DevOps from the basics

A course that starts at "what is a server?" and ends with Kubernetes, CI/CD pipelines, infrastructure as code, observability and DevSecOps. Each hard idea gets a step-by-step animation and a plain-language explanation first. Each module also traces its technology from where it started to the most recent changes in its architecture. Free GeeksforGeeks articles are linked throughout for deeper reading.

01

Computer & Software Basics

Before you can operate software you must understand what it runs on and how its pieces talk to each other. This module explains computers, operating systems, programs and processes, files, servers, the client-server model, frontends and backends, databases, APIs, environments and what "deploying" really means. No prior knowledge assumed.

Explain in detail

You will learn: CPU / RAM / disk · what an OS does · program vs process · what a server is · client-server round trip · frontend vs backend · databases · APIs · dev / staging / production · deployment · and how computing evolved from mainframes to containers and serverless.

Guess first

You are not expected to know these yet. Guessing before you read helps you remember the answer when you meet it.

A web server process crashes at 3 a.m. What brings it back?

A crashed process stays gone unless a supervisor restarts it.

A browser gets an HTTP 502 or 503 response. What does it usually mean?

5xx codes are server-side failures.

Why do application servers keep important data in a database instead of in their own files?

Servers are disposable; the data must not be.

Why start here? The problem this solves

  • DevOps talk mixes many ideas: API, staging, server, database, limits.
  • If those words are fuzzy, Linux, Docker and Kubernetes feel like magic.
  • Typical problems: code works on a laptop but not the server, or nobody finds the bottleneck.
ELI5: Explain like I'm 5

Before you run a restaurant, you learn its parts: the customer, the waiter, the kitchen and the storeroom. In a computer system, the browser is the customer, the API is the menu and waiter, the server is the kitchen and the database is the storeroom.

Explain in detail

This module introduces each of these parts; the rest of the course teaches you to run the whole restaurant.

DevOps engineers spend their days saying things like "the API in staging is returning 500s because the database connection pool on the app server is exhausted." That one sentence uses six ideas: API, staging, server, database, connection and resource limits. If any of those words is fuzzy, every later topic (Linux, Docker, Kubernetes, cloud) feels like magic.

Problem 1

"Works on my laptop" but not on the real server, because nobody understood what differs between the two.

Problem 2

Slow or crashing apps with nobody able to say whether CPU, memory, disk or network is the bottleneck.

Problem 3

Confusion about who does what: browser, server, database and API are mixed into one blur.

Everything in this course is built from the handful of ideas in this module. Every one of the words above (API, staging, server, database) gets its own slide. Take your time here.

History & Evolution

Computing changed shape many times. Each shift moved where software runs and who looks after the machines, and each shift created new work for operations people.

YearMilestoneWhy it mattered
1940sFirst electronic general-purpose computers such as ENIAC (completed 1945, unveiled 1946)Room-sized machines programmed by hand; one machine, a few specialists.
1964IBM System/360 mainframe familyA family of compatible machines: software could outlive one particular computer. Mainframes dominate business computing.
1969Unix created at Bell LabsAncestor of Linux and macOS; ideas of files, processes and the shell still shape every server.
1971Intel 4004, the first commercial microprocessorA whole CPU on one chip, which made small, cheap computers possible.
1977–1981Apple II (1977), IBM PC (1981)The personal computer era: a computer on every desk, and software sold on disks.
1980s–1990sClient-server computingWork is split: many "client" PCs ask a few powerful "servers" for data and services. Companies now run their own server rooms.
1989–1991Tim Berners-Lee proposes the World Wide Web at CERN (1989), runs the first web server and website there (late 1990), and the Web opens to the public (1991)Browser-and-web-server becomes the dominant client-server pattern. Linus Torvalds also releases the first Linux kernel in 1991.
1999VMware WorkstationVirtualisation reaches ordinary x86 PCs: one physical machine can host several "virtual" machines.
2006Amazon Web Services launches S3 and EC2Rent servers by the hour over the internet instead of buying them: the start of public cloud as we know it.
2007iPhone; KVM merged into the Linux kernelMobile apps multiply the number of clients; Linux gains built-in virtualisation that powers much of the cloud.
2013Docker is released as open sourceContainers become easy to use. A container is a lightweight, isolated package holding an app plus everything it needs, so it runs the same way on any machine (Module 08).
2014–2015AWS Lambda (2014) popularises "serverless" functions; Kubernetes announced 2014, version 1.0 in 2015Two new directions: do not manage servers at all (serverless: you upload code and the cloud provider runs it on demand), or manage fleets of containers automatically (orchestration).
2018AWS launches Graviton, its own Arm-based server processorThe start of a shift away from Intel/AMD-only servers in the cloud. Software now often has to be built for two CPU families (x86 and Arm).
2022Kubernetes 1.24 removes dockershimKubernetes drops its built-in adapter for Docker Engine and talks to container runtimes such as containerd through a standard plug-in interface (the Container Runtime Interface, CRI). Images built with Docker still work.
Late 2022 onwardChatGPT is released (November 2022) and generative AI spreads quicklyDemand for GPU servers (graphics processors used to run AI models) becomes a major driver of data centre and cloud growth, and AI assistants enter everyday developer and operations tools.
2020s (current state)Cloud-native is the common default; platform engineering growsMuch new software is designed for cloud, containers and APIs from day one, though plenty of systems still run on traditional servers and mainframes.

Dates are for first public availability or announcement. The pattern: machines get smaller, cheaper, more numerous and more automated, so humans must manage them with code.

A computer = CPU + RAM + disk (+ network)

  • The CPU does the work; more cores run more tasks at once.
  • RAM is fast working space that is wiped when power goes off.
  • Disk keeps files permanently; SSDs are faster than HDDs.
  • The network card connects the machine to other machines.
ELI5: Explain like I'm 5

Think of a chef in a kitchen. The chef's brain and hands are the CPU: they do the actual work, one step at a time, very fast. The kitchen counter is RAM: small, but everything on it is instantly reachable.

ResourceSpeedSurvives power-off?Typical symptom when exhausted
CPUfastest (it does the work; the others feed it)n/aeverything slow, high "load" (many processes waiting for CPU time)
RAMvery fastNoswapping, processes killed (OOM)
Diskslower (SSD) to slowest (HDD)Yes"No space left on device", write errors
Networklimited by link and distancen/atimeouts, slow downloads
Explain in detail

The pantry is the disk: huge, but it takes a walk to fetch things. When the kitchen closes for the night (the power goes off), the counter is cleared, while the pantry keeps everything.

CPU (processor)

The central processing unit executes instructions. It is described by its number of cores (independent workers inside the chip) and its clock speed in GHz (billions of steps per second). More cores means more things done truly at the same time. When a server is "CPU-bound" it is busy computing and everything else queues up.

RAM (memory)

Random access memory is fast, temporary working space. Programs and their data are loaded here to run. It is volatile: cleared when the machine powers off. When RAM runs out the OS may move some memory to a slower area on disk called swap, or kill a process to free memory (an "out of memory" or OOM kill).

Disk (storage)

Permanent storage: an HDD (hard disk drive, with spinning platters; cheaper and slower) or an SSD (solid-state drive, with flash chips; much faster). Keeps files after power-off. Running out of disk space is one of the most common causes of real outages, often because log files grew until the disk was full.

Network card (NIC)

The network interface card connects the machine to other machines. Speed is measured in bits per second (for example 1 Gbps, one billion bits per second). We study networking in Module 05.

Monitoring (Module 12) is largely about watching these four resources. Learn them now: CPU, memory, disk, network.

What is an operating system?

  • The OS manages hardware and lets programs use it safely.
  • Common examples: Linux, Windows and macOS.
  • Programs ask the kernel, the OS core, for help via system calls.
Operating system (OS): the core software that manages the hardware and gives other programs a safe, simple way to use it. It schedules the CPU, hands out RAM, organises the disk into files, talks to devices and enforces who may do what. The central part is called the kernel.
ELI5: Explain like I'm 5

The OS is the manager of a busy apartment building.

Explain in detail

Tenants (programs) do not fight over the elevator, the water or the electricity. They ask the manager, and the manager decides who gets what and keeps tenants out of each other's flats. Without the manager every tenant would have to know how the pipes work.

Linux

Open source (its code is public and free to use and change). It runs most of the world's web servers and cloud machines, so it is the OS DevOps engineers use the most. Module 04 covers it.

Windows / Windows Server

Common on desktops and in many company environments (for example, applications built on Microsoft's .NET platform, and Active Directory, Microsoft's system for managing company users and computers).

macOS

Unix-based; popular on developer laptops. Its terminal feels very similar to Linux's, so the commands you learn transfer.

What the kernel does for programs

  • Process management: starts, pauses and stops programs; shares the CPU between them.
  • Memory management: gives each program its own private memory so one program cannot read or corrupt another's.
  • File systems: turns raw disk blocks into folders and files with names and permissions.
  • Device and network drivers: lets programs use disks, keyboards and network cards without knowing the hardware details.
  • Security: users, permissions and isolation.

Programs ask the kernel for help via system calls (for example "open this file" or "send these bytes"). A shell (like bash) is just a program that lets you type commands to the OS. The window you type them in is called a terminal.

Programs vs processes

  • A program is a file on disk; a process is that program running.
  • One program can run as many processes at once.
  • A web server is a process that listens on a port.
  • A crashed process stays gone unless something supervises it.
Program: a file on disk containing instructions (a recipe). Process: a program that is currently running, with its own memory and a process ID (PID). The same program can be running as many processes at once.
ELI5: Explain like I'm 5

A program is a recipe in a cookbook: it just sits there.

TermMeaningExample
Program / executableInstructions stored on disk/usr/bin/python3, chrome.exe
ProcessA running instance, with a PIDPID 4812 running python3 app.py
ThreadA path of execution inside a process; threads share the process's memoryA web server handling many requests at once
Service / daemonA process that runs in the background, usually started at boot, waiting for worknginx, sshd, postgres
PortA numbered "door" on a machine where a process listens for network trafficWeb servers listen on 80 (HTTP) / 443 (HTTPS, the encrypted version). HTTP is the language of the web, explained a few slides later.
Explain in detail

A process is one meal being cooked from that recipe right now, with its own pots and ingredients (its memory) and its own order number (its PID). The same recipe can be cooked as ten meals at once (ten processes), while the chef (the CPU) moves between them.

A web server is simply a long-running process that listens on a port, receives requests and sends back responses. When people say "restart the service" they mean stop that process and start a fresh one.

If a process crashes, it is gone; nothing automatically brings it back unless another program is supervising it. Examples of supervisors you will meet later: systemd on Linux (Module 04), Docker (Module 08) and Kubernetes (Module 09). A big part of DevOps is making sure the right processes are always running.

Files, folders and configuration

  • Files hold source code, binaries, configuration, logs and data.
  • Common text formats are JSON, YAML, INI or .env, and Markdown.
  • In YAML, indented lines belong to the line above them.
  • Keep code and config separate; each environment reads its own.
File: a named chunk of data stored on disk. Directory (folder): a file that lists other files. Path: the address of a file, such as /etc/nginx/nginx.conf.
ELI5: Explain like I'm 5

A file system is a giant filing cabinet. Drawers are folders, papers are files, and the label on each is its name.


# A tiny YAML configuration file: settings, not code
app:
  name: shop-web
  port: 8080
  debug: false
database:
  host: db.internal
  name: shop
Explain in detail

A path is directions: "third drawer, second folder, the paper called report".

Kinds of files you will meet

  • Source code: app.py, index.js, Main.java (human-readable instructions)
  • Executables (binaries): programs translated ("compiled") into machine instructions the CPU can run directly
  • Configuration: settings like nginx.conf, .env, config.yaml
  • Logs: running diaries written by programs, for example /var/log/syslog on many Linux systems
  • Data: databases, images, uploads

Common text formats

  • JSON (JavaScript Object Notation): {"name": "web", "port": 8080}
  • YAML ("YAML Ain't Markup Language"): uses indentation to show structure, and is used everywhere in DevOps (Kubernetes, CI pipelines)
  • INI / .env: simple KEY=value lines
  • Markdown: plain text documentation, like the README files you see on GitHub

Here is the YAML format in practice. Indented lines belong to the line above them, so port: 8080 is a setting of app:

Code vs configuration: the same program behaves differently in different places simply by reading a different config file. Keeping the two separate is one of the key ideas behind environments (later in this module).

Check yourself

Two quick questions on the last few slides. Not graded; wrong answers explain themselves.

You start the same program three times. How many processes are running?

A program is a file; each run is a process.

In a YAML file, what does an indented line mean?

Indentation shows which setting belongs to which group.

What is a server?

  • A server waits for requests and answers them.
  • It runs service processes on ports and is meant to be always on.
  • Usually you control it remotely over SSH.
  • Servers come as web, application, database, file and mail servers.
Server: a computer (or a program on one) whose job is to serve other computers: to wait for requests and answer them. The word means both the machine and the software running on it.
ELI5: Explain like I'm 5

A server is a kitchen that never closes: it waits for orders (requests) and sends back dishes (responses).

Explain in detail

The customers placing orders are the clients. A server is not special hardware; it is an ordinary computer that is left running and well looked after, just as this is an ordinary kitchen that simply stays open.

What makes a machine a "server"?

  • It runs service processes that listen on ports.
  • It is meant to be always on and reachable on a network.
  • Usually it has no monitor or keyboard; you control it remotely over SSH (Secure Shell, an encrypted way to log in to another machine's terminal).
  • Often it runs Linux, in a data centre or in the cloud.

Server flavours

  • Web server: serves web pages and files (nginx, Apache)
  • Application server: runs the business logic (the rules of the app, such as "apply the discount, then charge the card")
  • Database server: stores and queries data
  • File, mail and DNS servers (DNS turns names like example.com into machine addresses), and many more
  • Physical ("bare-metal") machines, virtual machines (VMs: software-simulated computers sharing one physical machine) and containers

You can run a server on your own laptop (we will, in the hands-on exercise). Companies instead rent servers from a cloud provider or keep them in a data centre; a data centre is a building full of racks of servers with power, cooling and fast networking.

"Server" is overloaded. Always ask: do you mean the hardware or the program? On one physical machine you may run a web server, a database server and an SSH server at the same time.

The client-server model in motion

  • The client always starts the conversation.
  • The server waits for requests and sends back answers.
  • A network carries the request and the response between them.

Watch what happens when you open a website. A client (your browser) sends a request; the server processes it, perhaps asking a database, and sends a response. Use Replay to watch again.

Explain in detail

The client always starts the conversation, the server waits and answers. Between them is a network. The same pattern appears for loading a web page, tapping "refresh" in a mobile app, or a script calling an API.

Anatomy of a request and a response

  • Clients request; servers respond over a network, for example with HTTP.
  • A request has a method, URL and headers; a response adds a status code.
  • Status codes: 2xx success, 3xx redirect, 4xx client error, 5xx server error.
Client–server model: an architecture in which clients request services or data and servers provide them, communicating over a network using an agreed protocol such as HTTP.
ELI5: Explain like I'm 5

It is ordering pizza by phone.


$ curl -i https://example.com
response HTTP/2 200 content-type: text/html ... <!doctype html><html>...the page...</html>
Status codeMeaningThink of it as
200OK"Here you go."
301 / 302Redirect"We moved; go there."
404Not Found"No such page."
403Forbidden"You may not see this."
500Internal Server Error"We broke; it's our fault."
502 / 503Bad Gateway / Service Unavailable"Something behind me is down or overloaded." (A gateway or proxy is a server that passes your request on to another server behind it.)
Explain in detail

You (the client) call and say what you want in a language both sides understand (the protocol); the pizza place (the server) makes it and delivers it. You never see the kitchen. If the shop is closed or the line is busy, you get an error.

A protocol is an agreed set of rules for how two programs talk. The web uses the HTTP protocol (HyperText Transfer Protocol); HTTPS is the same protocol wrapped in encryption. An HTTP request has a method (what to do, such as GET), a URL (the address of what to act on, such as https://example.com/about) and headers (extra information, such as which browser is asking). A response has a status code (a three-digit result number), headers and usually a body (the actual content).

curl is a command-line program that acts as an HTTP client, like a browser without the graphics. The -i flag asks it to show the response headers as well as the body:

Codes starting with 2 mean success, 3 redirect, 4 the client made a mistake, 5 the server has a problem. DevOps engineers watch the 5xx rate (the share of requests that end in a 5xx code) very closely.

Frontend vs backend

  • The frontend is what users see, running in the browser or phone.
  • The backend runs on servers: business rules, databases and heavy lifting.
  • Users can modify frontend code, so it cannot be fully trusted.
Frontend: the part users see and interact with (it runs in the browser or on the phone). Backend: the part running on servers that holds the business rules, talks to the database and does the heavy lifting.
ELI5: Explain like I'm 5

In a restaurant the dining room (tables, menu, decoration) is the frontend; the kitchen and storeroom are the backend.

Explain in detail

Guests only touch the dining room, but nothing happens unless the kitchen works. An app's backend is the kitchen of that app.

Frontend

  • HTML (structure), CSS (looks), JavaScript (behaviour)
  • Frameworks (ready-made building blocks for apps): React, Vue, Angular
  • Runs on the user's device
  • Can never be fully trusted, because users can modify it

Backend

  • Languages: Python, Java, Go, Node.js, C#, Ruby, PHP...
  • Handles login, payments, rules, data access
  • Runs on servers you control
  • Talks to databases, caches, queues and other services

Static vs dynamic: a static site is just ready-made files (HTML, CSS, JavaScript, images) handed out as they are. A dynamic site or app has a backend that builds the answer for each request (your cart, your feed). Many modern apps are a static frontend plus a backend API (APIs are explained two slides from now).

A full-stack developer works on both. DevOps sits around both, making sure each part is built, tested, deployed and kept running.

Check yourself

Two quick questions on the last few slides. Not graded; wrong answers explain themselves.

Why can you not fully trust frontend code for security checks?

Enforce important rules on the backend.

A curl request returns HTTP 403. What does that mean?

403 is Forbidden.

Databases: where the data lives

  • A database stores data so it can be saved, found, changed and protected.
  • Relational (SQL) databases use tables; NoSQL databases use other shapes.
  • App servers keep no important data; it lives in the database.
  • Backups, replication and migrations are DevOps concerns.
Database: software that stores data in an organised way so it can be saved, found, changed and protected reliably, even when many users use it at the same time.
ELI5: Explain like I'm 5

A database is a very organised, very fast librarian.


-- SQL: ask the database a question
SELECT name, email FROM customers WHERE city = 'Pune';
Explain in detail

You do not search the shelves yourself; you ask "give me all orders from Alice" (a query) and the librarian brings back exactly those. The librarian also makes sure two people never write on the same card at the same moment. The cards are your data, and the librarian is the database software.

Relational (SQL)

Data in tables with rows and columns, plus relationships between tables (an order row points to a customer row). Queried with SQL (Structured Query Language). Examples: PostgreSQL, MySQL. They guarantee that related changes happen completely or not at all, which makes them the usual default.

Non-relational (NoSQL)

Other shapes: documents (MongoDB), key-value pairs (Redis), wide-column (Cassandra), graph (Neo4j). Chosen for flexible structure, special access patterns or very large scale.

  • Why not store data in the app server's own files? Servers get replaced, duplicated and restarted; the data must outlive them. So app servers are made stateless (they remember nothing important between requests) and the state (the data that must be remembered, such as accounts and orders) lives in a database.
  • Backups, replication (keeping live copies on other machines) and migrations (controlled changes to the table structure) are DevOps concerns: if the database is lost, the business is lost.
  • A cache (for example Redis) keeps frequently requested data in RAM to avoid asking the database again and again.
Never test with the production database, and never put its password in your source code. We will cover secrets properly in the DevSecOps module.

Why make app servers stateless?

Compare with ours

Because servers can be restarted, replaced or copied at any time, so the data has to live somewhere that outlives them.

APIs: how programs talk to programs

  • An API defines the requests a program accepts and the responses it returns.
  • Most web APIs use HTTP and JSON; the URL names the thing, the method the action.
  • DevOps tools such as GitHub, Kubernetes and AWS are all controlled through APIs.
  • An API is a contract, so it is versioned.
API (Application Programming Interface): a defined set of requests a program accepts and the responses it returns, so other programs can use it without knowing how it works inside.
ELI5: Explain like I'm 5

An API is the menu plus the waiter.

MethodTypical meaningExample
GETReadGET /users/42
POSTCreatePOST /users
PUT / PATCHReplace / partially updatePATCH /users/42
DELETERemoveDELETE /users/42

$ curl -s https://api.example.com/users/42
{"id": 42, "name": "Asha", "plan": "pro"}
Explain in detail

You cannot walk into the kitchen; you choose from the menu, and the waiter carries your order in and the dish back out. The menu is the list of requests the program accepts, the waiter carries each request and response, and the kitchen is the program's code, which you never see.

Most web APIs are REST-style APIs (REST is a common set of conventions for designing web APIs) that use HTTP and exchange data as JSON. The URL names the thing, the HTTP method says the action:

For example (illustrative: api.example.com is a made-up address, so this exact command will not work):

  • Your phone app, your website and a partner's system can all use the same backend API.
  • Almost all DevOps tools expose APIs too: GitHub, Kubernetes and AWS are all controlled through APIs, and tools such as Terraform work by calling them. That is why automation is possible.
  • Other styles you may hear of: GraphQL and gRPC.
An API is a contract. Changing it carelessly breaks every client, which is why APIs are versioned (/v1/users).

Environments: dev, staging, production

  • An environment is a separate copy of where software runs.
  • Typical environments: local or dev, test or CI, staging, production.
  • Differences should live in configuration, not in code.
  • Check which environment your terminal points at before destructive commands.
Environment: a complete, separate copy of the place where your software runs (servers, config, database), used for a specific purpose.
ELI5: Explain like I'm 5

Actors practise in a rehearsal room (dev), run the full show on an identical practice stage (staging), then perform for the audience (production).

EnvironmentPurposeWho uses itData
Local / devWrite and try codeDevelopersFake / sample
Test / CIAutomatic tests on every changeThe CI pipeline (an automated sequence of build and test steps, Module 07)Throw-away
Staging (pre-production)Final check in a copy that mimics productionQA, product ownersRealistic but not real customer data
Production (prod)The live system serving real usersCustomersReal, valuable, private
Explain in detail

Mistakes in the rehearsal room cost nothing. The audience only ever sees the real stage, so the show must already work on the practice stage.

  • The more similar the environments are, the fewer surprises. This goal is called "dev/prod parity".
  • Differences are meant to live in configuration (URLs, credentials, sizes), not in code.
  • "It works on my machine" almost always means the environments differ somewhere.
Be extremely careful which environment your terminal is pointed at. Running a destructive command against production instead of staging is a classic way to cause an outage.

Why have separate environments?

Compare with ours

So mistakes show up in a safe copy where nobody is hurt, before real users and real data are involved.

What does "deploying" mean?

  • Deployment puts a tested version onto an environment's servers.
  • Release makes that version available to users.
  • Manual deployment is slow, error-prone and hard to repeat.
  • DevOps automates every step so deploying is boring and reversible.
Deployment: the act of taking a finished, tested version of software and putting it onto the servers of an environment so that it is actually running and usable there. Release: making that version available to users (the two can be separate steps).
ELI5: Explain like I'm 5

Writing code is like baking a cake at home.

Explain in detail

Deploying is carrying the finished cake to the party and setting it on the table, without dropping it and without stopping the party. Inviting the guests to eat it is the release, which can happen later. Home is your laptop, the party is the environment's servers, and the guests are the users.

A manual deployment, the old way, looks like this:

  1. Developer finishes code and builds it into a package (a single file or folder that contains the finished program).
  2. Someone copies the package to the server, for example with scp (secure copy, a command that copies files over SSH).
  3. They log in with SSH, stop the old process, install the new version, change config.
  4. They start the new process and hope it works.
  5. If it breaks, they try to remember how to go back.

Why manual is painful

Slow, error-prone, different every time, scary on Friday evenings, impossible to repeat exactly, and only one person knows how.

What DevOps changes

Every step is scripted and automated (pipelines, containers, infrastructure as code, each covered later in the course) so deploying becomes boring, fast, repeatable, and reversible. Going back to the previous working version is called a rollback.

That is the whole motivation for this course: make getting working software to users safe and routine. The next modules show how software is planned and built (Module 02) and the culture and practices that automate its delivery (Module 03).

Check yourself

Two quick questions on the last few slides. Not graded; wrong answers explain themselves.

Which HTTP method is typically used to create a new user through an API?

GET reads, POST creates, PUT or PATCH update, DELETE removes.

Where should differences between staging and production mostly live?

Keep code the same and vary configuration.

Hands-on exercise: be a server for 10 minutes

  • Inspect your hardware and OS, then make a tiny website.
  • Start a web server process, then be the client with curl.
  • Find your process and stop it; the server is gone.

Task 1: worked example


$ uname -a          # kernel and OS info
$ df -h /           # disk size and usage
$ ps aux | head -5  # a few running processes (note the PID column)
$ mkdir -p ~/mysite && cd ~/mysite
$ echo '<h1>Hello from my own server</h1>' > index.html
$ python3 -m http.server 8000
output Serving HTTP on :: port 8000 (http://[::]:8000/) ...

Then, in a second tab:


$ curl -i http://localhost:8000/
output HTTP/1.0 200 OK Content-type: text/html ... <h1>Hello from my own server</h1>

Task 2: finish it


$ curl -i http://localhost:8000/nothing.html
$ ps aux | grep ____

Expect a 404, then fill the blank.

Show hint

Look at the command you used to start the server.

Show answer

ps aux | grep http.server lists the process; the PID is in the second column.

Task 3: on your own

Goal: serve a second page, then stop the server. Check: curl shows the page, then connection refused.

Show hint

The server serves whatever files are in the folder. Stop it with Ctrl+C in the first tab.

Show answer 

$ echo '<h1>About</h1>' > ~/mysite/about.html
$ curl -i http://localhost:8000/about.html
# press Ctrl+C in the first tab, then:
$ curl -i http://localhost:8000/
Explain in detail

You need a terminal on macOS, Linux, or Windows with WSL (Windows Subsystem for Linux, which runs a real Linux environment inside Windows), and Python 3. Python 3 is preinstalled on most Linux systems; on macOS, the first time you type python3 you may be asked to install Apple's command line developer tools, which include it. Type each command yourself rather than copying, and leave out the leading $: it only marks the prompt.

Everything after # is a comment for you to read; the shell ignores it. The | (pipe) sends the output of ps aux into head -5, which keeps only the first five lines. On Linux you can also run nproc (CPU cores) and free -h (memory). On macOS use sysctl -n hw.ncpu (CPU cores).

Python includes a small built-in web server. This command starts it as a process listening on port 8000 and serving the files in the current folder. You are now running a server.

Leave the server running and open a second terminal tab or window:

localhost is a special name that always means "this same computer", so your client and your server are on one machine, talking through port 8000.

Back in the first tab you will see a log line for your request. Also try curl -i http://localhost:8000/nothing.html and observe the 404 status code. Finally open http://localhost:8000 in a browser.

In the second tab run ps aux | grep http.server to see the PID, then press Ctrl+C in the first tab to stop it. Run curl again and notice connection refused: the server process is gone.

You just did client, server, request, response, status codes, ports, files and processes in one go.

Cheat sheet

TermOne-line meaning
CPUExecutes instructions; cores = parallel workers
RAMFast, temporary memory; lost at power-off
Disk (SSD/HDD)Permanent storage
OS / kernelManager of hardware for all programs; kernel is its core
Program vs processRecipe on disk vs a running instance (has a PID)
Daemon / serviceBackground process that waits for work
PortNumbered door where a process listens (80 HTTP, 443 HTTPS, 22 SSH)
ServerMachine or program that answers requests
ClientWhoever makes the request (browser, app, script)
Frontend / backendWhat the user sees / what runs on servers
DatabaseDurable, organised data store (SQL or NoSQL)
APIContract for programs to talk to each other, often REST + JSON
Environmentdev → test → staging → production
DeployPut a tested version onto an environment's servers
Status codes2xx ok · 3xx redirect · 4xx client error · 5xx server error

Interview questions

Q1: What is the difference between a program and a process?

A program is a passive set of instructions stored on disk. A process is an instance of it that is running, with its own memory, a PID and a state. One program can have many processes.

Q2: What does an operating system do?

It manages hardware resources (CPU scheduling, memory, storage, devices), provides files and networking, isolates processes from each other and enforces security and permissions. The kernel is its core part.

Q3: Explain the client-server model.

Clients initiate requests and servers listen and respond, over a network using a protocol such as HTTP. Examples: a browser asking a web server for a page, or a mobile app calling a backend API.

Q4: What is the difference between frontend and backend?

The frontend runs on the user's device and handles presentation and interaction. The backend runs on servers and contains business logic, authentication and data access, and talks to databases.

Q5: Why should application servers be stateless and data live in a database?

Servers can be restarted, replaced or duplicated at any time (especially in the cloud). If state is stored in a shared database, any server instance can handle any request and nothing is lost when one disappears.

Q6: What is an API and why does it matter for DevOps?

A defined interface by which programs communicate, often REST over HTTP using JSON. DevOps tools (cloud providers, Kubernetes, CI systems) are driven through APIs, so everything can be automated with code instead of clicking.

Q7: Why have separate environments?

To find problems safely before real users are affected. Dev is for building, staging mimics production for final checks, and production serves real customers. Differences should be configuration, not code.

Q8: What does a 502 or 503 mean and how is it different from a 404?

5xx codes mean the server side failed (502: a gateway got a bad reply from something behind it; 503: service unavailable or overloaded). 404 is a client-side error: the requested resource does not exist.

Quiz

1. Which resource loses its contents when the computer is powered off?

RAM is volatile. Disks (SSD/HDD) keep data without power.

2. A running instance of a program, with its own PID and memory, is called a:

A program is the recipe on disk; a process is it being run.

3. In the client-server model, who starts the conversation?

Clients request; servers wait and respond.

4. HTTP status 500 means:

5xx codes are server-side problems. 404 is "not found", 200 is success.

5. Which environment is closest to a copy of production, used for the final check before release?

Staging (pre-production) mimics production as closely as possible.

6. Which statement about APIs is true?

An API defines requests and responses so programs can use each other without knowing the internals.

02

How Software Is Built: SDLC, Waterfall & Agile

Software is not just typed into existence. Teams follow a repeatable process that takes an idea through requirements, design, coding, testing, release and maintenance. This module explains that process, the two big ways of organising it (Waterfall and Agile), the architectures that result (monolith and microservices), and the gap that Agile left open, which is exactly where DevOps begins.

Explain in detail

You will learn: the phases of the SDLC · Waterfall with its strengths and weaknesses · V-model and Spiral · the Agile Manifesto · Scrum and Kanban · monolith vs microservices · technical debt · why delivery to production stayed slow even after Agile.

Guess first

You are not expected to know these yet. Guessing before you read helps you remember the answer when you meet it.

In a Waterfall project, when do customers usually first see working software?

Waterfall gives late feedback.

A wrong requirement is found in production. Compared with catching it during planning, fixing it is usually:

Mistakes are cheapest to fix early.

Agile made teams much faster at writing code. What stayed slow?

The bottleneck moved to delivery.

Why do we need a process at all?

  • Without a shared process, teams build the wrong thing and find bugs late.
  • A process gives predictability, quality and coordination.
  • The SDLC covers the phases from first idea to retirement.
ELI5: Explain like I'm 5

Building software is like building a house with many workers.

SDLC (Software Development Life Cycle): the set of phases a piece of software passes through from the first idea to its retirement. Methodologies such as Waterfall and Agile are different ways of arranging those same phases.
Explain in detail

Someone must decide what rooms are wanted (requirements), draw the plan (design), build the walls (coding), check that the doors open and the pipes do not leak (testing), hand over the keys (release) and fix leaks later (maintenance). A process is the agreed order and rules so the plumber does not wall in the electrician's wires.

One person can build a small script without any process. A team of ten building a banking app for a million customers cannot. Without a shared process, people build the wrong thing, overwrite each other's work, skip testing and discover problems when they are most expensive to fix.

Predictability

Stakeholders want to know roughly what will be delivered, when, and at what cost.

Quality

Built-in checkpoints (reviews, tests) catch mistakes early.

Coordination

Dozens of people can work on one product without confusion about who does what.

History & Evolution

Every method below was an attempt to fix a pain the previous method caused.

YearMilestoneWhy it mattered
1968NATO conference on "software engineering" in Garmisch, GermanyThe term entered common use as the industry admitted that big software projects were routinely late, over budget and unreliable (the "software crisis").
1970Winston Royce presents the paper "Managing the Development of Large Software Systems"Shows a strictly sequential flow of phases, then says this simple version "is risky and invites failure" and recommends adding feedback loops, prototyping and early customer involvement. Despite that warning, the sequential diagram became the template for what people later called Waterfall. Royce never used the word "waterfall"; the label appeared later in the 1970s.
1986–1988Barry Boehm describes the Spiral model (1986, widely read 1988 article); Hirotaka Takeuchi and Ikujiro Nonaka publish "The New New Product Development Game" (1986)Spiral puts risk analysis in repeated loops. The Takeuchi and Nonaka article, with its rugby analogy for cross-functional teams, later inspired Scrum.
1992Ward Cunningham uses the "technical debt" metaphorGave teams a way to explain to managers why shortcuts have a cost that grows over time.
1990sV-model in widespread use; Rapid Application Development, Rational Unified Process, and Extreme Programming (Kent Beck, late 1990s) emergeTesting is tied explicitly to each design phase (V-model); lighter, iterative alternatives appear in reaction to heavy planning.
1995Ken Schwaber and Jeff Sutherland present Scrum publicly at the OOPSLA conferenceA simple framework of short iterations and small cross-functional teams (teams that contain every skill needed to finish the work).
Feb 2001Manifesto for Agile Software Development written by 17 practitioners at the Snowbird ski resort in UtahFour values and twelve principles that reframed software as collaborative and adaptive.
2004–2010David J. Anderson applies Kanban ideas to software teams (from about 2004; book in 2010); Schwaber and Sutherland publish the first Scrum Guide (2010)Visual flow management, and an official, shared definition of Scrum that the authors update over time.
2010"Continuous Delivery" by Jez Humble and David FarleyArgued that every change should be releasable at any moment through an automated pipeline. A key bridge from Agile to DevOps.
2011Scaled Agile Framework (SAFe) is published by Dean LeffingwellOne of several attempts to apply Agile across many teams in large organisations. Popular with big companies and also widely criticised as heavy.
2011–2014The word "microservices" is discussed at a 2011 workshop of software architects and described in a widely read 2014 article by James Lewis and Martin FowlerLarge applications are split into small, independently deployable services (explained later in this module).
Nov 2020Major revision of the Scrum GuideShorter and less prescriptive. Introduced the Product Goal, replaced the separate "Development Team" with one Scrum Team containing "Developers", and added a commitment to each artifact.
2021–2022GitHub Copilot, an AI assistant that suggests code inside the editor (preview 2021, generally available 2022)AI enters the coding phase of the SDLC for millions of developers.
2020s (current state)Most teams combine Agile planning with automated pipelines, trunk-based development (everyone merges small changes into one main branch often) and cloud platformsThe distinction between "how we plan" and "how we ship" has largely merged into the DevOps way of working (next module).
2024–2026 (ongoing trend)AI coding agents that can plan, write and change code across a whole project are adopted widelyCode can be produced faster than before, so reviewing, testing and safely delivering changes matter even more. Practices here are still settling and will keep changing.

SDLC phases, part 1: deciding what and how

  • Planning decides whether to build, with a rough scope, budget and timeline.
  • Requirements say what the system must do and how well.
  • Design plans architecture, data model, interfaces and security.
  • Mistakes are cheapest to fix in these first phases.
ELI5: Explain like I'm 5

Requirements are the customer saying "I want a treehouse with a slide."

Explain in detail

Design is the blueprint saying "four posts, a ladder here, the slide goes on this side, and we use these boards." You would never start sawing before the blueprint exists.

1. Planning and feasibility

Why are we building this? Who is it for? What will it cost? Is it technically possible? The output is a go or no-go decision and a rough scope, budget and timeline.

2. Requirements analysis

People who will use or pay for the software (stakeholders) say what it must do. Requirements are written down in a form everybody can check.

  • Functional requirements say what the system does: "a user can reset their password by email".
  • Non-functional requirements say how well: "the page loads in under two seconds", "available 99.9% of the time", "customer data is encrypted". Operations teams (the people who run the software once it is live) care about these a great deal.
  • In Agile teams (Agile is explained later in this module) requirements often appear as user stories, short descriptions written from the user's point of view: "As a shopper, I want to save items to a wishlist so that I can buy them later."

3. Design

Turn requirements into a plan: the architecture (which parts exist and how they talk), the data model (what is stored and how), interfaces and APIs (Module 01), technology choices, and security design.

Mistakes are cheapest to fix in these first phases. A wrong requirement found during planning costs a conversation; the same mistake found in production can cost a rewrite.

SDLC phases, part 2: building, checking, delivering

  • Implementation: developers write code in version control, with code review.
  • Testing covers unit, integration, end-to-end and acceptance tests.
  • Deployment puts tested software into production for users.
  • Maintenance keeps it running and is usually the longest phase.

Planning -> Requirements -> Design -> Code -> Test -> Deploy -> Maintain
    ^                                                             |
    +-------------------- feedback / new needs --------------------+
Explain in detail

4. Implementation (coding)

Developers write the code and store it in a version control system such as Git (a tool that records every change to every file, who made it and why, so any version can be restored). A code review means a second developer reads and approves each change before it is accepted.

5. Testing

  • Unit tests check one small piece (for example a single function) in isolation.
  • Integration tests check that pieces work together (app plus database).
  • System and end-to-end tests exercise the whole product like a user would.
  • Acceptance tests confirm it satisfies the original requirements.
  • Also performance, security and usability testing.

6. Deployment and release

Put the tested software into production (see Module 01) and make it available to users.

7. Maintenance and operations

Software is never finished. Operations keeps it running, monitors it, fixes bugs, patches security holes, adds features and eventually retires it. For long-lived software this is usually the longest and most expensive phase of the whole life cycle.

Notice who appears at the end of the chain: operations. In traditional organisations they were handed the finished software late, with little context. Keep that in mind for the last slides of this module.

The Waterfall model

  • Waterfall finishes each phase fully before the next one begins.
  • Strengths: clear phases, documentation and an upfront plan.
  • Weaknesses: late feedback, painful changes and one giant release.
Waterfall: a sequential model where each phase (requirements, design, implementation, testing, deployment, maintenance) is completed in full before the next begins, like water flowing down steps. Going back up is difficult and expensive.
ELI5: Explain like I'm 5

It is like making a big book: write every chapter, then edit, then print. Each step (phase) is finished before the next starts.

Variants and relatives

ModelIdeaBest for
V-modelEach development phase is paired with a test phase (requirements pair with acceptance tests, high-level design with system and integration tests, detailed design with unit tests). Drawn as a V: design goes down the left side, testing comes up the right.Projects where verification must be rigorous and traceable.
Iterative / incrementalBuild the product in several passes, each adding to the last.When a first working version is valuable early.
SpiralRepeat cycles of plan, risk analysis, build, evaluate.Large, risky, expensive projects.
Explain in detail

If the editor finds on page 300 that the story does not work, the whole book may need rewriting, and if readers dislike it, nobody finds out until every copy is printed.

Strengths

  • Easy to understand and manage; clear phases and milestones.
  • Thorough documentation as a by-product.
  • Works well when requirements are truly stable and well understood (for example, some regulated, safety-critical or hardware-linked projects).
  • Budget and schedule are planned upfront.

Weaknesses

  • Customers see nothing working until very late.
  • Changing requirements mid-project is painful, and requirements nearly always change.
  • Testing happens at the end, when bugs are expensive and deadlines near.
  • All the risk is pushed to one giant release.
  • Handover to operations happens late, often as a surprise.

Check yourself

Two quick questions on the last few slides. Not graded; wrong answers explain themselves.

Which of these is a non-functional requirement?

Functional is what, non-functional is how well.

In the V-model, unit tests are paired with which development phase?

Each phase on the left of the V has a matching test on the right.

The Agile Manifesto (2001)

  • Agile builds software in short cycles and adjusts to feedback.
  • Seventeen practitioners wrote the manifesto in February 2001.
  • Its four values each prefer one thing over another, but both still matter.

Individuals and interactions

over processes and tools

Working software

over comprehensive documentation

Customer collaboration

over contract negotiation

Responding to change

over following a plan

ELI5: Explain like I'm 5

On a hike, the Waterfall way plans the whole route at home and follows it no matter what. The Agile way walks a short stretch, looks around (feedback) and adjusts the route.

Explain in detail

You still carry a map, but you trust what you see more. Each short stretch is one iteration, and the route is the plan you keep updating.

Agile is a family of ways of working that build software in short cycles, deliver small working pieces often, and adjust the plan based on feedback. Its founding document is the Manifesto for Agile Software Development. In February 2001 seventeen software practitioners met at the Snowbird ski resort in Utah and wrote it. It began: "We are uncovering better ways of developing software by doing it and helping others do it." They agreed on four values:

The manifesto adds that while there is value in the items on the right, the items on the left are valued more. It does not say "no documentation" or "no planning".

Examples of the twelve principles (paraphrased)

  • Satisfy the customer through early and continuous delivery of valuable software.
  • Welcome changing requirements, even late in development.
  • Deliver working software frequently, from a couple of weeks to a couple of months, preferring the shorter timescale.
  • Business people and developers work together daily.
  • Working software is the primary measure of progress.
  • Maintain a constant pace that can be sustained indefinitely.
  • Continuous attention to technical excellence and good design.
  • At regular intervals the team reflects on how to become more effective, then adjusts.
Notice the phrase "deliver working software frequently". Agile asked for frequent delivery in 2001, but delivery to production stayed hard for years. DevOps grew out of the effort to fix that.

Scrum: roles, events and artifacts

  • Scrum works in sprints of one month or less, each ending with a usable increment.
  • Roles: Product Owner, Scrum Master and Developers.
  • Five events: Sprint, Planning, Daily Scrum, Review and Retrospective.
  • Artifacts: Product Backlog, Sprint Backlog and Increment.
Scrum: a lightweight Agile framework in which a small team works in fixed-length iterations called sprints (one month or less) and delivers a usable increment of the product at the end of each.
ELI5: Explain like I'm 5

Imagine a team building a LEGO city in two-week rounds (sprints).

The five events

EventPurpose
SprintA container for everything else; fixed length, one month or shorter.
Sprint PlanningDecide what can be done this sprint and how; produces a Sprint Goal.
Daily ScrumA 15-minute daily meeting where the Developers check progress toward the Sprint Goal and plan the next day of work.
Sprint ReviewShow the increment to stakeholders and gather feedback.
Sprint RetrospectiveThe team inspects how it worked and picks improvements.
Explain in detail

At the start they pick which buildings to finish this round from the list of wanted buildings (sprint planning from the product backlog). Every morning they talk for a few minutes about progress (the daily scrum). At the end they show the city to the neighbours (the sprint review) and then talk about how to build better next round (the retrospective).

The Scrum Team (Scrum Guide 2020)

Product Owner

Decides what is most valuable to build and orders the Product Backlog.

Scrum Master

Helps the team follow Scrum, removes blockers, and improves how the team works. Not a boss.

Developers

The people doing the work of building a usable increment each sprint (not only programmers; testers, designers and others count too).

The artifacts and their commitments

In Scrum, an artifact is a piece of information the team keeps visible. Since 2020, each artifact has a commitment: the goal or standard it is measured against.

  • Product Backlog: an ordered list of everything that might be needed (commitment: Product Goal).
  • Sprint Backlog: the items chosen for this sprint plus a plan (commitment: Sprint Goal).
  • Increment: a usable, finished step toward the goal (commitment: Definition of Done).

Kanban: visualising and limiting work

  • Kanban shows all work on a board with a column per stage.
  • Limits on work in progress keep work flowing.
  • It suits support, operations and maintenance work.
Kanban: a method that shows all work on a board with columns for each stage, and limits how many items may be in progress at once so work flows smoothly instead of piling up.
ELI5: Explain like I'm 5

A kitchen hangs order tickets on a rail (the board) and lets only a few dishes be cooked at once (the work-in-progress limit).


  To Do      |  In Progress (limit 3)  |  Review (limit 2)  |  Done
  ----------------------------------------------------------------
  Login page |  Search API             |  Cart bug fix      |  Signup
  Reports    |  Profile page           |                    |  Logo
  Dark mode  |                         |                    |
ScrumKanban
CadenceFixed-length sprintsContinuous flow
RolesProduct Owner, Scrum Master, DevelopersNo required roles
Change during the iterationThe Sprint Goal stays fixed; scope can be renegotiated with the Product OwnerNew items can be pulled in whenever capacity frees up
Key measureA usable Increment each sprint, measured against the Sprint GoalLead time (how long one item takes from request to done) and work in progress (WIP)
Good fitProduct developmentSupport, operations and maintenance work
Explain in detail

Tickets move from "waiting" to "cooking" to "ready" (the columns). If the counter is full of unfinished plates, nobody starts new orders until some go out. Fewer half-finished things means faster dishes for everyone.

"Kanban" is Japanese for "signboard" or "visual card". The origins lie in the Toyota Production System developed by Taiichi Ohno in the mid-20th century, which used cards to control how much work entered the factory. David J. Anderson adapted the idea for software teams. Operations and DevOps teams like Kanban because their work (incidents, requests) arrives unpredictably.

Many teams mix both ("Scrumban"). The labels matter less than the habits: visible work, small batches, limited WIP, regular reflection.

One big release versus many small releases

  • Waterfall stores up months of work and releases it in one risky step.
  • Small frequent releases are delivered and checked quickly.
  • Few changes per release makes problems easy to find and undo.

The left side shows the Waterfall habit, with months of work stored up and released in one risky step. The right side shows frequent small releases, each delivered and checked quickly. Use Replay to watch again.

Explain in detail

A big-bang release bundles hundreds of changes, so when something breaks nobody knows which change caused it. Small frequent releases carry few changes each, so problems are easy to locate and to undo, and users receive value sooner. This is the idea that Agile started and DevOps makes practical.

Why are small frequent releases safer than one big release?

Compare with ours

Each release carries few changes, so when something breaks the cause is easy to find and undo, and users get value sooner.

Check yourself

Two quick questions on the last few slides. Not graded; wrong answers explain themselves.

In Scrum, who orders the Product Backlog by value?

Product Owner decides the what.

Why are many small releases easier to fix than one big release?

Fewer changes per release means faster diagnosis.

Monolith versus microservices

  • A monolith is one application deployed as a single unit.
  • Microservices are many small services, each owning one business capability.
  • Microservices add operational complexity and are not automatically better.
Monolith: one application, built and deployed as a single unit, containing all features. Microservices: an application made of many small services, each owning one business capability, running separately and talking over the network (usually APIs).
ELI5: Explain like I'm 5

A monolith is one kitchen cooking every dish. Microservices are a food court: each stall cooks one thing and can be changed alone.

Explain in detail

Each stall is a service. The stalls must agree how they pass orders to each other (APIs over the network) and who looks after the shared tables, so a food court needs more coordination than one kitchen.

The way you organise the work influences how you structure the software, and vice versa.

Monolith

  • Simple to develop and test at first
  • One thing to deploy
  • Hard to scale one part alone
  • A bug or a slow build affects everybody, and every small change means redeploying the whole application
  • Large codebases become tangled

Microservices

  • Teams deploy their service independently
  • Scale only the busy parts
  • Different technologies per service possible
  • Much more operational complexity: networking between services, monitoring many moving parts, many separate deployments
  • Failures can cascade across services
Microservices are not automatically better. Many teams do well with a well-organised monolith. But when you do have many services, manual deployment collapses, which is a big reason container tools and Kubernetes (Modules 08 and 09) became popular.

Technical debt

  • Technical debt is the future cost of a quick shortcut taken now.
  • Debt can be deliberate or accidental.
  • Symptoms: changes slow down and new bugs appear with every fix.
  • Teams manage debt by making it visible and paying it down regularly.
Technical debt: the future cost of rework caused by choosing a quick, easy solution now instead of a better one. Ward Cunningham introduced the metaphor in 1992.
ELI5: Explain like I'm 5

You are in a hurry, so you shove all your toys under the bed instead of putting them away.

Explain in detail

The room looks tidy today (you borrowed time). Every day, finding anything gets harder, and that is the interest. Eventually you must spend an afternoon sorting it all out, or you can never find anything.

  • Deliberate debt: "Ship it now, fix it next sprint." Fine if you actually repay it.
  • Accidental debt: poor design or lack of knowledge, discovered later.
  • Examples: missing tests, copy-pasted code, outdated libraries, hand-edited servers, manual deployment steps, no documentation.
  • Symptoms: changes take longer and longer, new bugs appear with every fix, nobody dares to touch certain files.
Operations also accumulates debt: servers configured by hand until each one is unique and nobody can rebuild it (called "snowflake servers"), forgotten scripts, undocumented firewall rules. DevOps practices such as Infrastructure as Code (describing servers in files, Module 11) and automated pipelines (Module 07) largely exist to prevent this kind of debt.

Teams manage debt by making it visible (list it in the backlog), reserving regular time to pay it down, and agreeing on a Definition of Done that includes tests and review.

Why Agile alone was not enough

  • Agile sped up writing code, but delivery to production stayed slow.
  • Developers wanted change; operations wanted stability.
  • DevOps extends Agile ideas to cover operations.

Developer incentive

Change: add features quickly.

Operations incentive

Stability: change is what causes outages, so slow it down.

The bottleneck: Agile sped up the first half of the pipeline (idea to working code) but left the second half (working code to running in production) slow, manual and risky. Fast development was stuck waiting in a queue for delivery.
Explain in detail

Agile transformed how developers plan and write software. A team could now produce a working increment every two weeks. But look at what happened next:

  1. The developers finished a sprint and "threw the build over the wall" to a separate operations team. (A build is the packaged, ready-to-install version of the software.)
  2. Operations had its own priorities, its own change-approval process, and often a monthly or quarterly release window (the only dates when changes were allowed into production).
  3. Production servers were configured differently from development, so deployments broke in surprising ways.
  4. When it failed, developers said "it works on my machine" and operations said "your code is broken".

The industry's response was to take Agile's ideas (small batches, fast feedback, collaboration) and extend them to cover operations: shared ownership, automation of building, testing and deployment, and monitoring in production. That movement is called DevOps, and it is the next module.

Why was Agile alone not enough?

Compare with ours

Agile sped up writing code, but developers and operations still had opposite goals and a manual hand-over, so delivery stayed slow.

Check yourself

Two quick questions on the last few slides. Not graded; wrong answers explain themselves.

What extra cost do microservices add compared with a monolith?

Microservices trade simple deployment for operational complexity.

What is the 'interest' on technical debt?

Shortcuts make later work slower.

Hands-on exercise: a Kanban board in your terminal

  • Create a board with folders as columns and files as cards.
  • Add cards written as user stories.
  • Move cards across the board while respecting a WIP limit of 2.
  • Write three user stories and count hand-offs to production.

Task 1: worked example


$ mkdir -p ~/board/{todo,doing,review,done} && cd ~/board
$ ls
output doing done review todo

$ echo "As a shopper I want a wishlist so I can buy later. Created: $(date)" > todo/wishlist.txt
$ echo "As an admin I want to export orders so I can report. Created: $(date)" > todo/export.txt
$ echo "As a user I want password reset by email. Created: $(date)" > todo/reset.txt
$ ls todo
output export.txt reset.txt wishlist.txt

Task 2: finish it


$ mv todo/reset.txt doing/
$ mv todo/____ doing/
$ ls doing | wc -l

Expect 2, then fill the blank.

Show hint

Run ls todo to see which cards are left. One of them is the wishlist story.

Show answer

mv todo/wishlist.txt doing/, then ls doing | wc -l prints 2.

Task 3: on your own

Goal: finish the reset card, then pull export into doing within the limit. Check: todo 0, doing 2, review 0, done 1.

Show hint

Move the card through review into done first, so doing has space before you pull the next card.

Show answer 

$ mv doing/reset.txt review/ && mv review/reset.txt done/
$ mv todo/export.txt doing/
$ for c in todo doing review done; do echo "$c: $(ls $c | wc -l)"; done
Explain in detail

Build a working Kanban board using folders as columns and files as cards. You will also practise writing a user story and measuring how long work takes.

Step 1: create the board. mkdir -p makes folders, and the {todo,doing,review,done} part is expanded by the shell into four folder names, so one command creates all four columns.

Step 2: add cards. Each card is a user story with a creation time inside. $(date) inserts the current date and time, and > writes the text into a new file.

Step 3: set a WIP limit of 2 for "doing" and move cards across the board with mv (move). ls doing | wc -l lists the folder and counts the lines, which tells you how many cards are in progress.

The limit is now reached. Finish something before you start the third card:

On macOS, wc -l pads its number with spaces, so you may see todo: 0. The numbers are what matter.

Step 4 (thinking exercise): write three user stories for an app you use daily, each in the form "As a ..., I want ..., so that ...". Then draw your own team's real path from "code merged" to "running in production" and count how many manual hand-offs there are. That count is what the next module aims to reduce.

Cheat sheet

TopicRemember
SDLC phasesPlan, requirements, design, implement, test, deploy, maintain
WaterfallSequential, each phase finishes first; great for stable requirements, poor at change; late feedback
V-modelEvery development phase has a matching test phase
SpiralRepeated loops with risk analysis
Agile Manifesto2001; four values; twelve principles; respond to change, deliver working software often
Scrum rolesProduct Owner, Scrum Master, Developers
Scrum eventsSprint, Planning, Daily Scrum, Review, Retrospective
Scrum artifactsProduct Backlog, Sprint Backlog, Increment
KanbanVisual board, WIP limits, continuous flow
Monolith vs microservicesOne deployable unit vs many small independent services
Technical debtShortcuts that cost more later; make it visible and repay it
Agile gapFast development, slow and manual delivery to production; this is what DevOps addresses

Interview questions

Q1: What are the phases of the SDLC?

Planning, requirements analysis, design, implementation, testing, deployment and maintenance. Different methodologies arrange or repeat these phases differently.

Q2: What are the advantages and disadvantages of Waterfall?

Advantages: simple, clear milestones, good documentation, predictable for stable requirements. Disadvantages: late feedback, costly changes, testing and deployment at the end, big-bang release risk.

Q3: What are the four values of the Agile Manifesto?

Individuals and interactions over processes and tools; working software over comprehensive documentation; customer collaboration over contract negotiation; responding to change over following a plan.

Q4: Describe Scrum roles and events.

Roles: Product Owner, Scrum Master, Developers. Events: Sprint, Sprint Planning, Daily Scrum, Sprint Review, Sprint Retrospective. Artifacts: Product Backlog, Sprint Backlog, Increment.

Q5: How is Kanban different from Scrum?

Kanban is continuous flow with a visual board and WIP limits and no required roles or fixed iterations. Scrum has fixed-length sprints, defined roles and events.

Q6: Monolith or microservices: how do you choose?

Start from team size, scaling needs and operational maturity. A monolith is simpler for small teams; microservices help large organisations deploy and scale independently but demand strong automation, monitoring and networking skills.

Q7: What is technical debt?

The accumulated cost of shortcuts and design compromises that make future change slower. It should be tracked and repaid deliberately.

Q8: Why was Agile not enough, and how does DevOps relate?

Agile accelerated development but delivery and operations stayed siloed, manual and slow. DevOps extends Agile principles across build, test, release and operations through collaboration and automation.

Quiz

1. In which phase are mistakes cheapest to fix?

The earlier a mistake is caught, the cheaper it is to correct.

2. Which is a weakness of Waterfall?

Late feedback and costly change are the classic weaknesses.

3. The Agile Manifesto was written in:

Seventeen practitioners met at Snowbird, Utah in February 2001. 1970 is Royce's paper, 1995 is Scrum's first public presentation.

4. Which of these is not a Scrum event?

Scrum has five events: Sprint, Planning, Daily Scrum, Review and Retrospective.

5. What does a WIP limit in Kanban do?

Limiting work in progress reduces multitasking and exposes bottlenecks.

6. The main reason Agile alone was not enough is that:

Development sped up but operations and release processes did not, which created the bottleneck DevOps addresses.
