03

What Is DevOps?

DevOps is a way of working in which the people who build software and the people who run it share responsibility, and automate everything between a code change and a healthy production system. This module defines it precisely, shows the problem it solves, and introduces the frameworks, lifecycle, metrics, roles and tools you will meet for the rest of the course.

Explain in detail

You will learn: the Dev versus Ops conflict · CALMS · the Three Ways · the DevOps lifecycle phase by phase · DORA metrics · DevOps compared with Agile, SRE and platform engineering · roles and job titles · the toolchain map · common myths.

Guess first

You are not expected to know these yet. Guessing before you read helps you remember the answer when you meet it.

Developers are usually rewarded for one thing and operations for another. Which pair is correct?

Dev is measured on change, Ops on stability.

Research from DORA looked at how often teams deploy. What did it find?

Small, frequent changes are easier to test and to fix.

In the DevOps lifecycle loop, what feeds the next Plan phase?

What you learn in Monitor feeds the next Plan, so the loop never stops.

The problem DevOps solves

  • Developers are rewarded for new features, operations for keeping the site up.
  • That clash makes releases rare, huge and stressful.
  • When releases fail, people blame each other instead of fixing the system.
  • DevOps aims to deliver changes quickly and safely, then learn from them.
ELI5: Explain like I'm 5

Two kids share a playroom: one invents games (Dev), one keeps it tidy (Ops).

Slow

Weeks or months between "code done" and "users have it".

Risky

Large, manual, rarely practised releases that fail in surprising ways.

Blame-driven

Handovers between teams with unclear ownership, so outages become arguments.

Explain in detail

They argue all the time, because new games make a mess and tidying stops new games. DevOps is the idea that they are one team with one goal (a playroom that is both fun and tidy) and simple tidy-up rules that a robot helps with (automation).

Imagine a company where developers are rewarded for shipping new features and the operations team is rewarded for keeping the site up. Every release is a clash between those two goals. Releases become rare, huge and stressful, and when they fail, people blame each other instead of fixing the system.

Everything in DevOps, from culture to Kubernetes, is aimed at one outcome: deliver changes to users quickly and safely, and learn from what happens. Speed and stability are not opposites; as the research later in this module shows, the best teams are good at both.

History & Evolution

YearMilestoneWhy it mattered
2001Agile ManifestoDevelopers learn to deliver in small, feedback-driven steps, but operations is left behind (previous module).
2003Google begins what becomes Site Reliability Engineering (Ben Treynor Sloss leads the first team)An early model of treating operations as a software engineering problem.
2007–2008Patrick Debois, a Belgian consultant, is frustrated by the gap between developers and system administrators on a data centre migration project. At the Agile 2008 conference in Toronto, Andrew Shafer proposes a session called "Agile Infrastructure"; Debois is the only person who turns up, and the two meet afterwards and keep talkingThe seed conversation: apply Agile thinking to infrastructure and operations.
June 2009John Allspaw and Paul Hammond of Flickr present "10+ Deploys per Day: Dev and Ops Cooperation at Flickr" at O'Reilly's Velocity conferenceShowed that deploying many times a day is achievable when Dev and Ops cooperate, share tools and automate. Debois watched the talk remotely and was inspired to organise an event in Belgium.
Oct 2009The first DevOpsDays conference, organised by Debois in Ghent, BelgiumDebois named the event DevOpsDays; on Twitter the name was shortened to the hashtag #devops, which gave the movement its name. A community forms, and DevOpsDays events now run in cities worldwide.
2010"Continuous Delivery" by Jez Humble and David FarleyGave the movement its technical backbone: deployment pipelines and always-releasable code.
2013"The Phoenix Project" by Gene Kim, Kevin Behr and George SpaffordA novel about a failing IT project that explained DevOps ideas to a wide, non-technical audience; popularised the Three Ways (later in this module).
2014The annual State of DevOps Report (published with Puppet) is now led by researchers Dr. Nicole Forsgren, Jez Humble and Gene Kim; Kubernetes is announced the same yearRigorous survey research linking DevOps practices to business performance. The three researchers go on to found DORA (DevOps Research and Assessment), which continues the annual reports.
2016"The DevOps Handbook" and Google's "Site Reliability Engineering" bookPractical playbooks for adopting DevOps, and a public account of how SRE works.
2018"Accelerate" by Forsgren, Humble and Kim (March); Google acquires DORA (December)Statistical evidence for the four key metrics; DORA continues as part of Google Cloud and keeps publishing its annual report.
2019–2022"Team Topologies" by Matthew Skelton and Manuel Pais (2019) describes platform teams; Spotify open sources its Backstage developer portal (2020), which joins the CNCF (Cloud Native Computing Foundation) as a sandbox project in 2020 and becomes an incubating project in 2022The seed of the platform engineering movement: an internal developer platform that reduces the load on every product team.
2023DORA renames "time to restore service" to "failed deployment recovery time"The metric now focuses specifically on recovering from failures caused by deployments, rather than from any outage.
2022–2024Platform engineering becomes a mainstream job areaDevOps matures from "make teams collaborate" toward "give teams self-service paved roads" (ready-made, well-supported ways to build and ship).
2024The DORA report adds rework rate as a fifth software delivery metricRecognises that unplanned fix-up deployments are a sign of instability even when they are not counted as failures.
2025DORA's annual report, "State of AI-assisted Software Development", focuses on AIIts finding, broadly, is that AI amplifies a team's existing strengths and weaknesses: AI adoption went with higher throughput but still with lower stability, and teams with good pipelines, testing and platforms benefit most. The report keeps the five delivery metrics and adds seven "team profiles" that also describe well-being and friction.
Mid-2020s (ongoing trend)AI coding assistants, coding agents and AI-assisted operations spread through the toolchainFaster code generation raises the importance of automated testing, review and delivery pipelines. This is an ongoing trend, not a settled standard.

The Flickr talk and the Ghent event are the most commonly cited start of DevOps as a named movement. As with any movement, earlier ideas existed (Agile, lean manufacturing, ITIL (a widely used framework of IT service management processes), the Toyota Production System) and later practices keep evolving.

A definition of DevOps

  • DevOps joins development and operations to deliver software faster and safer.
  • It is culture, practices and tools, not a product.
  • Its four themes: culture, practices, automation and measurement.
DevOps: a set of cultural philosophies, practices and tools that unites software development (Dev) and IT operations (Ops) so that teams can build, test, release and operate software faster and more reliably, with shared responsibility and heavy automation.
ELI5: Explain like I'm 5

It is a relay race where the runners practise passing the baton together, instead of each runner only caring about their own leg.

Explain in detail

The runners are the Dev and Ops teams, and the baton is the working software. The team wins or loses together, so a good pass is smooth, quick and rarely dropped.

Culture

Shared ownership ("you build it, you run it"), blameless learning (after a failure, ask what in the system allowed it, not who to punish), collaboration across roles.

Practices

Version control for everything, continuous integration and delivery (automatically building, testing and preparing every change for release; defined later in this module), infrastructure as code (servers and networks described in files), monitoring, small frequent releases.

Automation

Anything repetitive and error-prone (builds, tests, deployments, server setup) is done by scripts and pipelines, not by hand.

Measurement

Decisions are guided by data: how often we deploy, how often it breaks, how fast we recover.

There is no single official definition or certification that defines DevOps. Treat it as an approach to organising people and work, supported by tools, not as a product you can buy.

The wall of confusion

  • The wall of confusion is the invisible barrier between Dev and Ops.
  • Dev is measured on change, Ops on stability, so their goals collide.
  • After DevOps, one team shares the pipeline, environments and on-call duty.
  • Incidents lead to learning, not blaming, and releases become routine.
Explain in detail

The term wall of confusion describes the invisible barrier between Dev and Ops. Animation: first the wall appears between the two teams and a release is thrown over it. Then the wall comes down and one team shares the whole path. Use Replay to watch again.

Before: siloed

  • Dev is measured on change (features shipped).
  • Ops is measured on stability (uptime).
  • Different tools, different environments, different vocabulary.
  • Hand-offs by ticket and document; blame when something breaks.

After: one team, shared goals

  • Same pipeline and same environments from laptop to production.
  • Developers share on-call duty for what they ship (they are the ones alerted, often by a phone "pager" app, when it breaks at night), and operators help design software that is easy to run.
  • Incidents lead to learning, not blaming.
  • Releases become small, routine and automated.
This is a mindset change first. Buying tools without changing how teams talk and share ownership simply produces the same wall with shinier bricks.

Why does the wall of confusion slow releases?

Compare with ours

Because Dev is rewarded for pushing change and Ops for keeping things stable, so changes are handed over rarely, in big batches, with unclear ownership when something breaks.

The CALMS framework

  • CALMS covers Culture, Automation, Lean, Measurement and Sharing.
  • It assesses how well an organisation is adopting DevOps.
  • Culture is the hardest part to change; automation is the easiest to buy.
CALMS: a way to assess how well an organisation is adopting DevOps, covering Culture, Automation, Lean, Measurement and Sharing. The acronym is credited to Jez Humble and builds on the earlier CAMS idea attributed to John Willis and Damon Edwards.
ELI5: Explain like I'm 5

CALMS is a table on five legs: Culture, Automation, Lean, Measurement and Sharing. If one leg is short, the table wobbles.

Explain in detail

A team with great tools (Automation) but no trust (Culture) wobbles just as much as a friendly team with no automation.

LetterMeaningWhat it looks like in practice
C: CultureCollaboration, trust, shared responsibility, blameless post-incident reviewsDevelopers and operators in the same chat and planning meetings; "what failed in our process?" rather than "who did it?"
A: AutomationAutomate builds, tests, deployments, infrastructure, repetitive tasksA pipeline that builds and deploys on every merge; servers created from code
L: LeanIdeas from lean manufacturing: small batches, limited work in progress, remove waste (anything that adds delay but no value), optimise the whole flowMany tiny releases instead of one giant one; visible queues; shorter feedback loops
M: MeasurementMeasure outcomes and system health, use data to improveDashboards for deployment frequency, error rate, latency; DORA metrics
S: SharingShare knowledge, tools and lessons across teamsRunbooks (step-by-step guides for handling known problems), internal wikis, shared pipeline templates, post-incident write-ups
Many companies start with Automation because it is the easiest to buy. Experience and the DORA research both point to culture as the hardest part to change and one of the strongest predictors of success.

The Three Ways

  • Flow: make work move quickly from development to operations and the customer.
  • Feedback: send fast signals back from production so problems are fixed at the source.
  • Continual learning: experiment, treat failure as learning, and keep improving.
ELI5: Explain like I'm 5

Think of a toy factory belt that carries work from developer to customer. Flow: keep the belt moving and clear any jam. Feedback: inspectors at every step speak up the moment a toy comes out broken.

WayExample practiceCourse module
FlowCI/CD pipelines, small pull requests, infrastructure as codeGit, CI/CD, IaC
FeedbackAutomated tests, monitoring, alerting, loggingCI/CD, Observability
LearningBlameless post-mortems (written reviews of an incident), game days (planned practice incidents), chaos experiments (deliberately breaking parts of a system to test resilience), shared runbooksObservability, Roadmap
Explain in detail

Learning: after every jam the workers sit together, find why it happened, and change the belt so it cannot happen again.

Gene Kim first described the Three Ways in 2012, and "The Phoenix Project" and "The DevOps Handbook" use them to explain DevOps. "Left" means where work starts (development) and "right" means where it ends (operations and the customer).

1. Flow

Make work move quickly from left (development) to right (operations and the customer). Make work visible, limit work in progress, make batches small, reduce hand-offs, automate, and remove bottlenecks.

2. Feedback

Create fast, constant feedback from right to left. Automated tests, monitoring, alerts and user data tell you at once when something is wrong so problems are fixed at the source.

3. Continual learning and experimentation

Build a culture of trying things, tolerating failure as a source of learning, practising recovery, and improving daily work.

Check yourself

Two quick questions on the last few slides. Not graded; wrong answers explain themselves.

Which statement best describes DevOps?

DevOps is culture, practices and tools, not a product.

A team adds automated tests and alerts so developers hear about production problems within minutes. Which Way is this mostly?

Feedback means fast signals back to the people who can fix the problem.

The DevOps lifecycle as a loop

  • Eight phases: Plan, Code, Build, Test, Release, Deploy, Operate, Monitor.
  • The left loop is mostly development, the right loop mostly operations.
  • What you learn in Monitor feeds the next Plan, so the loop never stops.
ELI5: Explain like I'm 5

It is like cooking for a family every day: you plan a meal, cook it and serve it, then look at what is left on the plates and use that to plan the next meal. The steps are the eight phases, and checking the plates is Monitor feeding the next Plan.

Explain in detail

The infinity loop shows eight phases in two halves. The left loop is mainly about development (Plan, Code, Build, Test); the right loop is mainly about operations (Release, Deploy, Operate, Monitor). The loop never stops: what you learn in Monitor feeds the next Plan. Use Replay to watch again.

Plan, Code, Build, Test, Release, Deploy, Operate, Monitor, then back to Plan. The next four slides explain each group in detail, with the typical tools. Different vendors draw slightly different versions of this loop (some merge Release and Deploy), but the idea is the same: a continuous cycle with feedback.

Phases 1 and 2: Plan and Code

  • Plan: decide what to build next and why, using feedback and monitoring data.
  • Code: write application, infrastructure and configuration, all in version control.
  • Planning tools include Jira and GitHub Issues; code lives in Git.
ELI5: Explain like I'm 5

Plan is choosing which dish to make next. Code is writing its recipe on a shared card that keeps every earlier version, so anyone can see who changed the salt and undo it. The card with its history is version control.

What this looks like in Git (Module 06 explains each command):


$ git checkout -b add-health-endpoint
$ git add app.py tests/test_health.py
$ git commit -m "Add /health endpoint with test"
$ git push origin add-health-endpoint     # then open a pull request for review
Explain in detail

Plan

Decide what to build next and why. Capture ideas as backlog items, break them into small tasks and prioritise using customer feedback and monitoring data.

  • Activities: backlog refinement (keeping the to-do list ordered and clear), user stories, sprint planning, roadmaps, incident follow-ups
  • Tools: Jira, Azure Boards, GitHub Issues and Projects, Trello

Code

Write the application and also the infrastructure and configuration, all stored in version control.

  • Activities: branching (working on a separate copy of the code), pull requests (asking for your change to be reviewed and merged) and code review, static analysis (tools that inspect code without running it), writing tests, pre-commit hooks (checks that run automatically before each commit)
  • Tools: Git with GitHub, GitLab or Bitbucket; editors and IDEs such as VS Code
"Everything in version control" is the foundation: application code, infrastructure code, pipeline definitions, even documentation. If it is not in Git, it cannot be reviewed, reproduced or rolled back.

Phases 3 and 4: Build and Test

  • Build turns source code into a runnable artifact, such as a container image.
  • Test automatically checks that the change works and breaks nothing else.
  • If the build or tests fail, the pipeline stops and the team is told.
Continuous Integration (CI): the practice of merging every developer's work into a shared branch frequently (at least daily) and automatically building and testing it each time, so integration problems appear immediately.
ELI5: Explain like I'm 5

Ten kids are each building one part of a giant LEGO ship.

Explain in detail

If they only snap parts together on the last day, nothing fits. CI means they snap their piece onto the ship many times a day, and each time a robot checks that the whole ship still holds together.

Build

Turn source code into a runnable artifact (the packaged output of a build): compile the code, download its dependencies (other people's libraries it relies on), and package everything, for example as a Java JAR file, a Python wheel or a container image. This is done by a build server, not on someone's laptop, so every build is made the same way.

  • Activities: compiling, dependency installation, creating a Docker image, tagging with a version, storing in an artifact registry (a server that stores built artifacts)
  • Tools: Maven, Gradle, npm, pip, Docker; CI servers such as Jenkins, GitHub Actions, GitLab CI

Test

Automatically check that the change works and has not broken anything else. Tests run on every change, within minutes.

  • Activities: unit, integration and end-to-end tests (Module 02), linting (automatic style and mistake checks), security scans, performance checks
  • Tools: JUnit, pytest, Jest, Selenium, SonarQube, Trivy

If the build or tests fail, the pipeline stops and the team is told at once. That is the second Way (Feedback) in action. Module 07 builds real pipelines.

Why test every merge?

Compare with ours

Because small changes tested automatically show integration problems immediately, while they are still easy to find and fix.

Phases 5 and 6: Release and Deploy

  • Release approves and versions a tested artifact so it is ready to go live.
  • Deploy puts the artifact on servers using a strategy that limits risk.
  • Always keep a tested way to roll back to the previous version.
StrategyIdeaRisk handling
RollingReplace instances (running copies of the app) a few at a timeOld instances stay up until new ones are healthy
Blue/greenRun two full environments (old "blue", new "green") and switch trafficSwitch back instantly if the new one misbehaves
CanarySend a small percentage of users to the new version firstExpand only if metrics stay healthy
Feature flagsDeploy new code switched off behind an on/off setting, then enable it graduallySeparate deploying from releasing to users
Continuous Delivery: every change that passes the pipeline is ready to be released to production at any time, with the final step approved by a person. Continuous Deployment: the same, but every passing change goes to production automatically.
ELI5: Explain like I'm 5

Releasing is deciding the cake is ready to serve.

Explain in detail

Deploying is carrying it to the table. A canary deployment is serving a small slice to a few guests first and checking they enjoy it before serving everyone. The cake is the tested build, and the guests are the users.

Release

Approve and version a tested artifact so it is ready to go live. It may need approvals, release notes and security checks.

Deploy

Put that artifact onto servers or clusters, using a strategy that limits risk.

  • Tools: Argo CD, Flux, Spinnaker, Jenkins, GitHub Actions, Ansible, Terraform, Helm, Kubernetes
  • Always keep a tested way to roll back (return to the previous working version).

Phases 7 and 8: Operate and Monitor

  • Operate: keep the live system healthy by scaling, patching, backing up and handling incidents.
  • Monitor: watch the system and users so problems are noticed early.
  • Observability rests on three kinds of data: metrics, logs and traces.
  • Monitoring results feed back into the next Plan phase.
ELI5: Explain like I'm 5

Operate is the caretaker keeping a school running: heating, repairs, cleaning. Monitor is the caretaker's meters and alarms, which show a problem before the pupils notice it. The school is the live system and the pupils are the users.

Explain in detail

Operate

Keep the live system healthy: run it on infrastructure, scale it, patch it, back it up, manage configuration and secrets, handle incidents.

  • Activities: capacity management, autoscaling, backup and restore, on-call rotation, incident response
  • Tools: Kubernetes, cloud platforms (AWS, Azure, Google Cloud), Terraform, Ansible, Vault (for secrets such as passwords and keys)

Monitor

Watch the system and the user experience continuously, so that you notice problems before customers complain, and so that the data feeds back into planning.

  • Observability is how well you can understand what a system is doing from the data it produces. It is often described with three pillars, or types of data: metrics (numbers over time), logs (event records) and traces (a request's path through services). Module 12 covers all three.
  • Tools: Prometheus, Grafana, the ELK/Elastic stack, Datadog, OpenTelemetry, PagerDuty for alerting
Monitoring closes the loop. A rise in errors, a slow page or a customer complaint becomes the first item in the next Plan phase. That is how DevOps teams continually learn (the third Way).

Check yourself

Two quick questions on the last few slides. Not graded; wrong answers explain themselves.

What does Continuous Integration mean?

CI merges at least daily and builds and tests every time.

Which deployment strategy sends a small share of users to the new version first?

Canary means a small percentage of users first, then expand if healthy.

Measuring DevOps: the DORA metrics

  • DORA research identifies which practices predict better software delivery.
  • Four key metrics: deployment frequency, lead time, change failure rate, recovery time.
  • Key finding: teams that deploy more often also tend to fail less.
  • Use metrics to improve systems, never to rank individual people.
DORA (DevOps Research and Assessment): a long-running research programme, part of Google Cloud since 2018, that surveys thousands of technology professionals every year and identifies which practices predict better software delivery and organisational performance. Its "four key metrics" are the most widely used way to measure delivery performance.
MetricQuestion it answersMeasures
Deployment frequencyHow often do we deploy to production?Throughput
Lead time for changesHow long from a code commit to running in production?Throughput
Change failure rateWhat percentage of deployments cause a failure in production that needs an immediate fix or rollback?Stability
Time to restore service (renamed failed deployment recovery time in 2023)How long does it take to recover when a deployment causes a failure?Stability
Explain in detail

The metrics keep evolving. In 2024 DORA added a fifth metric, rework rate: the share of deployments that were not planned but were made to fix a user-facing problem. DORA now groups the five into throughput (deployment frequency, change lead time, failed deployment recovery time) and instability (change failure rate, rework rate), so recovery time has moved to the throughput side. You will still see the original four in most articles and interviews. Check the latest DORA report when you need the current wording.

ELI5: Explain like I'm 5

A pizza shop can be judged by how often pizzas leave the kitchen and how long each order takes (speed), and by how many come out burnt and how quickly a burnt one is replaced (stability). A great shop is fast and rarely burns anything.

The key finding of the research: speed and stability go together. Teams that deploy more often tend to also have lower failure rates and faster recovery, because small changes are easier to test and fix.
Metrics are for improving systems, not ranking people. Turning them into individual targets makes people game the numbers.

DevOps, Agile, SRE and platform engineering

  • Agile, DevOps, SRE and platform engineering overlap and complement each other.
  • SRE, defined by Google, is one concrete way to put DevOps into practice.
  • Platform engineering builds an internal platform so teams can self-serve.
  • DevSecOps builds security into every phase of delivery.
ELI5: Explain like I'm 5

In a school, DevOps means teachers (developers) and caretakers (operations) work as one team. SRE is caretakers who set a measured target for how clean the school must be. Platform engineering is a shared toolbox (the internal platform) so each classroom can fix small things without waiting.

Explain in detail

These ideas overlap, and people often confuse them. They are complementary, not competing.

ApproachFocusTypical practicesRelation to DevOps
AgileHow to plan and build software iteratively with customer feedbackSprints, backlogs, user stories, retrospectivesDevOps extends Agile thinking past "code complete" to delivery and operations.
DevOpsCulture and automation across the whole delivery pathCI/CD, infrastructure as code, monitoring, shared ownershipThe broad philosophy.
SREReliability engineered with software, defined by GoogleService level objectives (SLOs), error budgets, toil reduction (toil is repetitive manual work that could be automated), on-call, post-mortemsA specific, prescriptive way to do operations. Google describes SRE as one concrete way to implement DevOps ideas, summarised in its phrase "class SRE implements DevOps".
Platform engineeringBuilding an internal developer platform so product teams self-serveGolden paths (a recommended, pre-built way to do a common task, such as creating a new service), templates, portals such as Backstage, self-service infrastructureA way to scale DevOps by reducing the cognitive load on every team.
DevSecOpsSecurity built into every phaseDependency scans, secret scanning, policy as codeDevOps with security as a shared responsibility (Module 13).

SLO and error budget (SRE ideas): a service level objective is a reliability target, such as "99.9% of requests succeed this month". If you promise 99.9%, the remaining 0.1% is your error budget. While budget remains you can ship quickly; when it is spent you slow down and fix reliability. It turns the Dev versus Ops argument into a shared number.

Roles, job titles and common myths

  • Common titles: DevOps Engineer, SRE, Platform Engineer, Cloud Engineer.
  • DevOps is not a tool, a separate team or just a job title.
  • Research shows the best teams are both faster and more stable.
TitleWhat they usually do
DevOps EngineerBuilds and maintains pipelines, infrastructure code and tooling that help teams ship reliably. The title varies a lot between companies.
Site Reliability Engineer (SRE)Owns reliability: SLOs, monitoring, incident response, capacity, automation.
Platform EngineerBuilds the internal platform and self-service tools developers use.
Cloud EngineerDesigns and runs cloud infrastructure and networking.
Release / Build EngineerMaintains build systems and the release process.
DevSecOps / Security EngineerIntegrates security checks and policy into the pipeline and platform.
Explain in detail

Common myths

"DevOps is a tool"

No single tool is DevOps. Tools enable the practices, but a team with Jenkins and Kubernetes can still have a wall between Dev and Ops.

"DevOps is a team"

A separate "DevOps team" that sits between Dev and Ops can become just a third silo. Some organisations call it that anyway, but the goal is shared responsibility.

"DevOps is a job title"

The title exists and is useful, but it describes someone who helps enable the culture and practices; it does not mean other people no longer care about operations.

"DevOps means no Ops (or no testers)"

The skills remain; they are shared, automated and moved earlier in the process.

"DevOps is only for startups or the cloud"

The practices apply to any size and to on-premises systems too, though cloud makes automation easier.

"Faster means less safe"

The research shows high performers are both faster and more stable.

This course teaches the ideas first and the tools second. Here is where each tool category lives in the lifecycle. Examples are illustrative, not an endorsement or a complete list.

You will never learn every tool. Learn the concept behind each category (a pipeline, an image registry, a metrics store) and switching tools becomes easy.

Check yourself

Two quick questions on the last few slides. Not graded; wrong answers explain themselves.

How should a team use the DORA metrics?

Use metrics to improve systems, not to rank people.

Which role mainly builds the internal platform and self-service tools that developers use?

Platform engineers build the self-service platform.

Hands-on exercise: a pipeline in 20 lines of bash

  • Build a tiny project and automate its build, test and deploy steps.
  • The script runs steps in order and stops at the first failure.
  • Break the code on purpose and watch the deploy step never run.

Task 1: worked example


$ mkdir -p ~/mini-pipeline && cd ~/mini-pipeline
$ cat > app.py <<'EOF'
def add(a, b):
    return a + b
EOF
$ cat > test_app.py <<'EOF'
from app import add
assert add(2, 3) == 5, "add is broken"
print("tests passed")
EOF


$ cat > pipeline.sh <<'EOF'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -e                      # stop at the first failing command
echo "== BUILD =="; python3 -m py_compile app.py
echo "== TEST  =="; python3 test_app.py
echo "== DEPLOY =="; mkdir -p deploy && cp app.py deploy/ && echo "deployed to ./deploy"
EOF
$ chmod +x pipeline.sh && ./pipeline.sh
output == BUILD == == TEST == tests passed == DEPLOY == deployed to ./deploy

Task 2: finish it

Break the code, then run the pipeline.


$ sed -i.bak 's/a + b/a - b/' app.py
$ ???
Show hint

Run the same script you ran in Task 1.

Show answer 

$ ./pipeline.sh
output == BUILD == == TEST == Traceback (most recent call last): File "/home/you/mini-pipeline/test_app.py", line 2, in <module> assert add(2, 3) == 5, "add is broken" AssertionError: add is broken

Task 3: on your own

Goal: restore app.py and get a passing run. Success: the output ends with "deployed to ./deploy".

Show hint

The sed command saved a backup called app.py.bak. Move it back over app.py.

Show answer 

$ mv app.py.bak app.py
$ ./pipeline.sh
$ grep "a + b" deploy/app.py
Explain in detail

Real pipelines run in tools like GitHub Actions, but the idea fits in a shell script: run steps in order, stop at the first failure. Create a tiny project and automate its build and test.

The cat > file <<'EOF' lines are a "here document": everything up to the line EOF is written into the file. Type them exactly, including the EOF lines.

sed edits the file in place (keeping a backup called app.py.bak), changing a + b to a - b:

The file path in the traceback will show your own home folder.

The DEPLOY step never ran. That is the heart of CI/CD: automated feedback prevents a broken change from reaching production. Restore the file with mv app.py.bak app.py and run the script again to see it pass.

Reflection: which parts of this script map to Plan, Code, Build, Test, Release, Deploy, Operate and Monitor? What is missing? (Answer: Plan, Release approval, Operate and Monitor. Later modules add them.)

Cheat sheet

ConceptRemember

MythsNot a tool, not just a team, not just a title

Interview questions

Q1: What is DevOps?

A culture and set of practices that brings development and operations together, with shared responsibility and automation, so software can be delivered quickly, reliably and safely, with continuous feedback.

Q2: Why did DevOps emerge?

Agile sped up development, but handoffs to a separate operations team with opposing incentives (change versus stability) made releases slow and risky. DevOps removes that conflict through shared goals and automation.

Q3: Explain CALMS.

Culture, Automation, Lean, Measurement, Sharing: five areas for assessing and guiding DevOps adoption.

Q4: What are the Three Ways?

Flow (left to right speed), Feedback (right to left signals) and Continual Learning and Experimentation.

Q5: List the phases of the DevOps lifecycle and a tool for each.

Plan (Jira), Code (Git), Build (Maven or Docker), Test (JUnit or Selenium), Release (artifact registry), Deploy (Argo CD, Jenkins), Operate (Kubernetes, Terraform), Monitor (Prometheus, Grafana).

Q6: What are the DORA metrics?

The original four: deployment frequency, lead time for changes, change failure rate and time to restore service (renamed failed deployment recovery time in 2023). Two measure throughput and two measure stability. Since 2024 DORA also tracks a fifth metric, rework rate, and groups recovery time with the throughput metrics.

Q7: Difference between Continuous Delivery and Continuous Deployment?

In delivery, every change is releasable and a person decides when to release. In deployment, every change that passes the pipeline goes live automatically.

Q8: How does SRE differ from DevOps?

DevOps is a broad philosophy. SRE is a specific discipline, originating at Google, that applies software engineering to operations with concrete tools such as SLOs and error budgets.

Q9: Is DevOps a role?

The job title exists, but DevOps is mainly a way of working. One person cannot "do DevOps" for everybody; the title usually means someone who builds the pipelines, infrastructure and tooling that make the culture possible.

Quiz

1. What best describes the wall of confusion?

Dev is rewarded for change and Ops for stability, creating friction at the handover.

2. In CALMS, what does the L stand for?

Culture, Automation, Lean, Measurement, Sharing.

3. Which is one of the Three Ways?

The Three Ways are Flow, Feedback and Continual Learning and Experimentation.

4. Which of these is not one of the four DORA key metrics?

The four keys are deployment frequency, lead time for changes, change failure rate and time to restore service. Lines of code says nothing about delivery performance and is easy to game.

5. In Continuous Delivery, who decides when a change goes to production?

Continuous Deployment is the automatic variant; Delivery keeps a manual release decision.

6. Which statement about DevOps is accurate?

Tools support DevOps, but shared ownership and automation are the core.

04

Linux Fundamentals & Bash

Almost every server you will ever manage as a DevOps engineer runs Linux. Containers run on Linux, Kubernetes nodes run Linux, cloud virtual machines are mostly Linux, and CI/CD runners are usually Linux. In this module you will learn to live in the terminal: move around the filesystem, read and edit files, control who may do what, manage programs and services, chain small tools together, connect to remote machines, and finally automate everything with Bash scripts.

Explain in detail

You will learn: what Linux really is (kernel, shell, distro) · the directory tree · core commands · users, groups and sudo · permissions and ownership · processes and signals · systemd services · package managers · pipes and redirection · grep/find/sed/awk · environment variables · SSH and keys · cron · Bash scripting.

Guess first

You are not expected to know these yet. Guessing before you read helps you remember the answer when you meet it.

Which part of a Linux system talks directly to the hardware?

The kernel talks to the hardware.

When you add up chmod numbers, what is the value of the read permission?

Read is 4, write is 2, execute is 1.

Which command asks a process to shut down politely so it can clean up?

kill sends SIGTERM (polite); kill -9 sends SIGKILL (forced).

Why does Linux matter? The problem it solves

  • An operating system shares CPU, memory, disk and network between programs.
  • Servers need to run for months, cost little and be controlled by scripts.
  • Linux is free, stable, scriptable and lightweight, with strict permissions.
  • Cloud VMs, containers, Kubernetes nodes and CI runners are mostly Linux.
ELI5: Explain like I'm 5

Many kids share one box of toys, so a referee decides whose turn it is with each toy. The kids are programs, the toys are the CPU, memory and disk, and the referee is the operating system.

Explain in detail

Linux is a referee whose rulebook is open for everyone to read, is free, and is used on almost every big company's servers.

A computer needs an operating system to share its CPU, memory, disk and network between many programs. Servers have special needs: they run for months without rebooting, nobody sits in front of them with a mouse, they must be cheap (hundreds of them), and they must be controllable by other programs (scripts, automation tools). Linux fits this perfectly.

Why servers love Linux

  • Free and open source: no per-server licence fee, so you can run 1 or 10,000 machines.
  • Stable: servers commonly run for months without a reboot.
  • Scriptable: everything can be done from the command line, so it can be automated.
  • Lightweight: no graphical desktop is needed on a server.
  • Strict permissions: a clear user, group and permission model.

Why DevOps engineers need it

  • Cloud VMs (AWS EC2, Azure, Google Cloud) are mostly Linux.
  • Docker containers use features of the Linux kernel.
  • Kubernetes nodes run Linux.
  • CI/CD runners, web servers (nginx), databases and monitoring tools are all Linux-first.
  • When something breaks at 3 a.m., you will fix it through an SSH terminal.
You do not need to memorise hundreds of commands. A few dozen commands cover most daily work, and this module teaches those.

Why do servers run Linux?

Compare with ours

Because Linux is free, stable, scriptable and lightweight, so one team can run and automate thousands of machines without per-server licences or a graphical desktop.

History & Evolution

Linux did not appear from nowhere. It stands on 20+ years of Unix ideas, and in the last decade its kernel features became the foundation of containers.

YearMilestoneWhy it mattered
1969Ken Thompson and Dennis Ritchie start Unix at Bell LabsIntroduced ideas still used today: "everything is a file", small tools that do one job, a hierarchical filesystem.
1973Unix is rewritten in the C languageAn OS written in a high-level language could be moved (ported) to different hardware.
Late 1970sBSD (Berkeley Software Distribution) grows out of Unix at UC BerkeleyGave the world many networking features; its descendants (FreeBSD and others) still exist.
1983Richard Stallman announces the GNU projectGoal: a completely free Unix-like system. GNU produced the compiler (gcc), the shell (bash), and most core tools (ls, cp, grep...), but not a finished kernel.
1991Linus Torvalds announces a hobby kernel; Linux 0.01 appearsThe missing piece: a free kernel. Combined with GNU tools it became a full OS (often called GNU/Linux).
1992Linux is released under the GNU GPL licenceAnyone may use, change and share it, as long as changes stay open. This fuelled worldwide collaboration.
1993Slackware and Debian appearTwo of the earliest distributions still alive (SLS and others came in 1992): kernel + tools + installer + packages bundled for users. Debian is still a pillar today.
1995Red Hat Linux 1.0 releasedStart of the commercial enterprise Linux family that later led to RHEL, Fedora, CentOS, Rocky and Alma.
2004Ubuntu first released (October)Made Linux easy to install and popular on desktops, cloud images and servers.
2008cgroups merged into the mainline kernel (2.6.24)Control groups limit and measure CPU, memory and I/O for groups of processes: half of what containers need.
2002–2013Namespaces added step by step (mount, UTS, IPC, PID, network, user)Each namespace gives a process its own private view of part of the system. Namespaces + cgroups = the foundation of containers (LXC, then Docker in 2013).
2010 →systemd created, then adopted by major distros (Fedora 2011, RHEL 7 in 2014, Debian 8 and Ubuntu 15.04 in 2015)Replaced the old SysV init scripts as the standard service manager. Today systemctl and journalctl are everywhere.
2016 →cgroup v2 declared stable; later the default on modern distros (e.g. Fedora 31, Debian 11, RHEL 9)A cleaner single-hierarchy design. Modern Docker and Kubernetes work with cgroup v2.
2020–2024CentOS Linux ends: CentOS Linux 8 ended in Dec 2021, CentOS Linux 7 in June 2024; focus moves to CentOS StreamFree RHEL-compatible rebuilds moved to Rocky Linux and AlmaLinux. Know all four names when reading job ads.
2022Kernel 6.0 released (October)Kernel major numbers are just a release counter: Linus bumps the first digit when the second gets large, not because of a redesign.
2022Kernel 6.1 merges initial Rust support (December)First time a language other than C (and assembly) is accepted for kernel code, aimed at fewer memory-safety bugs in drivers.
2024Kernel 6.12 (November): real-time support (PREEMPT_RT) merged into mainline, plus sched_ext (CPU schedulers written as eBPF programs)Features that lived as out-of-tree patches for about 20 years became standard; eBPF keeps growing as the way to extend the kernel safely at runtime.
2025Kernel maintainers declare Rust support no longer experimental (December); systemd 258 drops cgroup v1 supportRust becomes a permanent part of kernel development; cgroup v2 is now the only option on current systemd-based distros.
2026Kernel 7.0 released (April 2026), following 6.19Again only a numbering change (Linus moves to a new major number roughly every three and a half years). 7.0 also formally removed the "experimental" label from Rust. Expect current distros to ship 6.x LTS kernels (such as 6.12 or 6.18) or 7.x; check with uname -r.

Dates for distro default switches vary slightly by distribution; always check your distro's release notes for exact versions.

Kernel vs shell vs distro vs terminal

  • The kernel is the OS core and talks to the hardware.
  • The shell reads your commands; the terminal is the window you type in.
  • A distro bundles kernel, system tools, package manager and defaults.
  • Debian and Red Hat families differ mainly in package commands.
ELI5: Explain like I'm 5

Think of a restaurant. The kernel is the kitchen: it does the real work with the stove and fridge (hardware).

Distro familyExamplesPackage managerWhere you meet it
Debian familyDebian, Ubuntuapt (.deb files)Cloud VMs, Docker base images, laptops, tutorials
Red Hat familyRHEL, Rocky Linux, AlmaLinux, Fedora, CentOS Streamdnf / yum (.rpm files)Enterprises, banks, support-contract environments
Amazon LinuxAmazon Linux 2, Amazon Linux 2023yum (AL2) / dnf (AL2023)Default on many AWS EC2 instances
AlpineAlpine LinuxapkTiny container images (a few MB), very common with Docker

$ uname -r            # kernel version
$ cat /etc/os-release # which distro am I on?
$ echo $SHELL         # my login shell (the one started when I log in)
Explain in detail

The shell is the waiter: you tell the waiter what you want in words, the waiter takes it to the kitchen. The terminal is your table: the place where you sit and talk to the waiter. A distro is a whole restaurant brand (Ubuntu, Debian...) that packages the kitchen, waiters, menu and furniture together.

People say "Linux" for four different things. Here is how they differ.

Kernel: the core of the OS. It talks to hardware, schedules processes on the CPU, manages memory, files, devices and the network. "Linux" strictly means this kernel.
Shell: a program that reads the commands you type and asks the kernel to run them. bash is the most common; others are zsh, sh, fish.
Terminal: the window (program) where you type to a shell. It displays text. Examples: GNOME Terminal, iTerm2, Windows Terminal, or an SSH session.
Distribution (distro): kernel + system tools + package manager + defaults, bundled and maintained by a project or company.
Learn one Debian-family distro (Ubuntu) first and one Red Hat-family idea (dnf). The concepts are the same, only package commands differ.

The filesystem hierarchy

  • Linux has one single tree starting at / (root), not drive letters.
  • Configuration lives in /etc, user files in /home, logs in /var/log.
  • Programs are in /bin and /usr/bin; devices appear under /dev.
ELI5: Explain like I'm 5

It is a giant family tree of folders. The great-grandparent folder is /.

Everything is a file: Unix design idea: ordinary files, directories, devices and even running-process information are all accessed through the same file operations (open, read, write).
Explain in detail

Every other folder is its child, grandchild and so on. To find a file you name its whole line of ancestors from the top, such as /home/alice/notes.txt: that line is the path.

Windows has drives (C:, D:). Linux has one single tree that starts at / (called "root"). Everything, including disks and devices, hangs off this tree.

DirectoryWhat lives there
/The root of everything
/bin, /usr/binPrograms (commands like ls, cp). On modern distros /bin is usually a link to /usr/bin
/etcConfiguration files (text). e.g. /etc/ssh/sshd_config, /etc/hosts
/homePersonal folders of normal users, e.g. /home/abhi (also written ~)
/rootHome folder of the administrator user "root" (not the same as /)
/varData that changes: logs (/var/log), caches, databases, mail
/tmpTemporary files, may be wiped at reboot
/devDevices shown as files (disks like /dev/sda, /dev/null)
/proc, /sysVirtual files that expose live kernel and process information
/optOptional third-party software

Navigating and managing files

  • pwd shows where you are, ls lists what is there, cd moves.
  • Absolute paths start with /; relative paths start from where you are.
  • rm is permanent, so check the path before running it.
ELI5: Explain like I'm 5

Using the terminal is like walking around a big library: you always stand in exactly one room (the current folder).

Path: the address of a file. An absolute path starts with / (/etc/hosts). A relative path starts from where you are (../notes.txt). . = this folder, .. = parent folder, ~ = your home.

pwd                      # print working directory
ls                       # list files
ls -l                    # long format: permissions, owner, size, date
ls -la                   # include hidden files (names starting with .)
ls -lh                   # human-readable sizes (KB, MB)
cd /var/log              # go to an absolute path
cd ..                    # go up one level
cd ~                     # go home (also just: cd)
cd -                     # go back to the previous directory

mkdir project            # create a directory
mkdir -p a/b/c           # create nested directories in one go
touch notes.txt          # create an empty file (or update its timestamp)
cp notes.txt backup.txt  # copy a file
cp -r project project2   # copy a directory recursively
mv backup.txt old.txt    # move OR rename
rm old.txt               # delete a file (no recycle bin)
rm -r project2           # delete a directory and everything inside
rmdir emptydir           # delete an empty directory
ln -s /etc/hosts myhosts # create a symbolic link (shortcut)
Explain in detail

pwd asks "which room am I in?", ls asks "what is in this room?", and cd means "walk to another room". Rooms lead into smaller rooms, just as folders hold other folders.

rm is permanent. rm -rf / or a typo like rm -rf / tmp/stuff (note the space) can destroy a whole system. Always double-check the path, and use ls with the same path first.
Press Tab to auto-complete names, ↑ to recall previous commands, Ctrl+R to search your history, and Ctrl+C to stop a running command. Use man ls (or ls --help) to read the manual.

Viewing and editing files

  • Most Linux configuration is plain text, so reading and editing it matters.
  • nano is the friendly editor; its shortcuts are shown at the bottom.
  • vim has modes: i inserts text and Esc returns to normal mode.
  • tail -f watches a log live, for example after a deploy.

cat /etc/os-release        # print a whole file
less /var/log/syslog       # scroll a big file: space=next page, /word=search, q=quit
head -n 5 file.txt         # first 5 lines
tail -n 20 file.txt        # last 20 lines
tail -f /var/log/nginx/access.log   # follow a log live as new lines arrive (Ctrl+C to stop)
wc -l file.txt             # count lines
echo "hello" > hi.txt      # write text to a file (overwrites!)
echo "more" >> hi.txt     # append to a file
ELI5: Explain like I'm 5

Vim is like a TV remote with two modes. In normal mode the buttons give commands (move, delete, save); in insert mode the same buttons type letters, as in a search box.

Vim keys (in normal mode)Action
ienter insert mode (type text)
Escback to normal mode
:w + Entersave
:q + Enterquit
:wq or ZZsave and quit
:q!quit without saving
/word then nsearch, jump to next match
dd / yy / pdelete (cut) line / copy line / paste
uundo
Explain in detail

If you press keys and strange things happen, you are in the wrong mode: press Esc to return to normal mode.

Most Linux configuration is plain text, so reading and editing text is your most-used skill.

nano: the friendly editor

Run nano file.txt. Shortcuts are shown at the bottom (^ means Ctrl). Ctrl+O saves, Ctrl+X exits, Ctrl+W searches.

vim: the editor on every server

Run vim file.txt. It has modes. You start in normal mode (keys are commands). Press i to insert text, Esc to go back.

tail -f is the DevOps engineer's best friend: deploy, then watch the log live to see if errors appear.

Check yourself

Two quick questions on the last few slides. Not graded; wrong answers explain themselves.

Where would you look first for a server's configuration files?

Configuration lives in /etc.

You want to watch a log file live while you restart an app. Which command fits?

tail -f follows a log live.

Users, groups and sudo

  • Linux is multi-user: many people and programs share one machine safely.
  • root is the superuser; sudo runs one command with root rights.
  • Use usermod -aG to add groups; without -a, existing groups are replaced.
  • Use your normal user, and sudo only when needed.
ELI5: Explain like I'm 5

An apartment building: every resident has a key to their own flat (user).

root: the superuser with user ID (UID) 0 who can do anything. sudo: runs one command with root privileges if you are allowed to, and records it in a log.

whoami                      # my username
id                          # my UID, GID and groups
sudo apt update             # run one command as root
sudo -i                     # open a root shell (use sparingly)

sudo useradd -m -s /bin/bash alice   # create user alice with a home dir and bash
sudo passwd alice                    # set her password
sudo groupadd devs                   # create a group
sudo usermod -aG devs alice          # add alice to group devs (-a = append! don't forget it)
sudo userdel -r alice                # delete the user and her home folder
groups alice                         # list alice's groups
FileContains
/etc/passwdList of users (name, UID, home, shell). Despite the name, no passwords are stored here.
/etc/shadowPassword hashes, readable only by root
/etc/groupList of groups and members
/etc/sudoersWho may use sudo. Edit it only with sudo visudo (it checks syntax so you do not lock yourself out)
Explain in detail

Some residents are in the "gym club" (group) and so may use the gym. The building manager (root) has a master key to everything. sudo is borrowing the manager's master key for one job, only if your name is on the manager's approved list, and the borrowing is written in the logbook.

Linux is multi-user: many people (and programs) share one machine safely. Each has an identity and rights.

Without -a, usermod -G replaces all of a user's supplementary groups. Always use usermod -aG. And do not run everything as root: use your normal user and sudo only when needed (principle of least privilege).

Permissions and ownership

  • ls -l shows type, owner, group and permissions for each file.
  • Permissions come in three triplets: owner, group and others, each rwx.
  • Read is 4, write is 2, execute is 1; add them per triplet.
  • For example, -rwxr-xr-- adds up to 7, 5 and 4, written 754.
$ ls -l -rwxr-xr-- 1 alice devs 1204 Oct 3 10:12 deploy.sh drwxr-xr-x 2 alice devs 4096 Oct 3 09:50 configs
ELI5: Explain like I'm 5

Every file carries a small label with three sets of rules: what its owner may do, what its group may do, and what everybody else may do. The label is the permission string.

LetterNumberOn a fileOn a directory
r4read contentslist names inside
w2modify contentscreate / delete / rename files inside
x1run it as a programenter it (cd) and access items

# octal mode
chmod 754 deploy.sh        # owner rwx, group r-x, others r--
chmod 600 ~/.ssh/id_ed25519 # private key: only the owner can read/write
chmod 644 index.html       # common for normal files
chmod 755 script.sh        # common for scripts and directories

# symbolic mode: who (u g o a) + operator (+ - =) + permission (r w x)
chmod u+x deploy.sh        # give the owner execute
chmod g-w file             # remove write from the group
chmod o= file              # others get nothing
chmod -R 755 mydir         # recursive (be careful!)

# ownership
sudo chown alice file              # change owner
sudo chown alice:devs file         # change owner and group
sudo chown -R www-data:www-data /var/www/html
sudo chgrp devs file               # change group only
Explain in detail

For each person you can say: may read it? may write (change) it? may execute (run) it?

Run ls -l and you see something like this:

Permission string: 10 characters. The 1st shows the type (- file, d directory, l link). The next 9 are three triplets: user (owner), group, others, each as rwx (a dash means "not allowed").

Add the numbers of each triplet: rwx = 4+2+1 = 7, r-x = 4+0+1 = 5, r-- = 4. So -rwxr-xr-- is 754.

Permissions animated

  • Each triplet becomes a number: rwx is 7, r-x is 5, r-- is 4.
  • Together they form the command chmod 754.
  • umask removes permissions from newly created files.
  • Never use chmod 777 just to make an error go away.
Explain in detail

Watch the string -rwxr-xr-- turn into the numbers 7, 5, 4 and then into the command chmod 754.

The first triplet (owner) is rwx = 7, the second (group) is r-x = 5, the third (others) is r-- = 4.

umask

The umask removes permissions from newly created files. Typical umask 022: new files become 644 and new directories 755. Check it with umask.

Special bits (briefly)

setuid (4xxx) runs a program as its owner, e.g. passwd. setgid (2xxx) on a directory makes new files inherit its group. sticky (1xxx) on /tmp stops users deleting each other's files.

Avoid this

chmod -R 777 / or chmod 777 "to make the error go away". It gives everyone full control and is a security hole. Find the real owner/permission problem instead.

"Permission denied" is the most common Linux error. Debug it with ls -l file (who owns it?), id (who am I?), and check every directory on the path with ls -ld.

Processes, signals, disk and memory

  • A process is a running instance of a program with its own PID.
  • Signals stop processes: SIGTERM asks politely, SIGKILL forces.
  • Slow server? Check top, then free -h, then df -h.
  • A full disk is a common cause of mysterious failures.
Process: a running instance of a program. Each has a PID (process ID). A daemon is a process that runs in the background, such as a web server.
ELI5: Explain like I'm 5

A recipe is a program; a cook actually cooking it is a process.


ps aux                    # every process on the system
ps aux | grep nginx       # find a particular one
top                       # live view (q to quit); htop is a friendlier version if installed
pgrep nginx               # print PIDs by name

kill 1234                 # send SIGTERM (15): "please shut down gracefully"
kill -9 1234              # send SIGKILL (9): forced, cannot be caught - last resort
kill -HUP 1234            # SIGHUP (1): many daemons reload their config
pkill nginx               # kill by name

sleep 300 &               # run in the background
jobs                      # list background jobs of this shell
fg %1                     # bring job 1 to the foreground
# Ctrl+Z pauses a foreground job; bg resumes it in the background
nohup ./long.sh &         # keep running after you log out
SignalNumberMeaning
SIGHUP1Hang up (often "reload config")
SIGINT2Interrupt (what Ctrl+C sends)
SIGKILL9Kill immediately, cannot be ignored
SIGTERM15Polite request to terminate (the default of kill)

Disk and memory


df -h                     # free/used space per filesystem (human-readable)
du -sh /var/log           # total size of a directory
du -sh /var/log/* | sort -h   # which item is biggest?
free -h                   # RAM and swap usage
lsblk                     # list disks and partitions
Explain in detail

Many cooks can follow the same recipe at once, each with their own number badge (PID). A signal is a tap on the cook's shoulder: "please stop politely" (SIGTERM) or the emergency "stop right now!" (SIGKILL).

"Server is slow" checklist: top (CPU, memory hogs) → free -h (out of RAM?) → df -h (disk full?). A full disk is one of the most common causes of mysterious failures, especially full /var/log.

Why SIGTERM first?

Compare with ours

Because SIGTERM lets the program shut down gracefully and clean up, while SIGKILL stops it immediately with no chance to save work.

Check yourself

Two quick questions on the last few slides. Not graded; wrong answers explain themselves.

What do the permissions of chmod 640 mean?

6 = rw-, 4 = r--, 0 = ---.

You run usermod -G devs alice and alice loses her other groups. What did you forget?

usermod -aG appends; -G alone replaces her groups.

Services (systemd) and package managers

  • systemd starts, stops and supervises services.
  • systemctl controls them; journalctl shows their logs.
  • apt, dnf and apk install software packages.
systemd: the init system and service manager on most modern distros. It is the first process (PID 1) and starts, stops and supervises services (nginx, ssh, docker...). You control it with systemctl and read its logs with journalctl.
ELI5: Explain like I'm 5

systemd is the head teacher who arrives first (PID 1), opens each classroom in the right order and reopens any that shuts unexpectedly. The classrooms are services, and systemctl is the intercom you use to talk to the head teacher.


sudo systemctl status nginx      # is it running? last log lines
sudo systemctl start nginx       # start now
sudo systemctl stop nginx        # stop now
sudo systemctl restart nginx     # stop then start
sudo systemctl reload nginx      # re-read config without dropping connections (if supported)
sudo systemctl enable nginx      # start automatically at boot
sudo systemctl enable --now nginx   # enable and start in one go
systemctl is-active nginx

journalctl -u nginx              # logs of one service
journalctl -u nginx -f           # follow live
journalctl -u nginx --since "1 hour ago"
journalctl -p err -b             # errors (and worse) since this boot
TaskDebian / Ubuntu (apt)RHEL family (dnf)Alpine (apk)
Refresh package listssudo apt updatesudo dnf makecache (usually automatic)apk update
Installsudo apt install nginxsudo dnf install nginxapk add nginx
Removesudo apt remove nginxsudo dnf remove nginxapk del nginx
Upgrade allsudo apt upgradesudo dnf upgradeapk upgrade
Searchapt search worddnf search wordapk search word
Explain in detail

A service is described by a small unit file, for example /etc/systemd/system/myapp.service:


[Unit]
Description=My little app
After=network.target

[Service]
ExecStart=/usr/bin/python3 /opt/myapp/app.py
Restart=on-failure
User=appuser

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target

After creating or editing a unit file run sudo systemctl daemon-reload, then sudo systemctl enable --now myapp.

Package managers

Package manager: a tool that downloads, installs, updates and removes software (and its dependencies) from trusted online repositories.
yum is the older name of the RHEL package tool; on modern RHEL-family systems yum is generally just a compatible alias of dnf. In Dockerfiles with Alpine you will write apk add --no-cache ....

Pipes, redirection and environment variables

  • A pipe | connects one program's output to the next program's input.
  • Every program has three streams: stdin (input), stdout (output), stderr (errors).
  • Environment variables pass settings from the shell to programs.
  • The shell finds commands by searching the folders listed in PATH.
ELI5: Explain like I'm 5

Picture water filters joined by pipes: water (text) flows out of one filter into the next, and each filter does one small job (a command).

Every program has three standard streams: stdin (0, input), stdout (1, normal output) and stderr (2, error messages).

ls | wc -l                     # pipe: count the entries in a directory
cat access.log | grep 404 | wc -l   # count 404 lines

echo hi > out.txt               # stdout -> file (overwrite)
echo hi >> out.txt              # stdout -> file (append)
sort < names.txt                # file -> stdin
ls /nope 2> errors.txt          # only stderr -> file
./run.sh > all.log 2>&1        # stdout and stderr -> same file
./noisy.sh > /dev/null 2>&1    # throw all output away
cmd1 && cmd2                   # run cmd2 only if cmd1 succeeded
cmd1 || cmd2                   # run cmd2 only if cmd1 failed
cmd1 ; cmd2                    # run both, regardless
Explain in detail

The pipe symbol | is the pipe between two filters: it sends one command's output into the next command's input. Each command does one tiny job, but joined together they do powerful things.

Environment variables and PATH

Environment variable: a named value (NAME=value) that programs inherit from the shell. Used to pass settings such as the database URL, the language, or the location of programs.

echo $HOME                    # print a variable
env                           # list all environment variables
export APP_ENV=production     # create one that child programs can see
echo $PATH                    # colon-separated list of directories searched for commands
export PATH="$PATH:/opt/mytool/bin"   # add a directory to PATH
which python3                 # which file runs when I type python3?

When you type ls, the shell looks through each folder listed in $PATH until it finds an executable called ls. To make a variable permanent, put the export line in ~/.bashrc (then run source ~/.bashrc).

Never put real passwords or API keys in scripts that you commit to Git. Use environment variables or a secrets manager (see the DevSecOps module).

Finding and transforming text: grep, find, sed, awk and friends

  • grep searches inside text; find searches for files.
  • cut, sort, uniq, sed and awk transform text in pipelines.
  • Chained tools can answer questions, such as which IPs hit a server most.

grep: search inside text


grep "error" app.log
grep -i "error" app.log     # ignore case
grep -n "error" app.log     # show line numbers
grep -v "debug" app.log     # invert: lines without
grep -r "TODO" ./src        # recursive in a folder
grep -c "404" access.log    # count matching lines

find: search for files


find /var/log -name "*.log"
find . -type d -name "node_modules"
find / -size +100M 2>/dev/null
find /tmp -mtime +7          # modified >7 days ago
find . -name "*.tmp" -delete


cut -d: -f1 /etc/passwd             # field 1 (usernames), delimiter ':'
sort names.txt                      # alphabetical;  sort -n numeric;  sort -r reverse
sort names.txt | uniq               # remove duplicates (input must be sorted)
sort names.txt | uniq -c            # count how many times each appears
sed 's/http:/https:/g' urls.txt     # replace text, print result
sed -i 's/DEBUG/INFO/' app.conf     # edit the file in place
awk '{print $1}' access.log         # print the 1st whitespace-separated column
awk -F: '{print $1, $3}' /etc/passwd  # custom delimiter
find . -name "*.log" | xargs grep -l "ERROR"   # xargs: turn lines into arguments
$ awk '{print $1}' access.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -3 412 203.0.113.9 187 198.51.100.4 96 192.0.2.77

Example output; your counts and addresses will differ (the IPs shown are reserved documentation addresses).

Explain in detail

On a server you rarely open a GUI. Instead you slice logs and files with small text tools.

That one-liner answers "which 3 IP addresses hit my web server most?": take the first column, sort, count duplicates, sort by count descending, keep the top 3.

Make a safety copy before sed -i: sed -i.bak 's/a/b/' file keeps the original as file.bak.

Network commands, SSH keys and cron

  • SSH gives an encrypted terminal on a remote machine, on port 22 by default.
  • A key pair has a public key for servers and a private key you keep.
  • cron runs scheduled jobs; edit your schedule with crontab -e.
  • Cron jobs get a minimal PATH, so use absolute paths in them.

ip addr                    # my IP addresses (replaces old ifconfig)
ip route                   # routing table, default gateway
ping -c 4 example.com      # is the host reachable? (4 packets)
ss -tulpn                  # listening TCP/UDP ports and which program owns them
curl -I https://example.com   # fetch only the HTTP headers
curl -s https://example.com/health   # fetch a URL quietly

SSH: Secure Shell

SSH: an encrypted protocol (default port 22) to get a terminal on a remote machine, copy files securely and tunnel traffic.
ELI5: Explain like I'm 5

SSH keys are a lock and a key.


ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "me@laptop"       # create a key pair in ~/.ssh/
ssh-copy-id user@203.0.113.10              # install your public key on the server
ssh user@203.0.113.10                      # log in (no password needed now)
ssh -i ~/.ssh/mykey.pem ec2-user@203.0.113.10   # use a specific key file (typical on AWS)
scp app.tar.gz user@203.0.113.10:/tmp/     # copy a file over SSH
chmod 600 ~/.ssh/id_ed25519                # SSH refuses keys that others can read

cron: scheduled jobs


# minute hour day-of-month month day-of-week  command
  0      2    *            *     *            /home/abhi/backup.sh >> /var/log/backup.log 2>&1   # every day at 02:00
  */5    *    *            *     *            /usr/local/bin/check.sh                                # every 5 minutes
  30     8    *            *     1-5          /home/abhi/report.sh                                   # 08:30 Mon-Fri
Explain in detail

You make a pair: a public key (a padlock you can hand out to everyone) and a private key (the only key that opens it, which never leaves your pocket). You put the padlock on the server; only you can open it.

A quick preview of network commands (the Networking module goes deeper):

Handy shortcut file ~/.ssh/config:


Host web1
    HostName 203.0.113.10
    User ubuntu
    IdentityFile ~/.ssh/id_ed25519

Now just type ssh web1.

Edit your schedule with crontab -e; list it with crontab -l. Each line has five time fields and then a command:

Cron runs with a tiny environment and a minimal PATH. Use absolute paths to scripts and programs, and redirect output to a log so you can see failures.

Check yourself

Two quick questions on the last few slides. Not graded; wrong answers explain themselves.

What does ./run.sh > all.log 2>&1 do?

> file takes stdout; 2>&1 makes stderr follow it.

A script works when you run it by hand but fails from cron. What is a likely cause?

Cron has a minimal PATH, so use absolute paths.

Bash scripting basics

  • A shell script is a text file of commands run top to bottom.
  • Exit code 0 means success; anything else means failure.
  • Always quote variables so spaces in filenames do not break commands.
Shell script: a text file of shell commands run top to bottom. It turns something you type repeatedly into one command you can schedule, share and version in Git.
ELI5: Explain like I'm 5

A script is a recipe card: you write the steps once, and from then on you just say "make the cake" and every step runs, top to bottom.


#!/usr/bin/env bash
# The first line (shebang) tells the system which interpreter runs this file.

name="Abhi"                  # variable: NO spaces around =
echo "Hello, $name"          # double quotes expand variables
echo 'Hello, $name'          # single quotes print literally: Hello, $name
today=$(date +%F)            # command substitution: capture output (e.g. 2026-10-10)
echo "Today is ${today}"

# arguments: $1 $2 ... ; $# = count ; $@ = all ; $0 = script name
echo "First arg: $1"

# if / else  (note the spaces inside [[ ]])
if [[ -f /etc/hosts ]]; then
  echo "file exists"
elif [[ -d /etc/hosts ]]; then
  echo "it is a directory"
else
  echo "missing"
fi

# numeric comparison uses -eq -ne -lt -gt -le -ge
if [[ $# -lt 1 ]]; then echo "usage: $0 NAME"; exit 1; fi

# loops
for f in *.log; do echo "found $f"; done
for i in 1 2 3; do echo "round $i"; done
count=0
while [[ $count -lt 3 ]]; do echo "count=$count"; count=$((count + 1)); done

# functions
greet() { echo "Hi $1"; }
greet "team"
TestTrue when
-f pathis a regular file
-d pathis a directory
-e pathexists
-z "$x"string is empty
"$a" == "$b"strings are equal
Explain in detail

The steps on the card are shell commands. When the cooking ends, you get a note saying how it went: that note is the exit code, 0 for success and anything else for a problem.

Exit codes and safety

Exit code: a number every command returns when it finishes. 0 means success; anything else (1–255) means some kind of failure. Read the last one with $?.

ls /etc/hosts; echo $?     # prints 0
ls /nope;      echo $?     # prints a non-zero number (2 on GNU ls)

# Put this near the top of every serious script:
set -euo pipefail
#  -e          exit immediately if a command fails (but not for commands
#              tested by if, while, && or ||, which are allowed to fail)
#  -u          treat use of an unset variable as an error
#  -o pipefail a pipeline fails if any command in it fails, not only the last

To make a script runnable: chmod +x script.sh then ./script.sh (or run it as bash script.sh).

Always quote variables: "$file", not $file. Without quotes, a filename with a space would be split into two words and your command would act on the wrong things.

A real-world script: backup and health check

  • The script backs up a folder into a dated archive.
  • It deletes backups older than 7 days and checks disk space.
  • It logs everything and can run nightly from cron.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

# ---- settings (override by exporting variables before running) ----
SOURCE_DIR="${SOURCE_DIR:-/var/www/html}"
BACKUP_DIR="${BACKUP_DIR:-/var/backups/site}"
KEEP_DAYS="${KEEP_DAYS:-7}"
DISK_LIMIT_PERCENT=90
TIMESTAMP="$(date +%F_%H-%M-%S)"
ARCHIVE="${BACKUP_DIR}/site_${TIMESTAMP}.tar.gz"

log() { echo "[$(date '+%F %T')] $*"; }

# ---- sanity checks ----
if [[ ! -d "$SOURCE_DIR" ]]; then
  log "ERROR: source directory $SOURCE_DIR does not exist"
  exit 1
fi
mkdir -p "$BACKUP_DIR"

# ---- disk check: use% of the filesystem that holds the backups ----
USED="$(df --output=pcent "$BACKUP_DIR" | tail -n 1 | tr -dc '0-9')"
if [[ "$USED" -ge "$DISK_LIMIT_PERCENT" ]]; then
  log "ERROR: disk is ${USED}% full, refusing to back up"
  exit 2
fi

# ---- do the backup ----
log "Backing up $SOURCE_DIR to $ARCHIVE"
tar -czf "$ARCHIVE" -C "$SOURCE_DIR" .
log "Backup finished: $(du -h "$ARCHIVE" | cut -f1)"

# ---- remove old backups ----
log "Deleting backups older than $KEEP_DAYS days"
find "$BACKUP_DIR" -name 'site_*.tar.gz' -mtime +"$KEEP_DAYS" -print -delete

log "Done"
Explain in detail

This script backs up a folder into a dated archive, deletes backups older than 7 days, checks that a disk is not too full, and logs everything. Read each section; every line is something you have already learned.

Concepts used

  • set -euo pipefail for safety
  • ${VAR:-default} default values
  • a function (log)
  • if with [[ ]] tests
  • exit codes (1, 2)
  • pipes: df | tail | tr
  • find ... -delete

Run it on a schedule


chmod +x backup.sh
sudo ./backup.sh
# cron: every night at 02:30
30 2 * * * /opt/scripts/backup.sh >> /var/log/backup.log 2>&1
Test destructive commands like -delete first by removing that flag: find ... -print only lists what would be deleted.

Check yourself

Two quick questions on the last few slides. Not graded; wrong answers explain themselves.

Which line correctly assigns a variable in Bash?

Assign with name=value and no spaces.

Why does the backup script check disk usage before creating the archive?

A failing check stops the script before it can make things worse.

  • Use an Ubuntu VM, WSL, a cloud free-tier machine or a container.
  • Steps: explore, analyse a fake log, write a script, fix permissions.
  • Type each command yourself and compare with the example output.

Task 1: worked example


cd ~ && pwd
mkdir -p lab/logs lab/scripts && cd lab
ls -R
printf "INFO start\nERROR disk full\nINFO ok\nERROR timeout\n" > logs/app.log
grep ERROR logs/app.log
grep -c ERROR logs/app.log
$ ls -R .: logs scripts ./logs: ./scripts: $ grep -c ERROR logs/app.log 2

cat > scripts/hello.sh <<'EOF'
#!/usr/bin/env bash

echo "Hello, $1! Today is $(date +%F)"
EOF
./scripts/hello.sh Abhi        # permission denied?

Task 2: finish it

Break the log's permissions, then repair them.


chmod 000 logs/app.log
cat logs/app.log           # Permission denied
ls -l logs/app.log
???
???

If you are logged in as root (for example inside a Docker container), the cat still works after chmod 000, because root bypasses read and write permission checks. Do this step as a normal user to see the error.

Show hint

Give the owner read and write and everyone else read (mode 644), then read the file again.

Show answer 

chmod 644 logs/app.log
cat logs/app.log

Task 3: on your own

Goal: nginx running and enabled at boot, plus a cron job logging a line every minute. Success: curl -I http://localhost returns 200 OK and the cron log grows.

Show hint

Use apt to install nginx, then systemctl enable --now. For the schedule, use crontab -e and the five time fields.

Show answer 

sudo apt update && sudo apt install -y nginx
sudo systemctl enable --now nginx
systemctl status nginx
curl -I http://localhost
sudo ss -tulpn | grep :80
journalctl -u nginx --since "10 minutes ago"

Expected: curl shows HTTP/1.1 200 OK and ss shows nginx listening on port 80.

Then run crontab -e and add * * * * * echo "tick $(date)" >> $HOME/lab/logs/cron.log. Wait two minutes and run tail -f ~/lab/logs/cron.log. Then remove the line.

Explain in detail

Use an Ubuntu VM, WSL, a cloud free-tier machine, or a container (docker run -it ubuntu bash after you learn Docker; a container has no sudo, systemd or cron, so do steps 5 and 6 on a VM). Type each command yourself.

Interview questions

Q1: What is the difference between the kernel, the shell and a distribution?

The kernel manages hardware and resources. The shell is a program that takes your commands and passes them to the kernel. A distribution bundles a kernel with tools, a package manager and defaults (Ubuntu, RHEL...).

Q2: Explain the permission string -rwxr-xr--.

First char: file type (- regular file). Then owner has rwx (7), group has r-x (5), others have r-- (4). So the octal mode is 754.

Q3: What is the difference between kill and kill -9?

kill sends SIGTERM (15), a polite request that lets the program clean up. kill -9 sends SIGKILL, which the kernel enforces immediately without cleanup. Use it only as a last resort.

Q4: How do you find which process is using port 8080?

sudo ss -tulpn | grep :8080 (or lsof -i :8080 if installed). It shows the PID and program name.

Q5: What does 2>&1 mean?

It redirects stderr (file descriptor 2) to wherever stdout (descriptor 1) currently points, so both streams go to the same place, e.g. cmd > all.log 2>&1.

Q6: A disk is full. How do you find what is using the space?

df -h to see which filesystem is full, then du -sh /path/* | sort -h to drill down into the biggest directories. Logs under /var/log are a frequent cause.

Q7: What does set -euo pipefail do?

It makes a script stricter: exit on any command failure (-e), error on unset variables (-u), and fail a pipeline if any stage fails (pipefail).

Q8: How do you make a service start at boot and start it right now?

sudo systemctl enable --now servicename.

Q9: Hard link vs symbolic link?

A symbolic link is a small file pointing to another path (breaks if the target is removed). A hard link is another name for the same data on disk. Create a symlink with ln -s target link.

Q10: How do containers relate to the Linux kernel?

Containers are ordinary processes isolated with kernel features: namespaces give each its own view of processes, network and filesystems, and cgroups limit its CPU and memory. They share the host kernel, unlike virtual machines.

Quiz

1. Which command shows your current directory?

pwd = "print working directory".

2. What is the octal value of the permissions rw-r--r--?

rw- = 6, r-- = 4, r-- = 4, so 644.

3. Which command follows a log file live as new lines are written?

tail -f keeps the file open and prints new lines as they arrive.

4. What does an exit code of 0 mean?

0 = success; any non-zero value signals some kind of failure.

5. Which kernel features are the foundation of containers?

Namespaces isolate what a process can see; cgroups limit what it can use.

6. Which command starts nginx now and also at every boot?

enable = start at boot; --now also starts it immediately.
