05

Networking for DevOps

Every application you deploy talks to something else: a browser, a database, another service, a cloud API. When it stops working, the cause is very often the network. This module explains how data travels from one machine to another, what IP addresses, ports and DNS records are, how HTTP and HTTPS work, what routers, firewalls and load balancers do, and how to debug the classic problem "the website is down".

What you will learn

IP addresses and CIDR subnetting · MAC addresses · ports · the OSI and TCP/IP models · TCP and UDP · DNS · HTTP, TLS and certificates · routers, switches, NAT · firewalls and security groups · proxies and reverse proxies · load balancers · CDNs · troubleshooting tools.

Guess first

You are not expected to know these yet. Guessing before you read helps you remember the answer when you meet it.

1. On one machine many programs listen for network traffic. What tells the machine which program should get a packet?

The IP address finds the machine; the port finds the program.

2. You type www.example.com into a browser. What must happen before any data can be sent to the server?

DNS turns names into IP addresses before the connection starts.

3. Why do two computers using TCP exchange a few small messages before sending any real data?

The three-way handshake opens a reliable connection.

Why networking matters for DevOps

  • A network connects devices that exchange data as small packets.
  • One page view can touch a CDN, load balancer, server, API and database.
  • Containers, Kubernetes, VPCs and CI/CD all assume you know addresses, ports and DNS.
Computer network: two or more devices connected so they can exchange data. The data is cut into small pieces called packets, sent across cables or radio, and reassembled by the receiver. The biggest network of networks is the Internet.
ELI5: Explain like I'm 5

Think of the postal system. Every house has an address (IP address).

Explain in detail

Letters are put in envelopes with the address on the front (packets). Sorting offices decide which road each envelope takes (routers). Inside the house, each family member has their own room, so a letter also says "for the person in room 5" (port). The address book that turns a name into an address is DNS.

Software is no longer one program on one computer. A single page view may touch a CDN, a load balancer, a web server, an API, a cache and a database, each on a different machine. Containers, Kubernetes, cloud VPCs and CI/CD all assume you understand addresses, ports, DNS and firewalls.

Problems networking solves

  • How do two machines find each other? (addresses, DNS)
  • How is data delivered reliably? (TCP)
  • How do many programs share one machine's connection? (ports)
  • How do we keep strangers out? (firewalls, TLS)
  • How do we handle huge traffic? (load balancers, CDNs)

Where DevOps engineers meet it

  • Designing cloud networks (VPC, subnets, security groups)
  • "Connection refused" and "timed out" errors
  • Pointing a domain name at a server
  • Configuring nginx and load balancers
  • Kubernetes Services and Ingress

History and evolution

Today's Internet is built from layers designed over decades. Each row below solved a limit of the previous one.

YearMilestoneWhy it mattered
1969ARPANET, a US research network, connects its first nodesThe first large packet-switched network and the ancestor of the Internet.
1983ARPANET switches to TCP/IP on 1 JanuaryOne common language lets different networks interconnect. This date is often called the birthday of the Internet.
1983–1987DNS is designed by Paul Mockapetris: first specified in RFC 882 and RFC 883 (1983), replaced by the core specifications RFC 1034 and RFC 1035 (1987)Replaced a single shared hosts file with a distributed naming system. Names like example.com became practical.
1989–1991The Web: Tim Berners-Lee proposes it in 1989; the first website and browser follow, publicly announced in 1991HTTP, HTML and URLs turned the Internet into something everyone could use.
1993CIDR introducedClassless addressing (the /24 style) slowed the waste of IPv4 addresses and the growth of routing tables.
1994–1995SSL created by NetscapeFirst widely used way to encrypt web traffic. Later standardised as TLS.
1997 / 1999HTTP/1.1 (RFC 2068, then RFC 2616)Persistent connections and a mandatory Host header, which made hosting many sites on one IP address routine. It was the main web protocol until HTTP/2 arrived in 2015.
1998IPv6 specified (RFC 2460)128-bit addresses to replace the 32-bit IPv4 space. The final standard is RFC 8200 (2017).
1999TLS 1.0 (RFC 2246)The standardised successor of SSL.
2011IANA allocates the last free blocks of IPv4 addressesPushed the world to NAT everywhere and to IPv6 adoption.
2015HTTP/2 (RFC 7540)Many requests multiplexed over one connection, header compression.
2015–2016Let's Encrypt: public beta December 2015, general availability April 2016Free, automated certificates. HTTPS went from optional to the default for most of the web.
2017IPv6 becomes an Internet Standard (RFC 8200)Formal maturity of the replacement for IPv4.
2018TLS 1.3 (RFC 8446)Faster handshake (one round trip) and removal of old insecure options.
2021QUIC standardised (RFC 9000); TLS 1.0 and 1.1 formally deprecated (RFC 8996)A transport over UDP with built-in encryption; legacy TLS versions retired.
2022HTTP/3 (RFC 9114) runs over QUIC; HTTP semantics re-published as RFC 9110Removes TCP head-of-line blocking and handles network switches (Wi-Fi to mobile) better.
2024–2025Browsers and large sites turn on post-quantum hybrid key exchange in TLS 1.3 (X25519 combined with ML-KEM, standardised by NIST as FIPS 203 in August 2024)Protects today's recorded traffic against future quantum computers. It changes only the key exchange; certificates and HTTP stay the same.
2025The CA/Browser Forum votes (April) to shorten the maximum lifetime of public TLS certificates; Let's Encrypt shuts down its OCSP service (August)Maximum lifetime drops to 200 days from 15 March 2026, then 100 days from 15 March 2027 and 47 days from 15 March 2029. Manual certificate renewal stops being practical, so automation (ACME, certbot, cert-manager) becomes mandatory.
The pattern: the Internet was never replaced. New layers were added on top (TLS, HTTP/2, QUIC) while IP and DNS stay. Hence the same troubleshooting tools still work today.

IP addresses and MAC addresses

  • IP addresses locate devices: IPv4 uses 32 bits, IPv6 uses 128.
  • Private addresses are not routable on the Internet.
  • MAC addresses work inside one local network.
IP address: a number that identifies a device's network interface so packets can be routed to it. IPv4 uses 32 bits written as four numbers (octets) from 0 to 255, such as 192.168.1.25. IPv6 uses 128 bits written in hexadecimal, such as 2001:db8::1.
ELI5: Explain like I'm 5

An IP address is your home address, and it can change if you move to a new town (new network).


ip addr                  # IPs and MACs of my interfaces
ip route                 # routing table, shows the default gateway
ip neigh                 # the ARP table
hostname -I              # quick list of my IPs
curl -s https://checkip.amazonaws.com   # what public IP do I appear as?
Explain in detail

A MAC address is like your name written inside your shirt by the factory: it belongs to your network card and is only used to talk to neighbours on the same street.

Public vs private IPv4

Public addresses are unique on the Internet. Private addresses are reused inside homes, offices and cloud networks and are not routable on the Internet. The private ranges (RFC 1918) are:

RangeCIDR
10.0.0.0 – 10.255.255.25510.0.0.0/8
172.16.0.0 – 172.31.255.255172.16.0.0/12
192.168.0.0 – 192.168.255.255192.168.0.0/16

Special addresses

  • 127.0.0.1 (loopback, "this machine", name localhost); IPv6 equivalent ::1
  • 169.254.0.0/16: link-local, assigned when DHCP fails
  • 0.0.0.0: "all interfaces" when a server listens, or "unknown"
  • IPv6 link-local addresses start with fe80::
  • 2001:db8::/32 is reserved for documentation

MAC address and ARP

A MAC address is a 48-bit hardware address written like 00:1a:2b:3c:4d:5e, burned into the network card (it can be changed in software). Switches use MAC addresses to deliver frames inside one local network. ARP is the protocol that asks "who has IP 192.168.1.1? Tell me your MAC." Every device keeps a small ARP table of answers.

Computers get their address either by hand (static) or automatically from a DHCP server, which also hands out the gateway and DNS server addresses.

CIDR and subnetting with worked examples

  • CIDR writes a block as address/prefix, such as 192.168.1.0/24.
  • The prefix counts fixed network bits; the remaining bits identify hosts.
  • A bigger prefix number means a smaller block with fewer addresses.
  • Classic subnets lose 2 addresses to overhead; AWS reserves 5 per subnet.
CIDR notation: writes an address block as address/prefix. The prefix is how many of the 32 bits are the fixed network part. The remaining bits identify hosts inside it. A block with 32 - prefix host bits holds 2^(32 - prefix) addresses.
ELI5: Explain like I'm 5

An address is like a phone number 020-7946-0123.

PrefixSubnet maskAddressesUsable hosts (classic rule)
/8255.0.0.016,777,21616,777,214
/16255.255.0.065,53665,534
/24255.255.255.0256254
/26255.255.255.1926462
/28255.255.255.2401614
/30255.255.255.25242
/32255.255.255.2551one single host
Explain in detail

The first digits are the area code (network), the last digits are the person (host). The slash number says how many leading digits belong to the area code. A bigger slash number means a smaller area, so fewer houses.

In a classic subnet the first address is the network address and the last is the broadcast address, so usable hosts = addresses minus 2. Cloud providers reserve more: AWS keeps 5 addresses in every subnet, so a /28 gives 11 usable.

Worked example 1: what does 192.168.1.0/24 contain?


Prefix /24 -> 24 network bits, 8 host bits -> 2^8 = 256 addresses
Network address:   192.168.1.0
First usable host: 192.168.1.1
Last usable host:  192.168.1.254
Broadcast:         192.168.1.255

Worked example 2: split 192.168.1.0/24 into four equal subnets

Four subnets need 2 extra bits (2^2 = 4), so the prefix grows from /24 to /26. Each /26 has 64 addresses.

SubnetNetworkUsable rangeBroadcast
1192.168.1.0/26.1 – .62192.168.1.63
2192.168.1.64/26.65 – .126192.168.1.127
3192.168.1.128/26.129 – .190192.168.1.191
4192.168.1.192/26.193 – .254192.168.1.255

Worked example 3: is 10.0.5.20 inside 10.0.4.0/22?

A /22 has 10 host bits = 1024 addresses, which is four consecutive /24 blocks: 10.0.4.0, 10.0.5.0, 10.0.6.0, 10.0.7.0. The block runs from 10.0.4.0 to 10.0.7.255, so 10.0.5.20 is inside.

Cloud design rule of thumb: pick a big private block for the whole network (for example 10.0.0.0/16), then carve /24 subnets from it (public, private, database). Keep ranges of connected networks from overlapping, or you cannot connect them later.

Ports: which program should get this packet?

  • The IP address finds the machine; the port finds the program.
  • Ports run from 0 to 65535 and pair with a protocol.
  • A connection is four things: source and destination IP and port.
Port: a 16-bit number (0–65535) that identifies one service or connection endpoint on a machine, always used together with an IP address and a protocol (TCP or UDP). The pair IP:port is a socket address.
ELI5: Explain like I'm 5

One apartment building has one street address, but hundreds of apartments.

PortService
22SSH
53DNS (UDP and TCP)
80HTTP
443HTTPS
25SMTP (mail sending)
3306MySQL
5432PostgreSQL
6379Redis
27017MongoDB
3389Remote Desktop (RDP)

sudo ss -tulpn          # which programs listen on which ports
nc -zv example.com 443  # can I open a TCP connection to port 443?
Explain in detail

The IP address gets the postman to the building. The port number is the apartment number so the parcel reaches the right family.

The IP address finds the building, the port finds the apartment.

Port ranges

  • 0–1023: well-known ports. On Linux, by default only root (or a program given the CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE capability) can listen on them.
  • 1024–49151: registered ports (apps like 3000, 5432, 8080).
  • 49152–65535: dynamic (ephemeral) ports in the IANA plan. Your browser's operating system picks a temporary source port for each connection; Linux uses 32768–60999 by default.

A connection is identified by four things: source IP, source port, destination IP, destination port.

"Connection refused" usually means the machine is reachable but nothing listens on that port. "Connection timed out" usually means packets are being dropped on the way (often a firewall).

Check yourself

Two quick questions on the last few slides. Not graded; wrong answers explain themselves.

1. Which of these blocks contains the fewest addresses?

A bigger prefix number means a smaller block.

2. Your laptop has the address 192.168.1.25. What does that tell you?

Private addresses are not routable on the Internet.

The OSI model: seven layers

  • OSI splits networking into seven layers, each with one job.
  • Going down, each layer wraps the data in its own header (encapsulation).
  • On the other machine each header is removed in reverse order.
OSI model (Open Systems Interconnection): a seven-layer reference model that splits networking into jobs. Each layer only talks to the layer directly above and below it and to the same layer on the other machine. Encapsulation means each layer adds its own header to the data from above.
ELI5: Explain like I'm 5

You write a birthday card (data).

#LayerUnit of dataExamplesDevice
7ApplicationDataHTTP, DNS, SSH, SMTPProxies, L7 load balancers
6PresentationDataEncoding, compression, encryption (TLS is often placed here)
5SessionDataOpening, maintaining and closing conversations
4TransportSegment (TCP) / datagram (UDP)TCP, UDP, portsL4 load balancers, firewalls
3NetworkPacketIP, ICMPRouter
2Data linkFrameEthernet, Wi-Fi, MAC addresses, ARPSwitch
1PhysicalBitsCables, fibre, radio signalsCables, hubs, NICs
Explain in detail

You put it in an envelope with the friend's name (a header). The post office puts that envelope in a bag with a sorting label (another header). A lorry carries the bag. At the other end each wrapper is removed in reverse order until your friend reads the card.

Data is wrapped in a new header at each layer going down, crosses the wire, then each header is removed going up on the other side.

Memory trick from top to bottom: "All People Seem To Need Data Processing". Layer 1 up: "Please Do Not Throw Sausage Pizza Away".

Layers 7, 6 and 5: what the application sees

  • Layer 7 holds the protocols programs speak, such as HTTP, DNS and SSH.
  • Layer 6 translates and secures data: encoding, compression, encryption.
  • Layer 5 starts, keeps alive and ends a dialogue between programs.
ELI5: Explain like I'm 5

In the birthday-card picture, layer 7 is what you write and the words both of you understand (such as HTTP).


# A layer 7 conversation, typed by hand with netcat (plain HTTP)
printf 'GET / HTTP/1.1\r\nHost: example.com\r\nConnection: close\r\n\r\n' | nc example.com 80
Explain in detail

Layer 6 is the language the card is written in and whether it is in a secret code (data format and encryption). Layer 5 is keeping track of a long exchange of letters, so each reply belongs to the right conversation (the session).

Layer 7: Application

The protocols your programs speak: HTTP for web, DNS for names, SSH for remote shells, SMTP for sending mail, FTP, and many more. A browser or curl works here. When people say "L7 load balancer" they mean it understands HTTP.

Layer 6: Presentation

Translating and securing data: character encodings (UTF-8), compression, serialisation (JSON), encryption. In practice TLS is the best-known example, though it does not fit neatly into one OSI layer.

Layer 5: Session

Starting, keeping alive and ending a dialogue between two programs, such as login sessions or checkpoints in a long transfer. In the real Internet, layers 5 to 7 are mostly merged inside the application.

When a bug is in layer 7, you can see it in curl -v: wrong status code, wrong header, bad JSON. If curl cannot even connect, the problem is lower down.

Layers 4 to 1 and the TCP/IP model

  • Layer 4 uses ports, layer 3 uses IP routing, layer 2 uses MAC addresses.
  • Layer 1 is the physical signal: copper, fibre or radio.
  • The TCP/IP model has four layers and matches how real software is built.
  • Debug bottom-up: link, IP, port, then HTTP.

The TCP/IP model (what the Internet actually uses)

TCP/IP layerOSI layersTypical protocols
Application7, 6, 5HTTP, DNS, SSH, TLS, SMTP
Transport4TCP, UDP
Internet3IP, ICMP
Link (network access)2, 1Ethernet, Wi-Fi, ARP
Explain in detail

Layer 4: Transport

Delivers data process to process using ports. TCP gives reliable ordered delivery, UDP gives fast best-effort delivery (next slide). Firewall rules like "allow TCP 443" work here.

Layer 3: Network

Addressing and routing across networks using IP. Routers read the destination IP and pick the next hop. ping (ICMP) and traceroute work here.

Layer 2: Data link

Delivery between devices on the same local network using MAC addresses. Switches and Wi-Fi access points operate here. Data is in frames.

Layer 1: Physical

Electrical, light or radio signals: copper, fibre, Wi-Fi radio. "Is the cable plugged in?" is a real layer 1 question.

The TCP/IP model has fewer layers and is the practical model. OSI is the teaching vocabulary; TCP/IP is how real software is organised.

Debug bottom-up: cable and link first, then IP reachability (ping), then port (nc), then HTTP (curl). Each step rules out a whole layer.

TCP vs UDP and the three-way handshake

  • TCP opens with SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK, then delivers data reliably and in order.
  • UDP skips the handshake, so it is faster but offers no delivery guarantee.
  • DNS queries, voice, games and QUIC use UDP.
ELI5: Explain like I'm 5

TCP is a phone call: you say "hello?" (SYN), they say "hello, can you hear me?" (SYN-ACK), you say "yes" (ACK).

TCP (Transmission Control Protocol): connection-oriented, reliable, ordered transport. It numbers bytes, acknowledges them, retransmits lost data and controls speed. UDP (User Datagram Protocol): connectionless, no delivery guarantee, minimal overhead.

nc -zv 203.0.113.10 22       # try a TCP handshake to port 22
ss -tan state established    # list established TCP connections
Explain in detail

Only then do you talk, and you repeat anything the other person did not hear. UDP is shouting a message across the playground: it is fast, but nobody promises the other child heard it.

How a TCP connection is opened with SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK.

TCP

  • Handshake: client sends SYN, server replies SYN-ACK, client sends ACK
  • Reliable and ordered; closes with FIN
  • Used by HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2, SSH, databases, email

UDP

  • No handshake, no retransmission built in
  • Lower latency, small header
  • Used by DNS queries, video and voice calls, games, DHCP, and QUIC (so HTTP/3)

Common TCP states you will see in ss: LISTEN (waiting for connections), ESTABLISHED (active), TIME-WAIT (recently closed, waiting to be sure no stray packets remain).

DNS: how names become IP addresses

  • DNS maps names to records, most often IP addresses.
  • A resolver asks the root, then .com, then the domain's own servers.
  • Answers are cached, and the TTL controls how long caches keep them.
DNS (Domain Name System): a worldwide, distributed database that maps names (www.example.com) to records, most often IP addresses. Humans remember names; computers route on numbers.
ELI5: Explain like I'm 5

DNS is the phone book of the Internet.

RecordPurposeExample
AName to IPv4 addressapp.example.com. A 203.0.113.10
AAAAName to IPv6 addressapp.example.com. AAAA 2001:db8::10
CNAMEAlias to another namewww CNAME app.example.com.
MXMail servers for the domain, with priorityexample.com. MX 10 mail.example.com.
TXTFree text: email SPF/DKIM, domain verification"v=spf1 include:_spf.example.com ~all"
NSWhich servers are authoritative for the zoneexample.com. NS ns1.example.com.

dig example.com              # full answer with TTL
dig +short example.com A     # just the IPs
dig example.com MX           # mail records
dig NS example.com           # who is authoritative
dig @8.8.8.8 example.com     # ask a specific resolver
dig +trace example.com       # follow root -> TLD -> authoritative yourself
nslookup example.com         # older, simpler tool
cat /etc/hosts               # local name overrides, checked before DNS
cat /etc/resolv.conf         # which resolver this machine uses
Explain in detail

You look up "Grandma" and get a number. Because no single book can hold every name, the book is split: one book says which book lists ".com", and that book says which book lists "example.com".

A browser asks a resolver, which walks root, TLD and authoritative servers and brings back the answer.

Lookup order: browser cache, then the operating system (including /etc/hosts), then the configured recursive resolver (your ISP, router, or something like a cloud provider's resolver). The resolver asks a root server, then the TLD server for .com, then the domain's authoritative name server, and caches the answer for the record's TTL (time to live, in seconds).

A CNAME cannot share its name with any other record. The bare domain (example.com) always has SOA and NS records, so it cannot be a CNAME; DNS providers offer ALIAS/ANAME records or "CNAME flattening" for that case. A low TTL speeds up changes but increases lookups. After changing a record, old answers can live in caches until the previous TTL expires. "DNS propagation" is really just caches expiring.

Why do resolvers cache DNS answers, and why does each record carry a TTL?

Compare with ours

Caching saves repeating the full root, TLD and authoritative lookup on every visit, and the TTL limits how long an old answer is reused so changes eventually reach everyone.

Check yourself

Two quick questions on the last few slides. Not graded; wrong answers explain themselves.

1. Which statement about TCP and UDP is correct?

TCP is reliable and ordered; UDP is faster with no guarantee.

2. You change a DNS record, but some users still reach the old IP for a while. Why?

Answers are cached for as long as the TTL allows.

HTTP and HTTPS

  • HTTP is request and response: method, path and headers go out, a status code comes back.
  • Status classes: 2xx success, 3xx redirect, 4xx client error, 5xx server error.
  • HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 differ in transport; your code rarely changes.
HTTP (HyperText Transfer Protocol): the request/response protocol of the web. A client sends a request (method, path, headers, optional body); the server returns a response (status code, headers, body). HTTP is stateless: each request stands alone.
ELI5: Explain like I'm 5

HTTP is ordering at a counter. You say "give me the blue balloon" (request).


# A request (what the client sends)
GET /products/42 HTTP/1.1
Host: shop.example.com
Accept: application/json
Authorization: Bearer <token>

# A response (what the server returns)
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json
Cache-Control: max-age=60

{"id": 42, "name": "Mug"}
MethodMeaning
GETRead a resource
POSTCreate / submit data
PUTReplace a resource
PATCHPartially update
DELETERemove
HEADLike GET, headers only
OPTIONSAsk what is allowed (used in CORS)
StatusMeaning
200 / 201 / 204OK / Created / No content
301 / 302Moved permanently / temporarily (see Location header)
304Not modified (use your cache)
400 / 401 / 403 / 404Bad request / not authenticated / forbidden / not found
429Too many requests
500Server error (app crashed or bug)
502 / 503 / 504Bad gateway / unavailable / gateway timeout (often proxy or load balancer cannot reach the app)
Explain in detail

The shop answers "here it is" (200) or "we have none" (404). The shopkeeper forgets you after each order, so you may need to show your membership card (a cookie or token) every time.

Status classes: 2xx success, 3xx redirect, 4xx the client made a mistake, 5xx the server failed. Useful headers: Host, Content-Type, Authorization, Cache-Control, Set-Cookie, Location, User-Agent.

Versions in one line: HTTP/1.1 sends requests over TCP one after another per connection; HTTP/2 multiplexes many streams over one TCP connection; HTTP/3 does the same over QUIC on UDP. Your application code usually does not change between them.

HTTPS, TLS and certificates

  • HTTPS is HTTP inside a TLS tunnel, normally on port 443.
  • TLS gives encryption, integrity and authentication.
  • Certificates are signed by a Certificate Authority and expire, so automate renewal.
HTTPS: HTTP carried inside a TLS (Transport Layer Security) encrypted tunnel, normally on port 443. TLS gives three things: encryption (nobody can read the data), integrity (nobody can change it unnoticed) and authentication (you are really talking to the real server).
ELI5: Explain like I'm 5

You and a friend want to pass secret notes in a crowded classroom.


curl -vI https://example.com 2>&1 | head -30      # shows TLS version, certificate subject and issuer
openssl s_client -connect example.com:443 -servername example.com < /dev/null
# Let's Encrypt certificates (free, automated) are typically issued with certbot or by your cloud/ingress
sudo certbot --nginx -d example.com
Explain in detail

First the friend shows an ID card signed by the head teacher (the certificate), so you know it is really them. Then you agree on a secret code word quickly, in a way the class cannot work out. From then on every note is written in your secret code.

The handshake, simplified (TLS 1.3)

  1. ClientHello: the browser says which TLS versions and ciphers it supports, which site it wants (SNI, Server Name Indication) and sends its half of a key exchange (a "key share").
  2. ServerHello: the server picks the version and cipher and sends its own key share. Both sides can now compute the same secret keys, so everything after this message is encrypted.
  3. Still in that first reply, the server sends its certificate, a signature proving it owns the certificate's private key (CertificateVerify), and a Finished message.
  4. The browser checks the certificate (right domain, not expired, chains to a CA it trusts) and the signature, sends its own Finished, and then the HTTP request. That is one round trip before data can flow, compared with two in TLS 1.2.
Certificate: a signed file that ties a public key to a domain name. It is signed by a Certificate Authority (CA). Servers usually send a chain: the site (leaf) certificate, one or more intermediates, and the browser already trusts the root CA.
Common failures: certificate expired, certificate for a different hostname, missing intermediate certificate, or a client clock that is wrong. Never "fix" it permanently with curl -k, which turns verification off.

Let's Encrypt certificates are valid for 90 days (and industry-wide maximum lifetimes are shrinking, see the history slide), so renewal must be automated (certbot timer, cert-manager in Kubernetes, or your cloud's managed certificates).

Routers, switches, NAT and gateways

  • Switches join devices; routers join networks.
  • The default gateway forwards traffic bound for other networks.
  • NAT lets private machines share one public IP.
Switch: connects devices inside one network (layer 2). It learns which MAC address is on which port and sends each frame only where it needs to go.
Router: connects different networks (layer 3). It looks at the destination IP and consults its routing table to choose the next hop.
ELI5: Explain like I'm 5

A switch is an office's internal mail room: it delivers letters between desks.


ip route
# example output:
# default via 192.168.1.1 dev eth0         <- the default gateway
# 192.168.1.0/24 dev eth0 proto kernel     <- the local subnet
traceroute example.com   # list each router hop on the path (use tracepath if traceroute is missing)

In the cloud

IdeaAWS nameWhat it does
Your private networkVPC with subnetsAn isolated address space you carve into subnets
Door to the InternetInternet gatewayLets public subnets send and receive Internet traffic
NAT for private machinesNAT gatewayLets private instances reach out (updates, APIs) without being reachable from outside
Routing rulesRoute tablesDecide where each destination goes
Explain in detail

It learns which desk is which, so each letter goes only to the right desk. A router is the outgoing post desk that sends letters to other buildings (other networks) and chooses the next stop; the post desk you hand all outside letters to is your default gateway. NAT is that post desk putting the company's one return address on every outgoing letter and noting who sent it, so each reply reaches the right desk. The desks are devices, and the company's return address is its public IP.

Default gateway: the router a machine sends traffic to when the destination is not on its own subnet. Shown by ip route as default via ....
NAT (Network Address Translation): a router rewrites the source address of outgoing packets from a private IP to its public IP and remembers the mapping so replies can be sent back to the right device.

Networks are connected to each other by routers, and the Internet is tens of thousands of independently run networks (autonomous systems) exchanging routes with BGP. You will see these ideas again in the Cloud module.

Firewalls, security groups, proxies and reverse proxies

  • A firewall allows or blocks traffic by IP, port and protocol.
  • AWS security groups allow replies automatically; network ACLs need rules both ways.
  • A forward proxy fronts clients; a reverse proxy such as nginx fronts servers.
  • Never open SSH or database ports to the whole Internet.
Firewall: software or hardware that allows or blocks traffic using rules, usually based on source and destination IP, port and protocol.
ELI5: Explain like I'm 5

A firewall is a guard at the school gates with a list of who may enter through which gate (port).


# Ubuntu: simple host firewall with ufw
sudo ufw allow 22/tcp
sudo ufw allow 443/tcp
sudo ufw enable
sudo ufw status verbose


# /etc/nginx/conf.d/app.conf : reverse proxy to an app on port 3000
server {
    listen 80;
    server_name app.example.com;

    location / {
        proxy_pass http://127.0.0.1:3000;
        proxy_set_header Host $host;
        proxy_set_header X-Real-IP $remote_addr;
        proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for;
    }
}
# test and apply:  sudo nginx -t && sudo systemctl reload nginx
Explain in detail

For example: "Visitors may come in through gate 443 only. Nobody may use gate 22 unless they come from the teachers' room." Anyone not on the list is turned away. The gates are ports, and the list is the firewall's rules.

Security group (AWS)

A virtual firewall attached to an instance. Rules only allow traffic; everything not allowed is denied. It is stateful: if an incoming request is allowed, the reply is allowed automatically.

Network ACL (AWS)

A firewall at the subnet level. It is stateless, so return traffic needs its own rule, and it supports both allow and deny rules.

Always allow SSH before enabling a host firewall on a remote machine, or you will lock yourself out. And do not open SSH (22) or database ports to 0.0.0.0/0 (the whole Internet); restrict them to your own IP or a bastion host.

Proxy vs reverse proxy

Forward proxy

Sits in front of clients and makes requests on their behalf (company web filter, caching). The server sees the proxy, not the client.

Reverse proxy

Sits in front of servers. Clients talk to it; it forwards requests to the right backend. It can terminate TLS, cache, compress, rate-limit and hide internal servers. nginx is the most common one.

Seeing 502 Bad Gateway from nginx usually means the app behind it is down or listening on a different port. Check with ss -tulpn and the app's logs.

Load balancers and CDNs

  • A load balancer spreads requests across servers and skips unhealthy ones.
  • Layer 4 balances by IP and port; layer 7 understands HTTP.
  • A CDN caches content at edge locations close to users.
Load balancer: a single entry point that spreads incoming requests across several identical servers, stops sending traffic to unhealthy ones (health checks), and makes it possible to add or remove servers without downtime.
ELI5: Explain like I'm 5

A load balancer is the helper at a supermarket who sends each shopper to a checkout with a short queue.

AlgorithmHow it picks a serverGood for
Round robinTakes servers in turnEqual servers, similar requests
Weighted round robinBigger servers get more turnsMixed server sizes
Least connectionsServer with fewest active connectionsLong or uneven requests
IP hashSame client IP always maps to the same serverSimple stickiness

# nginx as a simple load balancer
upstream backend {
    least_conn;
    server 10.0.1.11:3000;
    server 10.0.1.12:3000;
    server 10.0.1.13:3000 backup;
}
server {
    listen 80;
    location / { proxy_pass http://backend; }
}
Explain in detail

If a checkout closes, the helper notices (a health check) and stops sending people there. The checkouts are the servers and the shoppers are the requests.

Requests are spread round-robin, then a health check removes a dead server.

Layer 4 load balancer

Decides using IP address and port only; forwards TCP or UDP connections. Very fast and protocol-agnostic. Example: AWS Network Load Balancer.

Layer 7 load balancer

Understands HTTP. Can route by host name or URL path (/api to one group, / to another), by headers or cookies, and terminate TLS. Example: AWS Application Load Balancer, nginx, HAProxy.

If a user's login lives in one server's memory, round robin will log them out on the next request. Keep servers stateless: store sessions in a shared store (for example Redis) or a signed token, rather than relying on sticky sessions.

CDN (Content Delivery Network)

A CDN is a worldwide group of cache servers (edge locations). The first visitor in a region fetches a file from your origin server; the edge keeps a copy and serves it to the next visitors nearby, which lowers latency and origin load. Typical providers: CloudFront, Cloudflare, Akamai, Fastly. Your Cache-Control headers tell the CDN how long to keep a file.

Check yourself

Two quick questions on the last few slides. Not graded; wrong answers explain themselves.

1. A user gets HTTP status 503 from your site. Which class of problem is this?

5xx codes are server errors; 503 means service unavailable.

2. One of three web servers behind a load balancer crashes. What should the load balancer do?

Health checks remove unhealthy servers from rotation.

The troubleshooting toolbox

  • Each tool tests one layer; use them from the bottom up.
  • ip, ping, dig, nc and curl check address, reachability, DNS, port and HTTP.
  • A failed ping does not prove the server is down.
ToolQuestion it answersExample
ip addr, ip routeDo I have an address and a gateway?ip route
pingIs the host reachable at the IP level? (ICMP)ping -c 4 8.8.8.8
traceroute / mtrWhere along the path do packets stop?traceroute example.com
dig / nslookupDoes the name resolve? To what?dig +short example.com
nc -zvIs this TCP port open?nc -zv example.com 443
curl -vWhat does the HTTP(S) conversation look like?curl -v https://example.com
ss -tulpn (replaces older netstat)What is listening on this server?sudo ss -tulpn
tcpdumpWhat packets really arrive?sudo tcpdump -i any port 80 -n

curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}\n" https://example.com   # print only the status code
curl -I https://example.com                                     # headers only
curl --resolve example.com:443:203.0.113.10 https://example.com # test a specific server IP, skipping DNS
sudo tcpdump -i any -n host 203.0.113.10 and port 443           # packets to/from one host and port

Reading common errors

MessageUsually means
Could not resolve hostDNS problem (typo, missing record, resolver down)
Connection refusedHost reachable, nothing listening on that port (service stopped or wrong port)
Connection timed outPackets dropped: firewall, security group, wrong IP, or host down
SSL certificate problemExpired, wrong name, or untrusted certificate
502 / 503 / 504Proxy or load balancer is up but the backend is not answering properly
Explain in detail

Each tool tests one layer. Use them in order from the bottom up.

Some networks and cloud security groups block ICMP, so a failed ping does not prove the server is down. Try nc -zv host port or curl as well. tcpdump needs root and can capture sensitive data; use it carefully.

Why do we troubleshoot a network problem from the bottom of the stack upward?

Compare with ours

Each layer depends on the one below it, so a low-level failure such as no route or no DNS makes every higher test fail too, and going bottom-up finds the first layer that is really broken.

Hands-on exercise: "the website is down" walkthrough

  • Work from the bottom of the stack to the top.
  • Check DNS, then reachability, then the port, then HTTP and TLS.
  • Then check the server, firewall and any recent change.
  • A recent change is the likeliest cause: roll back first, investigate after.

Task 1: worked example


ip addr                       # 1. my interfaces and addresses
ip route                      # 2. my default gateway
ping -c 3 8.8.8.8             # 3. can I reach the Internet by IP?

Expected: an address, a default via line, ping replies.

Task 2: finish it


dig +short example.com        # 4. does DNS work? (prints one or more IPs)
nc -zv example.com 443        # 5. is port 443 open?
# 6. ask the web server what it answers (headers only)
Show hint

One curl flag fetches headers only.

Show answer

curl -I https://example.com   # starts with HTTP/2 200 or HTTP/1.1 200 OK

Task 3: on your own

Goal: find which layer fails for app.example.com. Check: you can name it and show the output.

Show hint

Same tests, bottom to top. Stop at the first failure.

Show answer

dig +short app.example.com
nc -zv app.example.com 443
curl -v https://app.example.com
Explain in detail

Scenario: users report that app.example.com does not load. Work from the bottom of the stack to the top. Replace names and IPs with your own. First, practise the tools on a real site:

Expected: step 3 shows replies with times, step 4 prints at least one IP address, step 5 reports a successful connection, step 6 starts with HTTP/2 200 or HTTP/1.1 200 OK (the exact line depends on the server).

Debugging flow

  1. Is it only me? Try from another network or phone, or an online "is it down" checker. If only you fail, check your own connection and DNS.
  2. DNS. dig +short app.example.com. No answer: the record is missing or wrong. A wrong IP: fix the A record (and wait for the TTL). Compare with dig @8.8.8.8 ....
  3. Reachability. ping and traceroute the IP. Silence may be blocked ICMP, so continue anyway.
  4. Port. nc -zv IP 443. "Refused": nothing listens (go to server checks). "Timed out": firewall or security group blocks it.
  5. HTTP/TLS. curl -v https://app.example.com. Read the certificate lines and the status code. 5xx points to the proxy, load balancer or app.
  6. On the server (SSH in): 
    
systemctl status nginx myapp          # are services running?
sudo ss -tulpn | grep -E ':80|:443|:3000'   # are they listening on the expected ports?
journalctl -u myapp --since "30 min ago"    # application errors
sudo tail -n 50 /var/log/nginx/error.log    # proxy errors
df -h; free -h                        # disk or memory exhausted?
  7. Firewall. Check the security group, network ACL and ufw status for the port.
  8. Recent change? A deploy, certificate renewal, DNS edit or config change in the last hours is the most likely cause. Roll back first, investigate after.
Write down what you tested and the result at each step. In an incident, that log saves your team from repeating checks.

Interview questions

Q1: What happens when you type https://example.com in a browser and press Enter?

The browser checks its caches, resolves the name through DNS to an IP, opens a TCP connection to port 443 (three-way handshake), performs the TLS handshake and verifies the certificate, sends an HTTP request, receives the response (maybe via a CDN, load balancer and reverse proxy), and renders the page. With HTTP/3 the transport is QUIC over UDP instead of TCP.

Q2: Difference between TCP and UDP?

TCP is connection-oriented, reliable and ordered, using a handshake and retransmissions. UDP is connectionless and best-effort with less overhead, suited to DNS, streaming and games.

Q3: What is a subnet and how many hosts are in a /26?

A subnet is a range of addresses sharing the same network prefix. A /26 has 2^6 = 64 addresses, so 62 usable hosts in the classic rule.

Q4: Public vs private IP address?

Public addresses are unique and routable on the Internet. Private ranges (10/8, 172.16/12, 192.168/16) are reused in internal networks and reach the Internet through NAT.

Q5: Explain DNS resolution and TTL.

A resolver asks root servers, then the TLD servers, then the authoritative server, and caches the result for the TTL (seconds). Changes to a record are only seen after caches expire.

Q6: What is the difference between a forward proxy and a reverse proxy?

A forward proxy represents clients to servers. A reverse proxy represents servers to clients, handling TLS, caching, routing and load distribution. nginx is a typical reverse proxy.

Q7: L4 vs L7 load balancer?

L4 balances connections using IP and port. L7 understands HTTP and can route by path, host or header and terminate TLS.

Q8: Security group vs network ACL?

Security groups are stateful, attached to instances, allow rules only. Network ACLs are stateless, attached to subnets, and support allow and deny rules.

Q9: "Connection refused" vs "connection timed out"?

Refused: the host answered but nothing listens on the port. Timed out: no answer, typically a firewall dropping packets or a wrong or unreachable IP.

Q10: What does HTTP 502 mean?

A gateway or proxy received an invalid or no response from the upstream server. Check that the backend is running and listening on the port the proxy expects.

Quiz

1. How many usable host addresses are in 192.168.1.0/24 using the classic rule?

A /24 has 256 addresses; the network and broadcast addresses are not usable, leaving 254.

2. Which message order opens a TCP connection?

The three-way handshake is SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK.

3. Which DNS record type maps a name to an IPv6 address?

A is IPv4, AAAA is IPv6, CNAME is an alias, MX is for mail.

4. At which OSI layer do IP addresses and routers operate?

IP and routing belong to the Network layer. Switches and MAC addresses are layer 2.

5. A request to your site returns "Connection refused". What is the most likely cause?

Refused means the machine answered with a reset because no service accepts connections on that port. A firewall drop would normally cause a timeout.

6. Which transport protocol does HTTP/3 run on?

HTTP/3 is defined in RFC 9114 and runs on QUIC (RFC 9000), which uses UDP.
