06

Git & GitHub

Git is the tool that remembers every version of your code, lets many people work on the same project at the same time without overwriting each other, and lets you travel back in time when something breaks. GitHub and GitLab are websites that host Git projects and add teamwork features on top (pull requests, code review, automation). Every DevOps pipeline starts with a Git commit, so this module is the foundation for everything that follows.

What you will learn

Why version control exists · the three local areas of Git · what a commit really is · init/add/commit/log/diff/restore · branches, merges and conflicts · rebase vs merge · remotes (fetch/pull/push) · pull requests and branch protection · branching strategies · tags and semantic versioning · undoing mistakes safely · stash · commit conventions · SSH keys.

Guess first

You are not expected to know these yet. Guessing before you read helps you remember the answer when you meet it.

1. When you create a new Git branch, what does Git actually create?

A branch is a movable pointer to a commit.

2. You edited a file and want it in your next commit. Which step comes between editing and committing?

Edit in the working directory, stage with git add, then commit.

3. You committed a mistake and already pushed it to a shared main branch. What is the safest way to undo it?

git revert is the safe undo for shared commits.

Why does version control exist?

  • Version control records changes so you can recall and compare versions.
  • Without it, copies pile up and edits overwrite each other.
  • Git keeps full history, cheap branches and authorship.
ELI5: Explain like I'm 5

Think of a video game with save points. Every time you reach a good spot you press "save".

Version Control System (VCS): software that records changes to files over time so that you can recall specific versions later, see who changed what and why, and combine the work of several people.

Centralized vs distributed version control

Centralized (CVCS), e.g. Subversion, CVSDistributed (DVCS), e.g. Git, Mercurial
Where is the history?On one central server. You only have the files you checked out.Every developer has a full copy of the whole history on their own machine.
Working offlineMostly impossible: commit needs the server.Commit, branch, view history, all offline. Sync later.
SpeedMany operations talk over the network.Most operations are local and fast.
If the server diesDisaster unless backed up.Any clone can restore the project.
BranchingPossible but historically heavy.Very cheap, the normal way of working.

Free resources (GeeksforGeeks)

  • GfG, Version Control Systems
Explain in detail

If you later get stuck you do not start from zero, you load the last save. Git is a save-game system for your project, but better: every save has a name, a date and an author, you can see exactly what changed between two saves, and many friends can each play their own copy and then merge their progress together.

Imagine you are writing an essay. You save essay.doc. You make big changes, so you save essay_v2.doc. Your teacher suggests edits: essay_v2_final.doc. Then essay_v2_final_really_final.doc. Then a friend edits their own copy and emails it back. Which file is the latest? Which edits came from whom? What did you change last Tuesday? Nobody knows.

The problems a VCS solves

Without a VCS

  • Files named final_v2_really_final.doc
  • Two people edit the same file and one silently overwrites the other
  • "It worked yesterday!" and nobody can see what changed
  • No safe way to try a risky idea
  • No record of who did what, or why

With Git

  • One folder, complete history of every change
  • Each person works on a branch; Git merges the work
  • Compare any two versions line by line
  • Branches are cheap, so experiments are safe
  • Every commit records author, time and a message
Git is distributed, but teams still agree on one shared remote (usually on GitHub or GitLab) that acts as the "official" copy. Distributed describes the technology; a shared hub is a team convention.

History & Evolution

Version control is older than most programmers. Each generation fixed a pain point of the previous one.

YearMilestoneWhy it mattered
1972SCCS (Source Code Control System) at Bell LabsOne of the first tools to store the history of a file. Only one file at a time, and only one person could edit a file at once (locking).
1982RCS (Revision Control System)Improved per-file history storage. Still per-file and lock-based.
1986 / 1990CVS (Concurrent Versions System): started as scripts around RCS in 1986, rewritten in C in 1990Let many people edit at the same time and merge changes (no more strict locking) and introduced the client-server model for whole projects.
2000Subversion (SVN) started as "a better CVS"Atomic commits (all changes in one commit succeed or fail together), versioned renames and directories. Still centralized.
2002 – 2005BitKeeper used by the Linux kernelA proprietary distributed VCS. It showed kernel developers how good distributed work could be. In April 2005 the free-use arrangement ended.
April 2005Git created by Linus TorvaldsWritten in a matter of weeks as a replacement for BitKeeper for the Linux kernel. Goals: speed, simple design, strong integrity checks, fully distributed, cheap branching.
2008GitHub launchesPut Git repositories on a friendly website with forks and pull requests, which made "social coding" and open source easy.
2011GitLab beginsAn open-source alternative that grew into a full DevOps platform (repositories, built-in CI/CD, registry, issue tracking). Can be self-hosted.
2018Microsoft acquires GitHub (announced June, completed October)Cemented GitHub as the home of open-source and enterprise code.
2018 – 2019GitHub Actions: beta in 2018, generally available November 2019CI/CD built directly into the code host. See Module 07.
2019 (Git 2.23)git switch and git restore addedSplit the overloaded git checkout into two clearer commands: one to move between branches, one to restore files.
2020 (Git 2.28)init.defaultBranch config optionLets you choose the name of the first branch when running git init instead of the traditional master.
Oct 2020GitHub changes the default branch for new repositories to mainIndustry-wide shift away from master as the default name; GitLab and others followed.
2020 (Git 2.29)SHA-256 object format (experimental)Git identifies content by a hash. SHA-1 is no longer considered strong (a practical SHA-1 collision was published in 2017), so Git added an opt-in SHA-256 mode: git init --object-format=sha256.
2023 (Git 2.42)SHA-256 repositories no longer labelled experimentalSHA-256 repositories are usable, but they still cannot exchange history with SHA-1 repositories, and most hosting services do not yet accept them. Nearly every repository you meet is still SHA-1.
2024 (Git 2.45)Reftable backend for references (opt-in)Branches and tags have traditionally been stored as many small files. Reftable stores them in a compact binary format that scales to repositories with millions of refs: git init --ref-format=reftable.
2021 onwardGitHub Copilot and AI-assisted code reviewAI suggests code, writes commit and pull-request descriptions and reviews diffs. Humans still own the review and the merge.
Forward-lookingA planned Git 3.0 with deliberate breaking changesPlanned; check the official release notes for the current state. The Git project's list of planned breaking changes includes making main the default initial branch, SHA-256 the default object format and reftable the default ref storage, and requiring Rust to build Git (optional Rust code first appeared in Git 2.49 in 2025). As of Git 2.56 (September 2026) there is no release date for 3.0.
Notice the pattern: locking per file (SCCS/RCS) → concurrent editing (CVS) → atomic, project-wide commits (SVN) → distributed (Git). Git won because it was fast, free and made branching almost free.

Installing & configuring Git

  • Install Git with a package manager or Git for Windows, then check the version.
  • Set your name and email once per machine with git config --global.
  • Settings come from system, global and local levels.

Install


# macOS (Homebrew)            brew install git
# Debian / Ubuntu             sudo apt update && sudo apt install -y git
# Fedora / RHEL family        sudo dnf install -y git
# Windows                     download "Git for Windows" from git-scm.com (includes Git Bash)

git --version
$ git --version git version 2.43.0

First-time setup: tell Git who you are


git config --global user.name  "Abhi Rai"
git config --global user.email "abhi@example.com"
git config --global init.defaultBranch main     # new repos start on "main" (Git 2.28+)
git config --global core.editor "nano"          # editor used for commit messages
git config --global pull.rebase false           # explicit choice for what "git pull" does (merge)

git config --list --show-origin                 # see every setting and the file it came from
Config levels: Git reads settings from three files, each overriding the previous: --system (all users on the machine), --global (your user, stored in ~/.gitconfig), and --local (this repository only, stored in .git/config).
Explain in detail

Your version number will differ. Anything reasonably recent works for this course.

Every commit stores an author name and email. Git does not verify them; they are just labels. Set them once per machine with --global:

Use the same email as your GitHub account so GitHub links your commits to your profile. Many people use the private "noreply" address GitHub offers in the email settings.

The three local areas + the remote

ELI5: Explain like I'm 5

You are packing a gift box. Your desk is where you work and make a mess (working directory).

  • You edit files in the working directory.
  • git add stages chosen changes; git commit records them locally.
  • git push uploads your commits; git pull brings down other people's commits.
AreaWhat lives thereMoved by
Working directoryThe real files you see and edityour editor
Staging area (index)A draft of the next commitgit add
Local repositoryAll commits (the history) in .gitgit commit
Remote repositoryA shared copy on a server (GitHub, GitLab)git push / fetch / pull
Explain in detail

The tray is where you put the items you have chosen for the box (staging area). When you close the box, tape it and write a label on it, that is a commit (local repository). Posting the box to your friend's house is a push (remote).

You edit files in the working directory. git add copies the chosen changes into the staging area (also called the index). git commit takes everything staged and permanently records it as a snapshot in the local repository (the hidden .git folder). git push uploads your new commits to the remote (for example GitHub). git pull brings other people's commits down.

Why a staging area at all? It lets you craft clean commits. You may have changed 10 files, but only 3 belong to the same fix. Stage those 3, commit them with a clear message, then stage the rest separately.

What a commit really is

  • A commit is a snapshot of the whole project, plus author and message.
  • Its ID is a hash: a fingerprint calculated from its content.
  • A branch is just a movable label pointing at one commit.
ELI5: Explain like I'm 5

A commit is a photograph of your whole project at one moment.

Commit: an immutable snapshot of the project plus metadata: author, committer, timestamp, message, and the ID(s) of its parent commit(s). It is identified by a SHA hash, a 40-character hexadecimal fingerprint (in the default SHA-1 format) calculated from its content.
ObjectWhat it isAnalogy
blobThe contents of one file (no name, only content)A page of a book
treeA directory: a list of names pointing to blobs and other treesA table of contents / folder listing
commitPoints to one top-level tree, plus parent commit(s), author and messageThe photo with its sticky note
tag (annotated)A named pointer to a commit with its own tagger, date and message; it can be cryptographically signedA bookmark with a note

git cat-file -p HEAD           # show the latest commit object
git cat-file -p HEAD^{tree}    # show the tree (folder listing) it points to
$ git cat-file -p HEAD tree 9f3c1ab5d0e7c1a2b4f6e8d0a1c3e5f7a9b1c3d5 parent 3a1f9c27e0d4b6a8c2e4f6a8b0d2c4e6f8a0b2c4 author Abhi Rai <abhi@example.com> 1735689600 +0000 committer Abhi Rai <abhi@example.com> 1735689600 +0000 Add login page
Explain in detail

Each photo has a sticky note saying who took it, when and why, and it points to the photo taken just before it (the parent commit). The photo's unique fingerprint is the commit's SHA hash.

Git does not store "the changes"; it stores the photo, and (to save space) re-uses parts of earlier photos that did not change. When you ask "what changed?", Git compares two photos.

The four kinds of objects inside .git

Because the ID is a hash of the content, identical content gets the same ID and any change, even one character, produces a completely different ID. This makes history tamper-evident: changing an old commit would change every ID after it.

The hashes above are illustrative. Yours will be different.

Branches, HEAD and tags are just sticky labels

  • A branch is a tiny file containing the ID of one commit. Making a commit moves the label forward. That is why branches are so cheap.
  • HEAD is "where you are now": usually it points to a branch, which points to a commit.
  • Because every commit knows its parent, history is a chain (really a graph) you can walk backwards.
You almost never type a full hash. The first 7 characters are usually enough: git show 9f3c1ab.

Core commands I: start, stage, commit, look

  • git init creates the hidden .git folder, which is the repository.
  • git status shows what Git sees; run it constantly.
  • git add stages changes; git commit records the snapshot.
  • git log shows history; --oneline keeps it short.

1. git init: create a repository


mkdir myapp && cd myapp
git init
$ git init Initialized empty Git repository in /home/abhi/myapp/.git/

2. git status: what is going on?


echo "# My App" > README.md
git status
$ git status On branch main No commits yet Untracked files: (use "git add <file>..." to include in what will be committed) README.md nothing added to commit but untracked files present (use "git add" to track)

3. git add: stage changes


git add README.md        # stage one file
git add src/ docs/       # stage whole folders
git add -p               # interactively choose pieces ("hunks") of changes
git add .                # stage everything in the current folder (use with care)

4. git commit: record the snapshot


git commit -m "Add README"
$ git commit -m "Add README" [main (root-commit) 3a1f9c2] Add README 1 file changed, 1 insertion(+) create mode 100644 README.md

5. git log: see history


git log                       # full details
git log --oneline             # one line per commit
git log --oneline --graph --all --decorate   # ASCII picture of all branches
git log -p -2                 # last 2 commits with their diffs
git log --author="Abhi" --since="2 weeks ago"
$ git log --oneline b7e42d1 (HEAD -> main) Add login page 3a1f9c2 Add README
Explain in detail

This creates the hidden .git folder, which is the repository. Delete it and the project loses all history.

Untracked means Git sees the file but is not recording it yet. Run git status constantly; it is your compass.

Do not use git add . blindly. It can stage secrets (.env files), huge binaries or temporary files. Check git status first, and use .gitignore (next slide).

Check yourself

Two quick questions on the last few slides. Not graded; wrong answers explain themselves.

1. What does git add do?

Staging selects what the next commit will contain.

2. What is a commit's ID?

A commit ID is a fingerprint of its content.

Core commands II: diff, restore, rm, mv, .gitignore

  • git diff shows unstaged changes; --staged shows what you will commit.
  • git restore permanently discards uncommitted edits, or unstages files.
  • git rm and git mv delete and rename tracked files.
  • .gitignore tells Git to ignore untracked files, such as secrets and build output.

git diff: what exactly changed?


git diff                 # working directory vs staging area (unstaged changes)
git diff --staged        # staging area vs last commit (what you are about to commit)
git diff main..feature   # differences between two branches
$ git diff diff --git a/app.py b/app.py index 8f2a1c3..d41e7b9 100644 --- a/app.py +++ b/app.py @@ -1,2 +1,2 @@ def greet(): - print("Hello") + print("Hello, DevOps!")

git restore: discard or unstage (Git 2.23+)


git restore app.py             # throw away unstaged edits in app.py (cannot be undone!)
git restore --staged app.py    # unstage app.py, but keep the edits in the file
git restore --source=HEAD~2 app.py   # bring back app.py as it was 2 commits ago

git rm and git mv: delete and rename tracked files


git rm old.txt             # delete the file and stage the deletion
git rm --cached secret.env # stop tracking the file but keep it on disk
git mv a.txt b.txt         # rename (Git detects renames from content anyway)

.gitignore: files Git should pretend not to see


# dependencies and build output
node_modules/
dist/
__pycache__/
*.pyc

# secrets and local config: do not commit these
.env
*.pem

# OS / editor junk
.DS_Store
.vscode/

# but keep this one file even though *.log is ignored
*.log
!important.log
Explain in detail

Lines starting with - were removed, lines starting with + were added. @@ lines say where in the file the change is.

git restore <file> overwrites your uncommitted edits permanently. Git never saw those edits as a commit, so it cannot bring them back.

Create a text file named .gitignore in the repository root. Commit it so the whole team shares it.

.gitignore only affects untracked files. If you already committed a secret, ignoring it later does not remove it from history. You must treat that secret as leaked and rotate it (change it) immediately.

Branching: parallel timelines

ELI5: Explain like I'm 5

A branch is a name tag stuck on the latest photo of your project; each new photo moves the tag forward.

Branch: a movable pointer to a commit. Creating one costs almost nothing because Git just writes a 41-byte file. HEAD is the pointer to the branch you are currently on.
  • A branch is a movable pointer to a commit.
  • Work on a feature branch while main stays safe.
  • When the feature is ready, merge the branch back into main.

git branch                       # list local branches (* marks current)
git branch feature-login         # create a branch (stay where you are)
git switch feature-login         # move to it (Git 2.23+)
git switch -c feature-login      # create and move in one step
git checkout -b feature-login    # the older equivalent you will see in tutorials
git branch -d feature-login      # delete a merged branch (-D forces deletion)
$ git switch -c feature-login Switched to a new branch 'feature-login' $ git branch * feature-login main
Explain in detail

To try a new idea, you stick a second tag on the same photo and take new photos under it, while the main tag stays where it was. If the idea works, you join the two lines of photos (merge); if not, you remove the tag. Nothing is copied, so tags cost almost nothing. HEAD shows which tag you are using now.

All work starts on main. You create a feature branch, add commits there while main stays safe, and finally merge the feature back, which creates a merge commit with two parents. HEAD shows which branch you are standing on.

Why is a branch cheap?

Compare with ours

A branch is only a small pointer to a commit, so Git writes one tiny file instead of copying the project.

Merging: fast-forward vs 3-way

  • Merge from the receiving branch: switch to it, then run git merge.
  • Fast-forward just slides the label when main has no new commits.
  • A three-way merge creates a merge commit with two parents.
  • --no-ff forces a merge commit; --abort cancels a bad merge.

git switch main
git merge feature-login

Fast-forward merge


before:  A---B   (main)
              \
               C---D (feature)
after:   A---B---C---D (main, feature)

Three-way merge


before:  A---B---E   (main)
              \
               C---D (feature)
after:   A---B---E---M (main)
              \     /
               C---D (feature)
$ git merge feature-login Merge made by the 'ort' strategy. login.py | 12 ++++++++++++ 1 file changed, 12 insertions(+) create mode 100644 login.py

Free resources (GeeksforGeeks)

  • GfG, Git Merge
Explain in detail

To bring a branch's work into another, you stand on the receiving branch and run git merge <other-branch>.

If main has had no new commits since you branched, Git simply slides the main label forward to the tip of the feature. No new commit is created; history stays a straight line.

If main also moved on, the two histories have diverged. Git finds their common ancestor, compares both sides to it (three points: ancestor, yours, theirs) and creates a merge commit with two parents.

Useful options: git merge --no-ff feature forces a merge commit even when a fast-forward is possible (keeps a visible "this was a feature" bubble in history). git merge --abort cancels a merge that went wrong.

After merging, delete the finished branch (git branch -d feature-login). The commits are safe in history; you only remove the label.

Merge conflicts: don't panic

  • A conflict happens when two branches change the same lines.
  • Git inserts markers; you edit to the final text and delete them.
  • Then git add the file and git commit, or git merge --abort.
ELI5: Explain like I'm 5

You and your friend both color the same square of a drawing: you use red, your friend uses blue.

Merge conflict: happens when two branches changed the same lines of the same file (or one deleted a file the other edited) and Git cannot decide automatically.

What it looks like


git merge feature-login
$ git merge feature-login Auto-merging app.py CONFLICT (content): Merge conflict in app.py Automatic merge failed; fix conflicts and then commit the result. $ git status On branch main You have unmerged paths. (fix conflicts and run "git commit") (use "git merge --abort" to abort the merge) Unmerged paths: (use "git add <file>..." to mark resolution) both modified: app.py no changes added to commit (use "git add" and/or "git commit -a")

def greet():
<<<<<<< HEAD
    print("Hello from main")
=======
    print("Hello from the feature branch")
>>>>>>> feature-login
MarkerMeaning
<<<<<<< HEADStart. Everything below is your current branch's version.
=======Divider between the two versions.
>>>>>>> feature-loginEnd. Everything above (since the divider) is the incoming branch's version.

# after editing app.py by hand:
git add app.py
git commit                 # completes the merge
# or bail out and return to how things were before:
git merge --abort
Explain in detail

When you put the drawings together, the computer cannot guess which colour you want. So it puts both side by side and asks you to choose. That is a merge conflict: Git is being polite, not broken.

Open app.py. Git inserted conflict markers:

Resolve it, step by step

  1. Run git status to list files marked "both modified".
  2. Open each file and find the markers (search for <<<<<<<).
  3. Decide: keep yours, keep theirs, or combine both. Edit the text to the final version you want.
  4. Delete all three marker lines. If a marker stays in the file, you committed a broken file.
  5. Test that the code still works.
  6. git add app.py (this tells Git "resolved").
  7. git commit (the default merge message is fine) to finish the merge.
Editors like VS Code show buttons "Accept Current / Accept Incoming / Accept Both". Handy, but always read the result. To prevent conflicts: keep branches short-lived, pull often, and talk to teammates before editing the same file.

Rebase vs merge

  • Rebase replays your commits on top of another branch as new commits.
  • It gives a linear history but rewrites commit IDs.
  • Never rebase commits that other people already have.
ELI5: Explain like I'm 5

Two kids wrote chapters of a story at the same time.

Rebase: takes the commits of your branch, and replays them one by one on top of another commit (usually the latest main). The replayed commits are new commits with new IDs.

before:      A---B---E   (main)
                  \
                   C---D (feature)

git switch feature && git rebase main

after:       A---B---E   (main)
                      \
                       C'---D' (feature)     C' and D' are new commits
MergeRebase
HistoryPreserves the true history, with merge commitsLinear and tidy
SafetyNon-destructiveRewrites commits (new hashes)
ConflictsResolve onceMay resolve per replayed commit
Best forIntegrating shared/public branchesCleaning up your own local branch before a pull request

git rebase main                 # replay current branch onto main
git rebase --continue           # after fixing a conflict
git rebase --abort              # give up, go back to before
git rebase -i HEAD~3            # interactive: squash, reorder, reword the last 3 commits
git push --force-with-lease     # needed after rebasing an already-pushed private branch (safer than --force)
Explain in detail

Merge staples the two notebooks together and adds a note saying "joined here" (the merge commit). Rebase is one kid rewriting their chapter as if they had started after the other finished, so the book reads as one straight line. The book is tidy, but the rewritten pages are new copies (new commit IDs).

The golden rule of rebase: never rebase commits that other people already have (commits you have pushed to a shared branch). Rewriting shared history makes teammates' copies diverge and causes chaos. Rebase your private work; merge shared work.

Many teams also offer "Squash and merge" or "Rebase and merge" buttons on the pull request page.

Why must you never rebase commits that other people already have?

Compare with ours

Rebase replays commits as new ones with new IDs, so teammates who still have the old commits no longer match your history.

Check yourself

Two quick questions on the last few slides. Not graded; wrong answers explain themselves.

1. When does a merge become a simple fast-forward?

Fast-forward only moves the label.

2. A merge stops with a conflict. After you edit app.py to the final text and delete the markers, what next?

Resolve, add, commit, or abort with git merge --abort.

Remotes: fetch vs pull vs push + SSH keys

  • A remote is a named link to another copy, usually origin.
  • fetch downloads; pull is fetch plus merge; push uploads.
  • SSH keys let you log in to GitHub without a password.
Remote: a named link to another copy of the repository (usually on GitHub or GitLab). The conventional name for the main one is origin.

git clone https://github.com/OWNER/REPO.git     # copy a remote repo to your machine (also sets origin)
git remote -v                                    # list remotes
git remote add origin git@github.com:OWNER/REPO.git   # link a local repo to a remote
git push -u origin main      # upload main; -u remembers it so later "git push" is enough
$ git clone https://github.com/OWNER/REPO.git Cloning into 'REPO'... remote: Enumerating objects: 120, done. remote: Counting objects: 100% (120/120), done. Receiving objects: 100% (120/120), 48.20 KiB | 2.41 MiB/s, done. Resolving deltas: 100% (45/45), done.

fetch vs pull vs push

CommandWhat it doesChanges your files?
git fetchDownloads new commits from the remote into origin/* tracking branches. Looks, but does not touch your work.No (safe)
git pullgit fetch + merge (or rebase, if configured) into your current branch.Yes
git pushUploads your local commits to the remote branch.Changes the remote

SSH keys for GitHub (log in without typing a password)

ELI5: Explain like I'm 5

An SSH key is a matching lock and key.


ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "abhi@example.com"     # accept the default path; set a passphrase
eval "$(ssh-agent -s)"                          # start the agent that holds your key
ssh-add ~/.ssh/id_ed25519
cat ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub                       # print the public key so you can copy it
# GitHub -> Settings -> SSH and GPG keys -> New SSH key -> paste it
ssh -T git@github.com                           # test the connection
$ ssh -T git@github.com Hi your-username! You've successfully authenticated, but GitHub does not provide shell access.
Explain in detail

You give GitHub the lock (public key) and keep the key (private key) secret on your computer. When you connect, GitHub checks that your key fits its lock, with no password sent.

If unsure, run git fetch then git log --oneline main..origin/main to preview what is coming before you merge it.
If git push says "rejected: non-fast-forward", someone pushed before you. Pull (or fetch and merge/rebase) first, resolve any conflicts, then push again. Avoid git push --force on shared branches.
Never share, email or commit the file id_ed25519 (no .pub). That is the private key. Only the .pub file is safe to give out.

GitHub & GitLab: collaboration workflow

  • A pull request proposes merging one branch into another, with review and checks.
  • Typical flow: branch, commit, push, open a PR, pass CI, get review, merge.
  • Branch protection stops direct pushes to main and requires approvals and checks.
  • GitHub and GitLab both host repositories and offer built-in CI/CD.
Pull Request (PR) (called a Merge Request, MR, on GitLab): a proposal to merge one branch into another, with a page for discussion, automated checks and review before anything is merged.

Free resources (GeeksforGeeks)

  • GfG, GitHub Actions
Explain in detail

The standard flow

  1. Fork (open source) or just create a branch (in your own team's repo). A fork is your personal server-side copy of someone else's repository.
  2. git switch -c fix/typo-in-readme, make changes, commit.
  3. git push -u origin fix/typo-in-readme.
  4. Open a pull request. Write what changed and why; link the issue.
  5. Automated checks run (the CI pipeline from Module 07): tests, linting, builds.
  6. Code review: teammates read the diff, leave comments, request changes or approve.
  7. Push more commits to the same branch to address feedback; the PR updates automatically.
  8. Merge (merge commit, squash, or rebase) once approved and green. Delete the branch.

Good code review habits

  • Keep PRs small (a few hundred lines at most)
  • Review the idea first, style second
  • Be kind: comment on the code, not the person
  • Reviewers ask questions; authors explain "why"

Protected branches

A branch protection rule stops people pushing straight to main. Typical rules: require a pull request, require N approvals, require status checks (CI) to pass, require up-to-date branches, block force-pushes and deletion.

GitHub

Largest developer community. Pull Requests, Issues, Projects, GitHub Actions (CI/CD), Packages/Container registry, Codespaces, Copilot.

GitLab

Merge Requests, Issues, built-in GitLab CI/CD, container registry, environments, and a self-hosted option many enterprises use.

Other files teams add: README.md (front page), CONTRIBUTING.md (how to help), CODEOWNERS (who must review which folders) and a pull-request template.

Branching strategies

  • GitHub Flow: short branches off a single deployable main.
  • GitFlow: long-lived main and develop, plus feature, release and hotfix branches.
  • Trunk-based: merge into main at least daily, using feature flags.
  • Whatever you choose, keep branches short-lived to avoid painful merges.
GitHub FlowGitFlowTrunk-based
Long-lived branches12+1
Branch lifetimedaysweekshours
Release cadencecontinuousscheduledcontinuous
Needs strong automated tests?YesHelpfulEssential
Explain in detail

A branching strategy is the team's agreement on which branches exist and how code flows between them. Pick the simplest one that fits how often you release.

GitHub Flow

One long-lived branch: main, always deployable.

  1. Branch from main
  2. Commit, push, open PR
  3. Review + CI
  4. Merge to main
  5. Deploy

Best for: web apps and teams that deploy often. Simple.

GitFlow

Several long-lived branches: main (releases), develop (integration), plus feature/*, release/*, hotfix/*.

Best for: versioned software with scheduled releases and several supported versions. Cost: more ceremony, long-lived branches, bigger merges.

Trunk-based development

Everyone integrates into main (the "trunk") at least daily, using very short-lived branches (hours) and feature flags to hide unfinished work.

Best for: mature CI/CD teams. The DORA research programme (State of DevOps reports) links it to higher delivery performance.

Whatever you choose, keep branches short-lived. The longer a branch lives, the more it drifts from main and the more painful the merge: this is "integration hell", which Module 07 is all about.

Tags, semantic versioning & commit messages

  • A tag names one commit permanently, for example a release such as v1.4.2.
  • SemVer is MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH: breaking, feature, fix.
  • Conventional Commits use the form type(scope): summary.

Tags: permanent bookmarks for releases

Tag: a name attached to one specific commit that never moves (unlike a branch). Used to mark releases such as v1.4.2.

git tag v0.9.0                              # lightweight tag (just a name)
git tag -a v1.0.0 -m "First stable release"  # annotated tag (stores author, date, message)
git tag                                      # list tags
git push origin v1.0.0                       # tags are not pushed by default
git push origin --tags                       # push all tags

Semantic Versioning (SemVer): MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH

PartBump it when…Example
MAJORYou make breaking changes to the public API1.4.2 → 2.0.0
MINORYou add features in a backwards-compatible way1.4.2 → 1.5.0
PATCHYou make backwards-compatible bug fixes1.4.2 → 1.4.3

feat(auth): add password reset by email
fix(api): return 404 instead of 500 for unknown user
docs: explain how to run tests
refactor(db): extract connection pool setup
test: add cases for empty cart
chore(ci): bump node version in workflow

feat(api)!: remove v1 endpoints       <- the "!" marks a breaking change
Explain in detail

Pre-release versions look like 2.0.0-rc.1. A CI/CD pipeline can build and publish automatically whenever a tag such as v1.4.3 is pushed.

Writing good commit messages (Conventional Commits)

A commit message is a note to your future self and teammates. A common convention is Conventional Commits: type(scope): short summary. It also lets tools generate changelogs and choose the next SemVer number.

  • Summary line: about 50 characters, imperative mood ("add", not "added").
  • Blank line, then an optional body explaining why.
  • One logical change per commit. "fix stuff" and "wip" tell nobody anything.

Undoing things safely (and stash)

  • git commit --amend fixes the last commit, if it is not pushed yet.
  • git revert is the safe undo for commits already shared.
  • git reset moves the branch back; --hard also destroys uncommitted work.
  • git reflog lists where you have been, so lost commits can be recovered.
  • git stash puts unfinished work aside so you can switch branches.
ELI5: Explain like I'm 5

Git is a notebook written in pen.

SituationCommandSafe?
Discard edits to a file (unstaged)git restore fileEdits lost permanently
Unstage a filegit restore --staged fileSafe
Fix the last commit's message or add a forgotten filegit commit --amendSafe if not pushed (rewrites that commit)
Undo a commit that is already sharedgit revert <hash>Safe: adds a new commit that cancels the old one
Move the branch back, keep changes stagedgit reset --soft HEAD~1Safe if not pushed (rewrites history)
Move the branch back, keep changes unstagedgit reset --mixed HEAD~1 (the default)Safe for files; rewrites history
Move back and delete the changesgit reset --hard HEAD~1Destructive: uncommitted work is lost

The three flavours of reset

ModeBranch pointerStaging areaWorking files
--softmovesunchangedunchanged
--mixedmovesresetunchanged
--hardmovesresetoverwritten

git revert b7e42d1          # safe undo of a pushed commit
git reset --hard HEAD~1     # destructive: throws away last commit and uncommitted edits
git reflog                  # history of where HEAD has been: your safety net
git reset --hard HEAD@{2}   # jump back to a state listed in the reflog
$ git reflog b7e42d1 (HEAD -> main) HEAD@{0}: commit: Add login page 3a1f9c2 HEAD@{1}: commit (initial): Add README

Stash: put unfinished work in a drawer


git stash push -m "half-done login form"   # save changes and clean the working directory
git stash list                              # see the drawer
git switch main                             # ...fix the urgent bug...
git switch feature-login
git stash pop                               # take the work out of the drawer (and remove it)
git stash apply                             # take it out but keep a copy in the drawer
$ git stash list stash@{0}: On feature-login: half-done login form

By default stash saves tracked files only; add -u to include untracked files.

Explain in detail

You cannot erase, but you can (a) cross something out and write the fix on a new line (revert), (b) tear out recent pages and rewrite them (reset, dangerous if you already shared the notebook), or (c) check the list on the inside cover where Git notes, for a while, every page you have been on, even torn-out ones (reflog).

Never use reset --hard followed by push --force on a shared branch unless you really know the team is aligned. To undo public history, use revert. The reflog only exists on your machine and is eventually cleaned up (by default, entries for commits no longer on any branch expire after 30 days and the rest after 90 days), so recover quickly.

You are halfway through something and need to switch branches to fix an urgent bug, but you are not ready to commit.

Check yourself

Two quick questions on the last few slides. Not graded; wrong answers explain themselves.

1. What does git pull do?

git pull = git fetch + merge.

2. Your release only fixes a bug and keeps the API the same. Using SemVer, 1.4.2 becomes:

MAJOR is breaking, MINOR is a feature, PATCH is a fix.

Hands-on exercise: your first repo, branch, conflict and push

  • Create a repo, commit, then branch and create a conflict on purpose.
  • Resolve the conflict and view the history with --graph.
  • Revert a commit, read the reflog, and push to GitHub.

Task 1: worked example


# 1. Create a project
mkdir git-lab && cd git-lab
git init
echo "print('hello')" > app.py
git add app.py
git commit -m "feat: add hello app"

# 2. Make a branch and change the same line as main will
git switch -c feature-greeting
echo "print('hello from feature')" > app.py
git commit -am "feat: greet from feature branch"

# 3. Change the same line on main (creates a conflict later)
git switch main
echo "print('hello from main')" > app.py
git commit -am "feat: greet from main"

# 4. Merge and hit the conflict
git merge feature-greeting
$ git merge feature-greeting Auto-merging app.py CONFLICT (content): Merge conflict in app.py Automatic merge failed; fix conflicts and then commit the result.

# 5. Resolve: open app.py, keep one line (or combine), delete the conflict marker lines
git add app.py
git commit -m "merge: resolve greeting conflict"

Task 2: finish it


# 6. Look at the history as a picture
git log --oneline --graph --all

# 7. Make one more commit, undo it safely, then see the reflog
echo "notes" > notes.txt
git add notes.txt
git commit -m "docs: add notes"
# undo that commit with a new commit, then list where HEAD has been

Output of step 6:

$ git log --oneline --graph --all * 9c1d4e2 (HEAD -> main) merge: resolve greeting conflict |\ | * 5d0a7b3 (feature-greeting) feat: greet from feature branch * | e84f2a1 feat: greet from main |/ * 3a1f9c2 feat: add hello app
Show hint

Revert adds a new commit. Reflog lists past positions of HEAD.

Show answer

git revert HEAD --no-edit    # adds a new commit that removes notes.txt again
git reflog

Task 3: on your own

Goal: publish the repository to GitHub. Check: your commits appear on the repository page.

Show hint

Add a remote called origin, then push main and set its upstream. You need the SSH key from the remotes slide.

Show answer

# replace USER; needs an empty repository named git-lab on GitHub
git remote add origin git@github.com:USER/git-lab.git
git push -u origin main
Explain in detail

Do this on your own machine. You need Git installed and (for step 8) a free GitHub account with an empty repository called git-lab.

Hashes will differ, and the two middle lines can appear in either order. The branch is called main only if you set init.defaultBranch main earlier; otherwise use master. If a step fails, run git status; it nearly always tells you the next command.

Golden rules

Commit small and often. Pull before you push. Never rebase shared commits.

Never commit

Passwords, API keys, .env, private keys, node_modules, huge binaries.

Lost?

git status first. Then git log --oneline --graph --all. Then git reflog.

Interview questions

Q: What is the difference between Git and GitHub?

Git is the open-source version control tool that runs on your computer. GitHub is a company/website that hosts Git repositories and adds collaboration features such as pull requests, issues and Actions. GitLab and Bitbucket are alternatives.

Q: Explain the working directory, staging area and repository.

The working directory holds the files you edit. The staging area (index) holds the changes you have chosen for the next commit. The repository (.git) stores the committed snapshots. git add moves changes to staging; git commit moves them into the repository.

Q: What is the difference between git fetch and git pull?

fetch downloads remote commits without changing your branches or files. pull is fetch followed by a merge (or rebase) into your current branch.

Q: Merge vs rebase? When would you use each?

Merge keeps true history and creates a merge commit; it is safe for shared branches. Rebase replays commits on a new base for a linear history, but rewrites commit IDs, so use it only on local/private branches, never on commits others have pulled.

Q: How do you resolve a merge conflict?

Run git status to find conflicted files, open them, edit the area between <<<<<<<, ======= and >>>>>>> into the desired final content, remove the markers, test, git add the file, and git commit. Use git merge --abort to back out.

Q: git reset vs git revert?

reset moves the branch pointer backwards (rewriting history; --hard also discards changes). revert creates a new commit that undoes an earlier one, so history is preserved and it is safe for already-pushed commits.

Q: What is a detached HEAD?

HEAD points directly at a commit instead of a branch (for example after git checkout <hash> or git switch --detach <hash>). New commits there are not on any branch and can be lost. Create a branch with git switch -c name to keep them.

Q: What is a fork vs a clone vs a branch?

A clone is a local copy of a repository. A fork is a server-side copy under your own account (used to contribute to projects you cannot push to). A branch is a pointer to a line of development inside one repository.

Q: Describe GitHub Flow vs GitFlow vs trunk-based development.

GitHub Flow: short feature branches off a single deployable main. GitFlow: long-lived main and develop plus feature, release and hotfix branches, suited to scheduled releases. Trunk-based: everyone merges to trunk at least daily, with feature flags; best for continuous delivery.

Q: You committed a password to a repository. What do you do?

Treat it as compromised: revoke or rotate the secret immediately. Removing it in a later commit is not enough because it stays in history; cleaning history needs special tools and coordination, and rotation is still required. Then add it to .gitignore and use a secrets manager or CI secrets.

Quiz

1. Which command copies your staged changes into the permanent history?

git commit records the staged snapshot in the local repository. add only stages, push uploads.

2. What does git fetch do?

Fetch only updates the remote-tracking branches. pull = fetch + merge.

3. You must undo a commit that was already pushed to a shared main. The safest command is:

Revert adds a new commit that cancels the old one without rewriting shared history.

4. In a conflict, the lines between <<<<<<< HEAD and ======= are:

Top part = HEAD (the branch you are on). Bottom part, before >>>>>>>, = the incoming branch.

5. A release changes the API in a way that breaks old clients. Using SemVer, version 1.4.2 becomes:

Breaking change = bump MAJOR and reset MINOR and PATCH to 0.

6. The golden rule of rebase is:

Rebase creates new commit IDs, so rewriting shared history breaks teammates' copies.
