07

CI/CD Pipelines

A pipeline is an assembly line for software. Every time someone pushes code, machines automatically build it, test it, package it and (when you decide) deliver it to users. This replaces the old routine of "build it on my laptop, copy it to the server and hope". CI/CD is the engine room of DevOps: it turns the Git commits from the previous module into running software.

What you will learn

The integration-hell problem · continuous integration · continuous delivery vs continuous deployment · pipeline anatomy (triggers, stages, jobs, steps, runners, artifacts, caching, secrets, environments, approvals) · the test pyramid and quality gates · a full GitHub Actions workflow · a Jenkinsfile · GitLab CI · deployment strategies (rolling, blue/green, canary) · feature flags and rollbacks · GitOps · pipeline security.

Guess first

You are not expected to know these yet. Guessing before you read helps you remember the answer when you meet it.

A test fails halfway through a pipeline run. What should happen to the later stages, such as deploy?

A failing stage turns the run red and acts as a gate.

What is the single difference between Continuous Delivery and Continuous Deployment?

One decision: does a human approve the production release?

A release goes wrong. Which deployment strategy lets you go back to the old version almost instantly?

Blue/green keeps the old environment on standby.

The problem: integration hell

  • Work kept apart for weeks breaks badly when finally merged at release.
  • Merging often with automatic checks keeps problems small.
  • CI/CD makes builds, tests and deploys routine, not stressful.
ELI5: Explain like I'm 5

Five kids each build one part of a big LEGO spaceship in separate rooms and never look at each other's work.

Integration hell: the painful, unpredictable phase near a release when long-lived separate work is merged and tested together for the first time. The longer the gap between integrations, the bigger the pain.

Free resources (GeeksforGeeks)

  • What is CI/CD?
Explain in detail

Picture a team of five developers who each work alone on their own copy of the code for six weeks. On the last Friday they try to combine everything. Nothing fits. Function names clash, two people rewrote the same file, a library was upgraded by one person and broken for everyone else. The team spends weeks fixing the combination, and then discovers that the build also fails on the production server because "it worked on my machine".

ELI5, continued: At the end they try to join the parts and nothing lines up. Now imagine instead that every ten minutes the kids snap their piece onto the shared ship and a grown-up checks right away that it still holds together. Problems are tiny and found immediately. That grown-up checker is CI.

Without automation

  • Manual builds on someone's laptop
  • Tests run "when there is time" (often never)
  • Deployments done by hand from a checklist, usually late at night
  • A release is a rare, stressful event
  • Bugs are found weeks after they were written

With CI/CD

  • Every push is built and tested by a machine in minutes
  • The same steps run the same way every time
  • Deployment is a button, or fully automatic
  • Releases are small, frequent and boring
  • Bugs are found minutes after they were written
The core idea is to make hard things routine by doing them often. If deployment hurts, deploy more often so that each deployment is small and the process gets fixed.

Why merge small changes often?

Compare with ours

Because each merge is tested right away, so a problem is small and the author still remembers the change that caused it.

History & Evolution

YearMilestoneWhy it mattered
1990s"Integration hell" is the normal experience of large projectsTeams integrated rarely, often at the end of a project (the waterfall style from Module 02).
Late 1990sExtreme Programming (XP) promotes integrating continuouslyMade frequent integration with automated tests a core engineering practice.
2000 (revised 2006)Martin Fowler's article "Continuous Integration"The reference description of CI: shared mainline, automated build, self-testing build, everyone commits daily. It spread the practice worldwide.
2001CruiseControl (originating at ThoughtWorks)One of the first widely used open-source CI servers.
2004 / 2005Hudson created by Kohsuke Kawaguchi (then at Sun Microsystems)Easy to install with a huge plugin ecosystem. It became the most popular CI server.
2010Book Continuous Delivery by Jez Humble and David FarleyExtended CI into the whole path to production: the deployment pipeline, with every commit a potential release.
2011Jenkins forked from Hudson after a dispute with Oracle; Travis CI launchesJenkins became the community standard. Travis made hosted CI with a simple config file in the repository popular for open source.
2015 (GitLab 8.0)GitLab CI, previously a separate application, is built into GitLab itselfCode hosting and CI in one product, configured by a .gitlab-ci.yml file.
2016 / 2017Jenkins 2.0 (April 2016) puts Pipeline as code and the Jenkinsfile at the centre; the declarative syntax shown later in this module reaches 1.0 in early 2017Pipelines moved from clicking in a web UI to a text file stored in Git.
2017The term GitOps is coined at WeaveworksGit becomes the single source of truth for what runs in production; an agent in the cluster pulls changes.
2018 – Nov 2019GitHub Actions: beta in 2018, generally available November 2019CI/CD built straight into the code host, with a marketplace of reusable actions.
2021GitHub Actions supports OIDC for cloud logins; SLSA and Sigstore are announcedPipelines can get short-lived cloud credentials instead of stored long-lived keys, and supply-chain security (signed, traceable builds) becomes a mainstream concern.
2022Argo CD and Flux both graduate in the CNCFThe pull-based GitOps tools are recognized as mature, production-grade projects.
2024Weaveworks, the company that coined GitOps and started Flux, shuts downFlux carries on as a community CNCF project with other maintainers. A reminder that open-source tools can outlive the companies that created them.
March 2025The popular tj-actions/changed-files action is compromisedAttackers changed the action's version tags to point at malicious code that printed secrets into build logs. Pipelines that pinned the action to a full commit SHA were not affected, which made SHA pinning standard advice.
Recent yearsAI assistants write pipeline YAML, summarize failures and review pull requestsPipelines are easier to author. The need for human review, least privilege and signed artifacts has not gone away.
The direction of travel: from manual, rare, scary releases to automated, frequent, boring ones, and from long-lived secrets to short-lived identity-based access.

Continuous Integration in depth

  • Every push starts an automatic build, lint run and test run.
  • Only green changes may merge into the protected main branch.
  • Commit small and often, and keep the build fast.
Continuous Integration (CI): the practice of merging every developer's work into a shared main branch frequently (at least daily), where each change is automatically built and tested to detect problems early.
ELI5: Explain like I'm 5

Each time a child snaps a piece onto the shared LEGO ship (main), a grown-up tests the whole ship (automatic build and tests).

The habits that make CI work

HabitWhy
Commit small and oftenSmall changes are easy to review, test and revert.
Keep the main branch always workingIf main is red, fixing it comes before any new work.
Keep the build fast (ideally under ten minutes)Slow feedback makes people stop waiting for it.
Make tests reliableFlaky tests (random failures) teach people to ignore red builds.
Build once, deploy the same result everywhereWhat you tested must be exactly what you ship.
Explain in detail

ELI5, continued: If a new piece breaks the ship, the grown-up says so immediately, while the child still remembers what they changed. That is why pieces should be small and added often.

What happens on every push

  1. A developer pushes a commit or opens a pull request.
  2. The CI system notices (through a webhook) and starts a clean machine.
  3. It checks out the code, installs dependencies, and runs linting (style and simple mistakes), unit tests, and a build.
  4. It reports a green tick or a red cross on the pull request.
  5. Only green changes are allowed to merge (enforced by a protected branch).
A CI server with no real tests only proves the code compiles. The value of CI comes from the quality of the automated tests it runs.

Continuous Delivery vs Continuous Deployment

Both are abbreviated "CD", which confuses almost everyone. The difference is one single decision: does a human press the final button?

  • Continuous Delivery keeps every change release-ready, but a human triggers production.
  • Continuous Deployment sends every passing change to production automatically.
  • Most teams start with CI and earn trust in tests before deploying automatically.
ELI5: Explain like I'm 5

In a bakery with continuous delivery, every loaf is baked, checked and waiting on the back shelf, but the shopkeeper decides when it goes on the counter. The loaves are changes, the counter is production.


Continuous Integration:    commit -> build -> unit tests
Continuous Delivery:       ... -> package -> deploy to staging -> acceptance tests -> [ human approves ] -> production
Continuous Deployment:     ... -> package -> deploy to staging -> acceptance tests -> production (automatic)
CIContinuous DeliveryContinuous Deployment
Automated build and testYesYesYes
Always release-readyNo (not necessarily)YesYes
Production deployNot part of itManual triggerAutomatic
Explain in detail

ELI5, continued: In continuous deployment, every loaf that passes the checks goes straight onto the counter, with no one deciding. The shopkeeper's decision is the manual approval step.

Continuous Delivery

Every change that passes the pipeline is ready to release at any time. A human (or a business decision) triggers the production deployment, often with one click and an approval.

Use when: regulation, business timing, or lower confidence in tests require a gate.

Continuous Deployment

Every change that passes all automated checks is deployed to production automatically, with no manual step.

Use when: you have very strong tests, monitoring and fast rollback.

Most teams begin with CI, add Continuous Delivery to staging, and move to Continuous Deployment for low-risk services only after trust in the tests is earned.

Anatomy of a pipeline

  • A pipeline is a coded, ordered set of steps from commit to release.
  • Triggers start it, stages and jobs organise it, and runners execute it.
  • Artifacts are tagged with the commit SHA and promoted, not rebuilt.
Pipeline: an automated, ordered set of steps that takes a code change from commit to a running, verified release. It is defined as code (a YAML file or a Jenkinsfile) kept in the repository.
ConceptMeaningExample
TriggerThe event that starts the pipelinepush to main, pull request, tag, schedule, manual button
StageA phase; stages usually run in orderlint, test, build, deploy
JobA group of steps that runs on one machine; jobs in a stage can run in parallel"unit-tests" job
StepOne command or reusable action inside a jobnpm test
Runner / agentThe machine (or container) that actually executes jobsGitHub-hosted ubuntu-latest runner, a Jenkins agent, a self-hosted VM
ArtifactA file or image a job produces and later jobs or people consumetest report, .jar, Docker image
CacheSaved downloads to speed up later runsnode_modules or the npm download cache
SecretA sensitive value stored encrypted outside the coderegistry password, API token
EnvironmentA named deployment target with its own settings and rulesdev, staging, production
ApprovalA human gate before a job runs"release manager must approve production"
ELI5: Explain like I'm 5

A pizza kitchen: the trigger is the order slip.

Explain in detail

ELI5, continued: The stages are dough, toppings, oven, box. Each cook is a runner doing a job made of small steps. The finished box is the artifact. The key to the storeroom is kept in a locked drawer (secrets), and the manager must approve special orders (approval).

Artifact repositories and versioning

The output of a build (a Docker image, a package, a zip) is stored in an artifact repository or registry, for example GitHub Packages / GitHub Container Registry, Docker Hub, Amazon ECR, or tools such as Nexus and Artifactory. Each artifact gets an immutable version label.

  • Tag images with the commit SHA (precise and traceable) and optionally a SemVer tag such as 1.4.2.
  • Avoid relying on the latest tag in production: it does not tell you which build is running.
  • Build once, then promote the same artifact from staging to production instead of rebuilding.

A pipeline in motion

First a run where every stage passes, then a run where a test fails and the pipeline stops before anything is deployed.

  • A commit starts the pipeline and stages run left to right.
  • A failing stage turns the pipeline red and stops it.
  • Broken code never reaches production, because the failing stage is a gate.
Explain in detail

A commit starts the pipeline. The stages run left to right (for example build, test, package, deploy). When all pass, the new version reaches the target. In the second run a test fails, the pipeline turns red and stops. The broken code never reaches production. This is the main safety value of a pipeline: the failing stage is a gate that bad code cannot pass.

Failing fast is a feature. Put the cheapest, fastest checks (lint, unit tests) first so that a typo does not cost you a twenty-minute build.

Why should a failing test stop the pipeline before the deploy stage?

Compare with ours

Because the failing stage is a gate: code that is known to be broken must never reach production.

The test pyramid and quality gates

  • Many fast unit tests, few slow end-to-end tests.
  • Quality gates are automatic pass/fail rules in the pipeline.
  • Typical gates are tests, linting, scans and reviews.
Test pyramid: a guideline saying you should have many fast, small tests at the bottom, fewer medium tests in the middle, and very few slow, broad tests at the top.

          /\        End-to-end (UI) tests: few, slow, brittle
         /  \       "Open the browser, log in, buy something"
        /----\
       /      \     Integration / API tests: some, medium speed
      /        \    "Does the service talk to the real database correctly?"
     /----------\
    /            \  Unit tests: many, very fast
   /______________\ "Does this one function return the right value?"
LevelSpeedCatchesRuns
Unitmillisecondslogic bugs in one functionevery push
Integrationsecondswrong wiring between components or databaseevery push or pull request
End-to-endminutesbroken user journeyson merge, before release
ELI5: Explain like I'm 5

Checking a bicycle: testing each wheel on its own is quick (unit).

Quality gates

Quality gate: an automated pass/fail rule in the pipeline. If the rule fails, the change cannot move forward.
Explain in detail

ELI5, continued: Slower to check that the wheels, chain and pedals turn together (integration). Slowest to ride the whole bike around the block (end-to-end). You check parts all the time and ride the whole bike only a few times, and the bike is not sold until it passes every check (the quality gate).

  • All tests pass, and a minimum test coverage is kept (for example "coverage must not drop")
  • Linter and formatter report no errors
  • Static analysis (for example SonarQube) finds no new serious issues
  • Dependency and container image scans find no critical vulnerabilities (Module 13)
  • Required reviewers have approved the pull request

Check yourself

Two quick questions on the last few slides. Not graded; wrong answers explain themselves.

Your pipeline deploys to staging automatically, then waits for a manager to click Approve before production. Which practice is this?

A human gate before production means Delivery, not Deployment.

In a pipeline run, the unit-test job fails. What happens to the later deploy stage?

The failing stage stops the pipeline.

GitHub Actions: a complete workflow (part 1)

  • A workflow is a YAML file in .github/workflows/ made of jobs and steps.
  • The on: block sets triggers, and permissions: limits the automatic token.
  • A matrix runs the test job once per Node version in parallel.
  • Steps check out code, set up Node, install, lint and test.
GitHub Actions: GitHub's built-in automation. A workflow is a YAML file in .github/workflows/. It contains jobs, jobs contain steps, and a step runs a shell command (run:) or a reusable action (uses:).

name: CI/CD

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  pull_request:
    branches: [main]

permissions:
  contents: read

env:
  IMAGE_NAME: ghcr.io/${{ github.repository }}

jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    strategy:
      matrix:
        node-version: [22, 24]
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7

      - name: Set up Node.js ${{ matrix.node-version }}
        uses: actions/setup-node@v7
        with:
          node-version: ${{ matrix.node-version }}
          cache: npm

      - name: Install dependencies
        run: npm ci

      - name: Lint
        run: npm run lint

      - name: Unit tests
        run: npm test
Explain in detail

We will build one workflow for a small Node.js web app: lint, test, build a Docker image, push it, then deploy. Save it as .github/workflows/ci-cd.yml. Part 1 covers the triggers and the CI job.

Line by line

LinesExplanation
name: CI/CDThe label shown in the Actions tab.
on:The triggers. Run on every push to main and on every pull request that targets main.
permissions: contents: readLeast privilege: the automatic GITHUB_TOKEN may only read the repository unless a job asks for more.
env: IMAGE_NAMEA workflow-wide variable. ${{ ... }} is an expression; github.repository is "owner/repo". Registry paths must be lowercase, which holds for most repository names.
jobs: test:Defines a job called test.
runs-on: ubuntu-latestWhich runner to use: a fresh GitHub-hosted Ubuntu virtual machine.
strategy: matrix:Runs the job once per Node version (22 and 24), in parallel. This tests compatibility with several versions.
actions/checkout@v7Downloads your repository code onto the runner. Without it the runner has an empty folder.
actions/setup-node@v7 with cache: npmInstalls the requested Node version and caches the npm download cache between runs for speed.
npm ciClean, exact install from package-lock.json. Preferred over npm install in CI because it is repeatable.
npm run lint, npm testRun the scripts defined in your package.json. A non-zero exit code fails the step and the job.
Action versions such as @v7 change over time; the majors shown here were current in October 2026. Check each action's page on the GitHub Marketplace for the current major version, and consider pinning to a full commit SHA for sensitive pipelines (see the March 2025 incident in the history table).

GitHub Actions: a complete workflow (part 2)

  • The build job needs test to pass and only runs for pushes to main.
  • Images are built, tagged with the commit SHA and pushed to a registry.
  • The deploy job uses a production environment, which can require human approval.
  • Secrets are read from encrypted settings and passed through env:.

  build-and-push:
    needs: test
    if: github.event_name == 'push' && github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      contents: read
      packages: write
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7

      - uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v4

      - name: Log in to GitHub Container Registry
        uses: docker/login-action@v4
        with:
          registry: ghcr.io
          username: ${{ github.actor }}
          password: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}

      - name: Build and push image
        uses: docker/build-push-action@v7
        with:
          context: .
          push: true
          tags: |
            ${{ env.IMAGE_NAME }}:${{ github.sha }}
            ${{ env.IMAGE_NAME }}:latest
          cache-from: type=gha
          cache-to: type=gha,mode=max

  deploy:
    needs: build-and-push
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment: production
    steps:
      - name: Deploy over SSH
        env:
          DEPLOY_KEY: ${{ secrets.DEPLOY_KEY }}
          DEPLOY_HOST: ${{ secrets.DEPLOY_HOST }}
          DEPLOY_USER: ${{ secrets.DEPLOY_USER }}
        run: |
          install -m 600 /dev/null key.pem
          echo "$DEPLOY_KEY" > key.pem
          IMAGE="${{ env.IMAGE_NAME }}:${{ github.sha }}"
          ssh -i key.pem -o StrictHostKeyChecking=accept-new "$DEPLOY_USER@$DEPLOY_HOST" \
            "docker pull $IMAGE && { docker rm -f myapp || true; } && docker run -d --name myapp -p 80:3000 $IMAGE"
Explain in detail

These jobs go in the same file under jobs:, after test. They build and push the Docker image, then deploy to a server.

Line by line

LinesExplanation
needs: testOrder between jobs. This job waits for test and is skipped if it fails.
if: ... github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'Only build and push for pushes to main, not for pull requests from branches.
permissions: packages: writeThis job alone may publish packages to GitHub's container registry.
docker/setup-buildx-actionPrepares Docker Buildx, the modern image builder.
docker/login-actionLogs in to ghcr.io. The password is the built-in GITHUB_TOKEN, a short-lived token created for each run, so you store no password.
docker/build-push-actionBuilds the image from the Dockerfile in context: ., then pushes it. Tags include the commit SHA so every image is traceable.
cache-from / cache-to: type=ghaStores Docker layer cache in the GitHub Actions cache, so unchanged layers are not rebuilt (layers are explained in Module 08).
environment: productionLinks the job to an environment. In the repository settings you can attach required reviewers, so the job waits for a human approval. This is the "delivery" gate.
${{ secrets.DEPLOY_KEY }}Reads an encrypted secret defined in repository or environment settings. Values are masked in logs. Pass it through env: rather than writing it inline in the script.
run: |A multi-line shell script. It writes the key to a file with restricted permissions, then connects with SSH, pulls the new image, removes the old container (ignoring the error if none exists) and starts the new one. If the pull fails, nothing else runs.
This SSH deploy is deliberately simple for teaching. It stores a long-lived key and replaces the container with a brief gap. The server must also be able to pull the image: either make the package public or run docker login ghcr.io on the server once. Real systems usually deploy to Kubernetes, a managed container service or with a GitOps tool, and use short-lived OIDC credentials (see the security slide).

Jenkins: a declarative Jenkinsfile

  • Jenkins is a self-hosted automation server that runs jobs on agents.
  • Pipelines are described in a Jenkinsfile stored in the repository.
  • Declarative syntax uses stages, steps, options, environment and post blocks.
  • The input step pauses the pipeline until a human approves.
Jenkins: a long-established, self-hosted, open-source automation server. You install it yourself, connect agents (the machines that run jobs), and describe pipelines in a Jenkinsfile stored in your repository. Its large plugin library is both its strength and a maintenance burden.

pipeline {
    agent any

    options {
        timeout(time: 20, unit: 'MINUTES')
        buildDiscarder(logRotator(numToKeepStr: '20'))
    }

    environment {
        IMAGE = "myorg/myapp"
        REGISTRY_CREDS = credentials('dockerhub-creds')
    }

    stages {
        stage('Install') {
            steps {
                sh 'npm ci'
            }
        }
        stage('Lint and Test') {
            steps {
                sh 'npm run lint'
                sh 'npm test'
            }
            post {
                always {
                    junit 'reports/junit.xml'
                }
            }
        }
        stage('Build Image') {
            steps {
                sh 'docker build -t $IMAGE:$GIT_COMMIT .'
            }
        }
        stage('Push Image') {
            when { branch 'main' }
            steps {
                sh 'echo $REGISTRY_CREDS_PSW | docker login -u $REGISTRY_CREDS_USR --password-stdin'
                sh 'docker push $IMAGE:$GIT_COMMIT'
            }
        }
        stage('Deploy to Production') {
            when { branch 'main' }
            steps {
                input message: 'Deploy this build to production?'
                sh './deploy.sh $IMAGE:$GIT_COMMIT'
            }
        }
    }

    post {
        failure {
            echo 'Build failed. Notify the team here.'
        }
        cleanup {
            cleanWs()
        }
    }
}

Free resources (GeeksforGeeks)

  • Jenkins Tutorial
Explain in detail

Line by line

PartExplanation
pipeline { ... }Marks a declarative pipeline: a fixed, structured syntax that is easier to read and validate than the older scripted style.
agent anyRun on any available agent. You can instead require a label or a Docker container.
options { ... }Pipeline-wide settings: stop after 20 minutes, keep only the last 20 build records.
environment { ... }Sets variables. credentials('dockerhub-creds') loads a stored credential and exposes REGISTRY_CREDS_USR and REGISTRY_CREDS_PSW without printing them in the Jenkinsfile.
stages { stage(...) { steps { ... } } }The ordered phases. Each stage holds steps, and sh runs a shell command.
post { always { junit ... } }Actions that run after a stage regardless of result. junit (from the JUnit plugin) publishes test results so Jenkins can graph them. It assumes your test runner is configured to write a JUnit XML report to reports/junit.xml; if the file is missing, the step fails the build.
$GIT_COMMITA built-in environment variable holding the commit SHA, used as the image tag.
when { branch 'main' }Condition: run this stage only for the main branch. (Branch conditions need a multibranch pipeline job.)
input message: ...Pauses the pipeline until a human approves. This is Continuous Delivery's manual gate.
final post { failure / cleanup }Runs on failure (send alerts) and always cleans the workspace afterwards. cleanWs() comes from the Workspace Cleanup plugin.

GitLab CI and the platform comparison

  • GitLab CI reads .gitlab-ci.yml from the repository root.
  • Runners pick up jobs organised in stages with scripts, artifacts and cache.
  • Rules decide when a job runs, and manual jobs wait for a click.
  • Stages, jobs, secrets and caches carry over between CI tools.

stages: [test, build, deploy]

default:
  image: node:22

test:
  stage: test
  script:
    - npm ci --cache .npm --prefer-offline
    - npm run lint
    - npm test
  cache:
    key:
      files: [package-lock.json]
    paths: [.npm/]

build-image:
  stage: build
  image: docker:27
  services: [docker:27-dind]
  variables:
    DOCKER_TLS_CERTDIR: "/certs"
  script:
    - echo "$CI_REGISTRY_PASSWORD" | docker login -u "$CI_REGISTRY_USER" --password-stdin "$CI_REGISTRY"
    - docker build -t "$CI_REGISTRY_IMAGE:$CI_COMMIT_SHORT_SHA" .
    - docker push "$CI_REGISTRY_IMAGE:$CI_COMMIT_SHORT_SHA"
  rules:
    - if: $CI_COMMIT_BRANCH == "main"

deploy-prod:
  stage: deploy
  script: ./deploy.sh "$CI_REGISTRY_IMAGE:$CI_COMMIT_SHORT_SHA"
  environment: production
  rules:
    - if: $CI_COMMIT_BRANCH == "main"
      when: manual
GitHub ActionsGitLab CIJenkins
HostingHosted by GitHub (or self-hosted runners)GitLab.com or self-managedYou host it
ConfigYAML in .github/workflows/.gitlab-ci.ymlJenkinsfile (Groovy)
ReuseMarketplace actionsIncludes and templatesPlugins and shared libraries
MaintenanceLowLow to mediumHigher (upgrades, plugins, agents)
Explain in detail

GitLab CI reads a file named .gitlab-ci.yml in the repository root. Runners (GitLab's name for agents) pick up jobs. The same ideas apply: stages, jobs, scripts, artifacts and cache.

stages lists the order. script is the list of shell commands. Names starting with $CI_ are predefined variables GitLab fills in. rules decide when a job runs, and when: manual inside the rule makes the production job wait for someone to press the play button. The cache stores npm's download folder (not node_modules, which npm ci deletes on every run), keyed on the lock file. docker:27-dind is "Docker in Docker", a service container that gives the job a Docker daemon; it needs a runner that allows privileged containers, as GitLab.com's hosted Linux runners do.

Learn one tool well. Stages, jobs, secrets, artifacts and caches carry across all of them, and a new tool usually takes a few days to pick up.

Check yourself

Two quick questions on the last few slides. Not graded; wrong answers explain themselves.

Which kind of test should a team have the most of, and why?

Many unit tests, fewer integration tests, very few end-to-end tests.

In the GitHub Actions workflow, what does the matrix under strategy do?

A matrix repeats one job for each value in the list.

Deployment strategies: recreate, rolling and blue/green

  • Recreate stops the old version first, so there is downtime.
  • Rolling replaces servers a few at a time with no downtime.
  • Blue/green builds a second environment and switches traffic in one step.
  • Switching back to blue gives an instant rollback.
ELI5: Explain like I'm 5

A theatre has two stages. The audience watches stage Blue while the crew quietly sets up the next scene on stage Green.

Explain in detail

Deploying new code to servers that are already serving users is risky. A deployment strategy is the plan for swapping old for new while limiting damage.

Recreate

Stop the old version, start the new one.

Pro: simplest. Con: downtime between stop and start.

OK for internal tools or maintenance windows.

Rolling

Replace servers a few at a time. At every moment some are old, some are new.

Pro: no downtime, little extra cost. Con: two versions run together, and rollback is gradual. This is the Kubernetes default for Deployments.

Blue/green

Run two full environments. Build the new one (green) beside the live one (blue), test it, then switch traffic over in one step.

Pro: instant switch and instant rollback. Con: double the infrastructure while both exist.

ELI5, continued: When Green is ready, the curtain opens on Green. If something looks wrong, they open the curtain on Blue again right away. The stages are two identical environments, the audience is the users, and opening a curtain is switching the traffic.

The load balancer sends all users to the blue environment. The green environment is deployed and tested without users. Then the router is flipped so users go to green. Blue stays on standby, so rolling back is just flipping the switch back. One caveat: database changes must be compatible with both versions during the switch.

Canary releases, feature flags and rollbacks

  • A canary sends the new version to a small share of users first.
  • Traffic grows only while metrics stay healthy.
  • Feature flags separate deploying code from releasing a feature.
  • Plan the rollback before you deploy.
Canary release: send the new version to a small slice of real users first (for example 5 percent), watch the metrics, and increase gradually only if healthy. The name comes from canaries once used in coal mines to detect danger early.

Feature flags

ELI5: Explain like I'm 5

A new dish goes to a few tables first (canary).

Explain in detail

Traffic starts mostly on the stable version. The canary receives a small share. If error rate and latency look fine, the share grows step by step to 25 percent, 50 percent and finally 100 percent. If metrics turn bad, traffic returns to the stable version and few users were affected.

ELI5, continued: If those diners are happy, the new dish goes to more tables step by step; if not, everyone gets the old dish again and only a few diners noticed (rollback). The tables are users, and the diners' reactions are the metrics.

A feature flag is a condition in the code, such as if (flags.newCheckout) { ... }, controlled from a configuration or flag service. It separates deploying code from releasing a feature, which makes trunk-based development and canary rollouts easy. Remove old flags once a feature is fully launched.

Rollbacks

  • Redeploy the previous artifact: because you tagged images by commit SHA, you can run the last good one.
  • Switch traffic back (blue/green) or turn the flag off: usually the fastest options.
  • Revert the commit in Git (git revert) and let the pipeline redeploy. This is clean and traceable.
  • Rolling back code is easy. Rolling back database changes is hard, so design migrations in small, backward-compatible steps.
Decide how you will roll back before you deploy. A release plan without a rollback plan is a hope.

GitOps: Git as the source of truth

  • In GitOps, Git holds the desired state and is the single source of truth.
  • An agent in the cluster pulls changes and makes reality match.
  • Argo CD and Flux are the main pull-based tools.
GitOps: a way of operating infrastructure and applications where the desired state is described declaratively in a Git repository, and an automated agent continuously makes the real system match it.
ELI5: Explain like I'm 5

You keep a drawing of how your toy room should look pinned on the wall.

Push model vs pull model

Push (traditional CI/CD)Pull (GitOps)
Who deploys?The CI pipeline runs kubectl or ssh against the targetAn agent inside the cluster pulls from Git and applies changes
CredentialsThe pipeline needs access to productionCluster credentials stay inside the cluster
Drift (manual changes)Not noticed until the next deployDetected and corrected automatically
Audit trailPipeline logsGit history: who changed what, with review
RollbackRe-run an old pipelinegit revert and the agent syncs
Explain in detail

ELI5, continued: A helper robot looks at the real room every minute. If a block is missing or in the wrong place, the robot fixes the room to match the drawing. To change the room, you do not move blocks yourself, you change the drawing, and the robot follows. The drawing is Git, the robot is Argo CD or Flux.

A typical flow: CI builds and pushes a new image, then updates the image tag in a separate "config" repository (or opens a pull request there). After review and merge, Argo CD or Flux sees the change and updates the cluster. The tools are covered further in Module 09 (Kubernetes) and Module 11 (Infrastructure as Code).

GitOps works best with declarative configuration such as Kubernetes manifests, Helm charts or Kustomize. It is a pattern rather than a product.

Pipeline security basics

  • Treat the pipeline as production infrastructure, because attackers target it.
  • Keep secrets in a secret store and give each job least privilege.
  • OIDC gives short-lived cloud credentials, so no long-lived keys are stored.
  • Pin third-party actions, scan dependencies and sign artifacts.

OIDC instead of long-lived cloud keys

ELI5: Explain like I'm 5

The pipeline does not keep a permanent key (a stored access key) that could be copied. It shows a fresh ID badge (an OIDC token) at reception (the cloud provider), which checks it and hands out a short-lived visitor pass (temporary credentials).


jobs:
  deploy:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      id-token: write
      contents: read
    steps:
      - uses: aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials@v6
        with:
          role-to-assume: arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/gha-deploy   # example role
          aws-region: eu-west-1
      - run: aws sts get-caller-identity   # prints the temporary identity
Explain in detail

A pipeline holds powerful credentials and runs code automatically, so attackers target it. Treat the pipeline as production infrastructure.

Secrets

  • Never commit secrets to the repository or print them in logs
  • Use the platform's secret store (GitHub Secrets, GitLab CI/CD variables marked masked and protected, Jenkins credentials) or a vault
  • Scope secrets to environments (production secrets only for production jobs)
  • Rotate them regularly and immediately after any leak

Least privilege

  • Set GitHub permissions: to the minimum, per workflow or job
  • Give deploy roles access to only what they deploy
  • Protect branches and require reviews for workflow-file changes
  • Be careful running untrusted pull-request code with access to secrets

With OpenID Connect (OIDC), the CI platform issues a short-lived signed identity token for each run. The cloud provider (AWS, Azure, Google Cloud) is configured to trust tokens from your repository and exchanges them for temporary credentials. No access key is stored in the CI system at all. In GitHub Actions this needs permissions: id-token: write and a cloud-specific login step.

The AWS side needs a one-time setup: an IAM OIDC identity provider for token.actions.githubusercontent.com and a role whose trust policy only accepts tokens from your repository.

Supply-chain security

  • Pin third-party actions and base images to a version or digest and update them deliberately.
  • Scan dependencies and images in the pipeline; generate a software bill of materials (SBOM).
  • Sign artifacts (for example with Sigstore's cosign) and aim for verifiable build provenance (the SLSA framework describes levels of this).
Pipeline files are code that runs with real credentials. A pull request that edits a workflow can try to steal secrets, so require review for changes under .github/workflows/.

Check yourself

Two quick questions on the last few slides. Not graded; wrong answers explain themselves.

After a blue/green switch, users hit errors on green. What is the fastest fix?

Blue/green gives an instant rollback by switching back.

What does a feature flag let a team do?

Flags separate deploying from releasing.

Hands-on exercise: build your first pipeline

  • Create a tiny Node.js app with one test and a GitHub repository.
  • Add a workflow file and watch the run in the Actions tab.
  • Break the test on purpose in a pull request and see the red cross.
  • Add branch protection so red code cannot be merged.

Task 1: worked example


mkdir cicd-lab && cd cicd-lab
git init -b main
npm init -y
mkdir -p .github/workflows
cat > sum.js <<'EOF'
module.exports = (a, b) => a + b;
EOF
cat > sum.test.js <<'EOF'
const test = require('node:test');
const assert = require('node:assert');
const sum = require('./sum');
test('adds numbers', () => assert.strictEqual(sum(2, 3), 5));
EOF
npm pkg set scripts.test="node --test"
npm install        # creates package-lock.json, which npm ci in the workflow requires
npm test

Task 2: finish it

Add the workflow, then publish.


# .github/workflows/ci.yml: triggers and the test job from the earlier slide
git add . && git commit -m "ci: add workflow"
git remote add origin git@github.com:USER/cicd-lab.git
# last command: send main to GitHub
Show hint

The first push needs -u so that Git remembers the upstream branch.

Show answer

git push -u origin main

Then open the Actions tab and watch the run turn green.

Task 3: on your own

Goal: fail a pull request on purpose, then block red merges.

Success: red cross, then green, merge blocked while red.

Show hint

Change 5 to 6 in the test on a new branch. For the block, use a branch protection rule on main.

Show answer

Push the branch and open a pull request to see the red cross, then fix the test. In Settings, Branches, require the status checks test (22) and test (24) on main.

Explain in detail

You need a free GitHub account and Git installed. The app is tiny: a Node.js script with one test.

The expected result is a passing test. The exact wording varies by Node version, but you should see a pass count of 1 and a fail count of 0.

  1. Create .github/workflows/ci.yml with the triggers and the test job from the earlier slide (use npm test; skip the lint step if you have no linter).
  2. Commit (including package-lock.json) and push to a new, empty GitHub repository: git add . && git commit -m "ci: add workflow" && git remote add origin git@github.com:USER/cicd-lab.git && git push -u origin main
  3. Open the Actions tab on GitHub and watch the run. Click a step to read its logs.
  4. Break it on purpose: change 5 to 6 in the test, push to a branch, and open a pull request. See the red cross.
  5. Fix the test, push again, and watch the check turn green.
  6. In Settings, Branches, add a protection rule (or ruleset) for main requiring the status checks from the test job. Because of the matrix, the job reports one check per version: test (22) and test (24). Now red code cannot be merged.
  7. Stretch goal: add a second job that builds a Docker image (you will write the Dockerfile in Module 08) and an environment: production with a required reviewer.
If a workflow does not start, check that the file is under .github/workflows/, ends in .yml, and is valid YAML (indentation must use spaces, not tabs).

Interview questions

Q: What is the difference between Continuous Delivery and Continuous Deployment?

Both automate the path to production. In Continuous Delivery every passing change is ready to release but a human triggers the production deploy. In Continuous Deployment there is no manual step; every change that passes the pipeline goes live automatically.

Q: What problem does CI solve?

Integration problems found late. By merging small changes often and testing each automatically, conflicts and bugs are found within minutes while the author still remembers the code.

Q: Explain the stages of a typical pipeline.

Trigger (push or pull request), checkout, install dependencies, lint, unit tests, build, package (for example Docker image), push to a registry, deploy to staging, integration or end-to-end tests, approval (for delivery), deploy to production, and monitor.

Q: Compare blue/green and canary deployments.

Blue/green switches all traffic at once between two full environments, giving instant rollback at the cost of duplicate infrastructure. Canary shifts traffic gradually to a small share of users, giving real-world validation with limited blast radius, but needs good metrics and traffic routing.

Q: How do you handle secrets in a pipeline?

Store them in the platform's secret store or an external vault, scope them to environments, mask them in logs, never commit them, rotate them, and prefer OIDC short-lived credentials over long-lived keys.

Q: What is a flaky test and why is it harmful?

A test that sometimes passes and sometimes fails without code changes. It erodes trust in the pipeline, so people ignore real failures. Fix or quarantine flaky tests quickly.

Q: What is GitOps and how does it differ from push-based CD?

GitOps keeps desired state in Git and uses an agent (Argo CD or Flux) inside the cluster to pull and apply it, continuously correcting drift. Push-based CD has the pipeline run deploy commands against the target and needs production credentials outside the cluster.

Q: How would you speed up a slow pipeline?

Cache dependencies and Docker layers, run independent jobs in parallel, run cheap checks first, split or shard tests, run only what changed, and use faster or larger runners.

Q: What is the difference between a Jenkins agent and a GitHub runner?

Both are machines that execute pipeline jobs. Jenkins agents connect to a controller you host. GitHub runners are either GitHub-hosted virtual machines or self-hosted machines you register.

Q: How do you roll back a bad release?

Options in order of speed: turn off the feature flag, switch traffic back (blue/green), redeploy the previous image tag, or revert the commit and let the pipeline redeploy. Plan database changes so they stay compatible with the previous version.

Quiz

1. Which statement describes Continuous Deployment?

Continuous Deployment removes the manual production gate. With Continuous Delivery a human still presses the button.

2. In GitHub Actions, what does needs: test do?

needs creates a dependency between jobs.

3. Which deployment strategy sends the new version to a small percentage of users first?

A canary release exposes a small slice of traffic, then grows it if metrics are healthy.

4. Why is OIDC preferred over storing cloud access keys in CI secrets?

The cloud exchanges a signed token for temporary credentials, so nothing permanent is stored.

5. In the test pyramid, which tests should you have the most of?

Unit tests are fast and cheap, so they form the wide base of the pyramid.

6. What is the main idea of the GitOps pull model?

Git is the source of truth and Argo CD or Flux reconcile the cluster to it.
