08

Containers & Docker

A container is a way of packaging an application together with everything it needs to run (its libraries, its settings, its runtime) so that it behaves identically on your laptop, on your teammate's laptop, on a test server and in production. Docker is the tool that made containers easy and famous. In this module you will learn what containers really are under the hood, how to write a Dockerfile, how to run, network and store data for containers, and how to run a multi-container app with Docker Compose.

What you will learn

The "works on my machine" problem · containers vs virtual machines · namespaces, cgroups & overlay filesystems · Docker architecture (CLI, dockerd, containerd, runc) · images, containers & registries · every common Dockerfile instruction · layers & build cache · multi-stage builds · security best practices · essential commands · volumes · networking · Docker Compose · a hands-on exercise

Guess first

You are not expected to know these yet. Guessing before you read helps you remember the answer when you meet it.

What does a container share with the machine it runs on?

Shared kernel is why containers are light and fast.

You rebuild an image after changing one line of app code. Docker finishes in seconds. Why?

Layers are cached in order.

You delete a container that wrote files inside itself. What happens to those files?

Use a volume for data that must survive.

Why does this exist? "It works on my machine!"

  • Apps break between machines because versions, libraries and operating systems differ.
  • A container packages the app and everything it needs into one image.
  • The same image runs the same way in dev, test and production.
ELI5: Explain like I'm 5

Bring only a recipe to a friend's house and their oven may make the cake turn out wrong; bring the cake in a sealed box and it arrives the same. The recipe is your code; the sealed box is a container.

Explain in detail

Every developer has heard (or said) the most famous sentence in software: "But it works on my machine!" Why does an app work on one computer and break on another? Because an application never runs alone. It depends on a long list of invisible things:

The problem

  • Your laptop has Python 3.12, the server has Python 3.8.
  • You installed a library globally months ago and forgot; the server does not have it.
  • Your OS is macOS, production is Linux; paths, line endings and system libraries differ.
  • Two apps on one server need different versions of the same library, and they fight.
  • Setting up a new teammate's laptop takes a whole day of installing things.

The container solution

  • Package the app plus its exact Python version, libraries and files into one image.
  • Run that image anywhere there is a container runtime. It carries its own world with it.
  • Each container is isolated, so two apps with conflicting needs live side by side.
  • New teammate: docker compose up and the whole stack is running in minutes.
  • Dev, test and prod run the same artifact, which is the heart of reliable CI/CD.

ELI5, continued: The friend's kitchen is another computer. The box holds the cake plus the plate and fork it needs (your app plus its libraries and settings). It still needs a table to stand on: every container runs on a host and uses that host's operating system kernel.

ELI5: The shipping container

Before standard shipping containers, every sack and barrel was loaded by hand. Then the world agreed on one steel box with fixed sizes, so any crane, ship or truck can move it without caring what is inside. A Docker container is that standard box, and the computers that run it are the ships.

Why do images run the same everywhere?

Compare with ours

Because the image packages the app together with its libraries and settings, so the host machine no longer decides what the app depends on.

History & Evolution

Containers are not new. Docker did not invent isolation; it made isolation usable. The ideas were built up in the Linux kernel over many years.

YearMilestoneWhy it mattered
1979chroot arrives in Unix (Version 7)First trick to give a process a different "root" directory, so it cannot see the rest of the filesystem. The seed idea of isolation.
2000FreeBSD JailsIsolated not just files but processes and networking: a real "mini-server" inside a server.
2002 onwardLinux namespaces (first one: mount, in kernel 2.4.19)Kernel feature that gives a process its own private view of mounts, process IDs, network, hostname and more. More namespace types were added over the following years.
2004–2005Solaris Zones (Solaris 10)Commercial-grade OS-level virtualization with resource controls.
2008cgroups (started at Google) merged into Linux 2.6.24Kernel feature to limit and measure CPU, memory and I/O per group of processes. Namespaces = what you can see; cgroups = what you can use.
2008LXC (Linux Containers)First complete Linux container manager built from namespaces + cgroups. Powerful but hard to use.
March 2013Docker shown publicly at PyCon by dotCloud; open-sourced the same monthdotCloud was a Platform-as-a-Service company. Docker packaged images, a simple CLI and a sharing hub in one easy tool. The company renamed itself Docker, Inc. later in 2013.
2014libcontainer (Go) replaces LXC as Docker's default execution backend (Docker 0.9)Docker stopped depending on LXC and talked to the kernel directly.
June 2015Open Container Initiative (OCI) founded; Docker donates runcA vendor-neutral standard for image format and runtime, so containers are not owned by one company. runc became the reference runtime.
2016Docker 1.12 ships Swarm mode built inDocker's own simple orchestrator. It later lost the "orchestration wars" to Kubernetes (see the next module).
2017containerd donated to the CNCFThe core runtime was split out of Docker so Kubernetes and others could use it directly, without the whole Docker engine.
2019Podman 1.0 (Red Hat) releasedA daemonless, rootless-friendly, Docker-compatible CLI. Popularised rootless containers for better security.
Dec 2020Docker Engine 20.10: cgroup v2 support, rootless mode no longer experimentalDocker could run on modern distributions that switched to cgroup v2, and could run without root privileges on the host.
2021Docker Desktop licensing changeDocker Desktop became paid for larger companies (free for personal use, education, small businesses). Many teams looked at alternatives such as Podman, Rancher Desktop, Colima. The open-source Docker Engine on Linux was not affected.
2021–2023Compose V2 replaces V1The old Python tool docker-compose (with a hyphen) was rewritten in Go as the plugin docker compose (a space). Compose V1 reached end-of-life in mid-2023. Today you should always type docker compose.
2023BuildKit becomes the default builder on Linux (Docker Engine 23.0)Faster, parallel, cache-smart image builds and better secrets handling.
2022 onwardWebAssembly (Wasm) container experimentsDocker and containerd-based runtimes began experimenting with running Wasm modules next to Linux containers, as a lighter and more portable unit. Still evolving, not a replacement yet.
Nov 2024containerd 2.0 releasedFirst new major version of the runtime that powers Docker and most Kubernetes clusters; stabilised many long-running features and removed old, deprecated APIs.
2024–2025The containerd image store becomes the default for new installs (Docker Desktop in 2024, Docker Engine 29.0 in November 2025)Docker now stores images through containerd instead of its own older storage code, which brings multi-platform images and other OCI features and shares more machinery with Kubernetes.

Docker = a friendly layer on top of long-standing Linux kernel features, now split into small standard pieces (containerd, runc, OCI specs) that other tools reuse.

What is a container? Containers vs virtual machines

  • Containers are isolated processes sharing one kernel.
  • Each VM runs its own full operating system.
  • Containers are lighter and start faster.
Container: a normal Linux process (or group of processes) that the kernel has isolated: it gets its own view of the filesystem, process list, network and hostname, plus limits on CPU and memory. It shares the host's kernel instead of booting its own operating system.
ELI5: Explain like I'm 5

A VM is a house with its own foundation; a container is a flat sharing one foundation, the kernel.

AspectVirtual machineContainer
Isolation unitWhole machine with its own kernelProcess(es) sharing the host kernel
SizeGigabytes (includes a full OS)Often megabytes (app + libraries only)
StartupTens of seconds to minutes (boot an OS)Typically about a second or less (start a process)
DensityA few per hostDozens to hundreds per host
Isolation strengthStronger (hardware-level boundary)Weaker (shared kernel), so a kernel bug could affect all
Different OS?Yes, Windows VM on Linux host is fineMust match the host kernel family (Linux containers need a Linux kernel)
Best forStrong isolation, different OSes, legacy appsPackaging and scaling apps and microservices fast
Explain in detail
Virtual machine (VM): a complete pretend computer, run by a hypervisor, with its own virtual hardware and its own full guest operating system and kernel.

ELI5, continued: The house also has its own plumbing and wiring (a whole guest operating system), so it is private but slow and costly to build, and takes minutes to start. A flat is ready in seconds because the building already stands. The trade-off: every flat rests on the same foundation, so a weakness in it (a kernel bug) affects them all.

They are not enemies. In the cloud, containers usually run inside VMs (an EC2 instance running Docker). VMs slice up hardware; containers slice up a VM.
On macOS and Windows, Docker Desktop quietly runs a small Linux VM and puts your containers in it, because Linux containers need a Linux kernel. That is why Docker Desktop uses memory even when idle.

VM stack vs container stack

Watch how many layers each approach needs between your app and the hardware.

  • Each VM carries its own guest operating system on a hypervisor.
  • Containers share the host kernel through one container runtime.
  • That is why containers are small and start fast.
Explain in detail

On the left, every VM carries its own guest operating system on top of a hypervisor, so three apps means three full OS copies. On the right, the containers sit on one container runtime that shares the host operating system's kernel, so the only extra weight per app is the app and its libraries. That is why containers are small and start fast.

How containers really work: namespaces, cgroups, overlay FS

  • A container is a normal Linux process, not a special kernel object.
  • Namespaces control what a process can see.
  • cgroups control what a process can use.
  • A layered filesystem stacks read-only image layers under one writable layer.
Container: namespaces + cgroups + a layered root filesystem, started by a runtime such as runc. There is no "container" object inside the kernel; it is just a normal process with these restrictions.

You can prove it: on a Linux host, run a container and look at it from outside.


$ docker run -d --name demo nginx
$ ps aux | grep nginx              # the container's processes are visible on the host
$ docker exec demo cat /proc/1/comm  # inside, PID 1 is nginx (PID namespace)
$ docker exec demo cat /etc/hostname # inside, the hostname is the short container ID (UTS namespace)
Explain in detail

"Container" is not a single kernel feature. It is a recipe combining three Linux features. Docker just applies the recipe for you.

1. Namespaces = "what you can see"

ELI5

Each child works in a library study booth with high walls: they see only their own desk and books, as if they were alone. The other booths are still there, just out of sight. The booth walls are namespaces, which give a process its own view of files, processes and network.

A namespace wraps a global resource so a process thinks it has its own copy. Main types:

  • PID: own process list; your app is PID 1
  • NET: own network interfaces, IP, ports
  • MNT: own filesystem mounts
  • UTS: own hostname
  • IPC: own shared memory
  • USER: own user IDs, so root inside can map to an unprivileged user outside (Docker does not turn this on by default)

2. cgroups = "what you can use"

ELI5

At a shared lunch table, each child is served a fixed portion, so one hungry child cannot eat everyone else's food. The children are containers, the food is the machine's CPU and memory, and the fixed portion is a cgroup limit.

Control groups (cgroups) limit and count resources for a set of processes: CPU time, memory, disk I/O, number of processes. If a container exceeds its memory limit, the kernel kills a process inside it (an "OOM kill", OOM meaning out of memory), which usually stops the container.


docker run --memory=256m --cpus=0.5 nginx

3. Union / overlay filesystem = "stacked sheets"

ELI5

Stack clear sheets on an overhead projector and you see all the drawings combined. To change something, you draw on a new top sheet and leave the sheets below untouched, so other stacks can reuse them. The lower sheets are read-only image layers; the top sheet is the container's writable layer.

OverlayFS merges read-only lower layers (the image) with one writable upper layer (the container) into one view. Changing a file copies it to the upper layer first: this is called copy-on-write.

Check yourself

Two quick questions on the last few slides. Not graded; wrong answers explain themselves.

Which Linux feature limits how much CPU and memory a container may use?

Namespaces limit what a process sees, cgroups limit what it uses.

Why does a container start much faster than a virtual machine?

No guest OS to boot means a near-instant start.

Docker architecture: who does what?

  • The docker CLI talks to dockerd, which uses containerd and runc.
  • Each program in the chain has one job.
  • OCI standards make images portable between tools.
PieceRole
docker CLIThe command you type. It does very little: it converts your command into a REST API call.
dockerd (Docker daemon)The long-running background service. Listens on a Unix socket (/var/run/docker.sock). Manages images, networks, volumes, builds, and asks containerd to run containers.
containerdA container runtime manager. Pulls images, stores them, manages container lifecycle and snapshots. Also used directly by Kubernetes.
containerd-shimA tiny per-container helper that keeps the container alive and holds its I/O even if containerd restarts.
runcThe low-level OCI runtime. It talks to the kernel to create namespaces and cgroups and starts your process. Then it exits.

docker CLI  ──REST──▶  dockerd  ──gRPC──▶  containerd  ──▶  containerd-shim  ──▶  runc  ──▶  your process
ELI5: Explain like I'm 5

You (the docker CLI) give your order to the waiter (dockerd), who passes it to the head chef (containerd); the chef stocks the pantry (images) and hands the job to a cook (runc), who makes the dish (the container) and leaves. A helper (the shim) stays by your table watching the dish, so the kitchen can change shifts without disturbing your meal.

Explain in detail
OCI (Open Container Initiative): standards that make containers portable between tools. Three specs: the Image Spec (how an image is laid out), the Runtime Spec (how to run a container from it; implemented by runc) and the Distribution Spec (how registries serve images). Because of OCI, an image built by Docker can run under Podman, containerd or Kubernetes.

When you type docker run nginx, a chain of programs cooperates. Each has one job.

Access to /var/run/docker.sock is effectively root on the host. Never mount it into untrusted containers, and be careful adding users to the docker group.

Images, containers and registries

  • An image is a read-only template built from a Dockerfile.
  • A container is a running instance of an image with a thin writable layer.
  • A registry stores and serves images, for example Docker Hub.
ELI5: Explain like I'm 5

An image is a cookie cutter; a container is a cookie made with it. One cookie cutter makes many cookies.

An image name has parts: registry/namespace/repository:tag


docker.io/library/nginx:1.27        # registry / namespace / repo : tag  (docker.io and library are the defaults)
ghcr.io/myorg/api:2.4.1             # GitHub Container Registry
myrepo/web:latest                   # Docker Hub user "myrepo"
nginx@sha256:3f1c...                # pinned by immutable digest (safest)
Explain in detail

Image

A read-only template: a stack of layers holding your app, libraries and a minimal filesystem, plus metadata (default command, ports...). Built from a Dockerfile. Identified by a name and tag like python:3.12-slim and by a content hash (digest).

Container

A running (or stopped) instance of an image: the image layers + a thin writable layer + isolated process. You can start many containers from one image.

Registry

A server that stores and serves images. Docker Hub is the public default; others: GitHub Container Registry, Amazon ECR, Google Artifact Registry, Azure Container Registry, or a private one you host.

ELI5, continued: The registry is the shop where people share cookie cutters. If you smash a cookie, the cutter is still fine and you can bake another.

The latest tag is just a name, not "the newest". It moves around and is a common cause of "it worked yesterday". Use explicit version tags in anything real.

From Dockerfile to running containers

This is the life of an app in the Docker world, from source to running everywhere.

  • Write a Dockerfile, then docker build creates an image.
  • docker push uploads the image to a registry.
  • Any server can docker pull and run identical containers.
Explain in detail

Step 1: you write a Dockerfile. Step 2: docker build turns it into an image. Step 3: docker push uploads the image to a registry. Step 4: any server runs docker pull / docker run and gets identical containers. Build once, run anywhere.

Writing a Dockerfile, line by line (part 1)

  • A Dockerfile is read top to bottom to build an image.
  • RUN, COPY and ADD create layers, other instructions only set metadata.
  • Copy the dependency list first so the build cache is reused.
Dockerfile: a plain text file of instructions, read top to bottom, that tells Docker how to build an image. Instructions that change files (RUN, COPY, ADD) each create a new layer; the others (ENV, CMD, EXPOSE and so on) only record settings in the image's metadata.

A complete small Python web app Dockerfile:


# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1
FROM python:3.12-slim

WORKDIR /app

COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt

COPY . .

ENV PORT=5000
EXPOSE 5000

CMD ["python", "app.py"]
Explain in detail
ELI5: Explain like I'm 5

A Dockerfile is a packing list for a lunchbox, followed top to bottom: start from a ready-made base box (FROM), put in my sandwich (COPY), cut up the fruit (RUN), and when it is opened, eat the sandwich first (CMD). The packed lunchbox you end up with is the image.

InstructionWhat it does
FROMChooses the base image to start from. Every build stage starts with it (only comments, parser directives and ARG may come before it). FROM scratch means an empty image.
WORKDIRSets (and creates) the working directory for the following instructions and for the running container. Like cd but permanent.
COPY src destCopies files from your build context (your project folder) into the image. Prefer COPY for ordinary files.
ADDLike COPY but can also auto-extract local tar archives and fetch URLs. Because of that "magic", use COPY unless you specifically need extraction.
RUNExecutes a command at build time and saves the result as a new layer (install packages, compile code).
ENV KEY=valueSets an environment variable that exists at build time and in the running container.
EXPOSE 5000Documentation: "this app listens on port 5000". It does not publish the port; you still need -p at run time.
CMDThe default command that runs when the container starts.
Why COPY requirements.txt . first and the rest later? Docker caches layers. Your dependency list changes rarely, source code changes constantly. Installing dependencies before copying the code means a code edit doesn't re-download every library. We animate this soon.

Writing a Dockerfile, line by line (part 2)

  • CMD is an easily replaced default command.
  • ENTRYPOINT is the fixed program, and CMD gives its default arguments.
  • RUN happens at build time, CMD and ENTRYPOINT at container start.
ELI5: Explain like I'm 5

A coffee machine always makes coffee; press nothing and you get the default size, medium, or press "large" instead. Making coffee is the ENTRYPOINT, the default size is the CMD, and pressing "large" is passing arguments to docker run, replacing the CMD.

Exec form vs shell form


CMD ["python", "app.py"]     # exec form (JSON array): runs the program directly, receives signals (graceful stop). Preferred.
CMD python app.py            # shell form: wrapped in /bin/sh -c, so signals like SIGTERM may not reach your app

A hardened version of our Dockerfile with ARG, USER and HEALTHCHECK:


FROM python:3.12-slim
ARG APP_VERSION=dev
LABEL version="${APP_VERSION}"
WORKDIR /app
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt
COPY . .
RUN useradd --create-home appuser
USER appuser
EXPOSE 5000
HEALTHCHECK --interval=30s --timeout=3s --retries=3 \
  CMD python -c "import urllib.request; urllib.request.urlopen('http://localhost:5000/')" || exit 1
CMD ["python", "app.py"]
Explain in detail
InstructionWhat it does
ARG NAME=defaultA build-time-only variable, set with --build-arg NAME=value. Not available in the running container (unless you copy it into ENV). Do not pass secrets this way; they remain visible in image history.
USER appuserSwitches to a non-root user for following instructions and for the running process. Strongly recommended.
HEALTHCHECKTells Docker a command to run periodically to test if the app is really healthy (not just running). Status appears in docker ps as (healthy) or (unhealthy).
ENTRYPOINTThe fixed executable of the container. In exec form, arguments from CMD or from docker run are appended to it.
VOLUMEDeclares a mount point for persistent data (rarely needed; prefer the -v flag or Compose).
LABELAdds metadata key=value to the image (maintainer, version, source repo).

CMD vs ENTRYPOINT

CMD = default, easy to replace


CMD ["python", "app.py"]

docker run myimg runs python app.py.
docker run myimg bash replaces it with bash.

ENTRYPOINT = the program; CMD = its default arguments


ENTRYPOINT ["ping"]
CMD ["localhost"]

docker run myimg → ping localhost.
docker run myimg google.com → ping google.com.

ELI5, continued: You can swap the whole machine for a different one, but only with a special request (docker run --entrypoint), so that is rare.

RUN runs at build time; CMD/ENTRYPOINT run at container start time. Mixing these up is a very common beginner mistake.

Check yourself

Two quick questions on the last few slides. Not graded; wrong answers explain themselves.

What is the relationship between an image and a container?

Image is the template, container is the running instance.

Which Dockerfile instruction sets the default command that runs when the container starts?

RUN is build time, CMD is start time.

Image layers and the build cache

  • Each file-changing instruction makes one read-only layer.
  • Changing a layer rebuilds every layer above it.
  • Order instructions from least to most often changing.
ELI5: Explain like I'm 5

Each finished floor of a LEGO tower is kept. Change the top floor and only the top is rebuilt; change a lower floor and every floor above it must be rebuilt too. Each floor is an image layer, and the kept floors are the build cache.


$ docker history myapp:1.0     # see every layer and its size
Explain in detail
Layer: a read-only set of filesystem changes produced by one Dockerfile instruction (such as RUN or COPY). An image is a stack of layers identified by content hashes. Layers are shared: ten images based on python:3.12-slim store that base only once on disk.

So a good Dockerfile puts things that rarely change (the base image, installed packages) on the lower floors and things that change often (your code) near the top.

The animation shows Dockerfile instructions becoming layers, then a rebuild after a source-code change: layers above the change are rebuilt, the ones below are served from cache.

Bad order (cache busts every time)


COPY . .
RUN pip install -r requirements.txt

Any code change invalidates COPY . ., so pip reinstalls everything.

Good order (rarely-changing first)


COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install -r requirements.txt
COPY . .

Code edits only rebuild the last layer. Rebuilds take seconds.

Rule of thumb: order instructions from least-often-changing to most-often-changing. Combine related shell steps with && in one RUN and clean up in the same instruction (for example, delete package caches), otherwise the deleted files still live in an earlier layer.

Why should COPY requirements.txt and the install step come before COPY . . in a Dockerfile?

Compare with ours

Because dependencies change rarely, so their layer stays cached and only the code layers after it rebuild when you edit the app.

Multi-stage builds & .dockerignore

  • Multi-stage builds use several FROM lines in one Dockerfile.
  • Only the finished results are copied into the small final image.
  • .dockerignore keeps secrets and clutter out of the build context.
ELI5: Explain like I'm 5

A model ship is built in a messy workshop (the build stage); only the finished ship goes into a clean box (the final image).

Multi-stage build: a Dockerfile with several FROM lines. Early stages contain compilers and build tools; the final stage copies only the results (COPY --from=builder) so the shipped image is small and has fewer security holes.

# ---- Stage 1: build (large image with Node + dev tools) ----
FROM node:22 AS builder
WORKDIR /src
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci
COPY . .
RUN npm run build               # outputs static files into /src/dist

# ---- Stage 2: runtime (tiny image, only the result) ----
FROM nginx:1.27-alpine
COPY --from=builder /src/dist /usr/share/nginx/html
EXPOSE 80

.dockerignore


# .dockerignore
.git
node_modules
__pycache__/
*.pyc
.env
Dockerfile
docker-compose.yml
compose.yaml
*.log
Explain in detail

ELI5, continued: The glue, sawdust and tools (compilers and build tools) stay behind, so the customer gets a small box with fewer things that can go wrong. The .dockerignore file is a note on the workshop door listing things that should not even come in, such as old drafts and private papers (the .git folder, .env files).

The final image contains nginx and your built files, with no Node, no node_modules, no source code. Typically this shrinks images dramatically.

When you run docker build ., the folder . is the build context: everything in it is sent to Docker. A .dockerignore file lists what to leave out (same idea as .gitignore). It speeds up builds, keeps secrets out of images and avoids pointless cache busting.

If your .env file with passwords is copied by COPY . ., those secrets are baked into the image forever and anyone who can pull it can read them. Ignore it, and pass secrets at run time.

Smaller, safer images: best practices

  • Use slim or distroless bases and multi-stage builds to keep images small.
  • Do not run as root, and pin image versions.
  • Scan images and keep secrets out of them.
ELI5: Explain like I'm 5

Pack a small backpack with only what the trip needs: it is light to carry and there is little inside that can go wrong. The backpack is your image, so leave out shells, compilers and tools the app does not need to run.


$ trivy image myapp:1.0          # example scanner: lists known CVEs in your image
$ docker run --read-only --cap-drop ALL --user 1000:1000 myapp:1.0
Explain in detail

Keep it small

  • Use a slim or alpine base (python:3.12-slim, node:22-alpine). Alpine uses musl libc, which occasionally breaks compiled packages, so test it.
  • Consider distroless images (Google) for production: they contain only your app and its runtime, no shell or package manager.
  • Use multi-stage builds.
  • Install only what you need; use --no-install-recommends (apt) and --no-cache-dir (pip), and clean caches in the same RUN.
  • Use .dockerignore.

Keep it safe

  • Don't run as root: add a USER.
  • Pin versions: python:3.12-slim, never bare python or latest. For maximum safety pin the digest.
  • Scan images for known vulnerabilities (Trivy, Grype, Docker Scout) in CI.
  • No secrets in images (no ENV PASSWORD=..., no copied .env). Inject at run time or use BuildKit secrets.
  • Rebuild regularly to pick up base-image security patches.
  • Run with a read-only filesystem and dropped capabilities where possible (--read-only, --cap-drop ALL).

ELI5, continued: A suitcase stuffed with everything is slower to carry (to pull and start) and has more places for a problem to hide (more packages with known vulnerabilities).

Container security is a layered topic; see Module 13 (DevSecOps) for scanning in the pipeline.

Essential commands: run & manage containers

  • docker run starts a container, with flags for ports, names and volumes.
  • Use -d to detach, -it for a shell and --rm to clean up.
  • Publish ports with -p HOST:CONTAINER, then check with docker ps.

docker run -d -p 8080:80 -e GREETING=hi -v mydata:/data --name web nginx:1.27
PartMeaning
-dDetached: run in the background and print the container ID
-p 8080:80Publish: host port 8080 → container port 80 (HOST:CONTAINER)
-e KEY=valueSet an environment variable
-v mydata:/dataMount a volume named mydata at /data
--name webGive the container a friendly name (otherwise random like quirky_turing)
-itInteractive + terminal (for shells): docker run -it ubuntu bash
--rmDelete the container automatically when it stops

$ docker run -d -p 8080:80 --name web nginx:1.27
$ docker ps

Example output (your container ID will differ):

$ docker run -d -p 8080:80 --name web nginx:1.27 Unable to find image 'nginx:1.27' locally 1.27: Pulling from library/nginx ... Status: Downloaded newer image for nginx:1.27 b7e0c6c1f6a2d4a1d3c58f0e9d8a4e1c9a0b5d7f2e3c4b6a8d9e0f1a2b3c4d5e $ docker ps CONTAINER ID IMAGE COMMAND CREATED STATUS PORTS NAMES b7e0c6c1f6a2 nginx:1.27 "/docker-entrypoint.…" 5 seconds ago Up 4 seconds 0.0.0.0:8080->80/tcp web

docker ps -a                  # also show stopped containers
docker logs web               # print the container's output (stdout/stderr)
docker logs -f --tail 50 web  # follow the last 50 lines live
docker exec -it web bash      # open a shell inside the running container
docker exec web nginx -v      # run one command inside
docker stop web               # graceful stop (SIGTERM, then SIGKILL after a timeout)
docker start web              # start a stopped container again
docker restart web
docker rm web                 # delete a stopped container (docker rm -f to force)
Explain in detail
Visit http://localhost:8080 in a browser and you will see the nginx welcome page, served from inside the container.

Check yourself

Two quick questions on the last few slides. Not graded; wrong answers explain themselves.

You edit one app file that a late COPY . . step adds. Which layers does Docker rebuild?

Changing a layer rebuilds it and everything after it.

What is the main benefit of a multi-stage build?

Build tools stay behind, only the result is copied forward.

Essential commands: images, build, registry, cleanup

  • docker images lists images, and docker inspect shows object details.
  • docker system prune removes unused data, so read its warning.
  • Dangling images are untagged leftovers from rebuilding a tag.

docker pull python:3.12-slim          # download an image
docker images                         # list local images  (also: docker image ls)
docker build -t myapp:1.0 .           # build an image from ./Dockerfile, tag it myapp:1.0
docker tag myapp:1.0 myuser/myapp:1.0 # add another name (needed before pushing to Docker Hub)
docker login                          # authenticate to a registry
docker push myuser/myapp:1.0          # upload the image
docker rmi myapp:1.0                  # remove an image
docker inspect web                    # full JSON details of a container or image
docker system prune                   # delete stopped containers, unused networks, dangling images
$ docker images REPOSITORY TAG IMAGE ID CREATED SIZE myapp 1.0 3a9c1b2d4e5f 2 minutes ago 148MB nginx 1.27 a1b2c3d4e5f6 3 weeks ago 192MB $ docker inspect --format '{{range .NetworkSettings.Networks}}{{.IPAddress}}{{end}}' web 172.17.0.2 $ docker system prune WARNING! This will remove: - all stopped containers - all networks not used by at least one container - all dangling images - unused build cache Are you sure you want to continue? [y/N] y Total reclaimed space: 412.3MB
Dangling image: an untagged leftover image (shown as <none>), usually produced when you rebuild a tag and the old image loses its name.
Explain in detail

This is example output: IDs, dates and sizes will differ on your machine.

docker system prune -a --volumes also removes every image not used by a container, plus unused volumes, which can delete database data you wanted. Read the warning before pressing y.
Newer Docker also accepts the grouped form: docker container ls, docker image ls, docker image rm. They do the same as the short forms.

Data that survives: volumes vs bind mounts

  • A container's writable layer is temporary and vanishes with it.
  • Volumes are managed by Docker and suit databases and production data.
  • Bind mounts map a host folder, ideal for development.
  • tmpfs keeps data only in memory, never on disk.
ELI5: Explain like I'm 5

A container is a hotel room: at checkout it is cleaned and anything left behind is gone. A volume is the hotel's luggage room, where your bags wait for your next room. The room is the container's own filesystem; the luggage room is a volume Docker keeps outside it.

VolumeBind mount
WhereDocker-managed areaAny host path you choose
Use caseProduction data (DB)Local development, config files
PortableYesNo: depends on host folder layout

docker volume ls
docker volume inspect pgdata
docker volume rm pgdata        # only if no container uses it
Explain in detail

A container's writable layer is temporary. When you remove the container, everything written inside it is gone. For databases, uploads and logs you need storage that lives outside the container.

Volume

Created and managed by Docker (on Linux under /var/lib/docker/volumes). Best for databases and production data. Portable, can be backed up, works the same on all OSes.


docker volume create pgdata
docker run -v pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data postgres:16

Bind mount

Maps a specific folder from your host into the container. Perfect in development: edit code on the host, see changes instantly in the container.


docker run -v "$(pwd)":/app myapp

tmpfs

Stored in host memory only, never on disk; vanishes when the container stops. Good for sensitive temporary data.


docker run --tmpfs /tmp myapp
Add :ro to mount read-only: -v ./config:/etc/app:ro.

Docker networking

  • Each container has its own network namespace.
  • On a user-defined bridge, containers find each other by name.
  • Publish a port with -p to reach a container from outside.
DriverWhat it doesUse when
bridge (default)A private virtual switch on the host. Containers on it get private IPs and can talk to each other; outside traffic needs -p port publishing.Most single-host setups
hostThe container shares the host's network directly, with no isolation and no -p needed.Maximum network performance on Linux, special cases
noneNo network except loopback.Fully isolated jobs
overlaySpans multiple hosts (used by Swarm).Multi-host clusters
ELI5: Explain like I'm 5

Networked containers are classmates calling each other by name; outsiders enter through doors opened by -p.

Container DNS (what makes Compose service names work)

On a user-defined bridge network, Docker runs a small built-in DNS server, so containers find each other by name. (The default bridge does not provide this name lookup, so create your own.)


$ docker network create appnet
$ docker run -d --name db --network appnet -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=secret postgres:16
$ docker run -it --rm --network appnet alpine ping -c 2 db

Example output (your IP addresses and times will differ):

$ docker run -it --rm --network appnet alpine ping -c 2 db PING db (172.18.0.2): 56 data bytes 64 bytes from 172.18.0.2: seq=0 ttl=64 time=0.095 ms 64 bytes from 172.18.0.2: seq=1 ttl=64 time=0.112 ms --- db ping statistics --- 2 packets transmitted, 2 packets received, 0% packet loss round-trip min/avg/max = 0.095/0.103/0.112 ms

docker network ls
docker network inspect appnet
docker port web                # show published ports of a container
Explain in detail

Each container gets its own network namespace (its own IP and ports). Docker connects them with virtual networks.

ELI5, continued: The classroom is a user-defined bridge network, calling by name is Docker's built-in DNS, and the door is a published port. Children in another classroom (a different network) cannot call these children by name, and on the default bridge network there is no calling by name at all, which is why you create your own network.

The name db resolved to the container's IP automatically. Your app just uses the hostname db in its connection string. IPs may change, names don't.

-p 8080:80 binds on all host interfaces by default. For a service that should only be reachable from the host itself, use -p 127.0.0.1:8080:80.

Docker Compose: many containers, one file

  • Compose defines a multi-container app in one compose.yaml file.
  • One command starts, networks and stops the whole stack.
  • Use docker compose (V2), not the legacy docker-compose.
Docker Compose: a tool that defines and runs a multi-container application from one YAML file (compose.yaml). One command starts, networks and stops the whole stack. Use the modern V2 syntax docker compose (with a space), not the legacy docker-compose.
ELI5: Explain like I'm 5

The whole band plays from one sheet of music and starts on one count-in: the sheet is compose.yaml, the musicians are containers.


# compose.yaml  (no "version:" line needed in modern Compose)
services:
  web:                                  # service 1: our Flask app
    build: .                            # build image from ./Dockerfile
    ports:
      - "8000:5000"                     # host 8000 -> container 5000
    environment:
      DATABASE_URL: postgresql://app:secret@db:5432/appdb   # "db" = service name = DNS name
      REDIS_HOST: redis
    depends_on:
      db:
        condition: service_healthy      # wait until db passes its healthcheck
      redis:
        condition: service_started
    restart: unless-stopped             # restart on crash, unless manually stopped

  db:                                   # service 2: PostgreSQL
    image: postgres:16                  # pre-built image from Docker Hub
    environment:
      POSTGRES_USER: app
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: secret         # demo only! use secrets/.env in real life
      POSTGRES_DB: appdb
    volumes:
      - pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data # named volume keeps data
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U app -d appdb"]
      interval: 5s
      timeout: 3s
      retries: 5

  redis:                                # service 3: cache
    image: redis:7-alpine

volumes:
  pgdata:                               # declare the named volume
KeyMeaning
servicesThe containers that make up the app. Each key (web, db, redis) is a service and also its DNS hostname on the automatic network.
build / imageBuild from a Dockerfile, or pull a ready image.
portsPublished ports, "HOST:CONTAINER". Only web needs one; db and redis stay private on the internal network.
environmentEnvironment variables (or use env_file: .env).
depends_onStart order. With condition: service_healthy it waits for the healthcheck to pass, not just for the container to exist.
volumesMounts; top-level volumes: declares named volumes.
healthcheckHow Compose decides a service is ready.
restartRestart policy: no, always, on-failure, unless-stopped.

docker compose up -d           # create network + volumes, build, start everything in background
docker compose ps              # list the stack's containers
docker compose logs -f web     # follow logs of one service
docker compose exec db psql -U app -d appdb   # run a command in a service
docker compose down            # stop and remove containers and network (volumes kept)
docker compose down -v         # ... and delete volumes too (this deletes data)
Explain in detail

ELI5, continued: The count-in is docker compose up. Compose also puts the whole band (web, database, cache) on one stage (a shared network), so they can hear each other by name, and starts them in the order the sheet asks for (depends_on).

Passwords in a committed compose file are fine for a lab, never for production. Use an .env file excluded from Git, Docker/Compose secrets, or your cloud's secret manager.

Hands-on exercise: containerize a Flask app

Prerequisite: Docker installed (Docker Desktop, or Docker Engine on Linux) and docker version works.

  • Create a small Flask app, requirements.txt, Dockerfile and .dockerignore.
  • Build the image and run it, publishing port 8000.
  • Explore the container, then change code and watch the build cache.
  • Clean up the container and image.

Task 1: worked example

Step 1: create the project


mkdir flask-demo && cd flask-demo

app.py:


from flask import Flask
import os, socket

app = Flask(__name__)

@app.route("/")
def hello():
    return f"Hello from container {socket.gethostname()} (v{os.getenv('APP_VERSION', 'dev')})\n"

if __name__ == "__main__":
    app.run(host="0.0.0.0", port=5000)

requirements.txt:


flask==3.0.3

Dockerfile:


FROM python:3.12-slim
WORKDIR /app
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt
COPY . .
RUN useradd --create-home appuser
USER appuser
EXPOSE 5000
CMD ["python", "app.py"]

.dockerignore:


.git
__pycache__/
*.pyc
.env

Step 2: build and run


docker build -t flask-demo:1.0 .
docker run -d -p 8000:5000 --name flask flask-demo:1.0
curl http://localhost:8000

Example output:

$ curl http://localhost:8000 Hello from container 9f2c4d1e8a7b (vdev)

Task 2: finish it

Two commands are missing.


docker ps                         # see it running
docker logs flask                 # see the request log lines
docker exec -it flask sh          # step inside; try: whoami, ls, cat /etc/os-release
docker run -d -p 8001:5000 -e APP_VERSION=2 --name flask2 flask-demo:1.0   # a second container, different env
# last two: check the second container, then inspect the layers
Show hint

Call the second container on port 8001 with curl, and use the image name to list its layers.

Show answer

curl http://localhost:8001        # different container ID, version 2
docker history flask-demo:1.0     # inspect the layers

Task 3: on your own

Goal: edit greeting, rebuild as 1.1, clean up.

Success: CACHED shown, nothing left over.

Show hint

Edit app.py, run docker build with the tag 1.1, then stop, remove containers and remove both images.

Show answer

docker build -t flask-demo:1.1 .


docker stop flask flask2
docker rm flask flask2
docker rmi flask-demo:1.0 flask-demo:1.1
Explain in detail
The app must listen on 0.0.0.0, not 127.0.0.1. Inside a container, "localhost" means only the container itself, so the published port could never reach it.
We publish host port 8000 rather than 5000 because on recent macOS versions port 5000 is already used by the AirPlay Receiver.

Your container ID will differ. APP_VERSION is not set, so the app shows dev.

Step 4: change code and watch the cache

Edit the greeting text in app.py and rebuild: docker build -t flask-demo:1.1 .. Notice the pip install step reports CACHED; only the COPY . . layer onward is rebuilt.

Stretch goal: add a compose.yaml with your app plus redis:7-alpine, and make the page count visits using the redis Python package (add it to requirements.txt, connect to host redis).

Interview questions

Q1: What is the difference between an image and a container?

An image is a read-only, layered template containing the app and its dependencies. A container is a running instance of an image with an extra writable layer and an isolated process. Many containers can be created from one image.

Q2: How is a container different from a virtual machine?

A VM virtualizes hardware and runs a full guest OS with its own kernel under a hypervisor. A container is an isolated process sharing the host kernel, using namespaces and cgroups. Containers are lighter and start faster; VMs give stronger isolation.

Q3: What Linux features make containers possible?

Namespaces (isolation of PIDs, network, mounts, hostname, IPC, users), cgroups (resource limits and accounting) and union/overlay filesystems (layered, copy-on-write images).

Q4: CMD vs ENTRYPOINT?

ENTRYPOINT defines the fixed executable; CMD provides default arguments or a default command that is easily overridden by arguments to docker run. Often used together: ENTRYPOINT is the program, CMD its default flags.

Q5: COPY vs ADD?

Both copy files into the image. ADD can also extract local tar archives and download URLs, which makes it less predictable. Best practice is to use COPY unless you need those extras.

Q6: How does the Docker build cache work and how do you exploit it?

Each instruction produces a layer cached by its inputs. If an instruction and everything before it are unchanged, the cached layer is reused; a change invalidates it and all later layers. Put rarely-changing steps (installing dependencies) before frequently-changing ones (copying source code).

Q7: What is a multi-stage build and why use it?

A Dockerfile with several FROM stages where only the needed artifacts are copied into a final minimal image. It keeps compilers and build tools out of production, giving smaller, more secure images.

Q8: Volume vs bind mount?

A volume is created and managed by Docker and is best for persistent production data. A bind mount maps an existing host directory into the container, which is ideal for development but tied to the host's layout.

Q9: How do containers in Compose find each other?

Compose creates a user-defined bridge network with built-in DNS, so each service is reachable by its service name (for example db, redis).

Q10: How would you reduce image size and improve security?

Use slim/distroless base images, multi-stage builds, a .dockerignore, pinned versions, a non-root USER, no secrets in layers, and scan images for vulnerabilities in CI.

Quiz

1. What do containers share with the host machine?

Containers are isolated processes that share the host kernel; VMs are the ones with their own guest OS.

2. Which Dockerfile instruction runs a command at build time and creates a layer?

RUN executes during the build. CMD and ENTRYPOINT run when the container starts; EXPOSE only documents a port.

3. In docker run -p 8080:80 nginx, what is 8080?

The format is HOST:CONTAINER, so traffic to host port 8080 goes to container port 80.

4. Your database container is deleted and the data vanishes. What should you have used?

The container's writable layer is temporary. A volume lives outside the container and persists.

5. Why copy requirements.txt and install dependencies before copying all source code?

Layers are cached in order; putting rarely-changing steps first keeps rebuilds fast.

6. Which command is the modern way to start a Compose stack?

Compose V2 is the docker compose plugin (space, not hyphen). The old Python docker-compose is end-of-life.
