09

Kubernetes

Kubernetes (often written K8s) is a system that runs containers across many machines and keeps them running the way you described. You tell it "I want three copies of this app, always", and it places them, restarts them when they crash, scales them when traffic grows and replaces them with new versions without downtime.

What you will learn

Why orchestration exists, the control plane and worker node components, desired state and reconciliation, Pods, Deployments, Services, Ingress and Gateway API, configuration and secrets, storage, probes, autoscaling, RBAC, Helm, kubectl, debugging failing Pods, managed Kubernetes, and a hands-on exercise with kind.

Guess first

You are not expected to know these yet. Guessing before you read helps you remember the answer when you meet it.

You tell Kubernetes you want 3 copies of an app, and one copy crashes. What do you expect to happen?

Controllers keep comparing desired state with actual state.

Pods are replaced often and each new Pod gets a new IP address. How can other apps keep reaching yours?

A Service gives changing Pods one stable address.

Which part of a cluster stores the state of every object?

etcd is the cluster's memory.

Why orchestration, and what Kubernetes does

  • Production runs many services, with many copies, on many servers.
  • Placement, restarts, scaling and rollouts need constant attention.
  • Kubernetes automates this and keeps the cluster in your declared state.
ELI5: Explain like I'm 5

A conductor decides who sits where, when each musician plays, and who fills in for a missing player. Kubernetes is the conductor; your containers are the musicians.

Kubernetes: an open-source container orchestration platform that schedules containers onto a cluster of machines and continuously works to keep the cluster in the state you declared.
Explain in detail

One container on your laptop is easy. Production is different: dozens of services, each with several copies, spread over many servers. Someone has to answer questions like these all day:

  • Which server has enough free memory for this new container?
  • A server died at 3 a.m. Who restarts its containers elsewhere?
  • Traffic doubled. Who starts more copies, and who spreads requests among them?
  • We shipped version 2. How do we replace version 1 gradually, and roll back if it breaks?
  • How does the web container find the database container when IP addresses keep changing?

Doing this by hand or with scripts does not scale. A container orchestrator automates it.

ELI5, continued: The seats are the machines in the cluster. The conductor does not play an instrument: you hand over the score (your desired state), and the conductor keeps the music matching it as players come and go.

Scheduling

Picks a suitable machine for each Pod based on free CPU and memory and your rules.

Self-healing

Restarts failed containers, replaces Pods on dead nodes, and stops sending traffic to unhealthy ones.

Scaling

Change the replica count by hand or let an autoscaler do it from CPU or other metrics.

Rollouts and rollbacks

Rolling updates replace old Pods with new ones gradually; one command goes back.

Service discovery and load balancing

A stable name and virtual IP in front of changing Pods, with traffic spread across them.

Config and storage

Injects configuration and secrets, and attaches persistent storage to Pods.

History and Evolution

YearMilestoneWhy it mattered
c. 2003–2004Google builds Borg, an internal cluster managerProved that running everything as containers scheduled by software works at huge scale. Most Kubernetes ideas (Pods, labels, declarative jobs) descend from Borg experience.
2013Google's Omega research systemExplored a more flexible, shared-state scheduler. Lessons fed into Kubernetes design.
June 2014Kubernetes announced and open-sourced by GoogleBorg's ideas rebuilt as an open project, arriving just as Docker made containers popular.
July 2015Kubernetes v1.0; CNCF (Cloud Native Computing Foundation) foundedDeclared production-ready and handed to a neutral foundation, so no single company owned it.
c. 2017Kubernetes wins the "orchestration wars" against Docker Swarm and Apache MesosMajor cloud vendors adopted it, and Docker itself added Kubernetes support. It became the industry default.
2016–2019Custom Resource Definitions (CRDs) and the Operator patternYou can add your own object types (for example a "Database") and write controllers that manage them, extending Kubernetes into a general platform. CRDs reached GA in v1.16.
Dec 2020v1.20 deprecates dockershimKubernetes announced it would stop shipping a built-in adapter for the Docker Engine, because Docker does not implement the Container Runtime Interface (CRI).
May 2022v1.24 removes dockershimClusters now use CRI runtimes such as containerd or CRI-O directly. Images built with Docker still work, since they follow the OCI standard.
Aug 2022v1.25 removes PodSecurityPolicyReplaced by the built-in Pod Security Admission (namespace labels enforcing the Privileged, Baseline and Restricted standards).
Oct 2023Gateway API reaches v1.0 (GA)A more expressive, role-oriented successor to Ingress for routing external traffic.
2023–2025Native sidecar containers (alpha in v1.28, beta in v1.29, stable in v1.33 in April 2025)Init containers with restartPolicy: Always that start before the main container and keep running until it has stopped. This fixes startup and shutdown ordering for log shippers and proxies.
2023–2025In-place Pod resize (alpha in v1.27, beta in v1.33, stable in v1.35 in December 2025)Change a running container's CPU and memory requests and limits without recreating the Pod.
Aug 2024v1.31 moves cgroup v1 support to maintenance modeKubernetes is steering toward cgroup v2, the modern Linux resource-control interface. In v1.35 (December 2025) cgroup v1 support was deprecated and the kubelet refuses to start on cgroup v1 nodes by default.
April 2025v1.33: the nftables mode of kube-proxy becomes stableAn alternative to the older iptables mode for programming Service traffic rules, which scales better on large clusters.
Aug 2025v1.34: Dynamic Resource Allocation (DRA) becomes stableA standard way for Pods to request GPUs and other special hardware, important for AI and machine learning workloads.
Nov 2025Kubernetes project announces the retirement of the Ingress-NGINX controllerThe widely used controller received only best-effort maintenance until March 2026, when it was retired; since then there are no further releases or security fixes. Users are expected to migrate, usually to a Gateway API implementation. (The Ingress API itself still exists and other Ingress controllers are unaffected.)
Apr 2026v1.36: user namespaces for Pods become stableRoot inside a container can now map to an unprivileged user on the node, so a container escape no longer gives node-level root. v1.37 (August 2026) followed as the current release at the time of writing.

The pattern: Kubernetes keeps stable APIs but regularly replaces the pieces underneath (container runtime, security policy, traffic routing).

Architecture: control plane and worker nodes

  • A cluster has a control plane (brain) and worker nodes (muscle).
  • The control plane holds the API server, etcd, scheduler and controllers.
  • Worker nodes run the kubelet, a container runtime and kube-proxy.
Cluster: a set of machines (nodes) managed together. It has a control plane (the brain that makes decisions) and worker nodes (the muscle that runs your containers).
ELI5: Explain like I'm 5

In a school, the office assigns each child to a classroom. The office is the control plane, classrooms are worker nodes, and children are Pods.

Explain in detail

ELI5, continued: Each classroom has a teacher (the kubelet) who makes sure the assigned children are there and reports back to the office. The office's record book is etcd.

Control plane components

kube-apiserverThe front door. Every request (from kubectl, nodes, controllers) goes through this REST API. It validates and stores objects. Nothing talks to etcd except the API server.
etcdA consistent key-value database holding the entire cluster state. If you lose it without a backup, you lose the cluster's memory.
kube-schedulerWatches for Pods with no node, and chooses a node by filtering (does it fit?) then scoring (which fits best?).
kube-controller-managerRuns many control loops (controllers): Deployment, ReplicaSet, Node, Job... Each compares desired state with actual state and acts.
cloud-controller-managerTalks to the cloud provider API to create load balancers, attach disks and manage cloud nodes (only present on cloud clusters).

Worker node components

kubeletThe node's agent. Receives Pod specs from the API server, tells the container runtime to run them, runs probes, reports status.
Container runtimeActually runs containers, through the Container Runtime Interface (CRI). Common choices: containerd, CRI-O.
kube-proxyMaintains network rules on each node so traffic to a Service reaches one of its Pods.
Add-onsCoreDNS (cluster DNS), a CNI network plugin (Pod networking), metrics-server, and optionally a dashboard.
Controllers and the scheduler never send commands directly to kubelets. They write to the API server, and each component watches the API server for changes it cares about. This is why Kubernetes survives component restarts so well.

Kubectl apply flowing through the cluster

  • Follow one kubectl apply request from your terminal to a running Pod.
  • The API server validates the YAML and saves it in etcd.
  • Controllers create the ReplicaSet and Pods; the scheduler assigns each to a node.
  • The kubelet on that node asks the container runtime to start the containers.
Explain in detail

Follow one request from your terminal to a running Pod.

Kubectl sends your YAML to the API server. The API server authenticates and validates it and saves it in etcd. In the controller manager, the Deployment controller sees the new Deployment and creates a ReplicaSet, and the ReplicaSet controller creates the Pods. The scheduler notices unscheduled Pods and assigns each to a node. The kubelet on that node sees a Pod assigned to it and asks the container runtime to start the containers.

Declarative desired state and reconciliation

  • You declare what you want, not the steps to get there.
  • Scaling means changing the number you declared.
ELI5: Explain like I'm 5

You set a thermostat to 21 degrees, and it keeps measuring the room and switching the heater on or off to match. The 21 degrees is the desired state, the room is the actual state, and the thermostat is a controller: if a Pod disappears, it sees the gap and creates a new one without being asked again.

Explain in detail
  • A controller compares desired state with actual state and closes the gap.
  • The loop never stops, so crashed Pods are replaced automatically.
Reconciliation loop: a controller repeatedly compares the desired state (in etcd, from your YAML) with the actual state (what is really running) and takes the smallest action to close the gap. It never stops.

You rarely tell Kubernetes what to do. You tell it what you want.

Imperative (do this)

"Start container A. Start container B. Start container C. If B dies, start another."

Declarative (I want this)

"There should be 3 copies of this app." Kubernetes works out the steps and keeps correcting.

You never say "heat for five minutes" to a thermostat, only what you want.

With replicas set to 3, a Pod is killed and a replacement appears within moments; then the replica count is raised and extra Pods are created. The only thing that changed was the number you declared.

Why is a Pod replaced?

Compare with ours

Because when a Pod crashes, a controller keeps comparing the desired replica count with the actual one and creates Pods to close the gap.

Check yourself

Two quick questions on the last few slides. Not graded; wrong answers explain themselves.

In the kubectl apply flow, which component decides which node a new Pod runs on?

The scheduler assigns Pods to nodes.

What does desired state mean in Kubernetes?

Desired state is what you declared; controllers close the gap.

Pods, labels and selectors

  • A Pod is the smallest deployable unit, on one node.
  • Its containers share one IP address, localhost and volumes.
  • Every object has apiVersion, kind, metadata and spec.
  • Use a Deployment instead of bare Pods.
Pod: the smallest deployable unit in Kubernetes. One or more containers that share a network namespace (same IP, same localhost), can share volumes, and are always scheduled together on one node.
ELI5: Explain like I'm 5

A Pod is a pea pod: its peas (containers) share one shell and move together, meaning one IP address and one node.


apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: hello
  labels:
    app: hello
    tier: frontend
spec:
  containers:
    - name: web
      image: nginx:1.27
      ports:
        - containerPort: 80

Labels and selectors


kubectl get pods -l app=hello
kubectl get pods -l 'tier in (frontend,backend)'
Explain in detail

ELI5, continued: Sharing a shell also means the containers can talk to each other over localhost. Usually there is one pea. Sometimes a helper pea sits beside it, for example one that collects logs.

Every Kubernetes object has the same skeleton: apiVersion (which API group and version), kind (the type), metadata (name, labels, namespace) and spec (what you want). Objects also get a status that Kubernetes fills in.

Pods are mortal. If one dies it is replaced by a new Pod with a new name and a new IP. Never rely on a Pod's IP, and rarely create bare Pods. Use a Deployment.
Label: a key-value tag on any object (app=hello). A selector is a query over labels. This is how Services find Pods and Deployments find their ReplicaSets.

A Pod can also have several containers: init containers run to completion first (for example wait for a database), and sidecar containers run alongside the main one for the Pod's whole life.

ReplicaSets, Deployments, rolling updates and rollback

  • A ReplicaSet keeps a set number of identical Pods running.
  • A Deployment adds rolling updates and rollbacks on top.
  • maxSurge and maxUnavailable control the pace of an update.
  • kubectl rollout undo returns to the previous revision.
ReplicaSet: keeps a given number of identical Pods running. Deployment: manages ReplicaSets for you and adds rolling updates and rollbacks. You almost always create Deployments, not ReplicaSets.
ELI5: Explain like I'm 5

The office keeps exactly three children (Pods) on the team (ReplicaSet) and changes their uniform one at a time (Deployment).


spec:
  replicas: 4
  strategy:
    type: RollingUpdate
    rollingUpdate:
      maxSurge: 1          # at most 1 extra Pod above 4 during the update
      maxUnavailable: 0    # never drop below 4 ready Pods
    

kubectl set image deployment/web web=myrepo/web:2.0   # trigger a rolling update
kubectl rollout status deployment/web                 # watch progress
kubectl rollout history deployment/web                # list revisions
kubectl rollout undo deployment/web                   # roll back to the previous revision

Example output:

$ kubectl rollout status deployment/web Waiting for deployment "web" rollout to finish: 1 out of 4 new replicas have been updated... Waiting for deployment "web" rollout to finish: 3 of 4 updated replicas are available... deployment "web" successfully rolled out
Explain in detail

ELI5, continued: If a child goes home, the office sends a replacement. The uniform is your app's version: if the new one causes problems, the Deployment switches the team back to the old one (a rollback), because it keeps the old team rule (the previous ReplicaSet) on file.

When you change the Pod template (for example a new image tag), the Deployment creates a new ReplicaSet and slowly scales it up while scaling the old one down.

A rolling update only stays safe if Kubernetes can tell when a new Pod is ready. That needs a readiness probe (see the probes slide).

Services: stable addresses for changing Pods

  • A Service gives changing Pods one stable IP and DNS name.
  • It load-balances to Pods chosen by a label selector.
  • Types: ClusterIP, NodePort, LoadBalancer and ExternalName.
Service: a stable virtual IP and DNS name that load-balances traffic to a set of Pods chosen by a label selector. As Pods come and go, the Service endpoints update automatically.
ELI5: Explain like I'm 5

A helpline number (Service) stays the same while the people answering (Pods) change shifts.

TypeReachable fromUse for
ClusterIP (default)Inside the cluster onlyInternal services such as databases and backend APIs
NodePortOutside, at NodeIP:port on every node (default range 30000–32767)Quick tests, or as a building block for load balancers
LoadBalancerOutside, via a cloud load balancer with its own external IPExposing one service on a cloud cluster
ExternalNameMaps a Service name to an external DNS namePointing at something outside the cluster

apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: web
spec:
  type: ClusterIP
  selector:
    app: web          # send traffic to Pods with this label
  ports:
    - port: 80        # the Service's port
      targetPort: 8080  # the container's port
Explain in detail

ELI5, continued: Each call goes to one of the people on duty, chosen by their label. When someone starts or ends a shift, the list of who can take calls (the endpoints) updates automatically, so callers never notice.

Inside the cluster, other Pods reach it simply as http://web (same namespace) or http://web.myns.svc.cluster.local. CoreDNS provides these names. A headless Service (clusterIP: None) skips the virtual IP and returns the Pod IPs directly, which StatefulSets use.

Why put a Service in front of Pods instead of using Pod IPs?

Compare with ours

Because Pods are replaced and get new IPs, so a Service gives one stable address and DNS name that follows the Pods matching its label selector.

Ingress and Gateway API

  • One entry point can route many hostnames and paths to many Services.
  • Ingress rules need an installed Ingress controller to take effect.
  • Gateway API is the newer successor; Ingress-NGINX is retired.
Ingress: an object holding HTTP/HTTPS routing rules (host and path to Service). It does nothing alone; an Ingress controller (a Pod such as NGINX, Traefik or a cloud implementation) must be installed to act on the rules.
ELI5: Explain like I'm 5

A hotel receptionist (Ingress controller) follows the desk's list (Ingress rules) to send each guest to the right department (Service).


apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: HTTPRoute
metadata:
  name: web-route
spec:
  parentRefs:
    - name: public-gateway
  hostnames: ["app.example.com"]
  rules:
    - matches:
        - path: { type: PathPrefix, value: / }
      backendRefs:
        - name: web
          port: 80
Explain in detail

A LoadBalancer Service per app gets expensive: one cloud load balancer each. Ingress and Gateway API let one entry point route many hostnames and paths to many Services.

ELI5, continued: Guests arrive at one entrance and say where they want to go, such as the restaurant or the spa (a hostname or path). Without a receptionist the list does nothing, which is why an Ingress controller must be installed. Gateway API splits the job: the hotel sets up the entrance (the Gateway), and each department writes its own directions (HTTPRoutes).

Gateway API: the newer, more expressive successor to Ingress. It splits roles into GatewayClass (which implementation), Gateway (the listener, owned by the platform team) and routes such as HTTPRoute (owned by app teams). It reached v1.0 GA in October 2023 and supports header matching, traffic splitting and more without vendor-specific annotations.
The community Ingress-NGINX controller was retired: announced in November 2025, it received only best-effort maintenance until March 2026 and has had no releases or security fixes since. For new setups, use a Gateway API implementation or another maintained Ingress controller.

ConfigMaps, Secrets and Namespaces

  • ConfigMaps keep non-secret settings outside the image.
  • Secrets hold sensitive values, but base64 is not encryption.
  • Namespaces partition one cluster by team or environment.

apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: web-config
data:
  LOG_LEVEL: "info"
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
metadata:
  name: db-secret
type: Opaque
stringData:            # plain text here; Kubernetes stores it base64-encoded
  DB_PASSWORD: "change-me"
    

    containers:
      - name: web
        image: myrepo/web:1.0
        envFrom:
          - configMapRef: { name: web-config }
        env:
          - name: DB_PASSWORD
            valueFrom:
              secretKeyRef: { name: db-secret, key: DB_PASSWORD }

Namespaces

Namespace: a virtual partition of one cluster for grouping and isolating objects (teams, environments). Names must be unique within a namespace, not across the cluster. Built-in ones: default, kube-system, kube-public, kube-node-lease.
ELI5: Explain like I'm 5

Several companies share one office building (the cluster), each on its own floor (a namespace), so two companies can both have a "Meeting Room". The rooms are objects such as Pods.


kubectl create namespace staging
kubectl get pods -n staging
kubectl get pods -A          # all namespaces
Explain in detail

ConfigMap

Non-secret configuration (settings, feature flags, config files) kept outside the image, so the same image runs in dev and prod with different config.

Secret

Same idea for sensitive values (passwords, tokens, keys). Values are base64-encoded, which is encoding, not encryption.

Consume them in a Pod as environment variables or as files:

Anyone who can read the Secret object can decode it. By default Secrets sit unencrypted in etcd. Enable encryption at rest, restrict access with RBAC, and keep real secrets out of Git (use a secrets manager or tools like Sealed Secrets or External Secrets).

ELI5, continued: Floors keep things organised, but their doors are not locked by default: you still need rules (RBAC, network policies) to stop people wandering between floors. This is a different idea from the Linux kernel namespaces in the Docker module.

Check yourself

Two quick questions on the last few slides. Not graded; wrong answers explain themselves.

Why should you usually create a Deployment instead of a bare Pod?

Deployments add self-healing and rolling updates.

A Secret holds a database password. Which statement is true by default?

Base64 hides nothing; use RBAC and encryption at rest.

Volumes, PersistentVolumes and StorageClasses

A container's own filesystem disappears when it restarts. Kubernetes volumes attach storage to Pods; persistent storage outlives the Pod.

ELI5: Explain like I'm 5

A locker keeps a child's things when the child moves classroom. The child hands in a slip asking for "a 10 GB locker", and the locker supplier provides one if none is free. The locker is a PersistentVolume, the slip is a PersistentVolumeClaim, the supplier is a StorageClass.

ObjectMeaning
PersistentVolume (PV)A piece of real storage in the cluster (cloud disk, NFS share...).
PersistentVolumeClaim (PVC)A request for storage by a Pod: size and access mode. Kubernetes binds it to a matching PV.
StorageClassDescribes a kind of storage (for example fast SSD). With dynamic provisioning, a PV is created automatically when a PVC asks for that class.
emptyDirScratch space that lives as long as the Pod. Good for temporary files and sharing between containers.

apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  name: pgdata
spec:
  accessModes: ["ReadWriteOnce"]   # mountable read-write by one node
  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 10Gi
  # storageClassName: standard     # omit to use the cluster default
---
# in the Pod spec:
#   volumes:
#     - name: data
#       persistentVolumeClaim: { claimName: pgdata }
#   containers:
#     - volumeMounts:
#         - { name: data, mountPath: /var/lib/postgresql/data }
Access modes: ReadWriteOnce (one node), ReadOnlyMany (many nodes read), ReadWriteMany (many nodes write; needs storage that supports it, such as NFS). Check what your storage class supports.

StatefulSet, DaemonSet, Job and CronJob

  • StatefulSet gives Pods stable names and their own disks, for databases.
  • DaemonSet runs exactly one Pod on every node.
  • Job runs Pods until a task completes successfully.
  • CronJob creates Jobs on a schedule using cron syntax.
Explain in detail

StatefulSet

For apps that need stable identity and their own disk: databases, Kafka, ZooKeeper. Pods get ordered, stable names (db-0, db-1), stable DNS through a headless Service, and each gets its own PVC that stays with it.

ELI5

Deployment Pods are like children in a playground game: any child can take any place. StatefulSet Pods are like children with fixed seats and their own lockers: "db-0" always comes back to seat 0 and the same locker. The fixed seat is a stable name, and the locker is its own PersistentVolume.

DaemonSet

Runs exactly one Pod on every node (or every matching node). Use for node-level agents: log collectors, monitoring exporters, network plugins.

ELI5

Every classroom has exactly one class monitor, and a newly opened classroom automatically gets one too. The classrooms are nodes, and each monitor is the DaemonSet's Pod, such as a log collector on that node.

Job

Runs Pods until a task completes successfully (a data migration, a report), retrying on failure. Then it stops.

CronJob

Creates Jobs on a schedule using cron syntax.


apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: CronJob
metadata:
  name: nightly-backup
spec:
  schedule: "0 2 * * *"      # 02:00 every day
  jobTemplate:
    spec:
      template:
        spec:
          restartPolicy: OnFailure
          containers:
            - name: backup
              image: myrepo/backup:1.0

Resources, probes and autoscaling

  • The Horizontal Pod Autoscaler scales Pods based on metrics like CPU.

Requests and limits


resources:
  requests:
    cpu: "250m"        # 250 millicores = a quarter of one CPU core
    memory: "128Mi"
  limits:
    cpu: "500m"
    memory: "256Mi"

Probes

ProbeQuestion it answersIf it fails
startupProbeHas the app finished starting? (for slow starters)Container is restarted; other probes wait until it passes
livenessProbeIs the app still alive, or stuck?kubelet restarts the container
readinessProbeCan it take traffic right now?Pod is removed from Service endpoints, not restarted

readinessProbe:
  httpGet: { path: /healthz, port: 8080 }
  initialDelaySeconds: 5
  periodSeconds: 10
livenessProbe:
  httpGet: { path: /healthz, port: 8080 }
  periodSeconds: 20
  failureThreshold: 3
ELI5: Explain like I'm 5

The teacher (the kubelet) restarts a child who stops responding (liveness probe) and gives no work to one who is awake but not ready (readiness probe). Requests and limits are desk space: the request is reserved when choosing a classroom (the scheduler), the limit is the most the child may use. Over the memory limit the child is sent out (OOMKilled); over the CPU limit it is only slowed.

Horizontal Pod Autoscaler (HPA)


apiVersion: autoscaling/v2
kind: HorizontalPodAutoscaler
metadata:
  name: web
spec:
  scaleTargetRef: { apiVersion: apps/v1, kind: Deployment, name: web }
  minReplicas: 2
  maxReplicas: 10
  metrics:
    - type: Resource
      resource:
        name: cpu
        target: { type: Utilization, averageUtilization: 60 }
Explain in detail
  • Requests reserve CPU and memory; limits cap their use.
  • Failed liveness restarts the container; failed readiness stops its traffic.
Request: the amount of CPU or memory the scheduler reserves for a container when choosing a node. Limit: the maximum it may use. Exceeding the memory limit gets the container killed (OOMKilled); exceeding the CPU limit just slows it down (throttling).

Adds or removes Pods based on metrics, typically CPU. It needs metrics-server installed and CPU requests set on the containers.

RBAC basics and Helm

  • RBAC decides who may do what, using Roles and RoleBindings.
  • Give each application its own ServiceAccount with least privilege.
  • Helm packages YAML into charts; installing one creates a release.

RBAC (role-based access control)

RBAC: decides who may do what. A Role lists allowed verbs (get, list, create...) on resources within a namespace; a RoleBinding grants that Role to a user, group or ServiceAccount. ClusterRole and ClusterRoleBinding are the cluster-wide versions.

apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: Role
metadata: { name: pod-reader, namespace: staging }
rules:
  - apiGroups: [""]
    resources: ["pods"]
    verbs: ["get", "list", "watch"]
---
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: RoleBinding
metadata: { name: read-pods, namespace: staging }
subjects:
  - kind: User
    name: alice
    apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
roleRef:
  kind: Role
  name: pod-reader
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
    

kubectl auth can-i delete pods -n staging --as alice     # test a permission

Helm

ELI5: Explain like I'm 5

A Helm chart is a flat-pack furniture kit: all parts and instructions in one box, and you choose only a few options (values).


helm repo add podinfo https://stefanprodan.github.io/podinfo   # podinfo: a small demo app chart
helm install my-web podinfo/podinfo --set replicaCount=2
helm list
helm upgrade my-web podinfo/podinfo -f my-values.yaml
helm rollback my-web 1
helm uninstall my-web
Explain in detail
Give each application its own ServiceAccount with only the permissions it needs (least privilege). Avoid binding users to cluster-admin casually.
Helm: the package manager for Kubernetes. A chart is a bundle of templated YAML plus default values; installing a chart creates a named release that you can upgrade and roll back.

ELI5, continued: The assembled furniture in your room is a release. Want a different colour later? Change the option and reassemble (helm upgrade). Do not like the result? Go back to the previous version (helm rollback).

A full annotated example: Deployment, Service and Ingress


apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: web
  labels: { app: web }
spec:
  replicas: 3                       # desired number of Pods
  selector:
    matchLabels: { app: web }       # which Pods this Deployment owns
  template:                         # the Pod blueprint
    metadata:
      labels: { app: web }          # must match the selector above
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: web
          image: myrepo/web:1.0     # pinned tag, not latest
          ports:
            - containerPort: 8080
          env:
            - name: LOG_LEVEL
              value: "info"
          resources:
            requests: { cpu: "100m", memory: "128Mi" }
            limits:   { cpu: "500m", memory: "256Mi" }
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet: { path: /healthz, port: 8080 }
          livenessProbe:
            httpGet: { path: /healthz, port: 8080 }
            initialDelaySeconds: 10
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: web
spec:
  selector: { app: web }            # picks the Pods labelled app=web
  ports:
    - port: 80
      targetPort: 8080
---
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: web
spec:
  ingressClassName: nginx           # which controller handles this; depends on what is installed
  rules:
    - host: app.example.com
      http:
        paths:
          - path: /
            pathType: Prefix
            backend:
              service:
                name: web           # the Service above
                port: { number: 80 }

Traffic flow: browser, then the Ingress controller (matches host and path), then Service web (virtual IP), then one of three Pods on port 8080. The label app: web ties all three objects together.

The selector.matchLabels must match template.metadata.labels, or the API server rejects the Deployment. Likewise, a Service whose selector matches no Pods has no endpoints and silently sends traffic nowhere.

Check yourself

Two quick questions on the last few slides. Not graded; wrong answers explain themselves.

A container's readiness probe fails, but its process is still running. What happens?

Readiness controls traffic; liveness controls restarts.

A container writes data to its own filesystem and then restarts. What happens to the data?

Container filesystems are temporary; persistent storage outlives Pods.

Essential kubectl commands


kubectl get nodes                          # list machines in the cluster
kubectl get pods -o wide                   # list Pods with node and IP
kubectl get deploy,svc                     # several kinds at once
kubectl apply -f app.yaml                  # create or update from a file
kubectl delete -f app.yaml                 # delete what the file describes
kubectl describe pod web-abc123            # details and recent events
kubectl logs web-abc123                    # container output
kubectl logs -f web-abc123 -c web          # follow a specific container
kubectl logs web-abc123 --previous         # logs of the previous (crashed) container
kubectl exec -it web-abc123 -- sh          # shell inside a Pod
kubectl port-forward svc/web 8080:80       # tunnel localhost:8080 to the Service
kubectl scale deployment web --replicas=5
kubectl get events --sort-by=.metadata.creationTimestamp
kubectl config get-contexts                # which clusters kubectl can talk to
kubectl config use-context kind-demo

Example output:

$ kubectl get nodes NAME STATUS ROLES AGE VERSION demo-control-plane Ready control-plane 3m v1.xx.x $ kubectl get pods NAME READY STATUS RESTARTS AGE web-6d8f7c9b5d-4k2xj 1/1 Running 0 2m web-6d8f7c9b5d-9qwlp 1/1 Running 0 2m web-6d8f7c9b5d-tn7zr 1/1 Running 0 2m $ kubectl get deploy NAME READY UP-TO-DATE AVAILABLE AGE web 3/3 3 3 2m

This is example output: the version and the random name suffixes differ on your machine.

Generate YAML instead of typing it: kubectl create deployment web --image=nginx:1.27 --replicas=3 --dry-run=client -o yaml > web.yaml. Use kubectl explain pod.spec.containers to read built-in field documentation.

Debugging Pods: common failure states

Start every investigation with the same two commands: kubectl get pods to see the STATUS, then kubectl describe pod NAME and read the Events at the bottom.

StatusWhat it meansTypical causes and fixes
PendingThe Pod was accepted but is not running yet, usually because the scheduler found no node for it.Events show FailedScheduling. Causes: requests larger than any node's free resources, node taints with no matching toleration, a nodeSelector that matches nothing, or an unbound PVC. Fix: add nodes, lower requests, correct selectors, check kubectl get pvc.
ImagePullBackOff / ErrImagePullThe kubelet cannot download the image and is retrying with growing delays.Typo in image name or tag, tag does not exist, registry unreachable, or a private registry without credentials. Fix: correct the image, or create a docker-registry Secret and reference it with imagePullSecrets.
CrashLoopBackOffThe container starts, exits, and Kubernetes keeps restarting it with increasing delays.App crashes at startup: bad config or missing env var, cannot reach database, wrong command, or a failing liveness probe. Fix: kubectl logs POD --previous to see why it died; check exit code in describe.
OOMKilled (last state; exit code 137)The container exceeded its memory limit and was killed.Raise the memory limit or fix the memory leak.
CreateContainerConfigErrorThe container could not be configured.Referenced ConfigMap or Secret does not exist, or a key is missing.
Running but 0/1 ReadyContainer is up but failing its readiness probe, so it gets no traffic.Wrong probe path or port, or the app is slow to start (add a startupProbe).

kubectl get pods
kubectl describe pod web-abc123          # read the Events section
kubectl logs web-abc123 --previous       # why did the last run die?
kubectl get endpointslices -l kubernetes.io/service-name=web   # does the Service have any Pods behind it?
kubectl run tmp --rm -it --image=busybox:1.36 -- sh    # throwaway Pod to test DNS and connectivity
ELI5: Explain like I'm 5

A toy stops right after it starts, again and again, and the parent waits longer each time before switching it back on. To fix it, you open the toy and look. The toy is the container, the parent is the kubelet, the wait is the back-off, and opening it is reading the logs.

Check yourself

Two quick questions on the last few slides. Not graded; wrong answers explain themselves.

A Pod is in CrashLoopBackOff. Which command shows why the previous run died?

Read the previous container's logs, then describe the Pod.

A Pod stays Pending and describe shows FailedScheduling. What is a likely cause?

Pending usually means the scheduler found no suitable node.

Managed Kubernetes and local clusters

  • Running the control plane yourself is real work, so providers offer to run it.
  • EKS, GKE and AKS are the managed services from AWS, Google and Azure.
  • The Kubernetes API is the same everywhere, so your YAML and kubectl skills carry over.
  • kind and minikube give you local clusters for learning.
ServiceProviderWhat you manage
EKS (Elastic Kubernetes Service)AWSWorker nodes (or use managed node groups or Fargate); AWS runs the control plane
GKE (Google Kubernetes Engine)Google CloudStandard mode: you manage node pools. Autopilot mode: Google manages nodes too
AKS (Azure Kubernetes Service)Microsoft AzureNode pools; Azure runs the control plane

Local clusters for learning

Explain in detail

Running the control plane yourself (backups of etcd, upgrades, certificates, high availability) is real work. Cloud providers offer to run it for you.

The Kubernetes API is the same everywhere, so your YAML and kubectl skills carry over. Differences show up in networking, load balancers, storage classes, IAM integration and pricing.

  • kind (Kubernetes in Docker): nodes are Docker containers. Fast, ideal for labs and CI.
  • minikube: a single-node cluster in a VM or container, with handy add-ons.
Clusters cost money while they run. Delete test clusters when finished, and set budget alerts on your cloud account.

Hands-on exercise: run, scale, heal and update an app with kind

  • Needs Docker, kubectl and kind installed.
  • You create a cluster, deploy an app, then watch self-healing.
  • You scale, roll an update forward and back, and provoke a failure.
  • Clean up the cluster at the end.

kubectl cluster-info --context kind-demo

Example output (your version will differ):

$ kubectl get nodes NAME STATUS ROLES AGE VERSION demo-control-plane Ready control-plane 1m v1.xx.x

Save as web.yaml:


apiVersion: apps/v1

Task 2: finish it

Self-healing, then scaling.


kubectl get pods
kubectl delete pod web-xxxxxxxxxx-yyyyy     # use a real name from the list
kubectl get pods                            # a replacement is already starting
# now scale to 5 replicas and confirm there are 5 Pods
Show hint

The scaling command is kubectl scale on the Deployment, with a replicas flag.

Show answer

kubectl scale deployment web --replicas=5
kubectl get pods

Task 3: on your own

Goal: update to nginx:1.27 and roll back, break the image and recover, delete the cluster. Success: the Image line shows nginx:1.26.

Show hint

Use kubectl set image, then kubectl rollout undo. A tag that does not exist gives ErrImagePull. Clean up with kind delete cluster.

Show answer

kubectl set image deployment/web web=nginx:1.27
kubectl rollout status deployment/web
kubectl rollout history deployment/web
kubectl rollout undo deployment/web
kubectl describe deployment web | grep Image

kubectl set image deployment/web web=nginx:does-not-exist
kubectl get pods                 # new Pods show ErrImagePull / ImagePullBackOff
kubectl describe pod NAME        # read the Events
kubectl rollout undo deployment/web

kind delete cluster --name demo
Explain in detail

Prerequisites: Docker running, plus kubectl and kind installed.

In another terminal, curl http://localhost:8080 returns the nginx welcome page.

Notice that most of the old Pods kept serving traffic the whole time. With the default settings (maxUnavailable: 25%) a rolling update takes down at most about a quarter of the old Pods before new ones are ready, so a broken image never takes over the whole app.

Interview questions

Q1: What problems does Kubernetes solve?

It automates scheduling, scaling, self-healing, rolling updates, service discovery and configuration of containers across a cluster of machines.

Q2: Name the control plane components and their roles.

kube-apiserver (front door for all requests), etcd (cluster state store), kube-scheduler (assigns Pods to nodes), kube-controller-manager (runs control loops), and cloud-controller-manager (cloud integration).

Q3: What runs on a worker node?

The kubelet (node agent), a container runtime such as containerd, and kube-proxy (Service networking rules), plus add-ons like CoreDNS and a CNI plugin.

Q4: What is the difference between a Pod, a ReplicaSet and a Deployment?

A Pod runs containers. A ReplicaSet keeps a set number of identical Pods. A Deployment manages ReplicaSets and adds declarative rolling updates and rollbacks.

Q5: Explain the Service types.

ClusterIP exposes inside the cluster only; NodePort opens a port on every node; LoadBalancer provisions an external cloud load balancer; ExternalName maps to an external DNS name.

Q6: Liveness vs readiness probe?

A failing liveness probe makes the kubelet restart the container. A failing readiness probe removes the Pod from Service endpoints so it receives no traffic, without restarting it.

Q7: What does CrashLoopBackOff mean and how do you debug it?

The container keeps starting and crashing, and Kubernetes backs off between restarts. Run kubectl logs --previous and kubectl describe pod to find the cause (config error, failed dependency, bad command, failing liveness probe, or OOM kill).

Q8: What is the difference between requests and limits?

Requests are what the scheduler reserves when placing the Pod. Limits are the ceiling at runtime: CPU is throttled above it, memory over the limit leads to an OOM kill.

Q9: Is a Kubernetes Secret encrypted?

By default it is only base64-encoded and stored unencrypted in etcd. Enable encryption at rest, limit access with RBAC and consider an external secrets manager.

Q10: Why was dockershim removed and what does it mean for Docker images?

Dockershim was an adapter that let the kubelet use Docker Engine, which does not implement the CRI. It was removed in v1.24 so clusters use CRI runtimes (containerd, CRI-O) directly. Docker-built images still work because they follow the OCI image format.

Quiz

1. Which component is the only one that talks to etcd?

All other components go through the API server, which reads and writes etcd.

2. You declare replicas: 3 and one Pod crashes. What happens?

Controllers continually reconcile actual state with desired state.

3. Which Service type is reachable only from inside the cluster?

ClusterIP is the default and internal only.

4. A Pod shows ImagePullBackOff. What is the most likely cause?

The kubelet cannot pull the image. Check the name and tag, and imagePullSecrets for private registries.

5. What does a failing readiness probe do?

Readiness controls traffic; liveness controls restarts.

6. Which object runs exactly one Pod on every node?

DaemonSets suit node-level agents like log collectors.

10

Cloud Computing (AWS-focused)

Almost every modern DevOps job runs on someone else's computers: Amazon, Microsoft or Google. This module explains what "the cloud" really is, the vocabulary every engineer must know (IaaS, regions, availability zones, shared responsibility) and the core AWS services (IAM, EC2, VPC, S3, RDS, load balancers, Lambda, EKS…), finishing with a hands-on exercise on the AWS CLI.

What you will learn

Renting vs buying computers · IaaS/PaaS/SaaS · public/private/hybrid · regions & AZs · shared responsibility · IAM · EC2 · VPC · S3 · RDS/DynamoDB · ELB & Auto Scaling · Route 53 · CloudWatch · Lambda · containers on AWS · pricing & FinOps · Well-Architected

Guess first

You are not expected to know these yet. Guessing before you read helps you remember the answer when you meet it.

A whole data centre in your region loses power. Which design keeps your website running?

Spread across at least two AZs.

A company's customer files sit in a cloud bucket that anyone on the internet can read. Whose job was it to prevent that?

Misconfiguration is the customer's side.

A program on a cloud server must read files from storage. What is the safest way to give it access?

Roles give temporary credentials.

Why does the cloud exist?

  • Before the cloud, you bought servers up front and guessed your traffic.
  • Going viral or flopping both cost money: too few or too many servers.
  • Cloud means pay as you go, new servers in minutes, and easy scaling.
  • Servers created by an API call can be created by code.
ELI5: Explain like I'm 5

Factories once ran their own generators; now they plug into the grid and pay for what they use. The cloud is that grid for computing.

Explain in detail

Imagine it is 2003 and you want to launch a website. Before you can serve even one visitor you must:

  • Estimate how many visitors you will get (nobody can do this well).
  • Buy physical servers, network switches and cables, and wait weeks or months for delivery.
  • Rent space in a data centre with power, cooling and security guards.
  • Hire people to replace broken disks at 3 a.m.

If your site goes viral, you cannot buy servers fast enough. If nobody visits, you paid for machines that sit idle. Either way, you spent a lot of money up front (called CapEx, capital expenditure) before learning whether your idea works.

ELI5, continued: The power company's plants are the provider's data centres. Like electricity, you can use a little or a lot, switch it off when you are done, and pay only for what the meter recorded.

Pay as you go

No up-front purchase. A test server for 2 hours costs a few cents, not a few thousand.

Minutes, not months

A new server, database or network appears after one command or click.

Scale up and down

Handle a sale-day spike with 100 servers, then shrink back to 5 at night.

This is perfect for DevOps: if servers can be created by an API call, then code can create them. That is exactly what Infrastructure as Code (next module) does.

Why does pay-as-you-go suit a new project?

Compare with ours

Because you cannot predict traffic, so renting by usage avoids paying up front for servers that may sit idle or run out.

History & Evolution

The idea of "computing as a utility" is old. The technology to deliver it at scale arrived in the 2000s and keeps evolving.

YearMilestoneWhy it mattered
1960sTime-sharing mainframes; the idea of "utility computing" is proposed (John McCarthy spoke of computing as a public utility in 1961)Many users shared one expensive computer and paid for use. The seed of the cloud idea.
1999VMware ships its first product (VMware Workstation) and x86 virtualization starts to go mainstreamOne physical machine can be carved into many virtual machines. Without this, clouds could not exist.
1999Salesforce launches, delivering business software over the webAn early, famous example of SaaS: no installation, just a browser and a subscription.
Mar 2006Amazon S3 launches (storage by the gigabyte)Often considered the start of modern public cloud infrastructure services.
Aug 2006Amazon EC2 launches (beta): rent virtual servers by the hourInfrastructure becomes an API. Startups no longer need to buy hardware.
2008Google App Engine previewA mainstream PaaS: upload code, Google runs it.
2010Microsoft Azure becomes generally available; OpenStack open-source cloud software is launched (by Rackspace and NASA)Competition for AWS, and an open-source way to build your own private cloud.
2014AWS Lambda announcedBirth of mainstream serverless / FaaS: run a function, pay per execution, manage no servers.
2017AWS introduces the Nitro System (with C5 instances) and FargateNitro moves networking, storage and security work onto dedicated hardware cards and a thin hypervisor, which is the base of every modern EC2 instance. Fargate runs containers without you managing any servers.
2018Amazon EKS becomes generally available; AWS Graviton (Arm-based) processors debut in EC2; AWS open-sources FirecrackerKubernetes becomes a managed cloud product; Arm chips offer cheaper compute, and later generations of Graviton followed. Firecracker is the lightweight micro-VM technology that runs Lambda and Fargate workloads.
Late 2010s →Multi-cloud strategies and FinOps (cloud financial management) become common practiceCompanies learn that unmanaged cloud bills grow fast, and that cost is an engineering concern.
2023 →Generative-AI boom: demand for GPU and AI accelerator capacity explodesCloud providers race to add GPU/accelerator capacity and managed AI services; GPU availability and cost become a major planning topic.
Nov 2023Broadcom completes its acquisition of VMware and changes its licensingMany companies running private virtualization re-examine their costs, and some speed up moves to public cloud or other hypervisors.
2024AWS starts charging for every public IPv4 address (Feb); Google, AWS and Microsoft waive data-transfer-out fees for customers leaving their cloud, ahead of the EU Data ActIPv4 addresses are scarce, so they now carry an hourly cost, which pushes designs towards private subnets and IPv6. Leaving a cloud became cheaper, which reduces lock-in.
July 2025AWS changes its Free Tier for new accounts to a credit-based free planNew accounts get credits and a time-limited free plan instead of the old 12-month allowances. Always read the current Free Tier page.
Notice the pattern: each step makes you manage less (hardware → virtual machine → container → function). The industry keeps moving up the stack.

What is cloud computing?

  • Cloud is on-demand computing, billed as you go.
  • It replaces big up-front purchases with pay-for-what-you-use billing.
  • NIST lists five essential cloud characteristics.
Cloud computing: on-demand delivery of computing resources (servers, storage, databases, networking, software) over the internet, with pay-as-you-go pricing. A widely used definition is from NIST (the US National Institute of Standards and Technology).
ELI5: Explain like I'm 5

Owning your servers (on-premises) is like owning a house; the cloud is like a hotel: book a room when needed, stop paying when you leave.

On-premises vs cloud

On-premisesCloud
Cost modelBig up-front purchase (CapEx)Pay for what you use (OpEx)
Time to get a serverWeeks to monthsMinutes
CapacityGuess in advance; idle or overloadedGrow and shrink on demand
Hardware careYour team (disks, power, cooling)The provider
ControlTotal control, including of the physical machineControl of what you rent; the provider owns the rest
Good fitStrict data rules, steady predictable load, existing investmentVariable load, fast experiments, global reach, small teams

The five NIST essential characteristics

CharacteristicPlain English
On-demand self-serviceYou create resources yourself via console/CLI/API, without phoning anyone.
Broad network accessReach it from anywhere over standard networks (laptop, phone, other servers).
Resource poolingMany customers share the provider's big pool of hardware (multi-tenancy), kept isolated from each other.
Rapid elasticityResources can be added or removed quickly, even automatically, to match demand.
Measured serviceUsage is metered, so you are billed for exactly what you consume.
Explain in detail

ELI5, continued: Owning a house means paying a lot up front, fixing the roof yourself and paying for empty rooms; in a hotel, someone else does the repairs. The hotel chain also has branches in many cities, so you can stay close to wherever your friends (users) are.

Service models & deployment models

  • IaaS, PaaS and SaaS differ in how much you manage versus the provider.
  • FaaS (serverless) runs functions when triggered; CaaS runs your containers.
  • Public, private and hybrid describe where the resources live.
  • Multi-cloud adds complexity, so master one cloud first.
ELI5: Explain like I'm 5

Cook pizza in your own kitchen (on-premises), rent an equipped kitchen and cook yourself (IaaS), give your own recipe to a restaurant's cooks (PaaS), or order from the menu and just eat (SaaS). The kitchen is the hardware, your recipe is your code, the meal is the application.

LayerOn-prem (make at home)IaaS (take & bake)PaaS (delivery)SaaS (restaurant)
ApplicationYouYouYouProvider
DataYouYouYouYou (your content) / Provider (platform)
Runtime, middlewareYouYouProviderProvider
Operating systemYouYouProviderProvider
Virtualization, servers, storage, networkingYouProviderProviderProvider
ExamplesYour own data centreAWS EC2, Azure VMs, GCEElastic Beanstalk, Heroku, App EngineGmail, Salesforce, Microsoft 365

Deployment models

ModelWhat it isExample
Public cloudResources owned by a provider and shared (securely isolated) among many customers over the internet.AWS, Azure, Google Cloud
Private cloudCloud-style infrastructure used by one organisation only, in its own data centre or dedicated hosting.OpenStack in a company data centre
Hybrid cloudPrivate/on-prem and public cloud connected and used together.Database on-prem for compliance, web tier on AWS
Multi-cloudUsing more than one public cloud provider.Analytics on Google Cloud, apps on AWS
Explain in detail

ELI5, continued: The more "as a service", the less you manage but the less you can change: in a rented kitchen you choose every ingredient, while from a menu you take the dish as it comes.

FaaS / Serverless

Function as a Service: you upload a small function; the cloud runs it only when triggered and bills per execution (e.g. AWS Lambda). "Serverless" does not mean no servers; it means you do not manage them.

CaaS

Container as a Service: the provider runs and manages the platform for your containers (e.g. Amazon ECS, EKS, Azure AKS, Google GKE). A middle ground between IaaS and PaaS.

Multi-cloud sounds safe ("no lock-in!") but it multiplies complexity, skills and cost. Most teams are better off mastering one cloud first, and using portable tools (containers, Terraform) to keep options open.

Regions, Availability Zones & Edge locations

  • A Region is a geographic area with several isolated data-centre groups.
  • An Availability Zone is one or more separate data centres inside a region.
  • Edge locations sit near users to deliver content quickly.
  • Choose a region by latency, compliance, service availability and price.
ELI5: Explain like I'm 5

A courier has hubs in many cities, and each city has several depots with their own power, so if one closes the others keep delivering. Small lockers near homes hold popular parcels. The cities are Regions, the depots are Availability Zones, the lockers are edge locations.

Choosing a region, considerWhy
LatencyPick a region near most of your users.
Data-residency / complianceLaws may require data to stay in a country.
Service availabilityNot every service/feature exists in every region.
PricePrices differ per region.
Explain in detail

ELI5, continued: You choose which city handles your parcels (the Region your resources live in), and they stay there unless you ask for copies elsewhere (replication). Spreading work over two or more depots keeps deliveries going if one depot closes.

Region

A geographic area containing multiple, isolated data-centre groups, named like us-east-1 or ap-south-1 (Mumbai). Resources live in a region you choose. Regions are independent; AWS does not move your data out of the region you chose unless you (or a feature you turn on, such as replication) do so.

Availability Zone (AZ)

One or more discrete data centres within a region, with independent power, cooling and networking, connected by fast low-latency links. Named like ap-south-1a, ap-south-1b. Spreading your app across 2+ AZs protects you from a single data-centre failure.

Edge location

A point of presence close to end users, used by services such as CloudFront (CDN) and Route 53 to cache content and answer requests nearer to the user, reducing latency.

"Highly available" on AWS usually means: run at least two copies of everything in two different AZs behind a load balancer.

Check yourself

Two quick questions on the last few slides. Not graded; wrong answers explain themselves.

You rent a virtual machine and patch its operating system and run your own web server on it. Which service model is that?

IaaS means you manage the OS and above.

How does cloud billing differ from buying servers?

Pay as you go replaces up-front CapEx.

The Shared Responsibility Model

  • You secure what you put in it: data, access, code.
  • Most breaches come from customer misconfigurations, not the provider.
ELI5: Explain like I'm 5

The hotel looks after the walls, lifts and front entrance; you lock your door, use the safe and choose who gets a key card. The hotel is the cloud provider (security of the cloud); your room is your data, accounts and settings (security in the cloud). If someone walks in through a door you left open, that is not the hotel's fault.

Explain in detail
  • The provider secures the cloud itself: buildings, hardware, virtualization.
Shared Responsibility Model: the provider is responsible for the security of the cloud (physical data centres, hardware, the virtualization layer); the customer is responsible for security in the cloud (their data, identities and access, operating system patches on VMs, network rules, application code, configuration).

How much is yours depends on the room type: in a self-catering flat (a VM) you also look after the kitchen (patch the operating system); in a full-service room (a managed service) the hotel does more.

AWS handles ("of the cloud")

  • Physical buildings, guards, power
  • Servers, storage devices, network hardware
  • Hypervisor / virtualization layer
  • Managed-service internals (e.g. RDS patching of the engine host, if you use RDS)

You handle ("in the cloud")

  • Who can log in (IAM, MFA)
  • Your data and whether it is encrypted
  • Security groups and firewall rules
  • OS patches on EC2 instances
  • Your application code and its secrets
The most common cloud breaches are customer misconfigurations: a public S3 bucket, a database open to the whole internet, leaked access keys committed to GitHub. They are your side of the line.

The more managed the service (SaaS > PaaS > IaaS), the more the provider handles, but you always keep responsibility for your data and for who has access.

Why is a public bucket your fault?

Compare with ours

Because the provider secures the cloud itself, while access rules and configuration of your own resources are the customer's responsibility.

IAM: Identity & Access Management

  • IAM controls who can do what on which AWS resources.
  • Users hold long-term credentials; roles give temporary ones.
  • Everything is denied by default; an explicit Deny wins.
  • Apply least privilege and turn on MFA.
ELI5: Explain like I'm 5

In an office, everyone gets a key card, and a list says which doors it opens. Cards are users and roles, the list is a policy, and IAM checks every door.

AWS IAM: the service that controls who (authentication) can do what (authorisation) on which AWS resources. It is global and free to use.
ConceptMeaning
Root userThe all-powerful identity created with the account email. Enable MFA, create no access keys for it, and do not use it for daily work.
UserA person or application identity with long-term credentials (password and/or access keys).
GroupA collection of users; attach a policy once to the group (e.g. "developers").
RoleAn identity with temporary credentials that anyone/anything authorised can assume. EC2 instances, Lambda functions and CI pipelines should use roles instead of stored keys.
PolicyA JSON document defining allowed/denied actions on resources.
MFAMulti-factor authentication: password plus a second factor (authenticator app or hardware key).

{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Action": ["s3:GetObject", "s3:ListBucket"],
      "Resource": [
        "arn:aws:s3:::my-example-bucket",
        "arn:aws:s3:::my-example-bucket/*"
      ]
    }
  ]
}
Explain in detail

ELI5, continued: At the door, IAM can also ask for a second proof, like a code on your phone (MFA). A new employee gets a card for their own office, not a master card for the whole building. That is least privilege.

A policy that allows read-only access to one S3 bucket and nothing else:

Reading it: Effect = Allow or Deny; Action = which API operations; Resource = which things, identified by an ARN (Amazon Resource Name, AWS's unique ID for anything). By default everything is denied; an explicit Deny always wins over an Allow.

Least privilege: grant only the permissions needed, nothing more. Start narrow and widen when needed. Avoid "Action": "*" and "Resource": "*" except in throw-away labs.

EC2: Elastic Compute Cloud

  • An EC2 instance is a virtual server billed for the time it runs.
  • Type names encode family, generation and size, such as t3.micro.
  • Security groups are stateful firewalls with allow rules only.
  • Never open SSH or database ports to 0.0.0.0/0.
ELI5: Explain like I'm 5

EC2 is a computer rental shop: pick a size and software, log in with your key, return it to stop the meter.

EC2 instance: a virtual server running in an AWS data centre. You pay for the time it is running (plus its attached storage and data transfer).

Security groups

TypePortSourceMeaning
SSH22203.0.113.7/32 (your IP)Only you can log in
HTTP800.0.0.0/0Anyone on the internet can browse the site
HTTPS4430.0.0.0/0Anyone, encrypted
Explain in detail

ELI5, continued: The rented computer is an instance, the pre-installed software is an AMI, and the key is a key pair. You also decide who may connect to it (the security group): by default nobody from outside can until you allow them, and replies to allowed visitors are let out automatically (stateful).

Instance types

The name encodes family, generation and size, e.g. t3.micro = family t (burstable, general purpose), generation 3, size micro.

  • General purpose (t, m): balanced CPU/RAM
  • Compute optimised (c): CPU-heavy
  • Memory optimised (r): databases, caches
  • Storage optimised (i, d): fast local disks
  • Accelerated (p, g): GPUs for ML and graphics

A "g" in the family suffix (e.g. m6g) denotes Arm-based Graviton processors.

The four things you pick at launch

  • AMI (Amazon Machine Image): the template for the disk & OS (Amazon Linux, Ubuntu, Windows…)
  • Instance type: how much CPU and RAM
  • Key pair: public key stored on the instance, private key (.pem) kept by you, used for SSH
  • Security group: a virtual firewall
Security group: a stateful virtual firewall attached to an instance. It has allow rules only: all inbound traffic is denied unless you allow it (by default all outbound traffic is allowed). "Stateful" means if a request is allowed in, the reply is automatically allowed out.
Never open SSH (22) or database ports to 0.0.0.0/0 ("the whole internet"). Bots scan for open SSH within minutes. Restrict to your own IP (/32).

Storage: an instance's disk is usually an EBS volume (network-attached, survives stop/start). Some types have instance store disks which are erased when the instance stops. Lifecycle: pending → running → stopping → stopped, and shutting-down → terminated. A stopped instance stops compute charges but you still pay for its EBS disk; terminated deletes it.

VPC: your private network in the cloud

  • A VPC is your isolated virtual network with a CIDR range.
  • Subnets live in one AZ; route tables make them public or private.
  • An internet gateway connects the VPC to the internet.
  • NAT gateways cost money per hour, so delete them after labs.
ELI5: Explain like I'm 5

A VPC is your own gated neighbourhood; its streets are subnets.

VPC (Virtual Private Cloud): a logically isolated virtual network in an AWS region in which you launch resources. You choose its IP range in CIDR notation, e.g. 10.0.0.0/16.
PieceWhat it does
CIDR blockThe IP address range of the VPC (e.g. 10.0.0.0/16) and of each subnet (e.g. 10.0.1.0/24). See the Networking module.
SubnetA slice of the VPC's IP range living in one AZ. "Public" or "private" depends on its route table.
Route tableRules: "traffic to this destination goes to that target".
Internet gateway (IGW)The door between the VPC and the internet. A subnet is public if its route table has 0.0.0.0/0 → igw-… (and instances have public IPs).
NAT gatewayLets instances in private subnets start outbound connections (updates, API calls) but blocks unsolicited inbound ones. Route: 0.0.0.0/0 → nat-…. It lives in a public subnet.
Security groupInstance-level stateful firewall (allow rules).
Network ACLSubnet-level stateless firewall (allow and deny rules, checked in order).

Typical 3-tier layout:


VPC 10.0.0.0/16
 ├─ public-subnet-a  10.0.1.0/24 (AZ a)  → load balancer, NAT gateway   (route: 0.0.0.0/0 → IGW)
 ├─ public-subnet-b  10.0.2.0/24 (AZ b)  → load balancer
 ├─ private-app-a    10.0.11.0/24 (AZ a) → app servers                  (route: 0.0.0.0/0 → NAT)
 ├─ private-app-b    10.0.12.0/24 (AZ b) → app servers
 └─ private-db-a/b   10.0.21.0/24 ...    → databases (no internet route at all)
Explain in detail

ELI5, continued: Only the roads you build connect it to the outside. Public streets have a road to the highway (the internet gateway), so visitors can reach those houses; private streets have none, which suits the database. Houses on private streets can still send letters out through a post office at the gate (the NAT gateway) without letting strangers in. Route tables are the signboards telling each street where traffic should go.

A NAT gateway is billed per hour it exists plus per GB processed, even if idle. Forgetting one in a lab account is a classic surprise bill. Delete it when done.

Every AWS account also has a default VPC in each region with public subnets, which is why you can launch an EC2 instance without designing a network first. Real production systems use custom VPCs.

S3: Simple Storage Service

  • S3 is object storage: objects in buckets, found by key.
  • Versioning, encryption and Block Public Access protect data.
  • Storage classes cost less for data you touch less.
ELI5: Explain like I'm 5

S3 is a toy box with no bottom: drop in any number of toys, each labelled so you can find it again, and pay only for the space they use. The box is a bucket, each toy is an object, and its label is the key.

Amazon S3: object storage.

Storage classes (pay less for data you touch less)

ClassUse it for
S3 StandardFrequently accessed data
S3 Intelligent-TieringUnknown or changing access patterns; AWS moves objects between tiers for you
S3 Standard-IA / One Zone-IAInfrequently accessed data that needs quick access when requested (One Zone keeps data in a single AZ)
S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval / Flexible Retrieval / Deep ArchiveArchives, from instant access to cheapest-but-slowest retrieval (hours)
Explain in detail

ELI5, continued: It is not a cupboard of folders you browse like a disk: you ask for a toy by its label over the internet (an HTTPS request), and you get the whole toy back.

Data is stored as objects (the file plus metadata) in buckets, each object identified by a key such as photos/2026/cat.jpg. Bucket names are globally unique across all AWS accounts. It is designed for very high durability (11 nines, 99.999999999%), and you access objects over HTTP via API, not by mounting a normal disk.

Common uses

  • Backups and archives
  • Static website files and downloads
  • Application assets (images, videos)
  • Data lakes and logs
  • Terraform remote state (next module)

Useful features

  • Versioning: keep old versions, undo accidental deletes
  • Encryption at rest
  • Lifecycle rules: move or delete old data automatically
  • Block Public Access: safety switch against accidental exposure
  • Event notifications: trigger Lambda on upload

S3 is not a file system and not a database. Choose EBS for an instance's disk, EFS for shared file storage and RDS/DynamoDB for structured data.

Check yourself

Two quick questions on the last few slides. Not graded; wrong answers explain themselves.

A security group rule allows SSH (port 22) from 0.0.0.0/0. What is the problem?

Never open SSH or database ports to the whole internet.

Instances in a private subnet must download updates but accept no inbound connections from the internet. What do you add?

NAT gives private subnets outbound-only access.

RDS & DynamoDB: databases as a service

  • RDS gives managed SQL databases with backups, patching, Multi-AZ failover and read replicas.
  • DynamoDB suits simple lookups by key at huge scale.
  • ElastiCache puts a very fast cache in front of a database.
ELI5: Explain like I'm 5

You could run a database yourself: install it, patch it, back it up nightly and fix it when it breaks. Or you hire a librarian who does all that while you just say "shelve this book" and "find me that book". The librarian is a managed database such as RDS or DynamoDB.

NeedReach for
Tables with relations, joins, transactionsRDS / Aurora
Simple lookups by key at huge scaleDynamoDB
Super-fast cache in front of a databaseElastiCache (Redis/Valkey, Memcached)
Explain in detail

ELI5, continued: You pay the librarian, but you save your evenings.

Amazon RDS

Relational Database Service: managed SQL databases. Engines include MySQL, PostgreSQL, MariaDB, Oracle, SQL Server, IBM Db2 and AWS's own Aurora (MySQL/PostgreSQL compatible).

  • Automated backups and point-in-time recovery
  • Software patching handled for you
  • Multi-AZ: a standby copy in another AZ for automatic failover
  • Read replicas to spread read traffic

You still choose the instance size, storage, and decide who can connect. Put databases in private subnets.

Amazon DynamoDB

A fully managed NoSQL key-value / document database designed for very fast, predictable performance at any scale. No servers to size or patch.

  • You model data around a partition key (and optional sort key)
  • Two capacity modes: on-demand or provisioned
  • Great for sessions, shopping carts, IoT, leaderboards

Not great for complex joins or ad-hoc reporting. That is relational territory.

Load balancing & Auto Scaling

  • A load balancer hands requests to healthy servers in turn.
  • Health checks remove failed servers from rotation.
  • ALB works at Layer 7, NLB at Layer 4, Gateway LB for appliances.
  • Auto Scaling adds or removes instances as load changes.
ELI5: Explain like I'm 5

A busy shop has a greeter at the door who sends each customer to a free cashier and skips any till that is not working. The greeter is the load balancer, the cashiers are servers, and checking which tills work is the health check.

Explain in detail

ELI5, continued: The manager (Auto Scaling) watches the queue: if it gets long, she calls in more cashiers; when it is quiet, she sends some home.

The animation shows requests being handed out in turn (round robin) and a failed server being removed after it fails its health check. On AWS this is built from two services:

Elastic Load Balancing (ELB)

  • Application Load Balancer (ALB): Layer 7 (HTTP/HTTPS). Routes by URL path or host name (/api → one group, / → another).
  • Network Load Balancer (NLB): Layer 4 (TCP/UDP), very high performance.
  • Gateway Load Balancer: for virtual network appliances such as firewalls.

Key words: listener (port/protocol to listen on), target group (the servers to send to), health check (e.g. GET /health must return 200).

EC2 Auto Scaling

  • Launch template: the recipe for a new instance (AMI, type, security group…)
  • Auto Scaling group (ASG) with min / desired / max instance counts, spread across AZs
  • Scaling policy: e.g. "target tracking: keep average CPU near 50%"
  • Replaces unhealthy instances automatically

Together: users hit one DNS name → ALB spreads traffic to instances in several AZs → ASG adds or removes instances as load changes. This is the AWS version of the self-healing and scaling you saw in Kubernetes.

More core services: Route 53, CloudWatch, Lambda & containers

  • Route 53 is AWS's DNS service, with health checks and routing policies.
  • CloudWatch collects metrics and logs, and sets alarms.
  • Lambda runs short event-driven functions, billed per request and run time.
  • ECR stores images; ECS and EKS run containers, with Fargate hiding servers.
Explain in detail

Route 53: DNS

ELI5: Explain like I'm 5

A phone book for the internet: you look up shop.example.com and it gives you the address of the right server. Route 53 is AWS's phone book service (DNS) for your domains.

AWS's DNS service. Hosts DNS zones and records (A, AAAA, CNAME, MX…), and supports health checks and routing policies (simple, weighted, latency-based, failover). See the DNS animation in the Networking module. (The name comes from DNS using port 53.)

CloudWatch: monitoring

ELI5: Explain like I'm 5

A car's dashboard shows speed and fuel, and a warning light comes on when something is wrong. CloudWatch is that dashboard for your AWS resources: the gauges are metrics and the warning lights are alarms.

Collects metrics (CPU, requests), logs (CloudWatch Logs) and lets you set alarms (e.g. CPU > 80% for 5 minutes → notify or trigger Auto Scaling). Details in the Observability module.

Lambda: serverless functions

ELI5: Explain like I'm 5

A vending machine does nothing until someone presses a button, then does one small job and waits again, and you pay only per use. The button press is an event, the small job is your function, and the machine is Lambda.

Upload a function (Python, Node.js, Java, …); trigger it from an S3 upload, an HTTP request (via API Gateway), a schedule, a queue message… Billed by number of requests and execution time. Has limits (an invocation can run for at most 15 minutes; memory is capped), so it suits short event-driven tasks.

Containers: ECR, ECS, EKS

  • ECR (Elastic Container Registry): private Docker-image registry, like Docker Hub inside your AWS account
  • ECS (Elastic Container Service): AWS's own container orchestrator
  • EKS (Elastic Kubernetes Service): managed Kubernetes control plane
  • Fargate: serverless compute for ECS/EKS: you do not manage the worker servers

Flow: build image (Docker module) → push to ECR → run on ECS or EKS.

You do not need to learn 200+ AWS services. The ones on this slide and the previous slides are the core that most entry-level DevOps work builds on.

Check yourself

Two quick questions on the last few slides. Not graded; wrong answers explain themselves.

A server behind a load balancer fails its health check. What does the load balancer do?

Health checks remove failed servers from rotation.

You need a shopping-cart store with simple lookups by key at huge scale and no servers to manage. Which fits best?

DynamoDB is built for key lookups at scale.

AWS vs Azure vs Google Cloud: cheat map

  • Concepts transfer between clouds; only the names change.
  • The table maps AWS services to Azure and Google Cloud equivalents.
  • Learn one cloud well, then translate.
NeedAWSMicrosoft AzureGoogle Cloud
Identity & accessIAMMicrosoft Entra ID + Azure RBACCloud IAM
Virtual machinesEC2Virtual MachinesCompute Engine
Private networkVPCVirtual Network (VNet)VPC
Object storageS3Blob StorageCloud Storage
Managed SQLRDS / AuroraAzure SQL / Azure Database for PostgreSQL & MySQLCloud SQL
NoSQL key-value/documentDynamoDBCosmos DBFirestore / Bigtable
