Explain in detail

The concepts transfer between clouds; only the names change. Learn one, and translate.

The mapping is approximate: services in different clouds differ in features, limits and pricing.

Pricing models & FinOps

  • On-demand, commitment discounts and Spot are the main pricing models.
  • You pay for compute time, storage, data transfer and always-on managed parts.
  • Set budgets, tag resources and delete idle resources.
  • FinOps brings engineering and finance together to manage cloud spend.
ELI5: Explain like I'm 5

Train tickets: the counter price just before travel, a cheaper monthly pass for daily riders, or cheap leftover seats you may have to give up at short notice. These are on-demand, commitment discounts and Spot.

ModelHow it worksBest for
On-DemandPay for compute by the second (Linux; minimum 60 seconds) or hour, no commitment.Unpredictable or short-term workloads, experiments
Savings Plans / Reserved InstancesCommit to a steady amount of usage for 1 or 3 years in exchange for a discount versus on-demand.Steady, always-on workloads (production baseline)
Spot InstancesUse spare AWS capacity at a big discount (AWS advertises up to 90%), but AWS can reclaim it with a two-minute warning.Fault-tolerant batch jobs, CI workers, stateless workers

What you actually pay for

FinOps & cost hygiene checklist

Explain in detail

ELI5, continued: Commitment discounts are Savings Plans and Reserved Instances. FinOps is checking the travel budget regularly: seeing which trips you actually take and choosing the cheapest ticket that still gets you there.

  • Compute time (EC2 hours, Lambda invocations)
  • Storage (GB-months of S3, EBS volumes, snapshots)
  • Data transfer: moving data into AWS is generally free; moving it out to the internet, or between regions, costs money
  • Always-on managed bits: NAT gateways, load balancers, RDS instances, public IPv4 addresses (charged per hour since February 2024, whether in use or not)
  • Set a budget with alerts (AWS Budgets) on day one
  • Tag every resource (team, env, owner) so you know who spends what
  • Turn off dev/test environments at night
  • Delete unattached disks, old snapshots, idle load balancers
  • Right-size: do not run a large instance at 3% CPU
  • Use lifecycle rules to age S3 data into cheaper classes
  • Use Savings Plans for the steady baseline; Spot for flexible work
  • Review the Cost Explorer report weekly
The AWS Free Tier rules and offers change over time and differ by account age. Always read the current "AWS Free Tier" page before relying on it, and set a budget alert anyway.

FinOps is the practice of bringing engineering, finance and business together to manage cloud spend: make costs visible, assign ownership, and optimise continuously.

The AWS Well-Architected Framework

  • The Well-Architected Framework is AWS best-practice guidance for reviewing workloads.
  • It is organised into six pillars, each with a guiding question.
  • Use the pillars to structure answers about highly available, secure architecture.
ELI5: Explain like I'm 5

A doctor's yearly check-up follows a fixed checklist, so nothing important is missed. The Well-Architected Framework is that checklist for your cloud system, with six pillars: operational excellence, security, reliability, performance efficiency, cost optimization and sustainability.

PillarQuestion it asksExample practice
Operational ExcellenceCan we run and improve it smoothly?Everything as code, small frequent changes, runbooks, learn from incidents
SecurityIs data and access protected?Least privilege, MFA, encryption, logging
ReliabilityDoes it recover from failure?Multi-AZ, backups, health checks, auto scaling
Performance EfficiencyAre we using the right resources efficiently?Right instance type, caching, CDN, serverless where it fits
Cost OptimizationAre we avoiding waste?Right-sizing, tagging, commitments, turning off idle things
SustainabilityAre we minimising environmental impact?Efficient utilisation, appropriate regions and hardware
Explain in detail

A set of best-practice guidance from AWS for designing and reviewing cloud workloads, organised into six pillars:

Other clouds publish similar guidance. Interviewers love the question "how would you make this architecture highly available and secure?"; the pillars give you a ready structure for the answer.

Check yourself

Two quick questions on the last few slides. Not graded; wrong answers explain themselves.

A nightly batch job can safely restart if it is interrupted. Which pricing is the cheapest fit?

Spot suits fault-tolerant, interruptible work.

Which Well-Architected pillar asks whether the system recovers from failure?

Reliability is about recovering from failure.

Hands-on exercise: S3 and EC2 from the AWS CLI

  • The exercise may create billable resources, so set a budget alert.
  • You configure the AWS CLI, then create and use an S3 bucket.
  • You launch an EC2 instance, SSH in, then clean up.

Task 1: worked example


$ aws --version
$ aws configure
AWS Access Key ID [None]: <your IAM user's key id>
AWS Secret Access Key [None]: <your secret>
Default region name [None]: ap-south-1
Default output format [None]: json

$ aws sts get-caller-identity      # who am I? proves your credentials work
    

$ BUCKET=my-devops-lab-$RANDOM-$RANDOM         # names must be globally unique and lowercase
$ aws s3 mb s3://$BUCKET --region ap-south-1
make_bucket: my-devops-lab-12345-6789

$ echo "hello cloud" > hello.txt
$ aws s3 cp hello.txt s3://$BUCKET/
$ aws s3 ls s3://$BUCKET/

Task 2: finish it

Create a key pair, a locked-down security group and an AMI lookup, then launch the instance.


# 3a. Key pair (private key is shown only once, so save it!)
$ aws ec2 create-key-pair --key-name devops-lab \
    --query 'KeyMaterial' --output text > devops-lab.pem
$ chmod 400 devops-lab.pem

# 3b. Security group in the default VPC: SSH only from your IP
$ MYIP=$(curl -s https://checkip.amazonaws.com)
$ SG=$(aws ec2 create-security-group --group-name devops-lab-sg \
    --description "lab ssh" --query GroupId --output text)
$ aws ec2 authorize-security-group-ingress --group-id $SG \
    --protocol tcp --port 22 --cidr $MYIP/32

# 3c. Find the latest Amazon Linux 2023 AMI through the public SSM parameter
$ AMI=$(aws ssm get-parameters \
    --names /aws/service/ami-amazon-linux-latest/al2023-ami-kernel-default-x86_64 \
    --query 'Parameters[0].Value' --output text)

# 3d. launch the instance and wait until it is running
Show hint

Use aws ec2 run-instances with the AMI, instance type, key name and security group, then aws ec2 wait instance-running.

Show answer

# 3d. Launch (use your free-tier-eligible type)
$ ID=$(aws ec2 run-instances --image-id $AMI --instance-type t3.micro \
    --key-name devops-lab --security-group-ids $SG --count 1 \
    --tag-specifications 'ResourceType=instance,Tags=[{Key=Name,Value=devops-lab}]' \
    --query 'Instances[0].InstanceId' --output text)
$ aws ec2 wait instance-running --instance-ids $ID

Task 3: on your own

Goal: SSH into the instance, run uname -a, then delete everything you created. Success: the instance shows as terminated and the bucket is gone.

Show hint

Look up the public IP with describe-instances. For clean-up, terminate the instance first, then the security group, key pair and bucket.

Show answer

$ IP=$(aws ec2 describe-instances --instance-ids $ID \
    --query 'Reservations[0].Instances[0].PublicIpAddress' --output text)
$ ssh -i devops-lab.pem ec2-user@$IP
[ec2-user@ip-172-31-x-x ~]$ uname -a
[ec2-user@ip-172-31-x-x ~]$ exit
    
$ aws ec2 terminate-instances --instance-ids $ID
$ aws ec2 wait instance-terminated --instance-ids $ID
$ aws ec2 delete-security-group --group-id $SG
$ aws ec2 delete-key-pair --key-name devops-lab && rm devops-lab.pem
$ aws s3 rb s3://$BUCKET --force        # deletes the objects and then the bucket

# verify nothing is left running (terminated instances stay listed as "terminated" for about an hour)
$ aws ec2 describe-instances --query 'Reservations[].Instances[].[InstanceId,State.Name]' --output text
Explain in detail
This exercise may create billable resources. Use an account where you have set a budget alert, pick a small instance type (t3.micro or t2.micro depending on region; on accounts created before July 2025 these are the free-tier-eligible types, on newer accounts the cost comes out of your credits), and run the clean-up step at the end. Never leave instances running overnight "just in case". Do not use the root user's access keys; create an IAM user (or use IAM Identity Center) for the CLI.

Credentials are stored in ~/.aws/credentials. Never commit that file or paste keys into code, chats or Git.

If SSH times out, check that the security group allows your current public IP. If it says "UNPROTECTED PRIVATE KEY FILE", run the chmod 400 again.

Next module you will do the same thing with Terraform: one file, terraform apply to create, terraform destroy to clean up. Repeatable and much harder to forget.

Interview questions

Q1: What is cloud computing and what are its benefits?

On-demand delivery of compute, storage, databases and more over the internet with pay-as-you-go pricing. Benefits: no up-front hardware cost, fast provisioning, elasticity, global reach, and offloading hardware maintenance to the provider.

Q2: Explain IaaS, PaaS and SaaS with examples.

IaaS gives virtual infrastructure you manage from the OS up (EC2). PaaS gives a platform where you manage only the app and data (Elastic Beanstalk, App Engine). SaaS is a finished application you just use (Gmail, Salesforce).

Q3: What is the difference between a Region and an Availability Zone?

A region is a geographic area; an AZ is one or more isolated data centres inside a region. Deploy across multiple AZs for high availability, and across regions for disaster recovery or to be closer to users.

Q4: What is the Shared Responsibility Model?

The provider secures the underlying cloud infrastructure; the customer secures what they put in it: data, IAM, OS patches, network rules, application configuration. The split shifts with the service model.

Q5: IAM user vs role?

A user has long-term credentials and represents a person/app. A role has no long-term credentials; it is assumed to get temporary ones. Prefer roles for EC2, Lambda and CI/CD so there are no keys to leak.

Q6: What makes a subnet public?

Its route table has a route to an internet gateway (0.0.0.0/0 → igw) and resources have public IPs. A private subnet has no such route; it may reach the internet outbound through a NAT gateway.

Q7: Security group vs network ACL?

Security groups are stateful, attached to instances/ENIs and only have allow rules. NACLs are stateless, attached to subnets, and have numbered allow and deny rules, so return traffic must be allowed explicitly.

Q8: How would you make a web application highly available on AWS?

Put instances in an Auto Scaling group across at least two AZs behind an Application Load Balancer with health checks; use a Multi-AZ RDS database in private subnets; store static assets in S3 (with CloudFront); monitor with CloudWatch alarms.

Q9: How do you reduce an AWS bill?

Tag and monitor costs, right-size instances, turn off idle resources, use Savings Plans for steady load and Spot for fault-tolerant work, move cold S3 data to cheaper classes, and set budgets and alerts.

Q10: When would you choose Lambda over EC2?

For short, event-driven, spiky workloads where you want no server management and pay-per-use. Choose EC2 (or containers) for long-running processes, special runtime needs, or steady high load where it can be cheaper.

Quiz

1. In the shared responsibility model, which is the customer's job?

Security "in" the cloud (access, configuration, data) is yours; security "of" the cloud is AWS's.

2. What makes a subnet "public"?

The route to the internet gateway defines a public subnet.

3. Which pricing model offers the biggest discount but can be interrupted by AWS?

Spot uses spare capacity at deep discounts, and AWS can reclaim it.

4. Which service is object storage?

S3 stores objects in buckets. EBS is block storage for instances.

5. For an EC2 instance that needs to read from S3, the best practice is to…

Roles supply temporary credentials automatically; no secret to leak.

11

Infrastructure as Code: Terraform & Ansible

Clicking through a cloud console works for one server and fails for fifty. Infrastructure as Code (IaC) describes servers, networks and configuration in text files that live in Git, so environments can be created, reviewed, repeated and destroyed like software. This module covers the ideas (declarative, idempotent, immutable) and the two tools almost every DevOps team meets: Terraform for creating infrastructure and Ansible for configuring it.

What you will learn

ClickOps and snowflake servers · declarative vs imperative · idempotency · provisioning vs configuration management · Terraform (HCL, providers, resources, variables, state, modules, workflow) · Ansible (inventory, playbooks, handlers, roles) · tool comparison · a hands-on exercise

Guess first

You are not expected to know these yet. Guessing before you read helps you remember the answer when you meet it.

You run the same declarative Terraform configuration twice, with no changes in between. What happens the second time?

Declarative and idempotent: the result is the same however many times you apply.

You want to see what Terraform would change without touching anything. Which command do you run?

plan previews, apply executes.

Why must the terraform.tfstate file never be committed to Git?

State may hold secrets; use a protected remote backend instead.

The problem: ClickOps and snowflake servers

  • ClickOps means building servers by hand through a cloud console.
  • Hand-built environments cannot be repeated exactly or reviewed later.
  • Rebuilding production by hand after a disaster is slow and risky.
ELI5: Explain like I'm 5

Building a LEGO castle from memory works once, but if it ever falls apart you cannot build exactly the same castle again. The castle is a server set up by hand (a snowflake server), and a written instruction booklet is infrastructure as code.

Explain in detail

Suppose you build a web server by logging into the AWS console, clicking through twelve screens, then SSH-ing in to install packages and edit config files. It works. Six months later you need an identical server for testing, and nobody remembers exactly what was clicked or typed. This way of working is called ClickOps.

Not repeatable

Building the same environment twice gives two slightly different results, because humans forget steps.

No history

Who opened port 22 to the world last Tuesday? The console does not keep a reviewable history of reasons, only (at best) an audit log of clicks.

Slow and risky

Recreating production after a disaster takes days of manual work, performed under stress.

Snowflake server: a server that was configured by hand over time and is now unique and fragile. Nobody dares to touch or rebuild it because nobody knows exactly how it got that way. The opposite is a server that can be thrown away and rebuilt from code in minutes, sometimes called a "phoenix" server.

Infrastructure as Code is the instruction booklet. Anyone can follow it and get the same castle, you can fix a mistake in the booklet, and you can keep every old version of the booklet.

Why is ClickOps a problem?

Compare with ours

Because hand-built environments cannot be repeated exactly or reviewed later, so rebuilding or auditing them depends on human memory.

History and evolution

YearMilestoneWhy it mattered
Before ~1993Administrators use hand-run shell scripts, written checklists and "golden image" disk copiesAutomation existed but every site had its own fragile scripts, and a golden image slowly drifted from reality.
1993CFEngine (Mark Burgess) appearsThe first widely known configuration management tool, introducing the idea of declaring a desired state that the machine converges to.
2005Puppet releasedPopularised a declarative language and an agent that keeps servers in the desired state.
2006 onwardsPublic cloud (AWS EC2) turns servers into API callsInfrastructure can now be created by programs, making "infrastructure as code" possible, not only configuration as code.
2009Chef releasedConfiguration written in Ruby code; strengthened the "infrastructure is code" mindset.
2011AWS CloudFormation launchesFirst major provider-native template service for provisioning cloud resources from JSON files.
2012Ansible first releasedAgentless, SSH-based, YAML playbooks: much lower barrier to entry than agent-based tools.
2014Terraform first released by HashiCorpOne language and workflow for many providers (AWS, Azure, GCP, and hundreds of others), with a plan step before changes.
2015Red Hat acquires AnsibleAnsible becomes a core part of enterprise Linux automation.
2018 / 2019Pulumi launched (2018); AWS CDK generally available (2019)Define infrastructure in general-purpose languages such as Python, TypeScript or Go.
2020Ansible 2.10 splits content into ansible-core (then called ansible-base) plus collectionsModules moved into separately versioned collections, changing how you install and reference modules (for example amazon.aws.ec2_instance).
June 2021Terraform 1.0Stability promise: upgrades within 1.x should not break working configurations.
June 2023Terraform 1.5 adds import blocks and check blocksExisting hand-made resources can be adopted through code that goes through plan and review, instead of a one-off command.
Aug 2023HashiCorp moves Terraform from an open-source licence (MPL 2.0) to the Business Source License (BUSL 1.1), starting with Terraform 1.6The source stays visible but use in competing commercial products is restricted, so Terraform is no longer open source by the usual definition. Many in the community objected.
2023 to early 2024OpenTofu forked from the last MPL-licensed Terraform (1.5) and placed under the Linux Foundation; OpenTofu 1.6, its first stable release, ships in January 2024A community-governed, open-source alternative that stays largely compatible with Terraform.
April 2024OpenTofu 1.7 adds built-in state encryptionThe first major feature Terraform does not have, so the two tools start to diverge.
Apr 2024 to Feb 2025IBM announces (April 2024) and later completes (February 2025) its acquisition of HashiCorpTerraform's steward is now part of IBM, alongside Red Hat and Ansible.
Nov 2024 to Feb 2025Terraform 1.10 adds native state locking in S3 (experimental), made generally available in 1.11A remote S3 backend no longer needs a separate DynamoDB table for locking; DynamoDB-based locking is deprecated.
June 2025Terraform AWS provider 6.0A major version with breaking changes, including a per-resource region argument so one provider block can manage several regions. Version pins such as ~> 5.0 keep old code on 5.x until you upgrade deliberately.
Nov 2025Terraform 1.14 adds action blocks and list resources with terraform queryProviders can now expose operations outside the create/read/update/delete model (for example invoking a function or invalidating a cache), and existing infrastructure can be queried and imported from code. Terraform 1.15 (April 2026) followed with module sources that can take variables.
Two trends to remember: from imperative scripts to declarative desired state, and from mutable servers fixed in place to immutable images replaced wholesale.

What is Infrastructure as Code?

  • IaC manages servers, networks and databases through machine-readable definition files.
  • The files live in Git and are reviewed, tested and applied by automation.
  • Benefits: repeatable, versioned, reviewable, fast, and easy to rebuild.
  • Risks: mistakes apply at machine speed, and secrets and state need care.
Infrastructure as Code (IaC): managing and provisioning infrastructure (servers, networks, databases, permissions) through machine-readable definition files instead of manual processes, and treating those files like application code: stored in Git, reviewed, tested and applied by automation.
Explain in detail

Benefits

  • Repeatable: the same file produces the same environment (dev, staging, prod)
  • Versioned: Git history shows who changed what and why
  • Reviewable: a pull request shows the change before it happens
  • Fast: whole environments appear in minutes and can be destroyed to save money
  • Documented: the code is the documentation and it cannot go stale
  • Disaster recovery: rebuild from code

New responsibilities

  • Mistakes now apply at machine speed: a typo can delete a database
  • Secrets must never be committed in these files
  • State files (Terraform) must be protected and shared safely
  • The team must keep the code, not the console, as the source of truth

IaC tools fall into two overlapping jobs, covered on the next slide: provisioning (creating the infrastructure) and configuration management (setting up the software inside it).

Key ideas: declarative, idempotent, immutable

  • Declarative tools take the desired end state and work out the steps.
  • Idempotent operations leave the same result however many times they run.
  • Immutable infrastructure replaces servers instead of changing them in place.
  • Provisioning creates infrastructure; configuration management sets up the software on it.

Declarative vs imperative

ELI5: Explain like I'm 5

Directions ("turn left, then right") are imperative; telling a GPS "the train station" is declarative, and the GPS is the IaC tool.

Imperative (how)


# Run twice and you get two servers
aws ec2 run-instances --image-id ami-123 --count 1

Shell scripts, many ad-hoc commands.

Declarative (what)


# Apply twice and you still have one server
resource "aws_instance" "web" {
  ami           = "ami-123"
  instance_type = "t3.micro"
}

Terraform, CloudFormation, Kubernetes manifests.

Mutable vs immutable infrastructure

MutableImmutable
IdeaChange servers in place (patch, upgrade, edit config)Never change a running server; build a new image/server and replace the old one
RiskConfiguration drift: servers slowly become different from each otherEach deployment is a clean copy; rollback means switching back to the previous image
Typical toolsAnsible, Puppet, Chef against long-lived VMsContainer images, AMIs, Terraform replacing instances

Provisioning vs configuration management

ProvisioningConfiguration management
Question answeredWhat infrastructure exists?What is installed and configured on it?
ExamplesCreate VPC, subnets, servers, databasesInstall nginx, create users, deploy config files
Typical toolsTerraform, CloudFormation, Pulumi, OpenTofuAnsible, Puppet, Chef
Explain in detail

ELI5, continued: Turn-by-turn directions only work if you start from the expected place; the GPS plans the route from wherever you are. In IaC, you describe the end state ("three servers and one load balancer") and the tool works out what to create, change or delete to get there.

Idempotency

ELI5: Explain like I'm 5

Press the elevator button for floor 3 once and the elevator goes to floor 3; press it ten more times and nothing extra happens. Pressing the button is running your automation, and arriving at floor 3 is the end state, which is the same however many times you press.

Idempotent: running an operation once or many times leaves the system in the same state. "Ensure nginx is installed" is idempotent; "install nginx again" run blindly in a script is not. Idempotency makes automation safe to re-run after a failure.

Common pattern: Terraform creates the servers, Ansible configures them. With containers and immutable images, much of the configuration step moves into the Dockerfile or image build instead.

Terraform: the language and providers

  • Terraform uses declarative HCL files ending in .tf.
  • Providers are plugins that talk to one platform's API.
  • Terraform downloads providers during terraform init.
  • Always pin provider versions to avoid surprise upgrades.
Terraform: an IaC tool from HashiCorp. You write declarative configuration in HCL (HashiCorp Configuration Language) files ending in .tf; Terraform compares it to what exists and calls provider APIs to make reality match.
ELI5: Explain like I'm 5

Terraform reads your shopping list (.tf code) and adds only what your cart (cloud account) is missing.

HCL syntax in one minute


# A block has a type, optional labels, and a body in { }
block_type "label_one" "label_two" {
  argument_name = "value"         # string
  count_example = 3               # number
  enabled       = true            # bool
  list_example  = ["a", "b"]      # list
  map_example   = { env = "dev" } # map
  reference     = aws_vpc.main.id # refer to another resource's attribute
  interpolated  = "web-${var.env}" # insert a variable inside a string
}

Providers


terraform {
  required_version = ">= 1.5"
  required_providers {
    aws = {
      source  = "hashicorp/aws"
      version = "~> 6.0"     # allow 6.x updates, not 7.0
    }
  }
}

provider "aws" {
  region = "ap-south-1"
}
Explain in detail

ELI5, continued: You write what you want ("1 network, 2 servers"). Terraform checks what is already in your cart, adds only what is missing and takes out what you crossed off the list. The shop clerks are providers: one for AWS, one for Azure, one for GitHub, fetched when you run terraform init.

A provider is a plugin that knows how to talk to one platform's API. Terraform downloads providers during terraform init.

Credentials are not written here. Terraform's AWS provider reads them from the same places as the AWS CLI (environment variables, ~/.aws, or an IAM role).

Always pin provider versions. An unpinned provider upgrade can change behaviour between two runs of the same code.

Check yourself

Quick questions on the last few slides. Not graded; wrong answers explain themselves.

Which example is idempotent?

Idempotent means the same end state however many times it runs.

What does terraform init do with providers?

init prepares the folder; providers are plugins that talk to one platform's API.

Terraform building blocks

  • Resources are the things Terraform creates and manages.
  • Variables, locals and outputs handle inputs, reusable values and results.
  • Data sources read existing things; modules package reusable code.
  • References between blocks build a dependency graph.
BlockPurpose
resourceA thing Terraform creates and manages (a VPC, a server, a bucket)
variableAn input, so the same code can be reused with different values
outputA value printed after apply or passed to other modules (an IP, an ID)
localsNamed expressions computed once and reused inside the module
dataRead-only lookup of something that already exists or is published (latest AMI, an existing VPC)
moduleA reusable folder of Terraform code, called like a function

variable "env" {
  type        = string
  description = "Environment name"
  default     = "dev"
}

variable "instance_type" {
  type    = string
  default = "t3.micro"
}

locals {
  name_prefix = "demo-${var.env}"
  common_tags = {
    Project = "demo"
    Env     = var.env
  }
}

# data source: look up the newest Amazon Linux 2023 AMI
data "aws_ami" "al2023" {
  most_recent = true
  owners      = ["amazon"]
  filter {
    name   = "name"
    values = ["al2023-ami-2023.*-x86_64"]   # standard image, not "minimal"
  }
}

resource "aws_instance" "web" {
  ami           = data.aws_ami.al2023.id   # reference a data source
  instance_type = var.instance_type        # reference a variable
  tags          = merge(local.common_tags, { Name = "${local.name_prefix}-web" })
}

output "web_public_ip" {
  value = aws_instance.web.public_ip
}
Explain in detail

Terraform builds a dependency graph from these references: because the instance uses data.aws_ami.al2023.id, the lookup happens first. Independent resources are created in parallel.

Set variable values with a file (terraform.tfvars), the command line (-var "env=prod") or environment variables (TF_VAR_env=prod).

Terraform init, plan and apply

  • init downloads providers; plan previews changes; apply makes them.
  • plan compares code, recorded state and the real cloud.
  • apply runs in dependency order and records the result in state.

A Terraform configuration is initialised, planned and applied, creating a VPC, an EC2 instance and an RDS database.

Explain in detail

init downloads the providers. plan compares your code to the recorded state and the real cloud and prints what it would add, change or destroy, without touching anything. apply executes that plan, in dependency order, then records the result in the state file.

The Terraform workflow with real output

  • The workflow is init, plan, apply, and destroy when finished.
  • plan is a safe, read-only preview of what would change.
  • Symbols show create, destroy, change and replace; always read the plan.
  • Save the plan in CI so exactly what was reviewed runs.

init

Prepare the folder: download providers, set up the backend.

plan

Preview changes. Safe, read-only.

apply

Make the changes, after you type yes.

destroy

Delete everything this configuration manages.


$ terraform init
Initializing the backend... Initializing provider plugins... - Finding hashicorp/aws versions matching "~> 6.0"... - Installing hashicorp/aws v6.x.x... - Installed hashicorp/aws v6.x.x (signed by HashiCorp) Terraform has created a lock file .terraform.lock.hcl to record the provider selections it made above. Include this file in your version control repository so that Terraform can guarantee to make the same selections by default when you run "terraform init" in the future. Terraform has been successfully initialized!

$ terraform fmt        # auto-format files
$ terraform validate   # check syntax and references
$ terraform plan
Terraform will perform the following actions: # aws_instance.web will be created + resource "aws_instance" "web" { + ami = "ami-0abc..." + id = (known after apply) + instance_type = "t3.micro" + public_ip = (known after apply) ... } Plan: 1 to add, 0 to change, 0 to destroy.

$ terraform apply
Plan: 1 to add, 0 to change, 0 to destroy. Do you want to perform these actions? Enter a value: yes aws_instance.web: Creating... aws_instance.web: Creation complete after 32s [id=i-0123456789abcdef0] Apply complete! Resources: 1 added, 0 changed, 0 destroyed. Outputs: web_public_ip = "203.0.113.25"

$ terraform destroy
Plan: 0 to add, 0 to change, 1 to destroy. ... Destroy complete! Resources: 1 destroyed.
Explain in detail

Init also creates .terraform/ (downloaded plugins) and .terraform.lock.hcl (exact provider versions; commit this lock file, but not the .terraform folder).

Symbols: + create, - destroy, ~ change in place, -/+ destroy and recreate (replacement). Always read the plan. A -/+ on a database means the data is gone.

The IDs, addresses and timings above are examples; yours will differ.

In CI/CD, save a plan with terraform plan -out=tfplan and later run terraform apply tfplan, so exactly what was reviewed is what runs.

Check yourself

Quick questions on the last few slides. Not graded; wrong answers explain themselves.

In a Terraform plan, which symbol means destroy and recreate (replace)?

Always read the plan before applying.

An instance uses data.aws_ami.al2023.id. In what order does Terraform work?

References between blocks decide the order.

Terraform state, remote backends and drift

  • State maps each resource in code to a real cloud object.
  • Never commit state to Git; it can hold secrets.
  • Teams use a remote backend with locking so only one apply runs at a time.
  • Drift is real infrastructure differing from code; plan detects it.
ELI5: Explain like I'm 5

State is Terraform's notebook of what it bought.

State: a file (by default terraform.tfstate) mapping each resource in your configuration to the real object in the cloud, plus its last known attributes. Terraform uses it to compute plans.

Remote state with locking


terraform {
  backend "s3" {
    bucket       = "my-team-tf-state"        # create this bucket first, with versioning on
    key          = "prod/network/terraform.tfstate"
    region       = "ap-south-1"
    encrypt      = true
    use_lockfile = true   # S3 native locking (Terraform 1.10+, generally available in 1.11)
    # Older setups use a DynamoDB table instead (now deprecated): dynamodb_table = "tf-locks"
  }
}
Useful state commandsWhat they do
terraform state listList resources tracked in state
terraform state show aws_instance.webShow one resource's recorded attributes
terraform import / import blocksBring an existing, hand-made resource under Terraform management
terraform state rmMake Terraform forget a resource without deleting it
Explain in detail

ELI5, continued: The notebook says which real item in the cart belongs to which line of the shopping list, for example "web" is server i-0123. Without it, Terraform could buy a duplicate or forget to remove something. If someone swaps an item in the cart by hand, the cart and the list no longer match (drift); terraform plan checks the cart, spots the difference and shows it to you.

State can contain sensitive values in plain text (passwords, keys). Never commit it to Git. Add *.tfstate, *.tfstate.* and .terraform/ to .gitignore, and never edit it by hand.

A local state file does not work for teams: two people applying at once corrupt it, and a laptop failure loses it. Use a remote backend, commonly an S3 bucket (versioned and encrypted) with state locking, so only one apply runs at a time.

Locking options changed across Terraform versions (a DynamoDB table was the classic way). Check the documentation for the version you use.

Drift

Drift: the real infrastructure no longer matches the code and state, usually because someone changed it by hand in the console. terraform plan detects it by refreshing real values and shows the difference. Applying either reverts the manual change or you update the code to adopt it.

Modules, environments and best practices

  • A module is a reusable folder of Terraform code, called like a function.
  • A typical module has variables.tf for inputs, main.tf and outputs.tf.
  • Use workspaces or separate folders per environment; separate folders are preferred.
  • Pin versions, protect state and never hard-code secrets.
ELI5: Explain like I'm 5

A module is a LEGO set with an instruction booklet, such as "standard network". You can build it for every project, changing only a few choices like colour. The booklet is the module's code, the choices are its input variables, and each built copy is one environment.


module "network" {
  source   = "./modules/network"   # a local folder; could also be a registry module
  cidr     = "10.0.0.0/16"
  env      = var.env
}

# use an output of the module
resource "aws_instance" "web" {
  subnet_id = module.network.public_subnet_id
  # ...
}
Explain in detail

ELI5, continued: Write the booklet once and reuse it for dev, staging and production, instead of copying the same code three times and letting the copies drift apart.

A module is simply a folder with variables.tf (inputs), main.tf (resources) and outputs.tf (outputs). The public Terraform Registry hosts many ready-made modules.

Environments

  • Workspaces (terraform workspace new staging): several state files from the same code in one backend. Simple, but easy to apply to the wrong workspace.
  • Separate folders or state keys per environment (envs/dev, envs/prod) calling shared modules with different .tfvars: more explicit, widely preferred for production.

Best practices

  • Remote, locked, encrypted, versioned state
  • Pin Terraform and provider versions; commit .terraform.lock.hcl
  • Run fmt and validate in CI; review the plan in pull requests
  • Small, focused state files (network, app, data) instead of one giant one
  • Never hard-code secrets; use a secrets manager or environment variables
  • Tag every resource
  • Keep the console read-only for most people, so code stays the source of truth
  • Protect critical resources with lifecycle { prevent_destroy = true }

A complete annotated example: VPC, security group and EC2

  • The example builds a VPC, a public subnet and a security group.
  • It adds an internet gateway, a route table and one EC2 server.
  • The instance is billable, so finish with terraform destroy.

This configuration creates a network with one public subnet, a security group allowing SSH from your IP and HTTP from anywhere, and a server. Put it in a file called main.tf.


terraform {
  required_providers {
    aws = { source = "hashicorp/aws", version = "~> 6.0" }
  }
}

provider "aws" { region = "ap-south-1" }

variable "my_ip_cidr" {
  type        = string
  description = "Your public IP in CIDR form, e.g. 203.0.113.7/32"
}

variable "key_name" {
  type        = string
  description = "Name of an existing EC2 key pair, needed only if you want to SSH in"
  default     = null              # null = no key pair attached
}

# 1. The network (the gated housing society)
resource "aws_vpc" "main" {
  cidr_block           = "10.0.0.0/16"
  enable_dns_hostnames = true
  tags = { Name = "demo-vpc" }
}

# 2. A street inside it
resource "aws_subnet" "public" {
  vpc_id                  = aws_vpc.main.id      # depends on the VPC
  cidr_block              = "10.0.1.0/24"
  map_public_ip_on_launch = true
  tags = { Name = "demo-public" }
}

# 3. Door to the internet + signboard telling traffic to use it
resource "aws_internet_gateway" "igw" {
  vpc_id = aws_vpc.main.id
}

resource "aws_route_table" "public" {
  vpc_id = aws_vpc.main.id
  route {
    cidr_block = "0.0.0.0/0"
    gateway_id = aws_internet_gateway.igw.id
  }
}

resource "aws_route_table_association" "public" {
  subnet_id      = aws_subnet.public.id
  route_table_id = aws_route_table.public.id
}

# 4. Firewall
resource "aws_security_group" "web" {
  name   = "demo-web-sg"
  vpc_id = aws_vpc.main.id

  ingress {
    description = "SSH from my IP only"
    from_port   = 22
    to_port     = 22
    protocol    = "tcp"
    cidr_blocks = [var.my_ip_cidr]
  }
  ingress {
    description = "HTTP from anywhere"
    from_port   = 80
    to_port     = 80
    protocol    = "tcp"
    cidr_blocks = ["0.0.0.0/0"]
  }
  egress {
    from_port   = 0
    to_port     = 0
    protocol    = "-1"            # all protocols
    cidr_blocks = ["0.0.0.0/0"]
  }
}

# 5. Find the latest Amazon Linux 2023 image
data "aws_ami" "al2023" {
  most_recent = true
  owners      = ["amazon"]
  filter {
    name   = "name"
    values = ["al2023-ami-2023.*-x86_64"]   # standard image, not "minimal"
  }
}

# 6. The server
resource "aws_instance" "web" {
  ami                    = data.aws_ami.al2023.id
  instance_type          = "t3.micro"       # use a free-tier-eligible type for your region
  subnet_id              = aws_subnet.public.id
  vpc_security_group_ids = [aws_security_group.web.id]
  key_name               = var.key_name
  tags = { Name = "demo-web" }
}

output "public_ip" {
  value = aws_instance.web.public_ip
}
Explain in detail

Run it with terraform apply -var "my_ip_cidr=$(curl -s https://checkip.amazonaws.com)/32" (add -var "key_name=devops-lab" to use the key pair from the Cloud exercise). The instance is billable, so finish with terraform destroy.

Check yourself

Quick questions on the last few slides. Not graded; wrong answers explain themselves.

Two teammates run terraform apply at the same time against one local state file. What is the fix?

Teams need remote state with locking.

A teammate changed a security group by hand in the console. Which command reveals the difference from your code?

Drift is real infrastructure differing from code; plan detects it.

Ansible: agentless configuration management

  • Ansible configures machines over SSH and needs no agent.
  • Playbooks are YAML files mapping hosts to an ordered list of tasks.
  • An inventory lists and groups the managed machines.
  • Ad-hoc commands run one-off tasks without a playbook.
ELI5: Explain like I'm 5

A teacher writes one list of instructions on the board ("everyone: wear a hat") and all 50 children follow it; children already wearing a hat do nothing. The list on the board is a playbook, the children are servers, and the teacher is Ansible.

TermMeaning
Control nodeThe machine where you run Ansible (your laptop or a CI runner)
Managed nodesThe servers being configured
InventoryThe list of managed nodes, grouped
ModuleA unit of work (apt, copy, service, user)
TaskOne call to a module with arguments
PlaybookA YAML file mapping hosts to an ordered list of tasks

Inventory


# inventory.ini
[web]
web1 ansible_host=203.0.113.25
web2 ansible_host=203.0.113.26

[db]
db1 ansible_host=10.0.21.15

[all:vars]
ansible_user=ec2-user
ansible_ssh_private_key_file=~/.ssh/devops-lab.pem

Ad-hoc commands: one-off tasks without a playbook


$ ansible all -i inventory.ini -m ping                      # can I reach every host?
$ ansible web -i inventory.ini -a "uptime"                  # run a command
$ ansible web -i inventory.ini -b -m ansible.builtin.package -a "name=htop state=present"   # -b = become root
web1 | SUCCESS => { "changed": false, "ping": "pong" }
Explain in detail
Ansible: an automation tool that configures machines by connecting to them over SSH (or WinRM for Windows) and running small programs called modules. It is agentless: nothing needs to be installed on the managed machines beyond SSH and Python (for most Linux modules).

ELI5, continued: The teacher speaks to the class directly (over SSH), so no helper has to sit with each child first: that is what agentless means. Children who already wear a hat doing nothing is idempotency.

Ping here is Ansible's own check (SSH login plus a working Python), not an ICMP ping.

Playbooks, handlers, variables and templates

  • A play picks hosts and runs tasks in order.
  • Variables and facts feed Jinja2 templates that Ansible renders per host.
  • Handlers run once at the end, only if a task changed something.
  • Most modules are idempotent; command and shell are not.

A playbook is YAML. Each play picks hosts and runs tasks in order from top to bottom.


---
- name: Configure web servers          # a play
  hosts: web
  become: true                         # use sudo
  vars:
    app_port: 8080                     # a variable
  tasks:
    - name: Ensure curl is installed   # a task
      ansible.builtin.package:         # the module
        name: curl
        state: present                 # desired state, not an action
ELI5: Explain like I'm 5

A template is a form letter with blanks; Ansible fills them in for each server from its variables.

Templates (Jinja2)


# templates/app.conf.j2
server_name {{ inventory_hostname }};
listen {{ app_port }};
{% if app_env == "prod" %}
log_level warn;
{% endif %}
    

- name: Configure the app
  hosts: web
  become: true
  vars:
    app_port: 8080
    app_env: prod
  tasks:
    - name: Render the app config
      ansible.builtin.template:
        src: app.conf.j2               # looked up in templates/
        dest: /etc/app/app.conf
        mode: "0644"
      notify: Restart app          # triggers the handler only if the file changed

  handlers:
    - name: Restart app
      ansible.builtin.service:
        name: app
        state: restarted
Explain in detail

Variables

Defined in the play (vars), in files (vars_files), in inventory (group_vars/, host_vars/), or on the command line (-e "app_port=9000"). Used with Jinja2 syntax: {{ app_port }}. Ansible also gathers facts about each host automatically, such as ansible_facts['os_family'].

Handlers

Tasks that run only when notified by another task that reported changed, and only once at the end of the play. Perfect for "restart nginx, but only if its config file actually changed".

Ansible fills in the blanks differently for every server and writes out the finished file. A handler is like ringing the doorbell only if you actually changed something in the house.

Idempotency in Ansible

Most modules check the current state first. The first run reports changed; the second run reports ok and does nothing. That is why Ansible output ends with a recap:

PLAY RECAP ********************************************* web1 : ok=5 changed=0 unreachable=0 failed=0 skipped=0 rescued=0 ignored=0
The command and shell modules are not idempotent by themselves; they run every time. Prefer a dedicated module (package, copy, user), or add creates: / when: conditions.

Why use a handler to restart?

Compare with ours

Because a handler runs only when something actually changed, and only once at the end, so the service is not restarted needlessly.

A complete annotated playbook: install and configure nginx

  • The playbook installs nginx, writes a home page from a template and starts the service.
  • A handler reloads nginx only when the page changed.
  • Run with --check --diff first, then apply, then run again to see changed=0.

---
# site.yml
- name: Install and configure nginx
  hosts: web
  become: true
  vars:
    site_message: "Hello from {{ inventory_hostname }}"

  tasks:
    - name: Install nginx
      ansible.builtin.package:
        name: nginx
        state: present

    - name: Write the home page from a template
      ansible.builtin.template:
        src: index.html.j2
        dest: /usr/share/nginx/html/index.html
        owner: root
        group: root
        mode: "0644"
      notify: Reload nginx

    - name: Make sure nginx is running and starts on boot
      ansible.builtin.service:
        name: nginx
        state: started
        enabled: true

  handlers:
    - name: Reload nginx
      ansible.builtin.service:
        name: nginx
        state: reloaded
    

# templates/index.html.j2
<h1>{{ site_message }}</h1>
    

$ ansible-playbook -i inventory.ini site.yml --check --diff   # dry run: show what would change
$ ansible-playbook -i inventory.ini site.yml                  # apply
$ ansible-playbook -i inventory.ini site.yml                  # run again: changed=0
Explain in detail

On a brand-new server, the --check run can fail at the service task: in a dry run nginx is not really installed, so the service does not exist yet. The web root path /usr/share/nginx/html is the default on Amazon Linux and Red Hat style systems. Debian and Ubuntu use /var/www/html. Facts such as ansible_facts['os_family'] let a playbook handle both.

Check syntax first with ansible-playbook --syntax-check site.yml and use --check to preview changes, like terraform plan for configuration.

Roles and Ansible Galaxy

  • A role packages tasks, handlers, templates and variables for one purpose.
  • Playbooks list the roles they need.
  • Galaxy shares roles and collections; most modules now live in collections.
  • Read and pin third-party roles; keep secrets in ansible-vault.
ELI5: Explain like I'm 5

Split one long banquet recipe into recipe cards ("bread", "soup") and pick the cards each dinner needs. Each card is a role; each dinner is a playbook.

Role: a standard folder layout that packages tasks, handlers, templates, default variables and files for one purpose (for example, "nginx"), so playbooks can reuse it.

roles/
  nginx/
    tasks/main.yml        # the tasks
    handlers/main.yml     # handlers
    templates/            # Jinja2 templates
    defaults/main.yml     # lowest-priority default variables
    vars/main.yml         # higher-priority variables
    files/                # static files
    

- hosts: web
  become: true
  roles:
    - nginx
    - { role: app, app_port: 8080 }
Explain in detail

ELI5, continued: Each card holds everything for one dish: the steps (tasks), the ingredients (files and templates) and the usual amounts (default variables). Ansible Galaxy is a public exchange where people share their cards.

Ansible Galaxy is the public hub for sharing roles and collections. Since Ansible 2.10, most modules live in collections (bundles of modules, roles and plugins) such as amazon.aws or community.general.


$ ansible-galaxy role init --init-path roles nginx   # create the skeleton in roles/nginx
$ ansible-galaxy collection install amazon.aws     # install a collection
$ ansible-galaxy install -r requirements.yml       # install what a project needs
Third-party roles run with root power on your servers. Read them, pin their versions, and prefer well-maintained ones. Store secrets with ansible-vault, never in plain YAML.

Check yourself

Quick questions on the last few slides. Not graded; wrong answers explain themselves.

When does an Ansible handler run?

Handlers avoid needless restarts.

Which is the better way to install nginx in a playbook?

Prefer a dedicated module over command or shell.

Terraform vs Ansible vs CloudFormation vs Pulumi vs OpenTofu

  • Terraform and OpenTofu provision infrastructure declaratively and keep state.
  • Ansible configures machines; CloudFormation is AWS only; Pulumi uses real programming languages.
  • Learn Terraform first, then add Ansible for server configuration.
ToolMain jobLanguageStyleNotes
TerraformProvisioningHCLDeclarative, keeps stateMany providers across clouds and SaaS. Business Source License since Aug 2023 (version 1.6 onward). Owned by IBM since Feb 2025.
OpenTofuProvisioningHCLDeclarative, keeps stateOpen-source fork under the Linux Foundation; largely compatible with Terraform configurations.
AnsibleConfiguration management, also orchestration and some provisioningYAML (+ Jinja2)Mostly declarative tasks, run in order; agentlessNo state file; idempotent modules decide whether to change anything.
CloudFormationProvisioning on AWS onlyJSON or YAMLDeclarative, state managed by AWS ("stacks")Deep AWS integration; no separate state file to manage.
PulumiProvisioningPython, TypeScript, Go, C#, Java, YAMLDeclarative result, written in real programming languagesLoops and functions come naturally; state kept in a backend.
Explain in detail

Which should I learn?

Learn Terraform first: it is the most common in job descriptions, and OpenTofu skills transfer directly. Add Ansible for server configuration. Learn CloudFormation if your employer is AWS-only.

They combine well

A common pipeline: Terraform creates the VPC and servers, outputs the IPs, then Ansible (or a baked image) installs and configures software. Kubernetes manifests handle the app layer.

Hands-on exercise: Terraform and Ansible on your own machine

  • Part A runs the Terraform workflow with the local provider; no cloud needed.
  • Edit the file by hand to simulate drift and watch plan notice it.
  • Part B shows Ansible idempotency on localhost.
  • The exercise is free; stretch goals use a throw-away AWS account.

Task 1: worked example (Terraform with the local provider)


$ mkdir tf-lab && cd tf-lab
$ cat > main.tf <<'EOF'
terraform {
  required_providers {
    local = { source = "hashicorp/local", version = "~> 2.0" }
  }
}

variable "greeting" {
  type    = string
  default = "hello iac"
}

resource "local_file" "hello" {
  content  = var.greeting
  filename = "${path.module}/hello.txt"
}

output "file_path" {
  value = local_file.hello.filename
}
EOF
$ terraform init
$ terraform plan
$ terraform apply          # type: yes
$ cat hello.txt

Task 2: finish it (drift and change)

Work out the last steps: change an input, then clean up.


$ terraform apply                          # again: "No changes." (idempotent)
$ echo "tampered" > hello.txt              # simulate drift
$ terraform plan                           # Terraform notices and plans to restore the file
Show hint

Variables can be set on the command line with -var. Clean-up is the opposite of apply.

Show answer 

$ terraform apply -var "greeting=hello again"   # change an input: file is replaced
$ ls                                       # see terraform.tfstate and .terraform.lock.hcl
$ terraform destroy                        # hello.txt disappears

Task 3: on your own (Ansible idempotency)

Goal: create /tmp/ansible-demo.txt with a playbook. Success: changed=1, then changed=0.

Show hint

Use hosts: localhost with connection: local, and the ansible.builtin.copy module with content and dest.

Show answer 

$ mkdir ansible-lab && cd ansible-lab
$ cat > hello.yml <<'EOF'
---
- name: Idempotency demo
  hosts: localhost
  connection: local
  tasks:
    - name: Create a file with content
      ansible.builtin.copy:
        content: "managed by ansible\n"
        dest: /tmp/ansible-demo.txt
        mode: "0644"
EOF
$ ansible-playbook hello.yml
$ ansible-playbook hello.yml
Explain in detail

This exercise uses no cloud account and costs nothing, but teaches the real workflow. Install Terraform (or OpenTofu, whose command is tofu) and Ansible first (for example with your package manager or pip install ansible).

Expected: the plan says Plan: 1 to add, 0 to change, 0 to destroy., apply says Apply complete! Resources: 1 added, and cat prints hello iac.

First run shows changed: [localhost] and a recap with changed=1. Second run shows ok: [localhost] and changed=0. Delete the file and run again to see it re-created.

Stretch goals

  • Use the VPC + EC2 example from the Terraform slide in a throw-away AWS account (with a budget alert), then terraform destroy.
  • Run the nginx playbook against that instance, with the IP in an inventory file, then browse to the instance's public IP.
  • Move the Terraform state to an S3 backend.

Cheat sheet

Command or conceptMeaning
terraform initDownload providers and set up the backend
terraform fmt / validateFormat code / check it is valid
terraform planPreview changes (read-only)
terraform applyMake the changes
terraform destroyDelete everything managed
terraform outputShow output values
terraform state listList tracked resources
terraform workspace new NAMECreate another state in the same backend
Plan symbols+ create, - destroy, ~ update, -/+ replace
HCL blocksresource, variable, output, locals, data, module, provider
Never commit*.tfstate, .terraform/, secrets
ansible all -m pingTest connectivity to inventory hosts
ansible-playbook site.yml --check --diffDry run with diffs
ansible-playbook site.yml -e "var=value"Run with an extra variable
ansible-galaxy init / installCreate a role / install roles and collections
ansible-vault encrypt fileEncrypt secrets
Declarative / idempotent / immutableDescribe the end state / safe to re-run / replace instead of patch

Interview questions

Q1: What is Infrastructure as Code and why use it?

Managing infrastructure through versioned definition files instead of manual steps. It gives repeatability, review through pull requests, history in Git, faster environment creation and easier disaster recovery.

Q2: Declarative vs imperative?

Declarative describes the desired end state and the tool computes the steps (Terraform, CloudFormation). Imperative lists the steps to run (shell scripts). Declarative tools are safer to re-run.

Q3: What is idempotency?

Running an operation repeatedly gives the same result as running it once. Ansible modules and Terraform applies are designed to do nothing when the system already matches the desired state.

Q4: What is the Terraform state file and why is remote state important?

It maps configuration to real resources and caches their attributes. A remote backend (for example S3 with locking and encryption) lets a team share one source of truth, prevents concurrent applies and avoids losing state. It can contain secrets, so it must not be committed to Git.

Q5: What does terraform plan do and why does it matter?

It refreshes real values, compares them with code and state, and shows what would be created, changed or destroyed without changing anything. Reviewing the plan catches dangerous changes such as replacing a database.

Q6: What is drift and how do you handle it?

Real infrastructure diverging from code, often from manual console edits. Detect with terraform plan, then either re-apply to revert it or update the code to match. Restrict console write access to prevent it.

Q7: Terraform vs Ansible?

Terraform primarily provisions infrastructure declaratively with state. Ansible primarily configures software on machines, agentless over SSH, without a state file. They are commonly combined.

Q8: What is an Ansible handler?

A task that runs only when notified by another task that changed something, executed once at the end of the play. Typical use: restart a service after its config file changed.

Q9: Mutable vs immutable infrastructure?

Mutable servers are modified in place and can drift. Immutable servers are never modified: you build a new image and replace them, making deployments and rollbacks predictable.

Q10: Why was OpenTofu created?

After HashiCorp changed Terraform's licence to the Business Source License in August 2023, the community forked the last open-source version. OpenTofu is governed by the Linux Foundation and aims to remain open source and largely compatible.

Quiz

1. Which description best matches a declarative tool?

Declarative means describing the destination, not the turn-by-turn route.

2. What does terraform plan do?

Plan is a read-only preview. Providers are downloaded by init; resources are created by apply.

3. Which should never be committed to Git?

State can contain secrets. The lock file is meant to be committed.

4. Running an Ansible playbook a second time on an already-configured server should mostly report…

Idempotent modules detect that the desired state already exists and do nothing.

5. Which pairing is most accurate?

That is the usual division of labour. CloudFormation is AWS-only, and Ansible is agentless.

Keep learning

Free resources (GeeksforGeeks)

  • What is Terraform?
  • What is Ansible?
  • AWS Tutorial

Official docs: developer.hashicorp.com/terraform · docs.ansible.com · opentofu.org/docs
