Congratulations

  • You covered the whole path, from foundations to security.
  • Employers look for how well you connect the pieces.
  • Next, build projects on GitHub and keep learning while you apply.

What to do next

  1. Pick project 1 or 2 from the list and start today.
  2. Put every project on GitHub with a clear README.
  3. Revisit the modules you found hardest, and redo the exercises without looking.
  4. Apply for roles while you keep learning. You do not need to know everything first.

That completes the course. Press Esc for the overview map, or go back to any module to review.

Explain in detail

You have worked through the whole path: foundations, Linux, networking, Git, CI/CD, containers, Kubernetes, cloud, Infrastructure as Code, observability and security. No one masters all of it at once, and nobody expects you to. What employers look for is that you understand how the pieces fit together, that you can learn the next tool quickly, and that you have built things.

15

Capstone project

One small web service, taken the whole way: code, container, pipeline, cluster and dashboard. Each milestone reuses one earlier module, and the work gets less hand-held as you go.

You will build: a Flask app with tests, a Dockerfile, a GitHub Actions pipeline that pushes to GHCR, a kind deployment with probes, and Prometheus plus Grafana monitoring.

Why a capstone project

  • Tools make sense only once they hand work to each other.
  • A finished project on GitHub proves more than a list of tools.
  • You will hit real errors and learn to read them.
  • Everything runs free: GitHub, Docker Desktop, kind and Helm.
Work in your own public repository, for example capstone-app. Commit after every milestone so your history tells the story.
Explain in detail

Earlier modules each taught one tool in isolation. Real jobs are about the joins: the image the pipeline builds must be the image the cluster runs, and the metrics the app exposes must be the metrics the dashboard reads. This project makes you cross every join once.

You need Git, Python 3.12, Docker, kind, kubectl and Helm installed, plus a GitHub account. If a command fails, read the error first, then use the hint on the slide.

The finished architecture

A push to GitHub produces an image; a local cluster runs it and is watched.

StageToolWhat it produces
1. CodeFlask, pytest, GitAn app with /, /healthz, /metrics and tests
2. PackageDockerAn image that runs as a non-root user
3. PipelineGitHub Actions, GHCRLint, test, then an image tagged with the commit SHA
4. Runkind, kubectlA Deployment and Service with probes and resource requests
5. WatchPrometheus, Grafana (Helm)A dashboard with request rate and latency

Source

GitHub repository

Registry

ghcr.io image

Runtime

kind cluster, monitoring namespace

Explain in detail

The flow is: you push, GitHub Actions runs lint and tests, and only on the main branch it builds the image and pushes it to GHCR (GitHub Container Registry). For the local cluster you build the image on your machine and load it into kind, so the cluster does not need registry credentials. Prometheus finds your Service through a ServiceMonitor and scrapes /metrics; Grafana reads from Prometheus.

Milestone 1: the app and its tests

Goal: a tested Flask service in a Git repository with health and metrics endpoints.

  • Health endpoint tells Kubernetes the app is alive.
  • Metrics endpoint tells Prometheus how the app behaves.
  • Tests and lint run locally before any pipeline exists.

Approach: worked example

Create these four files, then run the commands below them.


# app.py
import os
import random
import time

from flask import Flask, Response, g, jsonify, request
from prometheus_client import CONTENT_TYPE_LATEST, Counter, Histogram, generate_latest

app = Flask(__name__)

REQUESTS = Counter("http_requests_total", "Total HTTP requests",
                   ["method", "path", "status"])
LATENCY = Histogram("http_request_duration_seconds", "Request latency in seconds",
                    ["path"])


@app.before_request
def start_timer():
    g.start = time.perf_counter()


@app.after_request
def record_metrics(resp):
    path = request.url_rule.rule if request.url_rule else "unmatched"
    LATENCY.labels(path).observe(time.perf_counter() - g.start)
    REQUESTS.labels(request.method, path, resp.status_code).inc()
    return resp


@app.get("/")
def home():
    return jsonify(service="capstone-app", version=os.getenv("APP_VERSION", "dev"))


@app.get("/healthz")
def healthz():
    return jsonify(status="ok")


@app.get("/work")
def work():
    time.sleep(random.uniform(0.0, 0.3))
    return jsonify(done=True)


@app.get("/metrics")
def metrics():
    return Response(generate_latest(), content_type=CONTENT_TYPE_LATEST)


# test_app.py
from app import app


def test_home():
    r = app.test_client().get("/")
    assert r.status_code == 200
    assert r.get_json()["service"] == "capstone-app"


def test_healthz():
    assert app.test_client().get("/healthz").get_json() == {"status": "ok"}


def test_metrics_counts_requests():
    client = app.test_client()
    client.get("/")
    body = client.get("/metrics").get_data(as_text=True)
    assert "http_requests_total" in body


# requirements.txt
flask==3.1.3
prometheus-client==0.26.0
gunicorn==26.2.0

# requirements-dev.txt
pytest==9.1.1
ruff==0.17.0


python3 -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate
pip install -r requirements.txt -r requirements-dev.txt
ruff check . && pytest -q
flask --app app run --port 8000      # then: curl localhost:8000/metrics
printf '.venv/\n__pycache__/\n.pytest_cache/\n.ruff_cache/\n' > .gitignore
git add . && git commit -m "Add Flask app with health and metrics"
Explain in detail

The two hooks time every request and count it by method, route and status. Using the route pattern (request.url_rule.rule) rather than the raw URL keeps the number of label values small, which matters for Prometheus. Keep gunicorn at its default of one worker for this project; several workers need extra setup in prometheus_client to combine their counters.

Milestone 2: containerise the app

Goal: a small image that runs the app as a non-root user.

  • Copy dependencies first so the layer cache survives code edits.
  • Run with gunicorn, not the Flask development server.
  • A .dockerignore keeps junk out of the build.

Approach: finish it

Replace the two TODO comments, then build and run.


FROM python:3.12-slim
ENV PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1 PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1
WORKDIR /app
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt
COPY app.py .
# TODO 1: create a user and switch to it
EXPOSE 8000
# TODO 2: start gunicorn on 0.0.0.0:8000 serving app:app


docker build -t capstone-app:dev .
docker run --rm -p 8000:8000 capstone-app:dev
Show hint

Use RUN useradd --create-home appuser then USER appuser. The start command is the exec form CMD [...] with gunicorn, --bind and app:app.

Show answer 

FROM python:3.12-slim
ENV PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1 PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1
WORKDIR /app
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt
COPY app.py .
RUN useradd --create-home appuser
USER appuser
EXPOSE 8000
CMD ["gunicorn", "--bind", "0.0.0.0:8000", "app:app"]


# .dockerignore
.venv/
__pycache__/
.pytest_cache/
.ruff_cache/
.git/

# check the user is not root
docker run --rm capstone-app:dev id -u

Milestone 3: CI pipeline with GitHub Actions

Goal: every pull request and push to main is linted and tested; pushes to main publish an image to GHCR.

  • Two jobs: test first, then image only if it passed.
  • The built-in GITHUB_TOKEN logs in to GHCR; no secret to create.
  • Tag the image with the commit SHA so every build is traceable.

Approach: skeleton given

Write .github/workflows/ci.yml. Complete the TODO steps.


name: ci
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  pull_request:
permissions:
  contents: read
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      # TODO: set up Python 3.12 with pip cache
      # TODO: install both requirements files, run ruff, run pytest
  image:
    needs: test
    if: github.event_name == 'push'
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      contents: read
      packages: write
    steps:
      # TODO: checkout, log in to ghcr.io, build and push
Show hint

Use actions/setup-python@v7, docker/setup-buildx-action@v4, docker/login-action@v4 and docker/build-push-action@v7. GHCR image names must be lowercase, so convert GITHUB_REPOSITORY in a shell step.

Show answer 

name: ci
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  pull_request:
permissions:
  contents: read
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - uses: actions/setup-python@v7
        with:
          python-version: "3.12"
          cache: pip
      - run: pip install -r requirements.txt -r requirements-dev.txt
      - run: ruff check .
      - run: pytest -q
  image:
    needs: test
    if: github.event_name == 'push'
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      contents: read
      packages: write
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - name: Lowercase image name
        run: echo "IMAGE=ghcr.io/${GITHUB_REPOSITORY,,}" >> "$GITHUB_ENV"
      - uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v4
      - uses: docker/login-action@v4
        with:
          registry: ghcr.io
          username: ${{ github.actor }}
          password: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}
      - uses: docker/build-push-action@v7
        with:
          context: .
          push: true
          tags: |
            ${{ env.IMAGE }}:${{ github.sha }}
            ${{ env.IMAGE }}:latest
Explain in detail

New packages on GHCR are private by default. To pull the image without a login, open the package settings and change its visibility to public. If the push step fails with a permission error, check the repository setting under Actions, Workflow permissions, and the packages: write line above.

Milestone 4: deploy to a kind cluster

Goal: two replicas running in a local cluster, reachable from your laptop.

  • Readiness decides when a Pod gets traffic; liveness decides when it restarts.
  • Resource requests tell the scheduler what each Pod needs.
  • Give the Service a named port; milestone 5 needs it.

Approach: write the manifests

Create the cluster and load your image. Then write k8s/deployment.yaml and k8s/service.yaml so the commands below succeed.


kind create cluster --name capstone
docker build -t capstone-app:dev .
kind load docker-image capstone-app:dev --name capstone
kubectl apply -f k8s/
kubectl rollout status deployment/capstone-app
kubectl port-forward svc/capstone-app 8080:80   # then: curl localhost:8080/
Show hint

Label Pods and the Service selector with app: capstone-app. Probes are httpGet on /healthz, port 8000. Set imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent so kind uses the loaded image.

Show answer 

# k8s/deployment.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: capstone-app
  labels:
    app: capstone-app
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: capstone-app
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: capstone-app
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: app
          image: capstone-app:dev
          imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent
          ports:
            - containerPort: 8000
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /healthz
              port: 8000
            initialDelaySeconds: 2
            periodSeconds: 5
          livenessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /healthz
              port: 8000
            initialDelaySeconds: 10
            periodSeconds: 10
          resources:
            requests:
              cpu: 50m
              memory: 64Mi
            limits:
              memory: 128Mi


# k8s/service.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: capstone-app
  labels:
    app: capstone-app
spec:
  selector:
    app: capstone-app
  ports:
    - name: http
      port: 80
      targetPort: 8000
Explain in detail

kind nodes are containers with their own image store, so kind load docker-image copies your local image into them. Rebuild and load again after every code change, then run kubectl rollout restart deployment/capstone-app.

To run the image from CI instead, set image: ghcr.io/your-user/capstone-app:COMMIT_SHA (all lowercase). If the package is private, create a pull secret with a personal access token that has the read:packages scope, then add imagePullSecrets: [{name: ghcr}] under the Pod spec:


kubectl create secret docker-registry ghcr --docker-server=ghcr.io \
  --docker-username=your-user --docker-password="$GHCR_TOKEN"

The CI image is built for linux/amd64 only. On an Apple Silicon Mac, either keep using kind load or add docker/setup-qemu-action@v4 and platforms: linux/amd64,linux/arm64 to the build step.

Milestone 5: monitoring with Prometheus and Grafana

Goal: a Grafana panel showing your app's request rate and 95th percentile latency.

  • kube-prometheus-stack installs Prometheus, Grafana and the operator in one chart.
  • A ServiceMonitor tells Prometheus which Service to scrape.
  • Generate traffic, or the graphs stay empty.

Approach: on your own, with hints

Install the stack with Helm, scrape /metrics on your Service, and chart request rate and p95 latency.

Show hint

Install into a monitoring namespace with release name monitoring. The chart only picks up a ServiceMonitor labelled release: monitoring. Keep it out of k8s/ itself, because kubectl apply -f k8s/ fails on it until the chart has installed the ServiceMonitor CRD. Port-forward the Prometheus and Grafana services to check.

Show answer 

helm repo add prometheus-community https://prometheus-community.github.io/helm-charts
helm repo update
helm install monitoring prometheus-community/kube-prometheus-stack \
  --namespace monitoring --create-namespace
kubectl get pods -n monitoring


# k8s/monitoring/servicemonitor.yaml  (apply with: kubectl apply -f k8s/monitoring/)
apiVersion: monitoring.coreos.com/v1
kind: ServiceMonitor
metadata:
  name: capstone-app
  labels:
    release: monitoring
spec:
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: capstone-app
  endpoints:
    - port: http
      path: /metrics
      interval: 15s


# Prometheus UI: http://localhost:9090/targets
kubectl port-forward -n monitoring svc/monitoring-kube-prometheus-prometheus 9090:9090
# Grafana UI: http://localhost:3000 (user admin)
kubectl port-forward -n monitoring svc/monitoring-grafana 3000:80
kubectl get secret -n monitoring monitoring-grafana \
  -o jsonpath="{.data.admin-password}" | base64 -d; echo
# traffic (run in another terminal, with the app port-forward from milestone 4)
for i in $(seq 1 200); do curl -s localhost:8080/work > /dev/null; done


# Panel 1: requests per second by route
sum by (path) (rate(http_requests_total[5m]))

# Panel 2: 95th percentile latency
histogram_quantile(0.95, sum by (le) (rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m])))

Milestone 6: harden and document

Goal: a scanned image, a clean teardown and a README a stranger can follow.

  • Scan the image for known vulnerabilities before you call it done.
  • Break something on purpose and watch the dashboard react.
  • A README that works on a fresh machine is the real deliverable.

Approach: goal only

Scan the image, then simulate a crash and a bad deploy, and describe what the dashboard and Kubernetes did.

Show hint

Trivy can run from a container. For the failure test, kubectl delete pod shows self-healing; kubectl set image with a tag that does not exist shows a stuck rollout while old Pods keep serving.

Show answer 

# scan: report HIGH and CRITICAL findings, fail with exit code 1 if any
docker run --rm -v /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock \
  aquasec/trivy:0.75.0 image --severity HIGH,CRITICAL --exit-code 1 capstone-app:dev

# failure 1: kill one Pod and watch the replacement (Ctrl+C to stop watching)
kubectl delete "$(kubectl get pods -l app=capstone-app -o name | head -n 1)" --wait=false
kubectl get pods -l app=capstone-app -w

# failure 2: bad image tag; the old Pods stay Ready, the new one is stuck
kubectl set image deployment/capstone-app app=capstone-app:does-not-exist
kubectl rollout status deployment/capstone-app --timeout=30s   # times out
kubectl get pods -l app=capstone-app   # one Pod in ErrImagePull or ImagePullBackOff
kubectl rollout undo deployment/capstone-app

# teardown
kind delete cluster --name capstone

Optional stretch goals

  • Add the Trivy scan as a CI step that fails the build.
  • Deploy the same image to a cloud cluster created with Terraform.
  • Add an alert rule for a high error rate.
Explain in detail

Trivy in CI: add a step in the image job after the image is built, and use the official Trivy action at the release tag its README recommends. Build with load: true first so the scan sees the image, then push only if the scan passes.

Terraform: use module 11 and module 10. Write a configuration for a managed Kubernetes cluster (for example EKS) or a single VM with k3s, keep the state in a remote backend, and run terraform destroy when finished. Cloud clusters cost money, so set a billing alert first and delete everything the same day.

Alert: a PrometheusRule resource with an expression such as the share of 5xx responses over five minutes, labelled release: monitoring like the ServiceMonitor.

Self-assessment rubric

Score each row honestly. Aim for good everywhere, excellent in two rows.

CriterionNeeds workGoodExcellent
App and testsRuns locally, no testsTests and lint pass, health and metrics endpoints workTests cover error paths; metrics use bounded labels
ContainerBuilds but runs as root or is hugeSlim base, non-root, dependency layer cachedPinned versions, .dockerignore, scanned with no high findings
CI pipelineRuns only tests, manual image pushLint, test, push to GHCR on main, SHA tagLeast-privilege permissions, caching, scan step, PR checks required
KubernetesPod runs but has no probesDeployment, Service, both probes, resource requestsLimits tuned, rollout and rollback demonstrated, labels consistent
MonitoringStack installed, nothing scrapedTarget UP, dashboard with rate and p95 latencyDashboard exported as JSON in the repo, alert rule added
DocumentationOne-line READMEPrerequisites, setup steps and architecture diagramA stranger reproduces it first try; known issues and teardown listed

Show your work

  • Pin the repository to your GitHub profile.
  • Lead the README with what it is and a diagram.
  • On a CV, state what you built and what it proves.
Explain in detail: how to describe it on a CV

Use one project entry with three or four short lines. Describe actions and checkable facts, and only claim numbers you measured. Example:


Capstone: containerised service on Kubernetes (github.com/you/capstone-app)
- Built a Flask API with pytest tests and Prometheus metrics; packaged as a non-root Docker image.
- Wrote a GitHub Actions pipeline: lint, test, build and push to GHCR tagged by commit SHA.
- Deployed to a kind cluster with readiness and liveness probes and resource requests.
- Monitored with kube-prometheus-stack: request rate and p95 latency dashboard.

In interviews, be ready to explain one failure you hit and how you debugged it. That story is worth more than the tool list.

Final self-check

1. Why does the Dockerfile copy requirements.txt and install before copying app.py?

Layers are cached top to bottom. Putting rarely changing steps first keeps rebuilds fast.

2. In the workflow, why does the image job use needs: test?

needs creates a dependency: if test fails, image is skipped.

3. A Pod is Running but its readiness probe keeps failing. What happens?

Readiness controls traffic; liveness controls restarts.

4. Prometheus shows no target for your app although the Service exists. What is the most likely cause?

Check the ServiceMonitor selector against the Service labels and the release label.

5. Why load the image into kind with kind load docker-image?

kind runs nodes as containers, so images must be copied into them or pulled from a registry.

6. Why use the route pattern (/work) rather than the full URL as a metric label?

High-cardinality labels are a classic way to break a Prometheus server.
